title: How a South African billionaire is turning a corner of Somerset into ‘one man’s estate’ | The super-rich | The Guardian
description: Koos Bekker’s Newt estate encompasses luxury hotels, pubs and high street business, with local concerns including flooding
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Koos Bekker’s Newt estate encompasses luxury hotels, pubs and high street business, with local concerns including flooding
Content: The Newt is a beloved destination for celebrities such as Charli XCX and Kate Moss.Photograph: Commission Air/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Newt is a beloved destination for celebrities such as Charli XCX and Kate Moss.Photograph: Commission Air/AlamyThe super-richHow a South African billionaire is turning a corner of Somerset into ‘one man’s estate’Koos Bekker’s Newt estate  encompasses luxury hotels, pubs and high street business, with local concerns including floodingHelena HortonandMichael GoodierSat 10 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 09.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen South African billionaire Koos Bekker bought an old country estate in a sleepy corner ofSomersetto turn it into a luxury hotel, residents thought it was a sign their area was on the up.Walking through his peaceful manicured gardens, which feature a maze of apple trees twisted into perfect shapes using the espalier method, it’s easy to feel that all is well in this quiet, picturesque pocket ofEngland.But if you venture beyond the orchards and into the local pubs, where the local cider sets tongues wagging, you’ll hear a very different story.Bekker has been embroiled in a row with local people over a number of issues ranging from the vast expansion of his estate, the use of pesticides on it and branding deals – described as “brazen” by one local person – which have seen the local train station named after his hotel, the Newt in Somerset.View image in fullscreenKoos Bekker has been buying thousands of acres around Bruton and Castle Cary.Photograph: Dave Benett/Getty Images for The Newt in Somerset & BurberryThe businessman has a net worth of about £3bn and is the chair of Naspers, one of the world’s biggest technology firms. He has been buying thousands of acres around Bruton and Castle Cary – more than 2,700 acres (1,090 hectares), according to Guardian analysis – through his company Emily Estate (UK) Limited, which trades as the Newt.As well as swathes of the countryside, Bekker has also snapped up high street businesses from a deli to a beauty parlour, as well as pretty former farmhouses and local pubs.map of the area of Somerset with the lands owned by Emily Estate marked according to date of purchase.And it is this expansion of Bekker’s influence beyond the boundaries of the Newt – beloved of celebrities such as Charli xcx and Kate Moss – into the heart of the local Somerset villages where tensions have begun to emerge.Bekker is not the only moneyed arrival in this corner of Somerset. The area boasts famous residents including former chancellor George Osborne, fashion designer Stella McCartney, and broadcaster Mariella Frostrup.The George pub in the centre of Castle Cary currently serves senior citizens a hot dinner for just £12, but local people do not expect these prices will remain now the Newt has bought the inn: a bag of chocolate buttons in its farm shop costs £11.95, while a bottle of “cyder” grown on the estate is £12.50.View image in fullscreenBekker acquired Hadspen House in 2013, along with 16 acres of land, and converted it into the luxury hotel.Photograph: Nick Scott/AlamyBekker bought the 17th-century manor Hadspen House in 2013, along with 16 acres of land, converting it into the luxury hotel. Last year he acquired Yarlington Lodge, a Grade II-listed Georgian house a mile away, and converted it into a 32-guest property with its own pool, tennis court and cinema room.He is hardly a silent investor – the sign for the local train station, Castle Cary, now reads “Castle Cary for the Newt”. By the tracks is the new Creamery cafe, which serves afternoon tea in a vintage Pullman carriage at £45 a head.Hugh Thomas, afood writerfrom Frome, said the renaming of the station seemed “arrogant and brazen”, adding: “The station does feel somewhat colonised by the Newt regardless, which I find an encroaching thing, given it is supposed to be a public service.”View image in fullscreenGardens at the Newt.Photograph: Victor Watts/AlamySome, though, have welcomed the investment, saying it has cheered up a previously unloved train station and the Bekker family were creating jobs as well as bringing new people to the area to eat in the restaurants and drink in the pubs.Visitors to the £800-a-night Newt hotel are invited to enjoy being immersed in the nature of deep Somerset. The hotel recently welcomeda cage of endangered red squirrels. But there, too, lay a problem.The Newt consulted rewilding expert Derek Gow about keeping five red squirrels in a pen. They became extinct in most of England after invasive grey squirrels were introduced from America which carry a virus that causes a disease called squirrelpox, which kills off the reds.Gow said: “The Newt did talk to me about it; we did have one conversation. I said: ‘It is not going to be viable.’ It is performative – [the squirrels] are in the cage to show guests. That’s it. Keeping five squirrels in a cage does nothing for wildlife. If they do release them, they will just get squirrelpox and die.”While the Newt has created spectacular gardens around the hotel, including a historically accurate Roman villa, a “four seasons” garden featuring marble water fountains and a treetop walkway, these are not freely accessible to the public. Only hotel guests and those with an £85 annual pass can enter the grounds.View image in fullscreenThe grounds of the Newt are only accessible to hotel guests and those buying an £85 annual pass.Photograph: OBNW/AlamyPeople living nearby have also been concerned that there has been an increase in flooding since the Newt was built. The hotel has acknowledged this, and has been digging pools to hold any run-off water from the farm and paved areas.Local people have set up a group to coordinate complaints about the issue. Emma Craigie, a writer who lives nearby, said: “I live in a village below the hill the Newt is on. In our immediate locality there were incidents of flooding which seemed clearly exacerbated by their road building and hardcore use.”The worst incident was in May 2023, when rain over the Newt caused flash-flooding down the Pitt and Cam valleys, which the local council described as “beyond levels seen in living memory”. The local authority declared an emergency that evening.Villagers have also set up a petition against the spraying of pesticides on the Newt’s farmland.The model and actor Gabriella Wilde, who also lives locally, said: “I was surprised and a little disappointed to learn that they are using such harmful chemicals in their farming operations. That is certainly not the image they project to their guests and local fans. Is it really necessary, especially given how many local farms are making great strides in moving away from old school harmful practices, and towards more nature friendly farming?”View image in fullscreenThe croquet lawn to the rear of the hotel building.Photograph: Peter Titmuss/AlamyFarmers have been suspicious that new boreholes drilled by the hotel have dried up sections of the River Brue, the stream that Bruton is named after. The cider-maker Oliver Dowding, the nextdoor neighbour of the hotel, has entered negotiations with the Newt via the Environment Agency over his section of the river, which runs through his land. He said, ironically, that the newts which used to live on his land had disappeared.Though the Newt boasts that its food is “locally produced”, its farms do not have organic certification. John Sykes, who lives nearby, pointed to the severely trimmed hedges around the estate as well as the sterile lawns.“Look, there are no berries for the birds here. And what bothers me is the land immediately adjacent to our village used to be an organic farm, now they’ve bought it, and it isn’t any more. They are continuing to buy farmland, and I don’t know when they will stop. I don’t want to live somewhere that’s just one man’s estate,” Sykes said.A spokesperson for the Newt in Somerset said: “Fundamental to our philosophy is a love of gardens, respect for the land and a determination to share that passion with a broad audience. To ensure best practice, we employ experts across our operations, including agronomists, horticulturists, arborists, conservationists, educationalists, beekeepers, nutritionists, livestock and wildlife specialists, alongside our hospitality teams.“We are equally committed to our local community, maintaining close relationships with local organisations and proudly employing more than 650 people, who are either from or live within the local area.”Explore more on these topicsThe super-richHospitality industrySomersetFarmingEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘There is no secret agenda’: Nara Smith on home-making absolutely everything, raising four kids at 25 – and why she’s definitely not a tradwife | Social media | The Guardian
description: The model, actor and influencer is known for making her own frozen yoghurt, bubblegum or even toothpaste while dressed in immaculate haute couture. But she insists she is not who the internet thinks she is
Author: Charlotte Edwardes
Headline: The model, actor and influencer is known for making her own frozen yoghurt, bubblegum or even toothpaste while dressed in immaculate haute couture. But she insists she is not who the internet thinks she is
Content: Portrait: Mary Rozzi/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPortrait: Mary Rozzi/The GuardianSocial mediaInterview‘There is no secret agenda’: Nara Smith on home-making absolutely everything, raising four kids at 25 – and why she’s definitely not a tradwifeCharlotte EdwardesThe model, actor and influencer is known for making her own frozen yoghurt, bubblegum or even toothpaste while dressed in immaculate haute couture. But she insists she is not who the internet thinks she isSat 10 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNara Smith is not a tradwife, she wants you to know that. Nor is she an ex-tradwife –pacethe New York Times who included her in a feature on how ex-tradwives are as popular a movement now as the tradwives were in the first place. Nor was she peddling a tradwife-adjacent lifestyle choice by marrying at 18, having four children by 24, and devoting hours to cooking and documenting it online. Nor is she Mormon, by the way. Although, yes, her husband, the model and former teen heart‑throb Lucky Blue Smith, was raised Mormon, but we’ll get to that. Nor was she telegraphing subliminal religious messages in her content: “There is no secret agenda.” Nor was she abandoning her biracial heritage by wearing her hair in a sleek little bob. Nor was she leaning into a 1950s housewife archetype – even when dressed in a pink and red polka-dot minidress to batch-cook sourdough.Smith wants you to scrap everything you think you know about her and start again. She also doesn’t care if you don’t.As with her content:“Those that get it, get it. Those that don’t, don’t. And that’s totally fine. I tell people: ‘If you don’t like my content, I won’t see you scroll past me.’ ‘If you need to block me for your own sanity, please do. I promise I won’t know.’ And if you want to stick around, that is beautiful, I’m grateful, welcome.”For those new to Nara Smith, she is a model and influencer with 12.5m TikTok followers (plus 879m likes) and 4.8m on Instagram, who makes eccentric, seductive cooking videos in which she narrates each step in a passive hushed voice while making dupes of everyday supermarket products from scratch. Her videos start with the same shtick: her husband or children have a request – eg “Lucky leaned over, asking me whether I wanted to go grab some frozen yoghurt after the kids go to bed. I turned to him and told him it wouldn’t be as good as if I just made it. And, even though he was reluctant at first, he just went with it.” In a custom-made$900 white-satin corset dress– no apron – she’s straining the yoghurt starter, combining it with kefir, vanilla, sugar, cork gum; juicing apples and cherries to make gummy bears for the topping, whisking in gelatine and honey. Throughout, Smith stays expressionless. Throughout, her movements are mannequin smooth. Nothing splatters on her front, ever (luck, she insists, not because she exceeds all standards of perfection).View image in fullscreenThese clips blow people’s minds.Her grilled cheese video has been viewed 49.6m times. Elsewhere she’s made Nutella, ketchup, Cheez-Its, Pop-Tarts, Skittles and Snickers. She’s even made bubblegum. There’s the novelty of the recipes – she now has a cookbook of scratch-made ones, Homemade, coming out. Then there’s the outfits. She wore a$5,000 cashmere Prada suit to make chicken drumsticks, a $10,000 Schiaparelli to grate tomatoes for a gnocchi sauce. Nigella, Gwyneth, your domestic goddessing has been out-luxed.All of which brings me to Deborah Ann’s Sweet Shoppe in the white clapboard town of Ridgefield, Connecticut, where Smith is sitting opposite me in the narrow red booth, tapping her phone with acrylic nails. Around us is the loud hum of ice-cream refrigeration units, the smell of hot fudge and candy floss. There are sugar pourers and napkin dispensers and Jay & the Americans sing Come a Little Bit Closer on the radio. Smith surely had a sense of humour when she chose this as the backdrop to talk about not being a 1950s homemaker? “They have the best soft serve,” she says, a hint of smile. “And Lucky comes for the cotton-candy ice-cream.”View image in fullscreenPortrait: Mary Rozzi/The GuardianToday, a fortnight shy of her 25th birthday, Smith, is in jeans, a white vest, Chanel flats and a lot of flashing jewellery (“I love a diamond ring”). For the record, she drove here in her own car. And, while it is true that Lucky once said that he drove “no matter what”, that he was “bothered” by the sight of a woman driving a man, she loves driving. She listens to her favourite podcasts while doing so – Aspire With Emma Grede, founder of Skims, and for fun, The Girls Bathroom – “so entertaining. And I do love an audiobook also. I love fantasy. Are you into fantasy?” I ask if she made the gum she’s chewing. She laughs. “Not today.”Smith’s content attracts millions from advertising (among others, she works with Marc Jacobs, Miu Miu and YSL). As well as her cookbook, she acts, and has two films in post-production. One is an indie film she can’t talk about. The other is Tyrant, “a culinary thriller” starring Charlize Theron, Demi Moore and Paapa Essiedu. Then there’s a “consumer goods brand”. I ask what. “We’ll talk about that later. We’re still figuring it all out.”Does she make more money than her husband? “That’s a loaded question. How do I even answer that?” She can answer it with a broad smile? “Yes, I will do that.” She has excellent teeth.What is staggering about Smith is that as well as devising and researching the recipes themselves, she does all her own styling, makeup, art direction, video editing, voiceover and mixing, spending upwards of eight hours a day on one 90-second clip. Her agents and managers beg her to take on help. “I always say no. I am very type A.” Type A? “Very rigid, very scheduled.” Her assiduous attention to detail and devotion to her “art” mean “I’m still figuring out where to relinquish control”, she says.I ask if she’s like The Princess and the Pea when something is not quite right. “That’s literally me. That should be the title. I can’t sleep. I’ll be tossing and turning, bruised.” The cookbook is a sumptuous, high-production volume, but the recipes are down-to-earth in a homely way. They include some from her German childhood: milchreis, schnitzel, rouladen. She doesn’t shy away from refined sugar. There’s meat, there’s chicken in cream, there’s roast potatoes in duck fat. “Do I have sugar and duck fat all day every day? Absolutely not. But roast potatoes occasionally? Absolutely. A little dessert once in a while? Absolutely.”What I try to keep in mind while she’s telling me all this is that Smith has four children: Rumble Honey, Slim Easy, Whimsy Lou and Fawnie Golden. (“Unusual names build character; Lucky had an unusual name and it helped him in ways.”) The book photoshoot took place three weeks after the youngest was born. So, as well as organising and slipping into, for instance, the Rodarte custom-made gingham dress on the cover, she was breastfeeding a newborn and overseeing renovations to the family home they had just moved into here in Connecticut.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: TikTok.com/ @naraazizasmithThen not long after, while the cookbook was still being edited, her daughter Whimsy Lou was diagnosed with cancer. It was Lucky’s mother who first noticed “this thing on her body” (for her daughter’s privacy, Smith doesn’t want to go into specifics) while they were all together on a family photoshoot for the holiday season late last year. “My mother-in-law was, like, ‘I don’t want to alarm you, but maybe you should go to the ER.’ Long story short, the doctors did a bunch of tests, from biopsies to ultrasounds, and then called us back and said: ‘She has cancer. She needs to start treatment immediately.’”Smith’s world “flipped”. Until that point, the couple didn’t even have childcare. Suddenly they were juggling work, kids, chemotherapy appointments, “while also making sure that we weren’t falling apart for her”. Five days out of every fortnight or so, depending on her blood count, Lucky stayed with Whimsy in hospital when she went through treatment while Smith was at home breastfeeding. They couldn’t explain to Whimsy what was happening to her. “She was under two years, so there wasn’t a lot she’d understand.” But they explained it to the older two, “and we got children’s books about cancer that would explain the hair loss and different parts of this journey through stories”.They found “a community” of mutually supportive parents – the reason Smith publicly disclosed Whimsy’s condition once she was in remission. “You don’t realise how many parents or children go through similar experiences until you’re in that situation in the hospital,” she says. “People speaking about it makes you feel less alone.”The shellshock is palpable. She sounds dazed as she runs through the litany of family upheaval that preceded diagnosis – new house, new book, new baby, big dose of postpartum anxiety. “I was still in the thick of dealing with all of it mentally, being pulled multiple different directions [when it happened]. Then all I wanted was to be present for Whimsy. It was hard.” Smith’s mother, Joyce, a nurse, not long free of her own treatment for breast cancer, flew in from Germany to help. “Everyone rallied in my family, and it was beautiful to see.”double quotation markI want people to feel like a grandma lives in my house, not a 24-year-old. Grandma chic with an English twistView image in fullscreenPortrait: Mary Rozzi/The GuardianWithout doubt she’s been changed by the experience. “When you come that close to a life-changing thing, you view the world a little differently.” On the one hand, she appreciates the beauty of “mundane moments”; on the other, she’s tougher. A lot of thought now goes into what her job means in terms of exposure of her children online. “But I’ve always had a boundary around my kids. I show as little of them as possible while acknowledging that they are part of my life.” When people come up to ask for her photograph, her children automatically turn their backs, or stand behind her, or move to a corner of whatever store they are in. “I try to avoid certain places if I can during peak hours.”Will she keep them off screens? “Like phone screens?” Her face is a picture of horror. “Oh, I’m not going to get them phones! No, I’m going to get them a little – I don’t know what they’re called, a Firefly? A Brick? I want them to be able to communicate with me and get a hold of me. I’ll get them a camera because my kids love taking pictures. But I don’t see the need in having them be on social media, or playing video games, or any of that. I deliberately moved to an area where there’s nature, stuff they can do and explore outside; not be on screens.” Until what age? “I don’t know, 18? I mean, if I could have my time again, I would have done it so different.” Does she ever wonder what her life would look like if she hadn’t done all these videos?“All the time. All. The. Time.” Later, she says: “The landscape on social media has changed so much. I had to learn the hard way and reconsider what I put on the internet.”Most nights, Smith takes her computer to bed. Her bedtime routine is specific. “I need clean sheets, that’s non-negotiable. I love freshly washed sheets.” Every night? She stalls. “Twice a week, probably. Linen sheets. I need a shower every night, take my makeup off, do my skincare, brush my teeth, have water on my bedside table, and then I just work in bed until my eyes are rolling.” Often, she’ll look over and Lucky is already asleep. “Sometimes, he’s, like, ‘You can go to bed, and I promise the email is still going to be there in the morning.’” She gets up around six after one night‑time interruption (she insists on doing nights with Fawnie: a, because of the guilt of travelling a lot, and, b, because this baby is her “last”). First thing, she takes their dog Archie out back. He’s a pyrenees-pitbull cross (He’s adopted. Lucky wanted a puppy, but she said no). It something of a relief to learn she doesn’t exercise. “I wish I could. That just feels … too much.”View image in fullscreenPortrait: Mary Rozzi/The GuardianA common theme in her stories is meticulousness in being willing to start from scratch. Three months after her kitchen had been done here in Connecticut, it flooded because of an ice dam on the roof. Ripping the whole thing out was not the headache you imagine because, she says, “I hated every decision that the designers made. I trusted them instead of my gut. So, we redid it the way I wanted and now it’s beautiful and totally different.“I feel like an adult now, having bought a home and furnishing it for the first time.” The vibe: “I want people to feel like a grandma lives here, not a 24-year-old. Grandma chic with an English twist” – because Ridgefield reminds her of the Cotswolds, she says, where she would have moved “in a heartbeat”.I ask what makes her lose her shit. “Mess,” she shoots back. “I get very stressed out by mess. I don’t like a messy house. I don’t like a messy kitchen. I don’t like a messy closet. Messes are overstimulating. On top of everything else that’s going on in the home, four kids running around, screaming and everything, messes then set me over the edge. So, I don’t necessarily lose my shit. I’m, like, ‘Let’s just tidy it up, OK? Everyone, start picking up your stuff.’”The children tidy? “I make the kids do their stuff. Anything they may need help with, like, putting socks together, sometimes they can’t do that, I’ll help. But usually the kids do their messes, I do our messes, and we’ll get it whipped super quick.”View image in fullscreenNara Smith with her husband, Lucky Blue Smith, at Milan fashion week, 2024.Photograph: Independent Photo Agency/Alamy Live NewsTwice a month she has a cleaner who comes to “deep clean”. Everything else, she and Lucky do themselves. Laundry? “I do it.” Ironing? “I steam.” If I opened her cupboards, would they be neat and ordered? “They would. Because it just makes everything more efficient. I love a system when it comes to getting dressed or doing laundry or schedules or routines or the kitchen. It makes life so much easier if you don’t have to think about all these small things.”While she talks, Smith is miming tidying on the laminate-top table between us. She is funny on the potential hazards of her daughter choosing her own outfits. “My eldest is very opinionated. She’s got good taste, so usually I don’t have an issue with it.” If she had bad taste, would she? “I would.” She laughs. “Sometimes it’s the craziest combinations. I have to intervene and kind of bargain a little bit. I’m, like, ‘Tights and socks over pants? That’s crazy.’”Elsewhere, the need for this level of control can be “stressful”. “A lot has changed over the last six years. Being very type A makes it hard when things happen that I can’t control,” she says. Any “wildcard” causes excessive anxiety. “When it came on, I didn’t know what it was.” She read self-help books, had individual therapy, she and Lucky went to couples counselling.She’s laughing when she says she’d been convinced she was a “brilliant” communicator until she got to couples therapy. They go in person, when they need it. “We married so young and have so much life ahead, so it’s more a prevention than cure, if that makes sense.“I grew up in Germany. He’s American. Sometimes, we kind of miss each other a little bit. One time I said ‘I don’t care’ about something, and he was, like, ‘You don’t care?’ It was just, like, ‘I don’t care about talking about it any more.’ Because I speak German, and the language is different, when I translate it into English, it comes across harshly, blunt, to an American. He was, like, ‘Whoa, that’s a little crazy, honey.’ But it’s small things.”Nara Aziza Smith was born in South Africa to a German father, a teacher of history and biology, and Mosotho mother, who grew up under apartheid (“She saw things no person should ever see or go through or have to deal with”). After Smith was born, the family moved to Frankfurt and two younger siblings followed. As a child, Smith had a host of allergies including to eggs and was hospitalised twice at young age for eczema (she also remembers a later operation on her “janky” toes). She describes herself as a child who wanted to hang out with adults, who saw the kids’ table as a punishment: “Like what am I going to do with these kids my age? Play tag?” She was fascinated by figures from history and mythology: Marie Antoinette, Medusa, Athena. She could recite Maya Angelou’s Still I Rise.Banned from Facebook by her parents, she signed up toInstagram, which they’d never heard of, and used it as a way into modelling. She was scouted at 14 by IMG Models through an online programme and her parents took her to castings. In many ways it was a great experience. “But it was also taxing on my 14-year-old mind: the pressure to look a certain way; the focus being only on how you look.” Back then, measurements were very particular, she says. “Getting older, your body changes. So, it was hard on me at times to maintain the standard [weight].” She wouldn’t “necessarily” want her children to go into the business, but if they did she would support them. “But would I recommend it over other interests that they may have? No.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: TikTok.com/ @naraazizasmith“Obviously” she knew who Lucky Blue Smith was before she met him. “He was a crush of mine aged 15. I watched his Ellen interview and I remember thinking, ‘That guy is really fit.’ Then when he DM’d me on Instagram years later, I was, like” – dramatic intake of breath – “it’s him!” In that first message, Lucky asked her where she was from. He didn’t text back to her reply. Sometime later he messaged: “I’m going camping with a friend so I’ll be off grid for a little bit. But when I’m back, I would love to hop on a phone call.” He was in Los Angeles; night-time in Frankfurt. They spoke all night and she watched the sun come up. Over seven hours, they covered family, hobbies, interests, teen stuff. “After that there wasn’t a day that we didn’t spend time on the phone, whether it was two hours or seven hours. We would fall asleep on the phone.”She was attracted by his calmness. How mature he seemed. “Also he’s beautiful, which was a bonus.” They decided to marry not long after their first meeting. Posted it all online, photos of them in bath towels, the ring. It was cute, until you looked at the comments. How did she deal with the racism? “Race has been something that I’ve always talked about with my parents. I’ve always been aware of it growing up in Germany and not looking like the other blond girls. I remember this specific time: I left the school bathroom with my hair out of a ponytail for the first time, and as I walked out one of my friends burst out laughing. I was mortified. I never wore my hair out in school again.“When Lucky and I got together … I don’t know, I kind of just brushed it off because it said more about the other person and how they choose to treat people. Did I talk to Lucky about it? Sure. Did I sometimes get sad about it? Yes. But I just tried to ignore it.”When she relocated to the US to be with Lucky, old health issues started to flare up. She started checking the labels on the food she was eating. “I wasn’t aware how many ingredients were involved. Bread had 20‑plus ingredients, some of which didn’t necessarily belong. I realised it would be easier and healthier if I started making things myself.” In this way, cooking from scratch became “a necessity … I wasn’t just coming up with crazy recipes.”double quotation markI’m very ambitious. But it’s one-upping myself. I couldn’t care less about one-upping other peopleView image in fullscreenPortrait: Mary Rozzi/The Guardian. Fashion stylist: Magdalena Bryk at Art Department. Assistant: Vienna Davies. Hair and makeup: Dindi Hojah at Forward Artists. Set stylist: Natalie Shriver at Art Department. Turquoise dress: Saint Laurent. Shoes: Jude. Beige skirt and blazer: Schiaparelli. Black top and skirt: Jil Sander. Pink dress: Rodarte. Silver blazer outfit: Alexander McQueenLike other gen Zs, Smith’s early content was “fit checks” and get-ready-with-me videos. And she wasn’t wildly different from other “mommy” influencers when she began propping her phone on a tripod to film herself cooking dupes of, say, Oreo ice‑cream or ranch dressing. But something about the package – the exquisite face, the heart-throb husband who goosed her at the stove, the fashion, the breathy monotone used because she was recording at nap time and didn’t want to wake the children, but which everyone compared to ASMR – elevated her above the rest.Then there was her willingness to keep taking it to the next level. She made cough drops. She made sun cream. She made Coca-Cola. She coordinated outfits and recipes so that she made Capri-Sun in a yellow gown with balloon sleeves. Fellow chef Ruby Tandoh wrote of Smith’s content: “It’s addictive. The low-stakes suspense of seeing just how much Too Much she’s going to do this time.” In less than a year, Smith went from under 1 million to 9 million followers. Among them, Bella Hadid, Ariana Grande, Selena Gomez, SZA and Doja Cat.All this coincided with a new and toxic movement online: tradwives. They were a domestic expression of the rightward swerve in American politics. Religion often played a part in their commitment to maintaining patriarchal structures.Womenclaiming their sole ambition was to serve men were suddenly all over the internet packing their husband’s lunchboxes. What Smith did seemed of a piece. Internet sleuths spied The Book of Mormon behind her in one clip. It’s a backstage prop, they argued, an attempt at mass conversion.It didn’t help that Smith was friendly with Hannah Neeleman, the 36-year-old Juilliard graduate and mother of nine who makes home-cooking videos dressed in vintage prairie dresses at Ballerina Farm in Mormon Utah. The internet ecosystem encourages influencers to cross-fertilise. Smith and Neeleman milked cows together. They posed on the farm porch, babies dandled on hips, husbands looking cocky in jeans and cowboy boots. Smith was accused of promoting regressive gender roles, of promoting teenage pregnancy, as well as “culturally appropriating” Mormon life, and distancing herself from her black heritage. Thinkpieces followed. Memes. Reams of Reddit discussion.Smith sighs when I put all this to her. “To begin with, I didn’t think too deeply about what I was doing. Cooking was something I did for health and because I enjoy it, and I also enjoy fashion. I had fun. I put it on the internet. People started reading into things, deciphering outfits, deciding I was saying things that would never even cross my mind.”Now she thinks that making your living in the kitchen is always going to be political. “It just is,” she says. “I feel people always want to put women in boxes, to try to explain them, to read into things they do. This is an expression of myself through food and fashion. People tune in for the voice, or the fashion, or the recipes, or all of it.”Does she see herself as a feminist? “Yes, absolutely. A woman should have the right to do it all, to do whatever she needs to do.”View image in fullscreenPhotograph: TikTok.com/ @naraazizasmithDoes she vote? “I would vote in the United States, but I’m not an American citizen so I’m not allowed.” But she worries about politics. “It’s scary everywhere right now.” She talks to family, to friends, to Lucky, about the rise of the AfD in Germany, deliberately keeps it offline. “People who see me know what I stand for. I have four kids. I’m a mum. I’m a woman. I would hope that people can put the pieces together. I don’t feel the need to speak about it on my socials because that’s for my artistic expression.”The Mormon thing? Well, she was curious, she admits. It was her husband’s background, she was open to hearing about it, to seeing if she identified with any of it. “If you marry someone that grew up that way, and you’re building a family, you’re figuring things out. That was happening when my social following exploded.” Are her children Mormon? “No. Our family isn’t. It’s a perception that people hold, but I’m not a Mormon, I was never a Mormon. I never got baptised. I never did anything that would make me Mormon. We figured out what we’re doing for our family, and it’s not being part of the [Mormon] church.”Every Wednesday and Thursday, Smith does three hours of acting class over Zoom with a teacher in Los Angeles,which she tops up with individual in-person sessions when she is in the city. She caught the acting “bug” on the set of Tyrant. She watched the big Hollywood names make mistakes, try it again, interpret lines in different ways, and realised you didn’t have to be perfect first time. Somehow, that blew her mind. She realised acting was an extension of what she was doing anyway. “I called my team after. Like, ‘We need an acting manager.’” She signed with a big agent and has started auditioning.Can she envisage a time where she’s not doing her cooking videos any more, or at least there’s less emphasis on that? “Yeah. I could see a time where my content evolves. I’ll never not be on social media because it’s such a pillar of my work, my business and the way I connect with people.”Is she competitive? She hmms and tilts her head to the side. “I wouldn’t say competitive. I’d say, what’s the word?” She snaps her fingers in the air. “Ambitious. That’s the word I was looking for. I’m very ambitious. But it’s one-upping myself. I couldn’t care less about one-upping other people. I’m in my own lane, and I have a goal I want to get to.”We’re ready to leave. As we rise from our chairs, a sea of teenage girls I hadn’t noticed converge. They look tiny next to Smith’s towering 6ft frame. They’ve been waiting, phone cameras at the ready. “You’ve, like, inspired me. I’ve been making stuff from scratch,” one says, grinning in train-track braces. “I love that,” says Smith. “What have you been making?” “I’m trying to make bread. It hasn’t gone well … ” “You know what? That takes a hot minute. It took me a hot minute. But you’re going get there.” She gives them a little hug.Homemade by Nara Aziza Smith is published by 4th Estate on 13 October. To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsSocial mediaTikTokInstagramFoodFood and drink booksDigital mediaWomen (Life and style)featuresShareReuse this content

title: Angry French students take to the streets. British students don’t – and I think I know why | Kitty Sayers | The Guardian
description: I grew up in France, where all children are taught about the revolutionary roots of their nation and the responsibility of the state towards its citizens, says Kitty Sayers, a master’s student in journalism
Author: Kitty Sayers
Headline: I grew up in France, where all children are taught about the revolutionary roots of their nation and the responsibility of the state towards its citizens, says Kitty Sayers, a master’s student in journalism
Content: Student protesters in the Place de la Bastille in Paris, 8 October 2026Photograph: Orin Louis/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenStudent protesters in the Place de la Bastille in Paris, 8 October 2026Photograph: Orin Louis/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionFranceAngry French students take to the streets. British students don’t – and I think I know whyKitty SayersI grew up in France, where all children are taught about the revolutionary roots of their nation and what the state owes its citizens. The lessons leave their markSat 10 Oct 2026 05.45 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTShareYoung British people have plenty to be angry about. Crushing student debt, private-school privilege, a housing market they can’t enter. Yet unlike their French counterparts, they have little tradition of turning that frustration into collective action. I grew up inFranceas a Briton, and for years I have watched my French friends do something my British ones never seem to: take to the streets.“To arms, citizens! Form your battalions! Let’s march, let’s march!” It shouldn’t be too surprising, given the rousing lyrics of La Marseillaise, that France’s revolutionary spirit is not a relic of the past.Thelycéeprotests in the past week have displayed the organisation and bravery of the French students. In Lens, a 15-year-oldlost his handto a police grenade during a blockade. More than6,000 people have been arrested, many of them under 18. Hundreds of schools across France are either blockaded or closed. These teenagers know the risks and commit to turning up anyway, day after day. I can’t imagine that happening in Britain, so what makes the French so different?First, there’s the history. France’s republic was born of insurrection and has never forgotten it. French pupils learn that protest, uprising and rioting are the origin story of their freedoms, so these methods are championed in promoting change. We grew up in school with the idea that if you don’t like something, you have the power to change it. The language of rights, citizenship and collective power is woven into French education. The French Revolution appears in the curriculum twice, for pupils aged 12 and then again at 16; the student protests of 1968 are taught at age 14 and again at 17. Debating is encouraged in schools from as early ascollège, or at about 11 years old.Young peopleare expected to have an opinion and not be afraid to defend it.Even I, at 11, started to feel patriotic during our moral and civic education classes, despite not having a French passport. Protesting is taught as a legally framed fundamental right and a civic responsibility. Of course, withlycéensnot yet being old enough to vote, protest is the next best thing.In the final year oflycée, pupils study Rousseau’sDu Contrat Social(The Social Contract), which argues that citizens should only surrender their unrestricted natural liberty in exchange for civil and moral freedoms. You give up your individual interests for thevolonté générale(general will) – put simply, you pay heavy taxes and in return you expect the country to work. That bargain is how the French understand their relationship with the state. When the government raises the retirement age, lets electricity bills soar or cuts school budgets, that is seen as a breach of the social contract. Protest is the automatic response.Britons, on the other hand, are subjects of the UK and are characterised more by an American-style individualism and a desire to live and let live. There is less collective spirit.Britain has an extraordinary history of protest, spanning Peterloo, the Chartists, the suffragettes and the poll tax riots, but there is arguably a different cultural relationship to these events. They can be remembered as stand-alone episodes and interruptions to the national story rather than as the story itself. The Thatcher era also did permanent damage to unions, contributing to the British public being a grumbling but compliant one, lacking in organising power.I see what’s happening here in Paris: reasonable student demands met with awful violence | Helen Massy-BeresfordRead moreBecause these values are ingrained across French society, and in every generation,the student protestersare emboldened by the firefighters, nurses, lawyers and teachers who have joined them in solidarity. Across social media, you can see these moments of support and unity. Aviral videoof the mayor of Saint-Denis,Bally Bagayoko, protecting students from the police is a striking example of this. It’s difficult to imagine British teenagers taking to the streets, because they would be alone.Parents have joined their children in protesting, and have called on other parents to do the same for the planned general strike on 17 October. (This is also a response to the police brutalitywitnessedin the past week.) Many parents were themselveslycéestudents and marched against education reforms and cuts. The anti-Macroniste parents (of whom there are many) don’t treat their children as delinquents, but as citizens exercising their rights.That does not mean every French parent supports every protest, or that French society is wholly united behind its students. While the French state technically encourages protest through the curriculum, the force and violence with which it has met its students says otherwise. And there is resentment of the protests among some students, particularly those who come from conservative households and believe that the blockades are a leftwing plot.Students in France are not necessarily more political than their British counterparts – young British people are active, but tend to take part in established and larger movements such as Extinction Rebellion or the Gaza protests rather than initiate protests themselves. The biggest difference lies in the French willingness to take to the streets, suddenly and en-masse. Unlike in the UK, the state is something the French are taught to engage with as citizens, and to challenge when necessary. If anything, thelycéensare just being good students.Kitty Sayers is a master’s student in journalismExplore more on these topicsFranceOpinionProtestYoung peopleEuropeStudentscommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Like a drill going into my eye’: why the mystery over Havana syndrome refuses to die  | CIA | The Guardian
description: Dozens of CIA officers have been afflicted by debilitating symptoms over the past decade. Are they the result of ‘mass hysteria’? Or are they from attacks with an energy weapon and, if so, who is responsible? And has there been a cover-up?
Author: Shaun Walker
Headline: Dozens of CIA officers have been afflicted by debilitating symptoms over the past decade. Are they the result of ‘mass hysteria’? Or are they from attacks with an energy weapon and, if so, who is responsible? And has there been a cover-up?
Content: The mystery of Havana syndrome refuses to die.Illustration: Alex Mellon for the Guardian : Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe mystery of Havana syndrome refuses to die.Illustration: Alex Mellon for the Guardian : Getty ImagesThe Saturday readCIA‘Like a drill going into my eye’: why the mystery over Havana syndrome refuses to dieDozens of CIA officers have been afflicted by debilitating symptoms over the past decade. Are they the result of ‘mass hysteria’? Or are they from attacks with an energy weapon and, if so, who is responsible? And has there been a cover-up?Shaun WalkerSat 10 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTShareShortly after 1am one night in April 2019, aCIAofficer on a work trip to London was jolted awake in his hotel room by the most intense head pain he had ever experienced. His body was soaked with sweat and he felt like his eyes were spinning in their sockets. He manoeuvred his way out of bed, hoping to make it to the bathroom to vomit, but found his sense of balance had deserted him. Eventually, he fell back into a fitful, shallow sleep.The next day, arriving at the work meeting he had travelled for, the officer found he could not remember the names of colleagues in the room, people he knew well. As the meeting got under way, he could barely follow the discussion. Initially, he chalked it up to a terrible – if rather odd – case of food poisoning. But over subsequent weeks, worrying symptoms persisted: brain fog, loss of balance and increasingly harsh tinnitus.By September, he had started to feel better and was on another work trip, this time to Poland. Asleep in his Warsaw hotel room, he was again woken by terrifying head pain, even worse than in London. He later described the sensation as “someone standing over me with a baseball bat and just repeatedly hitting me on the head”. It was a nine or 10 on the pain scale, he felt, worse than anything he could remember.Two hours later, the same feeling returned, and he started to suspect that what was happening might not be an internal process but rather some external attack. He dragged himself off the bed and curled up on the floor, where the intense pain subsided somewhat. That was the last time he had the “attack” sensation, but he went on to suffer chronic nerve pain, fatigue and other severe health problems for years.View image in fullscreenThe incidents acquired the name Havana syndrome after the Cuban city where mass reports of the phenomenon first emerged.Photograph: Manon Levet/Hans Lucas/AFP/Getty ImagesSources described the man in question as a senior CIA officer who had recently been assigned an important job relating to worldwide operations againstRussia. At the time, he was only vaguely aware of the stories that had emerged from Cuba two years previously, about US diplomats who believed they may have been attacked with a sonic weapon.These incidents, in which people reported feeling a variety of unusual sounds, pressure and pain, followed by residual symptoms that could last for years, had acquired the name Havana syndrome, after the city where mass reports of the phenomenonfirst emerged.Later, dozens of CIA officers around the world reported Havana syndrome episodes, which in official documents were called anomalous health incidents (AHIs). Many believed AHIs were the result of a Russian intelligence operation to wound or intimidate covert US operatives using a previously unknown weapon that delivered sonic or pulsed microwave energy.There was sustained pushback against that theory. Some scientists insisted the idea of a portable weapon that could deliver these injuries belonged in the realm of science fiction. They said a whole range of conditions could cause pain, dizziness and cognitive issues.Various experts suggested AHIs could be down to environmental factors, toxins or even the sound of chirping crickets. One explanation was that the symptoms were psychogenic and the result of “mass hysteria”, while some inside the CIA even accused those involved of faking their injuries in the hope of a medical payout. The disagreements over what was causing Havana syndrome led to bitter arguments and broken friendships at the spy agency.In 2022, a panel of scientific experts convened by the US government concluded that “the signs and symptoms of AHIs are genuine and compelling” and “could be due to external stimuli”.But the next year,a long-awaited report delivered the official assessmentof the US intelligence community: “The available intelligence consistently points against the involvement of US adversaries in causing the reported incidents,” read an unclassified summary. It was “very unlikely” that a sinister Russian campaign was behind AHIs, it concluded.World map showing locations of Havana syndrome incidentsYet the mystery of Havana syndrome refuses to die. This summer, the “very unlikely” assessment from 2023 was rescinded by Donald Trump’s outgoing director of national intelligence, who claimed it was based on flawed analysis.Now, a decade after the first reports emerged from Havana, two CBS journalists who have covered the story from the start are to release a book that sets out the case for Russia being behind at least some of the episodes. It also accuses parts of the US government and intelligence community of covering up the evidence.This article is based on early access to their findings, as well as on the Guardian’s own interviews with intelligence sources, AHI patients and scientists.David Relman, the Stanford professor who led the official scientific panel on Havana syndrome in 2022, told the Guardian he believed there was a subset of AHI cases that were “most plausibly explained by exposure to pulsed microwave energy”.His panel had access to patient records and to more than 1,000 classified documents on the topic. “To any reasonable person looking at all the evidence I was able to see, it inevitably leads to the conclusion that there may have been a cover-up,” he said.Michael Rey and Oriana Zill de Granados are longstanding producers for the CBS programme 60 Minutes. In an interview at the programme’s studios in midtown Manhattan, the pair recounted how they first came across the story a decade ago.They covered the Obama administration’s policy of re-establishing diplomatic relations withCubain 2015, so when reports emerged the next year of a mysterious new condition afflicting employees at the reopened embassy in Havana, they contacted a senior US diplomat who had been posted there. “I expected him to say: ‘This is all bullshit,’” said Zill. “But he said: ‘Oh no, this is completely true. And I can put you in touch with a bunch of people who were hit.’”The pair spoke to more than a dozen of them, off the record, but by the time they were ready to put a story together there were new reports of similar cases occurring among US diplomats stationed in China. Then there were whispers about it happening in other locations around the world.View image in fullscreenOriana Zill de Granados and Michael Rey, producers for 60 Minutes and authors of the forthcoming book The Havana Syndrome.Photograph: Pete Kiehart/The GuardianOnce the first 60 Minutes episodes devoted to the topic aired, victims started contacting the producers, keen to tell their stories. Many of these new sources were – or had been – undercover operatives for the CIA, meaning they could not speak openly as most details of their work were classified. But people stationed around the world who had not known each other told stories that seemed remarkably similar.A pattern linked some of the key cases: the alleged victims were working, or had previously worked, on beats where they rubbed up against Russian interests.In some cases, the location of the supposed hits was notable in itself: allies of Moscow where some part of the elite was looking to improve relations with the west. This was the case in Cuba, where the original cluster of cases had come during the Obama-era thaw in relations with the US, which had irritated hardliners in the Cuban regime and their backers in Moscow.It was also the case in Georgia, Kyrgyzstan, Serbia and Vietnam. Several CIA officers who had been stationed in Kyiv around the time of the 2014 Maidan revolution in Ukraine, decried by the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, as a US-backed coup, later suffered AHIs in different locations across the world.“I went through years of doubts about the story, and all the crazy things we were hearing,” said Zill. But the more source meetings she and Rey had, the more they felt there really was something there. “We’re meeting these highly effective intelligence officers and they’re all telling versions of the same story,” said Rey.The origins of Havana syndrome go back long before Cuba. A cornerstone case is that ofMike Beck, a counter-intelligence officer at the National Security Agencywho got sick while on temporary assignment to an undisclosed location in the 1990s to check a US diplomatic facility for bugs.Beck developed a rare form of Parkinson’s disease at the age of 45 and died this year. A declassified NSA statement, included in his 2014 workplace compensation claim, noted that “there is intelligence information from 2012 associating the hostile country to which Mr Beck travelled in the late 1990s with a high-powered microwave system weapon that may have the ability to weaken, intimidate or kill an enemy, over time, and without leaving evidence”. The unnamed “hostile country”, sources said, was Russia.View image in fullscreenMike Beck, pictured in 2017, died this year after developing a rare form of Parkinson’s disease aged 45.Photograph: The Washington Post/Getty ImagesThe first known AHIs among the contemporary batch of cases occurred in late 2014, when several US government employees at the consulate in Frankfurt, Germany, became ill. One was found unconscious in a consulate stairwell after feeling sudden, intense pressure on her chest and hearing a “high-pitched squeal”, Rey and Zill reported.The next year, a researcher at a US defence institute – who asked the Guardian not to use her name – was on a tour of the Balkans, attending meetings with military officers from the host nations alongside US defence attaches. Her itinerary took in Montenegro, which was in the process of applying for Nato membership, and Serbia, a Russian ally that harboured resentments towards the US over the 1999 Nato bombing of Yugoslavia.On her final evening in Belgrade, as she walked through lively pedestrianised streets to her hotel, the researcher was sure she spotted someone following her. Later, as she approached her hotel room, she felt “a sinking feeling, as though I was in a lift that was descending suddenly”, she recalled in a telephone interview.Inside her room, she continued to feel odd sensations. “I just had this falling sensation, a feeling of gravity pulling at me, and nausea.” At one point, she turned on her government laptop and found the screen was flickering with blue static. The computer never worked again.She said she was able to continue her trip, but in the subsequent weeks she felt weak, had difficulty speaking clearly and developed pain that felt “like a drill was going into my eye”. She was unable to focus at work. “I used up all my vacation, then my sick leave, then colleagues donated their leave. Eventually, I had to leave my job,” she said. It was only much later that she connected what had happened to her with reports about Havana syndrome.View image in fullscreenMarc Polymeropoulos has symptoms associated with Havana syndrome.Photograph: Pete Kiehart/The GuardianThe next cohort of AHI patients included people at the heart of a new CIA policy on Russia. In 2017, as Donald Trump took office for the first time, the agency launched a drive to push back against the increasingly brazen global reach of Moscow’s intelligence agencies.“They wanted us to take the same kind of tactics and spirit we used in the global war on terror to the Russians,” said Marc Polymeropoulos, who was made deputy chief of operations forEuropeand Eurasia in 2017. Polymeropoulos, who had spent most of his career in the Middle East, was one of several veterans of the “war on terror” who were moved to senior roles focused on Russia. Even as Trump publicly denied that Russia had interfered in the 2016 election, the agency made plans to push back hard against Russian activity.“Obviously, we didn’t have permission to run lethal operations against the Russians, but we could do things we hadn’t done as much previously, such as enlist the help of multiple friendly services and expose the Russians for what they were doing,” said Polymeropoulos, in an interview at a restaurant just outside Washington.In early December 2017, Polymeropoulos and another senior CIA executive made a liaison trip to Moscow, to meet their counterparts in Russia’s SVR and FSB intelligence services. The official meetings were ill-tempered and lacking in substance. Late one night, Polymeropoulos woke up suddenly in his hotel room. “I had vertigo and a splitting headache. I thought it was food poisoning at first, I thought I was going to puke and crap my brains out, and I remember being like, holy shit, the room is spinning and my ears are ringing,” he said.On his return to Washington, Polymeropoulos struggled with a persistent migraine that would not subside, and with superiors who insisted his symptoms were unrelated to other AHIs. He saw a variety of doctors on his own time, but owing to the classified nature of his job he could not share details of where he had been when he became ill.He left the CIA in 2019 and, frustrated at being stonewalled in his requests for medical assessment, became the first CIA officer to go public with a Havana syndrome story under their real name,tellingthe journalist Julia Ioffe about what happened in Moscow.The resulting publicity prompted the CIA to send him to the Walter Reed military medical centre, where he was diagnosed with mild traumatic brain injury. In 2023 he was found eligible for compensation under theHavana Act, which authorised payments to “personnel who incur brain injuries from hostilities while on assignment”. The financial payout was modest, but he saw it as a moral victory after years of fighting for recognition.View image in fullscreenMarc Polymeropoulos struggled with a persistent migraine that would not subside.Photograph: Pete Kiehart/The GuardianOne early theory was that AHIs could be the result of data collection attempts gone wrong – a machine designed to pull classified data from operatives’ electronic devices that had unfortunate side-effects when turned up too high. That is still seen by some as a possibility, although even if intelligence collection was the initial idea, the damaging health effects would have quickly become apparent to the operators.Some observers insisted the whole concept of “Havana syndrome” was an invention. They asked why, if Russia possessed a brain-frying weapon, it was not using it on a wider range of its enemies. Why were there not more reports of collateral victims?The sociologist Robert Bartholomew and the neurologist Robert Baloh co-authoreda bookthat declared the whole story a hoax – “a case study in the social construction of mass psychogenic illness” – borne of high-stress work environments and propagated by excitable journalists.Douglas Fields,a cellular neuroscientist and author of several books about the brain, claimed in a journal article that the medical studies of patients which showed cognitive changes had used unsound methodology, and that theories of an energy weapon “defy the laws of physics”. Reports of Havana syndrome should be taken no more seriously than sightings of the Loch Ness monster, he suggested.Other scientists, including some who had reviewed patients’ medical records, strongly disagreed. “The early scepticism was perfectly appropriate, but over time we started to see an increase in the number of individuals who have gone through clinical evaluations that cannot be faked,” said James Giordano, a professor emeritus of neurology at Georgetown University Medical Center and the forensic neuroscientist on the original cohort of cases from Havana.“We are talking about objective signs that are presenting with a very distinct pattern,” Giordano said. Key symptoms included “a profound tumbling or falling sensation” as well as pressure in the head, chest and throat, and cognitive effects. It was true that chemical or drug exposure could cause similar symptoms, he said, but this would be visible on blood tests. Another key factor was the sudden onset and the sense of a specific location where the apparent attack felt strongest.When the Biden administration took office in 2021, the then CIA director, Bill Burns, and the director of national intelligence, Avril Haines, vowed to get to the bottom of the issue. Burns met many of the AHI cohort, including Polymeropoulos, listening carefully to their stories and promising them a full investigation.Burns also fired the CIA’s chief medical officer, who had infuriated some AHI patients by accusing them of faking their symptoms. The same year, more than 100 CIA operatives and other US government officials reported AHIs in locations around the world. In Vienna, there were so many hits that the work of the CIA station was essentially paralysed and the station chief recalled. A spate of government employees also reported incidents on US soil, including several who claimed to have been hit on the grounds of the White House. Was this an adversary stepping up its campaign, or was the increasing publicity about AHIs leading more people to misidentify other conditions or episodes as Havana syndrome?Burns and Haines launched two investigations, one to re-examine intelligence on whether a foreign adversary was behind Havana syndrome, and another that convened a panel of scientists and physicians to determine whether it was even possible for a weapon to cause the symptoms.View image in fullscreenDavid Relman said there were dozens of cases ‘that were unusual in the distinctness of their features’.Photograph: Lea Suzuki/San Francisco Chronicle/Hearst Newspapers/Getty ImagesRelman, a Stanford professor who chaired the scientific panel, said its members were given access to open source and classified scientific studies into pulsed radio frequency energy, which suggested that the science behind there being a “device” that could cause AHI symptoms was plausible. Scientists who disagreed were simply unaware of the research into such technology that had been taking place for decades in several countries, especially in the Soviet Union and then Russia, he said.Regarding the medical results, Relman conceded that plenty – perhaps the vast majority – of AHI claims could be explained by other factors. But there were dozens of cases “that were unusual in the distinctness of their features and the near impossibility of explaining them based on known medical and environmental conditions”. In short: the publicity around AHIs may have prompted a wave of false reporting, but a core subset of cases seemed real.Determining who may have carried out such attacks was beyond Relman’s purview. That fell to the second expert group, which in 2023 issued the assessment that it was “very unlikely” to be caused by a foreign adversary, dismaying many AHI patients who had hoped to finally receive closure on what caused their health problems.Even people who have seen the intelligence on Havana syndrome can disagree on what it suggests. Two sources offered the Guardian radically different interpretations of what the classified data shows on possible Russian involvement.One highlighted the lack of a “smoking gun”; a piece of human intelligence or an intercept that showed Russian operatives discussing a programme to use directed energy against Americans.“Everyone has seen how strong our collection capabilities on Russia are,” the source said, referencing howUS intelligence got hold of Putin’s war plansbefore his February 2022 invasion of Ukraine. “If this was really a large-scale Russian programme, we would have expected to see something in some of these channels, but we didn’t.”Another former intelligence official disagreed: “If you’re waiting for an intercept of someone saying: ‘My name is Igor and I’m going to press the button on my secret laser’ before you have confidence, that’s probably never going to happen. But for any reasonable person who has access to the intelligence and knows how to read it, the Russian fingerprints are clear.”If that is the case, it raises the question of why the 2023 intelligence community assessment found it “very unlikely” that a foreign actor was involved. At the end of the Biden administration, atweaked versionsaid that while five US intelligence agencies still found it “very unlikely”, one agency now believed there was a “roughly even chance” that a foreign actor had used “a novel weapon or prototype device” in a number of attacks.This summer, both of those Biden-era assessments were rescinded by Trump’s director of national intelligence, Tulsi Gabbard, in amemo issued just before she left office. Gabbard said the earlier assessments were marred by “selective exclusion of evidence” and “mischaracterisation of sources”, though the statement did not release any new evidence or provide a revised assessment.While Gabbard had achequered reputation among the intelligence community, Mark Zaid, a lawyer who represents more than 30 AHI patients, welcomed her memo and said it was a first step to overturning a CIA cover-up. When asked why the CIA might have perpetrated such a cover-up, Zaid suggested it could be to protect its reputation after prior negligence. “This has built up to a level that the agency can’t let the truth get out because it’s going to reflect so poorly on them,” he said.Burns, in a comment for Rey and Zill’s book, said it was “simply not true that there was a ‘cover-up’ by the CIA” and described the earlier investigation as “a rigorous effort across the entire intelligence community”.Rey and Zill believe the purported cover-up was a result of multiple factors over many years. “There’s not a single cigar-filled backroom meeting that led to decisions getting made,” said Rey. “There was a lot of, ‘This is a pain in the ass’ or ‘The president’s not going to want to hear this’. There was bureaucratic dysfunction, careerism and things that just got in the way of proper investigation.”One example he gave is the fact that the FBI sent criminal investigators, rather than counterintelligence investigators with access to classified information, to Havana after the attacks there. Another is a nascent investigation at CIA headquarters in late 2019 which reportedly found that, in some cases, phones linked to Russian intelligence operatives had been in the vicinity of suspected Havana syndrome incidents. These included the hits that year on the senior CIA officer in London and Warsaw.View image in fullscreenRey and Zill believe the purported cover-up was a result of multiple factors over many years.Photograph: Pete Kiehart/The GuardianIn London, a suspicious phone had supposedly been just 10 metres (30ft) away from his hotel room. But when the then CIA director, Gina Haspel, was briefed on these findings, she allegedly complained it was not solid enough to take to the president, given how sensitive he was on Russia-related matters. “The meeting abruptly ended after Haspel shouted that if she took reports like this to President Trump, she would be fired as director,” Rey and Zill write.Outside the CIA, some have uncovered intriguing leads about possible links between Russian operatives and AHIs.Christo Grozev, a journalist and investigatorwho has exposed several Russian intelligence operations, claimed leaked travel data suggested at least four potential crossovers between suspected AHIs and travel by officers from Unit 29155 of Russia’s GRU military intelligence, known for its campaign of sabotage and assassinations in western countries. He also said he had traced travel by “members of what appears to be a technical unit adjacent to 29155” to Cuba during the initial attacks.Perhaps the most significant piece of evidence to emerge recently has been the alleged US government acquisition of a “Havana syndrome-style device” in an undercover operation.First reportedby the independent journalist Sasha Ingber this year, two sources confirmed to the Guardian that a device had been acquired and brought to the US in late 2024 for testing, after a purchase from a dark-web seller.Rey and Zill’s book recounts a meeting with a person who claimed to be part of the undercover team that acquired the device. The source told them the device was “man-portable”, shot non-thermal pulsed microwaves and was acquired from “a complex Russian illicit network”.It was not believed to have been used in a Havana syndrome incident, but testing on animals has reportedly shown it may cause similar symptoms to AHIs, which could prove that building such a device is scientifically possible.That would make the case for a weapon being involved in some incidents more plausible, and would also raise new and worrying questions. If such weapons have proliferated to the extent that one can be bought on the dark web, how many devices could be out there and who may have access to them? Could AHIs thus have not one perpetrator, but many? And is there a future in which such weapons become a widespread element of warfare? “We know the technology has reached a level that enables it to be used in weaponisable ways,” said Giordano. “I see that as a clear and present threat.”For those who have had symptoms for years, the acquisition of the device and the rescinded intelligence assessments provide some hope that, one day, they will receive official confirmation that they were targeted by a foreign adversary. For many of them, the lack of recognition at home has angered them more than the attack itself.“The Russians are our enemy, I put them in the same bucket as al-Qaida or the Taliban, or any other groups I worked against,” said Polymeropoulos. “Do I want to see them held accountable? Of course. But I’m actually more upset and feel more of a betrayal from my own government.”The Havana Syndromeby Michael Rey and Oriana Zill de Granados is published by Crown Publishing in the US on 13 October and by WH Allen in the UK on 15 October.

title: How to storm-proof your home, from roof tiles to garden fences | Property | The Guardian
description: With an extremely wet and windy winter forecast, take steps to keep you and your home safe and dry
Author: Zoe Wood
Headline: With an extremely wet and windy winter forecast, take steps to keep you and your home safe and dry
Content: Total payouts for storm damage to UK homes surged 32% in 2025 after Storm Éowyn and Storm Floris.Photograph: Charles McQuillan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTotal payouts for storm damage to UK homes surged 32% in 2025 after Storm Éowyn and Storm Floris.Photograph: Charles McQuillan/Getty ImagesPropertyHow to storm-proof your home, from roof tiles to garden fencesWith an extremely wet and windy winter forecast, take steps to keep you and your home safe and dryZoe WoodSat 10 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith theMet Officewarning that this year’s supersizedEl Niñocould mean a wet and stormy winter lies ahead, it’s never been more important to maintain your home.Payouts for storm damage to UK homes surged 32% to £244m in 2025 amid the destruction caused by the heavy rain and strong winds that accompanied the likes of Storm Éowyn and Storm Floris.But that is just part of the picture, with total claims for weather damage to homes and possessions hitting £758m last year, according to the Association of British Insurers (ABI). It says this figure points to “the toll that increasingly severe weather is taking on homes”.However, experts say regular maintenance can help prevent damage to your property. With that in mind, here are practical steps you can take to make sure your home is best-placed to ride out the storms.Inspect your roofAlex Peters, a cost guide expert at Checkatrade, says: “The primary line of defence begins at roof level, where high winds will dislodge weak structures and create hazardous flying debris that could damage your home.”Tiles often become broken or loose, or slip. Ideally you would get up there to have a look, but only do so if you have the proper safety equipment – otherwise, call a professional.View image in fullscreenExperts advise regular roof and chimney inspections. A standard professional inspection averages about £250 a visit.Photograph: Paul Glendell/AlamyPeters says: “It is important to undertake regular roof and chimney inspections to make sure they’re structurally sound. A standard professional roof inspection averages about £250 per visit to check for loose tiles or mortar decay.”Most roof repairs cost between £110 and £160 a sq metre, depending on roof type and materials, according to Checkatrade.A buildup of moss can cause moisture damage to tiles and the wood underneath them, so remove it if you can. The best time is after a dry spell, when you can brush it off with a stiff broom (but don’t attempt this without the proper safety equipment).Roof “furniture” such as chimneys, skylights and vents is sealed with metal strips called flashing, which should sit flush, with no gaps where water can seep in. If yours does not, you can buy flashing strips, roof sealant and caulk in mostDIYstores but, again, this repair job might be better-suited to a professional.Maintain your guttersPeters says: “Gutters channel heavy rain safely away from your roofline down to external drains, but if they’re blocked, water can pool and lead to a range of issues.”These include water seeping into brickwork and causing internal damp, or uncontrolled drainage which erodes the soil around your home’s foundations and, over time, can destabilise them.View image in fullscreenYou can clear your gutters yourself, or hire a professional for about £20-£30 an hour.Photograph: Roy Morsch/Getty ImagesNow is a good time to clean them out and make any repairs. The cost depends on the size of your home but sits at about £20-30 an hour for a skilled tradesperson, according to Checkatrade.Andy Simms, of home service marketplace MyBuilder, says that any trees near your house should be checked now, adding: “Overhanging or unhealthy trees can cause all sorts of property damage, alongside clogging drains.”Pruning can usually be completed for about £100, but for bigger jobs, a tree surgeon typically costs £240-£400 a day depending on where you live.… and don’t forget the brickworkInspect walls for obvious weak spots, including cracked render, staining or places where rainwater collects.Michael Davie, from specialist home improvement firm PureBuilt, says one of the biggest issues homeowners underestimate is damp caused by small external defects. “A cracked or damaged section of render might not look serious at first, but if water is able to get behind it, the problem can spread quickly,” he says.View image in fullscreenRoof furniture such as chimneys, skylights and vents are sealed with metal strips called flashing, which should sit flush, with no gaps where water can seep in.Photograph: Paul Maguire/Alamy“We regularly see cases where what could have been a relatively straightforward repair becomes a much bigger job because the source of the moisture has been left untreated. A repair of about £500 can turn into thousands of pounds once damp has affected plaster, internal finishes or larger areas of the property.”Seal your windows and doorsRepair any cracks or seals around your doors and windows. Peters says: “If there are any gaps or cracks, apply draught excluder tape or caulk to help prevent drafts and water from getting in.”View image in fullscreenWindow sealant costs about £10 perfor a 300ml tube.Photograph: Elizaveta Galitckaia/AlamyWindow sealant costs about £10 for a 300ml tube, while draught-proofing tape works out at £5-£15 a roll. Another low-cost fix is a door seal – typically a piece of rubber, vinyl or silicone fitted around the frame or on the door edge. You can use basic self-adhesive foam strips or spend more on brush seals and compression strips (and don’t forget letterbox and keyhole covers).Hiring a professional to weatherstrip drafty openings runs at about £50 a window or £100 for each external door, according to Checkatrade.Secure your gardenPlant pots, garden furniture and trampolines should be stored inside or secured before a storm. Gates and fences are particularly susceptible to wind damage and for this reason most standard buildings insurance policies will not let you claim for the cost of repairing them.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYou could reinforce your fence with concrete posts and look at replacing the panels with ones that are 50% wind-permeable (these have gaps that let the wind through without toppling over). For repairs, the price varies depending on the material, but for fence panels it typically costs £45 while fence posts cost about £25. The big cost is labour, and this varies depending on where you live and the amount of work involved, but £950 is a ballpark figure.View image in fullscreenGates and fences are particularly susceptible to wind damage, which is why most standard buildings insurance policies will not let you claim for the cost of repairing them.Photograph: Glyn Kirk/AFP/Getty ImagesInsulate your pipesDamage caused by frozen and burst pipes can be significant. Household insurers settled roughly 8,000 claims for weather-related pipe damage in 2024, paying out £250m in total, according to the ABI. The average claim was almost £33,000.Insulating exposed hot water pipes is an easy DIY job. Inexpensive pipe insulation (often called pipe lagging) is available from most DIY stores, and fitting it could also shave about £6 off your annual energy bill, according to theEnergy Saving Trust.Most modern hot water tanks have plenty of insulation, but an older tank might only have a small amount. Adding an 80mm jacket to a tank with 25mm foam built in can save homeowners in Great Britain £45 a year, says the Trust. The jackets cost about £20 and are widely available from DIY retailers.View image in fullscreenInsulating exposed hot water pipes is an easy DIY job.Photograph: Laurence Berger/Getty Images/iStockphotoAlso locate your stopcock – it is usually under the kitchen sink. This valve allows you to turn off the incoming water supply. That’s vital if a pipe bursts, and you might also want to use it if you are leaving your property unoccupied. It is a good idea to clear remaining water from the pipes after turning the supply off.Get emergency suppliesThe government is urging people to“get prepared”for emergencies by stocking up on essentials such as bottled water and tinned food. Your emergency kit should include a portable mobile phone charger, torches and batteries, blankets and warm clothing. Also keep a list of emergency numbers to hand. These should include 105 for a power cut or 0800 111999 for a gas leak.Think about getting your boiler serviced. “Freezing storm conditions can cause indoor temperatures to drop rapidly, forcing boilers to work harder,” Peters says. “Servicing catches pressure drops, sediment buildup or worn components that could trigger a system lockout under heavy load.” A service typically costs about £100, but prices vary depending on the type of boiler.Prevent floodingFlood resilience champion Mary Long-Dhonau, who is behind theFlood Mary campaign, has adirectory of builders who specialisein flood-related work on her website.Long-Dhonau warns that an “awful lot of water can enter your home via the airbricks – in fact, it is often the first place flood water can enter into a home”.
