She recommends replacing them with Kitemarked self-closing airbricks. Alternatively, you can buy temporary covers. In an emergency she suggests creating a temporary seal using wide aluminium tape – one large roll can cover multiple airbricks and can be bought online or in DIY shops. (Once the danger of flooding has passed, you should remove any temporary coverings to allow for proper air circulation and temperature regulation.)View image in fullscreenIf you already own flood-protection equipment, now is the time to test it.Photograph: Oli Scarff/Getty ImagesPeople often assume that flood protection means spending many thousands of pounds – and it can, says FPS Group founder Simon Crowther, who is also known as“The Flood Guy”. But some individual measures are more accessible.“A basic domestic flood pump setup can be in the low hundreds of pounds, and a door barrier may be a few hundred pounds,” he says. “Current examples on the market put small complete pump kits at about £150 upwards, and some domestic door barriers at about £400-£600.”If you already own flood-protection equipment, now is the time to test it.“Check flood barrier seals and fixings, make sure all the parts are actually there, and practise fitting it,” he says. “If you have a pump, run it and check the hose, connections, float switch or sensor.”View image in fullscreenCheck your insurance cover to see what damage qualifies for repair.Photograph: Nicholas.T Ansell/PAWill my home insurance cover me?Buildings and contents insurance typically provides some cover for weather or storm damage, says Amy Rootham, an insurance expert at price comparison website Compare the Market. It may also fund alternative accommodation if your home is uninhabitable.But insurers have specific criteria for what constitutes a storm, which may include wind speed or rainfall intensity. Also, this sort of insurance is designed to cover sudden and unforeseen damage, so they will assess whether the storm was the direct cause of the problem, or if it exposed an issue already in need of repair.Rootham says home insurance premiums have been falling over the past two years but warns not to “focus on price alone” when comparing policies. “Check the cover limits, excesses and exclusions carefully,”she says.Explore more on these topicsPropertyDIYConstruction industryHome insuranceInsuranceHome improvementsHomesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Blind date: ‘Most awkward moment? When she squished an insect that was on my forehead’ | Dating | The Guardian
description: Holly, 42, a horticulturist, meets Graeme, 47, a forest manager
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Holly, 42, a horticulturist, meets Graeme, 47, a forest manager
Content:
Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianBlind dateDatingBlind date: ‘Most awkward moment? When she squished an insect that was on my forehead’Holly, 42, a horticulturist, meets Graeme, 47, a forest managerSat 10 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGraemeon HollyView image in fullscreenWhat were you hoping for?Really, just a fun night with minimal awkwardness was my fairly low expectation before the meeting.First impressions?A very positive, engaging lady with a beautiful smile.What did you talk about?Growing food, the joys of seeds, birdwatching, the failings of young people when it comes to proper raving, epigenetics and breaking generational cycles.Most awkward moment?Holly destroying an aphid, which had landed on my forehead, with a firm thumb squish. I should make clear that the poor aphid wasn’t in the lovely restaurant; it was outside an entirely different place, which had hanging baskets.Good table manners?Impeccable.Best thing about Holly?Holly was incredibly easy to converse with. Her assured nature and wide range of interests meant she was a joy to be with.Would you introduce Holly to your friends?In a heartbeat.Q&AFancy a blind date?ShowBlind date is Saturday’s dating column: every week, two 
strangers are paired up for dinner and drinks, and then spill the beans 
to us, answering a set of questions. This runs, with a photograph we 
take of each dater before the date, in Saturday magazine (in the
 UK) and online attheguardian.comevery Saturday. It’s been running since 2009 – you canread all about how we put it together here.What questions will I be asked?We
 ask about age, location, occupation, hobbies, interests and the type of
 person you are looking to meet. If you do not think these questions 
cover everything you would like to know, tell us what’s on your mind.Can I choose who I match with?No,
 it’s a blind date! But we do ask you a bit about your interests, 
preferences, etc – the more you tell us, the better the match is likely 
to be.Can I pick the photograph?No, but don't worry: we'll choose the nicest ones.What personal details will appear?Your first name, job and age.How should I answer?Honestly
 but respectfully. Be mindful of how it will read to your date, and that
 Blind date reaches a large audience, in print and online.Will I see the other person’s answers?No. We may edit yours and theirs for a range of reasons, including length, and we may ask you for more details.Will you find me The One?We’ll try! Marriage! Babies!Can I do it in my home town?Only if it’s in the UK. Many of our applicants live in London, but we would love to hear from people living elsewhere.How to applyEmailblind.date@theguardian.comWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Describe Holly in three wordsNuanced, sparkling, niche.What do you think Holly made of you?I reckon she was hugely impressed I could name every species of bird she had tattooed on her leg.Did you go on somewhere?Yes, a nearby pub then a little nightclub.And … did you kiss?Yes, we did.If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be?I would tone down my oversharingMarks out of 10?9.8.Would you meet again?I’m hugely looking forward to doing so.View image in fullscreenGraeme and Holly on their dateHollyon GraemeView image in fullscreenWhat were you hoping for?To meet someone interesting and fun.First impressions?Warm, confident. Graeme quickly made me feel at ease.What did you talk about?Our mutual nerves about the evening. The joys of working outside. Forestry management for biodiversity. Rural living. The importance of dancing.Most awkward moment?I got overexcited about the menu and ordered quite a lot of food. We didn’t need the extra salad.Good table manners?Excellent: he kept our glasses topped up and was open to sharing dishes.Best thing about Graeme?He’s got a very curious mind and is a great listener.Would you introduce Graeme to your friends?He’d get along well with them.Describe Graeme in three wordsWarm, intelligent, open.Blind date: ‘We talked about how I don’t like Clapham gays – guess where he lives?’Read moreWhat do you think Graeme made of you?I hope he thought I was easy to talk to.Did you go on somewhere?We did. We made the most of being in the city and sought out some music and dancing!And … did you kiss?Yes.If you could change one thing about the date, what would it be?Nothing – I had a really fun evening. Graeme is a lovely guy who is very easy to talk to and up for a laugh.Marks out of 10?A solid 8.Would you meet again?We live quite far apart, but we’ll see …Holly and Graeme ate at thePalmerstonin Edinburgh. Fancy a blind date? Emailblind.date@theguardian.comExplore more on these topicsDatingBlind dateRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Camden council was warned about paedophile nursery worker years before arrest | Children | The Guardian
description: Vincent Chan went on to abuse children after being cleared of ‘significant concerns’ following council-overseen inquiry
Author: Sirin Kale
Headline: Vincent Chan went on to abuse children after being cleared of ‘significant concerns’ following council-overseen inquiry
Content: Chan, who was jailed for 18 years in February, was described by prosecutors as a ‘prolific sexual predator’.Photograph: Metropolitan police/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChan, who was jailed for 18 years in February, was described by prosecutors as a ‘prolific sexual predator’.Photograph: Metropolitan police/AFP/Getty ImagesChildrenCamden council was warned about paedophile nursery worker years before arrestVincent Chan went on to abuse children after being cleared of ‘significant concerns’ following council-overseen inquirySirin KaleSat 10 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA paedophile nursery worker was cleared by an investigation overseen by a local authority three years before he was arrested.In February, Vincent Chanwas jailed after pleading guilty to 56 offences, including assault by penetration on three-year-old girls in his care at a Bright Horizons nursery on Finchley Road in north-west London. After his conviction, prosecutors described him as a “prolific sexual predator”.The Guardian can now reveal that Chan was the subject of an earlier safeguarding investigation, carried out by Bright Horizons, with the oversight of Camden council. It followed what were described as “significant concerns” raised with the nursery in 2021 about Chan’s conduct and behaviour by the parent of a young girl, including concerns about what her daughter was saying to her about Chan.Bright Horizons referred the matter to Camden council, which advised the nursery to investigate. Chan was put on duties that involved no contact with children while the investigation by Bright Horizons took place. After it was completed, Chan was cleared to return to his role caring for young children in the nursery.A year later, in 2022, Chan filmed himself sexually abusing three-year-old girls at the Bright Horizons nursery.Chan was first arrested in June 2024, initially on suspicion of child cruelty, after nursery staff discovered videos Chan had filmed of distressed children in his care.After Chan’s devices were searched by police as part of this investigation, they discovered that he was a prolific sexual offender, with tens of thousands of child abuse images on his computer. He had also committed sexual offences in his previous job as a teaching assistant at St Mary’s Church of England primary school in Dollis Park, northLondon, including upskirting female pupils. In February this year, Chan was sentenced to 18 years in prison.The revelation that Camden council and Bright Horizons were aware of concerns about Chan three years before his arrest, and that there had been an investigation into his behaviour, will raise questions about whether there were earlier opportunities to stop him. It will also raise wider questions about whether existing safeguards for nurseries are adequate.In early 2024, prior to Chan’s arrest, other parents say that they raised concerns with Bright Horizons about Chan’s conduct at work. They say they warned Bright Horizons that their children were telling them that Chan shouted at them, was “angry” and a “bad man”. These parents say these concerns were dismissed. After Chan’s first arrest, the Bright Horizons nursery on Finchley Road closed in June 2025.Nurseries have a responsibility to refer to local authority designated officers (LADOs) when there are concerns that a nursery worker has been accused of harming or posing a risk of harm to children, may be guilty of criminal conduct, or has exhibited behaviour that makes them unsuitable to work with children.Local authorities have the ultimate responsibility for managing allegations raised that relate to adults who work with children.LADOs can recommend that a matter be referred to the police if they believe it meets a criminal threshold. It is understood that the Metropolitan police did not receive a referral in 2021 regarding Chan, and were only notified of the concerns subsequently.After Chan’s sexual offending came to light, Camden council carried out a rapid review of the decision to clear him to return to work after the Bright Horizons investigation. The review concluded in November 2025, and Camden council subsequently commissioned a local child safeguarding practice review, led by an independent reviewer, to examine how Chan was able to abuse children at the Finchley Road nursery, in addition to offences committed in his previous role.The review, which has been pushed back repeatedly, is expected to be published in early 2027 according to Camden council. It is expected to be critical of the safeguarding culture within Bright Horizons. But Camden council has said publicly that it cannot investigate Bright Horizons under health and safety laws because it is conflicted due to its participation in the safeguarding review. Local authorities have the power to prosecute businesses that do not comply with health and safety legislation.In a letter to the parent of a child at the nursery, seen by the Guardian, Camden council said that the purpose of the safeguarding review was “not conducted to hold individuals, organisations, or agencies to account”. The review is not expected to satisfy the parents of Chan’s victims because it is unlikely to apportion blame to executives at Bright Horizons.There has been no explanation of why the review was pushed back from summer 2026, when the independent reviewer was initially expected to submit her report. The council has also rejected a freedom of information request from the Guardian relating to Chan’s employment at the nursery, citing a desire to “manage” the release of information.It is understood that, in addition to the 2021 referral involving Chan, Camden council received other unrelated safeguarding referrals from Bright Horizons between 2017 and 2024, the time Chan worked at the nursery.Get in touchContact our investigations teamThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu. Select ‘Secure Messaging’.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can emailinvestigations.contact@theguardian.com.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreA spokesperson for Camden council said: “Children deserve the best care in a safe environment and the ongoing independent local child safeguarding review into this case presents a pivotal opportunity to prevent abuse like this from happening again. Our participation in the review is thorough, and we have disclosed all relevant documents and information.“We are ready to receive the review’s recommendations once it is published and take action. We are determined to make a real and tangible impact on safeguarding arrangements for the future.”A spokesperson for Bright Horizons said: “Our thoughts remain with the victims of Chan’s shocking crimes and their families. As the Camden local authority’s child safeguarding practice review is ongoing, we will not be able to comment without the express written authorisation of that committee as we do not wish to prejudice that process. We will respond as soon as we are able, once we have received the committee’s response.”In the UK, theNSPCCoffers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In the US, call or text theChildhelpabuse hotline on 800-422-4453. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact theKids Helplineon 1800 55 1800; adult survivors can seek help atBlue Knot Foundationon 1300 657 380. Other sources of help can be found atChild Helpline InternationalExplore more on these topicsChildrenEarly years educationCrimeLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump says Ukraine needs a new leader after diesel deal with Russia | Volodymyr Zelenskyy | The Guardian
description: US president suggests Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has not done enough to end war
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: US president suggests Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has not done enough to end war
Content: Rescuers evacuate a wounded woman from under the debris of an apartment building hit by a Russian airstrike in Zaporizhzhia.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenRescuers evacuate a wounded woman from under the debris of an apartment building hit by a Russian airstrike in Zaporizhzhia.Photograph: ReutersVolodymyr ZelenskyyTrump says Ukraine needs a new leader after diesel deal with RussiaUS president suggests Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has not done enough to end warOliver HolmesSat 10 Oct 2026 16.42 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 10.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has said Ukraine needs “a new leader”, a day after making a deal withVladimir Putinto buy large quantities of Russian diesel.The US president suggestedVolodymyr Zelenskyyhas not done enough to end the war with Russia and blamed him for high diesel prices in the US.“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does,” Trump said.Trump made the comments as Russia launched deadly strikes on civilians inUkraine, which Zelenskyy said were a “thanks” to Trump for the diesel deal.The Ukrainian president has expressed outrage at theagreement announced by Trumpon Friday, which the US president said was needed to reduce diesel prices, and comes ahead of November’s midterm elections in which fuel costs are a key voter issue.The deal, which appeared to blindside Kyiv as it was announced while Ukrainian negotiators were in Miami for peace talks, was described by Zelenskyy as a “gift” to Russia’s president.He said Russia would use the money it raised from the fuel sales to invest in its war and that “any easing of sanctions” would play into Russia’s hands, “allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer”.That prediction was realised hours later, when Ukrainian officials announced that a barrage of Russian strikes on the country’s south-east early on Saturday had killed 20 people, including three children.View image in fullscreenRescuers working at the site of an apartment building damaged by a Russian strike in Zaporizhzhia.Photograph: Reuters“Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy saidon social mediaon Saturday.“Last night confirmed once again that in Russia, they take any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed,” he said.There were also “large-scale power outages” in the capital, Kyiv, the country’s largest private energy provider said.Map of Russian-controlled territory in UkraineAndy Burnham reiterated his “complete solidarity” in a call with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the leaders agreed to meet in person in the coming days to continue talks.The prime minister said he recognised the past day had been “difficult for Ukraine” and the two talked about the importance of keeping up pressure on Russia, No 10 said.In stark contrast to Zelenskyy’s open frustration with Trump, a Kremlin readout of Friday’s call between the US president and Putin was glowing, with the Russian ⁠news agency Interfax ⁠quoting ​an aide as saying it was “very substantive and friendly”.“Neither wanted to be the first to hang up,” the Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said of the two leaders. “They hung up simultaneously, literally at the same time.”​Zelenskyy has previouslysaidPutin is playing games with Trump.The diesel deal disrupts four years of western financial pressure on Moscow and leaves Kyiv’s allies inEuropeand Nato scrambling to adapt their sanctions plan. The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the diesel deal “provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war”.“This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won’t,” shesaidon Saturday. “On Monday, EU foreign ministers intend to approve the biggest set of sanctions listings targeting Russia’s war machine since the start of the war.” She was referring to plans to formally add 1,600 new individuals and entities to the EU’s sanctions blacklist.View image in fullscreenKaja Kallas with Volodymyr Zelenskyy at a summit in Copenhagen last year.Photograph: Piroschka Van De Wouw/ReutersMajor European governments have attempted to balance their diplomatic and trade relationships with a mercurial Trump and their support for Ukraine.The more Putin escalates his attacks on Europe, the more Europe should support Ukraine | Timothy Garton AshRead moreThe German government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said Berlin “remains committed to the sanctions imposed on Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions”, adding that support for Ukraine “remains unwavering”.Ulf Kristersson, the Swedish prime minister, expressed “regret” at the US agreement, saying energy revenues were “a vital source of funding Russia’s war of aggression”.Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia “must feel its losses” and has promised to respond. In the Russian-occupied ‌Luhansk ‌region, Ukrainian attacks in the past 24 hours had killed four ⁠civilians and wounded ⁠five, the region’s ‌Russian-installed governor, Leonid Pasechnik, said ​on Saturday.Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was ready to take “de-escalatory steps” in the war but only if Russia did the same.Russia’s fuel production has become a key point of contention between Zelenskyy and Trump, who has attempted to stop Ukraine from bombing Russian refineries, which he says exacerbates a global diesel shortage. The Ukrainian leader has rejected such requests unless Russia stops attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.The Financial Timesreportedthat during the talks in Miami, Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner raised the possibility that US intelligence sharing could be cut off if Kyiv did not halt the strikes.Explore more on these topicsVolodymyr ZelenskyyUkraineRussiaTrump administrationDonald TrumpVladimir PutinUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Nuclear war and malicious use of AI threaten end of humanity by 2100, says Lancet assessment | Global health | The Guardian
description: Newly established commission identifies 17 catastrophic threats to human health but says ‘realistic route to act’ on each exists
Author: Kat Lay
Headline: Newly established commission identifies 17 catastrophic threats to human health but says ‘realistic route to act’ on each exists
Content: An environmental protest at Cop28, the UN climate summit in Dubai, 2023.Photograph: Karim Sahib/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn environmental protest at Cop28, the UN climate summit in Dubai, 2023.Photograph: Karim Sahib/AFP/Getty ImagesGlobal healthNuclear war and malicious use of AI threaten end of humanity by 2100, says Lancet assessmentNewly established commission identifies 17 catastrophic threats to human health but says ‘realistic route to act’ on each existsSupported byAbout this contentKat LaySat 10 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHumans could become extinct by the year 2100 due to malicious use of AI or nuclear conflict, according to a new global risk assessment.They top a list of 17 major threats to human health over the next 75 years, which also includes cuts to aid spending by wealthy countries, the climate crisis and childhood malnutrition.The experts behindThe Lancet Commission on 21st Century Global Threats to Healthsaid all the threats interact, meaning they must be addressed together – but stressed that there was “a realistic route to act” on each.“Decisions made by leaders today will shape the health and wellbeing of the next generation,” said Prof Christopher Murray, commission co-chair and the director of the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, University of Washington.To create its list, the commission modelled how many years in good health might be lost due to sickness, disability or early deaths due to each threat, based on current trajectories – a measure known as disability-adjusted life years (Dalys).“Malicious use of AI, including bioweapons, and nuclear conflict with nuclear famine carry risks of extinction in the next 75 years,” the report said, adding that while their likelihood remained low, they had the potential to end humanity in the case of nuclear conflict by injecting enough particles into the upper atmosphere to block sunlight and cause famine, or via AI-created biological weapons. An accompanying Lancet editorial, published alongside the report, warned: “The scale of harm, should they be realised, would inflict an apocalypse on humanity.”Other risks that could cause more than 1bn cumulative Dalys, and therefore deemed “major catastrophic threats”, includedair pollution,antimicrobial resistance,childhood malnutritionand climate breakdown, as well as conventional conflict,declining overseas aid,high alcohol use, high blood pressure, income inequality, low educational attainment,naturally occurring pandemics,obesity, poormental health,smokingand unhealthyageing.To be included on the list, threats not only had to potentially cause a high number of lost healthy years, but also to have potential solutions.Ibrahim Abubakar, commission member and professor of infectious disease epidemiology at UCL, said: “We are not starting from a point of view of ‘oh look, we want to scare you – we’ve got X many threats facing humanity’. We’re starting from the premise that if you are a policymaker today, whether at the global multilateral level or at the national level, these are the potential threats that you could face, and this is the magnitude by which, if you act, you can actually make a difference.”Action to limitglobal heating to about 1.8C (3.2F)rather than letting it reach 4.4C could prevent 1.89bn years of healthy life being lost, according to the report, which modelled best and worst case scenarios for each threat.In higher income regions, non-communicable diseases such as obesity and poor mental health were the dominant threats, while in lower income regions health loss was driven by issues such as low educational attainment.Many major donor nations, including the US and UK, have announcedlarge cuts to aid spendingover the past year. The potential collapse of, or steep reduction in, international health aid could cause up to 1.5bn Dalys before 2100, the commission found, nearly 70% of which would be in sub-Saharan Africa. The region also bears the brunt of child malnutrition.The commission was made up of 35 experts, and its findings will be shared on Sunday at the World Health Summit in Berlin, Germany. Their assessment will be updated annually to re-evaluate the 17 threats identified, incorporating new data and any emerging hazards.The authors urged leaders to address the risks before they escalated into crises, including via investment in technological innovations and by strengthening health systems.“We started this process three years ago, thinking that there were three big threats: conflict, climate, and pandemics,” said Murray. “There’s a much larger number of threats that we need to worry about, and governments really need to dedicate some money and staff to the task of anticipation, prevention and preparation for this more diverse set of threats.”Explore more on these topicsGlobal healthAI (artificial intelligence)Nuclear weaponsClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Skies across the UK illuminated by the northern lights | Northern lights | The Guardian
description: Though mostly visible near the Arctic Circle, the natural phenomenon dazzled sky-gazers as far south Devon, Hampshire and Kent
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Though mostly visible near the Arctic Circle, the natural phenomenon dazzled sky-gazers as far south Devon, Hampshire and Kent
Content: The breath-taking aurora borealis was visible from locations as far south as Sheerness in Kent – pictured here – despite heavy light pollution in the area.Photograph: James Bell/Alamy Live News/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenThe breath-taking aurora borealis was visible from locations as far south as Sheerness in Kent – pictured here – despite heavy light pollution in the area.Photograph: James Bell/Alamy Live News/Alamy Live News.Northern lightsSkies across the UK illuminated by the northern lightsThough mostly visible near the Arctic Circle, the natural phenomenon dazzled sky-gazers as far south Devon, Hampshire and KentNadeem BadshahSat 10 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 18.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe northern lights illuminated the skies across the UK on Friday and Saturday evening.Sky-gazers as far south as Devon, Hampshire and Kent were treated to the dazzling natural phenomenon, also known as the aurora borealis.The Met Office said sightings could continue during clear skies until Tuesday.0:38Spectacular aurora captured from space by Russian cosmonaut – videoSuch occurrences are mostly visible near the Arctic Circle and northern Scotland.The aurora borealis is a natural light display in Earth’s sky, driven by solar activity and geomagnetic storms interacting with the upper atmosphere.Sightings will remain possible until Tuesday across Scotland and similar geomagnetic longitudes during clear skies, the Met Office said.Aurora displays occur when charged particles collide with gases in the Earth’s atmosphere around the magnetic poles. As they collide, light is emitted at various wavelengths, creating colourful displays in the sky.According to the Met Office, the sun emits charged particles known as solar wind, which travel at bout 1m mph.Intense geomagnetic storms could make auroras visible in southern USRead moreThe forecaster said: “When these particles interact with Earth’s magnetic field – especially when the solar wind’s polarity is opposite to Earth’s – they are funnelled toward the magnetic poles.“As these energetic particles collide with gases in the upper atmosphere, they release energy in the form of light. Oxygen produces green and, at higher altitudes, rare red auroras, while nitrogen creates blue and purple hues.”Last year, experts said 2026 will be a peak year for aurora-spotting, as the sun has been in a heightened state of activity as part of its 11-year natural cycle.Explore more on these topicsNorthern lightsThe sunSpacenewsShareReuse this content

title: Christa Pike out of hospital and back in prison after botched execution attempt | Christa Pike | The Guardian
description: Pike’s lawyers said she is back in same prison she’s lived in for last 30 years and will continue to receive medical care
Author: Alba Asenjo Domínguez
Headline: Pike’s lawyers said she is back in same prison she’s lived in for last 30 years and will continue to receive medical care
Content: Christa Pike cries after being sentenced to death on 30 March 1996 in Knoxville, Tennessee.Photograph: WBIR-TV/APView image in fullscreenChrista Pike cries after being sentenced to death on 30 March 1996 in Knoxville, Tennessee.Photograph: WBIR-TV/APChrista PikeChrista Pike out of hospital and back in prison after botched execution attemptPike’s lawyers said she is back in same prison she’s lived in for last 30 years and will continue to receive medical careAlba Asenjo DomínguezSat 10 Oct 2026 13.10 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 15.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChrista Pikehas been discharged from the hospital after survivingTennessee’s botched 30 September attempt to execute her by lethal injection and is back in prison, her lawyers said on Saturday.Pike, 50, returned to the Deborah K Johnson rehabilitation center, where she has been imprisoned for the last three decades, her attorneys, Stephen Ferrell, Luke Ihnen, Randy Spivey and Kelly Gleason, said in a statement.“She is grateful to the first responders and her medical team for their care in these extraordinary circumstances,” Pike’s lawyers added. “She is continuing to receive medical care at the prison, and we will continue to track her recovery.”Saturday’s update about Pike came 10 days after the death row prisoner was given two doses of pentobarbital, a lethal injection drug, in what proved to be a failed execution attempt. She was hospitalized after surviving the botched execution and was declared brain dead on Monday.Texas kills man in first US execution since botched lethal injection of Christa PikeRead moreBut in a shocking turnaround, on Thursdayher lawyer said that she was “up and walking”– though she remained “somewhat foggy” and wasn’t able to use her arms very much.Pike said that her arms were burning during the failed execution and asked if it was supposed to feel that way.Witnesses present in the chamber saidthat “nothing was normal” while officials have maintained that they followed every step of Tennessee’s approved execution protocol.There has been no official explanation about why Pike survived the execution. Medical experts speculate that perhaps some or much of the drug missed her vein and went into surrounding tissue, that one of her veins blew, that the drug was faulty, or a combination of such factors.Her lawyers months earlier had flagged that Pike’s veins were problematic.Pike was convicted in 1995 for the torture and murder of Colleen Slemmer, then 18 and her classmate at Knoxville Job Corps. According to court filings, Pike, who was also 19 at the time, was worried Slemmer was trying to take her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, then 17.Shipp and Pike were convicted of taking Slemmer into a wooded part of the University ofTennesseecampus and murdering her. She was given the death penalty, and Shipp was sentenced to life in prison because he was younger than 18.After Slemmer’s murder, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar and post-traumatic stress disorders, her attorneys said.“It took me numerous years to even realize the gravity of what I’d done,” Pike said in an earlier petition for clemency. “Even more to accept how many lives I affected. I took the life of someone’s child, sister, friend. It sickens me now to think I had the ability to commit such a crime.”Pike’s survival of the botched execution has shocked many in the US and overseas and galvanized critics of the death penalty.Tennessee’s top prison official has announced hisresignation.Meanwhile, the state’s governor, Bill Lee, has paused executions in Tennessee for the rest of the year. And Florida’s governor, Ron DeSantis, on Fridaycanceleda planned lethal injection execution in the state.But they continue elsewhere.For instance, the Pentagonconfirmed on Thursdaythat it planned to livestream the execution by firing squad in December of former army psychiatrist Nidal Hassan, who killed 13 people at Texas’s Fort Hood, prompting condemnation from the United Nations.Donald Trump on Saturday said Hassan “was vicious – he was violent” and that he would “make a decision” about the plans to livestream his execution.“There are two thoughts: don’t show it and show,” the president remarked. “Because you know by showing it, maybe other people won’t be doing what he did. So I’ll make a decision ultimately. I know what the military would like to do, but we’ll make a decision.”Explore more on these topicsChrista PikeTennesseeCapital punishmentUS prisonsUS justice systemnewsShareReuse this content

title: Twelve killed and hundreds injured in Houthi attack at Riyadh airport | Saudi Arabia | The Guardian
description: Donald Trump evaluating whether US should join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Yemeni rebels
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Donald Trump evaluating whether US should join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Yemeni rebels
Content: Thick black smoke and flames rising from a fire at King Khalid International airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, 9 October 2026.Photograph: UGC via APView image in fullscreenThick black smoke and flames rising from a fire at King Khalid International airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, 9 October 2026.Photograph: UGC via APSaudi ArabiaTwelve killed and hundreds injured in Houthi attack at Riyadh airportDonald Trump evaluating whether US should join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Yemeni rebelsPatrick WintourDiplomatic editor and agenciesSat 10 Oct 2026 19.37 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 11.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYemen’s Houthis have launched a missile attack on Riyadh’s international airport inSaudi Arabia, killing at least 12 people and leaving hundreds wounded, the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority has said.Operations at King Khalid international airport in Riyadh were suspended as ambulances rushed to the airport. More than 300 people were reported injured in the deadliest attack in any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war.Donald Trump said he was evaluating whether the US should join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouringYemen.“We may. We’re going to look at it,” Trump said. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”The US secretary of ⁠state, Marco ⁠Rubio, called the attacks “​reprehensible” and said “they must ​stop ‌now”.A Saudi government statement said the dead included four Saudi citizens, as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese.One witness at the Riyadh airport reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board a flight, and another said they saw a strike that left people wounded.“I was on gate 403,” at the domestic terminal, the witness told the Agence France-Presse news agency. “I saw [gate] 401 hit, I saw injured [people] in front of my eyes. Everyone was running.”The relative of one injured person said they had been wounded in the shoulders and arms by shattered glass and taken to hospital.A missile struck an airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorised to speak to the media.Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved?Read moreA projectile also fell near the King Fahd international airport in Dammam, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting theHouthis. The Dammam airport has become an important alternative to Riyadh amid the recent spate of attacks.Saturday’s incident comes amid an escalation of missile strikes by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis ⁠on the kingdom. The airport has already been attacked twice this ​week, leaving four people dead and ‌others wounded, and ‌badly damaging an aircraft.The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government unravelled in July.The attack came as forces allied to the UN-recognised government in Yemen claim to have mounted a successful offensive to retake the Bab al-Mandab strait from Houthi rebels, but accounts vary as to whether the push has been repelled.View image in fullscreenFighters from the Southern Giants Brigades clash with Houthis near the Bab al-Mandab strait in Taiz province, 6 October.Photograph: Yemen Giants Brigades Media Centre/AFP/Getty ImagesA Houthi spokesperson said forces from the Saudi-backed government based in Aden “were targeted with a large number of ballistic missiles, artillery support and heavy weapons, resulting in the destruction of more than 22 armoured vehicles and the killing and wounding of dozens, including a number of commanders.“More than 30 ambulances arrived in Aden to transport the dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations.”By contrast, the Saudi ambassador to Yemen, Mohammed al-Jaber, said: “Blessed Friday and victory for every Yemeni and Arab. Bab al-Mandab has been cleared of the remnants of the Houthi terrorist militia.”View image in fullscreenThe Southern Giants, linked to the STC, are the chief pro-government force fighting around the Bab al-Mandab strait.Photograph: Yemen Giants Brigades Media Centre/AFP/Getty ImagesThe exposed 5 sq mile (13 sq km) Perim Island straddles the strait, acting as a lookout point for all traffic from the Red Sea into the Gulf of Aden and towards the Indian Ocean. Aidarous al-Zubaidi, the president of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), one of the main political forces in the south of Yemen, claimed the island and coastal area had been recaptured from Houthi hands.An official military spokesperson for the UN-recognised government forces qualified the claim, saying only half the area had been recaptured so far. Waddah al-Dabish said newly established Houthi defensive lines had been broken on the land next to the strait, leading to the death of thousands of Houthi fighters.It is thought that as many as 500 Houthi fighters are stationed on the island, and Saudi Arabia is desperate to be able to report that the strait has been reclaimed to show thatthe land counteroffensive it launchedat the beginning of the week is advancing.View image in fullscreenSouthern Giants fighters fire at Houthis near the Bab al-Mandab strait in Taiz province, 6 October.Photograph: Yemen Giants Brigades Media Centre/AFP/Getty ImagesThe report came as the United Nations’ special envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, admitted to the UN security council in New York that Yemen – one of the poorest countries in the world – had lapsed back into full-scale war and said the first victims would be women and children.The Houthis seized control of the strait two weeks ago and said no Saudi-linked commercial traffic would be permitted to go through the narrow waterway. The Houthis are waging a war to remove Saudi influence from Yemen, and have been mounting missile attacks on Riyadh in support of this objective.There have been previous prematurereports of military breakthroughsby the Saudi-backed Yemeni government since it launched its counteroffensive at the start of the week, but the recapture of the land by the strait and Perim Island (also known as Mayyun Island) is a military prize western governments desperately need.Explore more on these topicsSaudi ArabiaYemenHouthisUnited NationsMiddle East and north AfricaAir transportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Man dies after jumping into tiger enclosure at Yorkshire zoo | Zoos | The Guardian
description: Police say man was pronounced dead at the scene after being attacked by tiger
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Police say man was pronounced dead at the scene after being attacked by tiger
Content: Police at Yorkshire Wildlife Park which has been evacuated and closed after an incident in the tiger enclosure.Photograph: Charley Atkins/SWNSView image in fullscreenPolice at Yorkshire Wildlife Park which has been evacuated and closed after an incident in the tiger enclosure.Photograph: Charley Atkins/SWNSZoosMan dies after jumping into tiger enclosure at Yorkshire zooPolice say man was pronounced dead at the scene after being attacked by tigerNadeem BadshahSat 10 Oct 2026 13.13 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 12.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man has died after being attacked by a tiger after jumping into its enclosure at a zoo inYorkshire, police have said.Emergency services were contacted shortly after 1.30pm on Saturday when the man entered the enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, nearDoncaster, and was set upon by the tiger.He was pronounced dead at the scene, South Yorkshire police said, adding his family had been informed.Videos circulating online appear to show a man being pawed at and grappled by a tiger in an enclosure.A police spokesperson said the tiger attacked the man and inflicted “serious injury”.“Emergency services attended and sadly, despite the best efforts of medical personnel, the man was pronounced dead at the scene,” they added.“Regarding rumours surrounding the condition of the tiger, the animal was uninjured and remained in the enclosure following the incident and there is no wider risk to the public.”The force urged people not to share “distressing” video footage of the attack, circulating on social media.Yorkshire Wildlife Park said a “serious incident” occurred inside the enclosure.It said in a statement: “Our emergency response procedures were immediately activated, and emergency services are currently attending the scene.“We are working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened.” It added that the “safety and wellbeing of visitors, staff and animals remain our highest priority”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYorkshire Wildlife Park opened in 2009, with the Land of the Tigers attraction opening in 2011.The attraction is on a purpose-built two-acre reserve for Amur tigers, an endangered subspecies with about 500 left in the wild.Photos of the enclosure on the park’s website shows a high walkway for visitors and fencing above the section where the tigers can roam.A Yorkshire ambulance service spokesperson said it sent a number of resources to the scene including two ambulances, Yorkshire air ambulance and a doctor.Explore more on these topicsZoosDoncasterYorkshireAnimalsnewsShareReuse this content

title: US man shoots off-duty ICE agent who allegedly attacked him and daughter | California | The Guardian
description: ICE official, who was sleeping on man’s lawn and appeared ‘intoxicated’, faces felony charges, California police say
Author: José Olivares
Headline: ICE official, who was sleeping on man’s lawn and appeared ‘intoxicated’, faces felony charges, California police say
Content: ICE agents walk outside the Ventura county government center in Ventura, California, on 27 July 2026.Photograph: Blake Fagan/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenICE agents walk outside the Ventura county government center in Ventura, California, on 27 July 2026.Photograph: Blake Fagan/AFP/Getty ImagesCaliforniaUS man shoots off-duty ICE agent who allegedly attacked him and daughterICE official, who was sleeping on man’s lawn and appeared ‘intoxicated’, faces felony charges, California police sayJosé OlivaresSat 10 Oct 2026 15.03 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 16.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 72-year-old manshotan off-duty Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) official inCaliforniaearly on Friday morning after the “intoxicated and agitated” official assaulted him and his daughter on their property, local authorities allege.The Fresno police department said that the ICE official was receiving medical care after being shot in the midsection. The official, identified as David Gonzalez, is facing felony charges for assaulting the father-daughter duo, Fresno policesaid.It was not immediately clear for how long Gonzalez had been with ICE and what exactly he did for ICE. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, referred all questions about Gonzalez to Fresno police.According to Fresno police, at about 3am, a woman found Gonzalez sleeping on her and her father’s front lawn. She told her 72-year-old father, who was inside, and then attempted to shoo Gonzalez off their property.New York City’s Marble Hill residents furious after ICE shooting: ‘Why do this?’Read moreBut when Gonzalez was awakened, “he appeared intoxicated and agitated” and physically assaulted the 72-year-old father, forcing him to the ground, police said. When the father’s daughter tried to intervene, Gonzalez physically attacked and took her to the ground as well, police said.The father feared for his and his daughter’s physical safety and shot Gonzalez once, police said. Shortly thereafter, the daughter’s boyfriend, an off-duty police officer, arrived and placed handcuffs on Gonzalez.“It is unknown at this time why Gonzalez was in the area at the time of the [shooting], but it has been confirmed he was off-duty and alone,” local authorities said.Fresno police on Friday said the investigation into the shooting was continuing while Gonzalez was in custody and receiving medical treatment. He was booked with battery likely to cause great bodily injury, felony vandalism and battery.The father and daughter were not booked with any crimes as they recovered from injuries of their own, police said.The confrontation that led to Gonzalez’s shooting is one of the latest cases in which federal ICE officials have fallen underscrutinyfor alleged criminal behavior. ICE has alsobeenmetwithnationwidecriticismthroughoutDonald Trump’ssecond termfor the agency’s aggressive arrest, detention and deportation tactics.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLawmakers have alsocriticizedICE’s hiring practices amid theagency’s rushto bring on more officials to carry out the Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda. In August 2025, an ICE supervisor filed awhistleblowercomplaint to the DHS office of inspector general alleging that the agency was skirting basic vetting and violating federal rules during its hiring spree.In July, anICE officershot and killeda Colombian immigrant in Biddeford, Maine. The ICE officer in question had reportedly been a recent hire by the agencydespite an alleged historyof violence and mental health problems.Meanwhile, in April, a longtime ICE officer in Cincinnati was arrested after allegedly lying to DHS about domestic violence allegations against him. Local newsreportssay police had been called more than 20 times in the past to years to the home he shared with his girlfriend.The Ohio Immigrant Alliance, a pro-immigrant group,released a reportin August documenting more than 150 federal immigration officials accused of abuse and crimes. One of the latest entries in their report citedallegationsthat an ICE official reportedly broke into an ex-girlfriend’s apartment in south-east Louisiana.Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaICE (US Immigration and Customs Enforcement)US crimeUS immigrationWest CoastnewsShareReuse this content

title: Thousands gather in London to express support for Palestinians after three years of ‘genocide’ | Israel-Gaza war | The Guardian
description: Twenty arrested in first march since Ed Miliband declared UK’s position was that Israel’s occupation of West Bank was unlawful
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Twenty arrested in first march since Ed Miliband declared UK’s position was that Israel’s occupation of West Bank was unlawful
Content: Pro-Palestinian march in LondonIsrael-Gaza warThousands gather in London to express support for Palestinians after three years of ‘genocide’Twenty arrested in first march since Ed Miliband declared UK’s position was that Israel’s occupation of West Bank was unlawfulSammy GecsoylerSat 10 Oct 2026 12.52 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThousands of people have gathered in central London to express their support for Palestinians after three years of “genocide” carried out against them byIsrael.The demonstrators, many wearing keffiyehs and holding Palestine flags, gathered on the Embankment at midday on Saturday. Some carried placards reading “End the genocide” and “Free Palestine” as they marched towards parliament. A bride and groomappearedto be among those in attendance and a two-minute silence was held to reflect on the lives lost in Gaza.The Metropolitan police said 20 arrests had been made, including for criminal damage after demonstrators climbed on to the Battle of Britain memorial, havingPalestineAction placards, making a Nazi salute and assaulting police as officers made arrests.Protesters were calling for the UK government to stop supplying arms to Israel, which various bodies – including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based – have said is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.View image in fullscreenProtesters at the National March For Palestine.Photograph: Guy Smallman/Getty ImagesA ceasefire was declared a year ago but Israeli airstrikes have continued in Gaza. In the last year, the overall death tollhas risenby a further 1,400 people. Settlers have also ramped up their attacks against Palestinians in the West Bank. According to UN figures, 230 Palestinians were killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces and settlers in 2025.Husam Zomlot, the Palestinian ambassador to the UK, shared a video from the march on social media. “Three years on, Israel’s atrocities in Gaza and the West Bank continue, and so does the solidarity of the British people. Louder, bigger and not going anywhere. Thank you all,” he said. By Saturday afternoon, organiserssaid250,000 people were at the march.‘Neither war nor peace’: Palestinians in Gaza on existing amid disease, despair and ruinsRead moreThe Met have imposed conditions on the event – which is organised by the Palestine Coalition, which has organised more than 30 mass demonstrations since October 2023, with a counter-protest by Stop The Hate – to “minimise the risk of serious disruption to communities”.The Met posted on X saying: “The front of the procession has now entered Whitehall where a rally will take place.“Several arrests have been made so far including a woman and a man with placards declaring support for proscribed organisation Palestine Action.“We have also arrested a number of protesters on suspicion of criminal damage after they climbed on to the Battle of Britain memorial on Victoria Embankment.”The national march is the first held since the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements and declared the UK government would take the official position that Israel’s occupation of theWest Bankwas unlawful in its entirety. He also told the Commons that settler terrorists supported by Benjamin Netanyahu’s government are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank.View image in fullscreenA pile of placards at the end of the pro-Palestinian protest march through London to mark the third anniversary of the war in Gaza.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersAt Labour party conference last month,Miliband appeared to reference the marches, which at their peak regularly numbered hundreds and thousands of people, telling the audience in Liverpool: “I want to say to the millions of people in this country and indeed elsewhere who have been moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people: we hear you, you were right.”Deputy assistant commissioner Carl Galvin said: “We know Saturday’s event, so close to the third anniversary of the terror attack on Israel, has the potential to have a greater impact on communities than the previous national marches.”Galvin, who is leading the policing operation this weekend, said the force’s presence on Saturday will be “significant”.“We will also be using powers under the Public Order Act requiring anyone in the protest area wearing face coverings to deliberately conceal their identity to remove them,” Galvin continued.The Met have imposed conditions on the march and require the group to travel via Westminster Bridge, York Road, Waterloo Bridge and The Strand on to Whitehall, with a rally concluding by 6.30pm. The force has said that any speeches and music must conclude by 5.30pm.British consulate in East Jerusalem will stay open as UK mission, says Ed MilibandRead moreA counter-protest by Stop The Hate is also taking place, with about 30 people gathered outside New Scotland Yard, some with flags.The force has also imposed conditions on the demonstration “to minimise the risk of serious disruption”. The demonstrators must remain within a designated area outside the Met’s headquarters, with the assembly concluding at 2.30pm.View image in fullscreenPeople clash with police officers during the pro-Palestine march in London.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PALast Saturday, on the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks, when Hamas militants broke across the Israeli border to launch a wave of attacks on kibbutzim, border towns, military bases and music festivals, killing at least 1,209 people, a small pro-Palestine student demonstration in centralLondonwas held.The Met publicly appealed to those behind the demonstration to “exercise [their] right to protest on a different date” and admitted that finding the organisers had been “frankly difficult”. In the end, it went ahead and about 100 people attended. Five people were arrested for breaching conditions imposed on the march.The Palestine Coalition organising the march includes Palestine Solidarity Campaign, Stop the War, CND, the Muslim Association of Britain, Friends of Al Aqsa and the Palestinian Forum in Britain.Explore more on these topicsIsrael-Gaza warLondonProtestFreedom of speechIsraelPalestineGazanewsShareReuse this content

title: Parents fear YouTubers are bringing ‘brain rot’ to Netflix. But are kids wising up to ‘slop’? | Children's TV | The Guardian
description: As streamers poach viral creators to appeal to children, digital whack-a-mole has become a new kind of family challenge
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: As streamers poach viral creators to appeal to children, digital whack-a-mole has become a new kind of family challenge
Content: Parents with a ‘no YouTube’ policy have noticed Netflix Kids is ‘suddenly more shouty, more gamified and more focused on dares’.Composite: Getty Images/Guardian designView image in fullscreenParents with a ‘no YouTube’ policy have noticed Netflix Kids is ‘suddenly more shouty, more gamified and more focused on dares’.Composite: Getty Images/Guardian designChildren's TVParents fear YouTubers are bringing ‘brain rot’ to Netflix. But are kids wising up to ‘slop’?As streamers poach viral creators to appeal to children, digital whack-a-mole has become a new kind of family challengeSophie QuickSat 10 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 19.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleExasperated dad Simon Hooper shakes his fist at the camera in aviral video. “We managed to get rid of YouTube in our household six months ago and the kids are finally OK with it,” he says – but Netflix is “now commissioning YouTubers to make their brain rot and putting it back in front of my kids’ faces”.The precise “brain rot” he’s referring to is the arrival of a polarising show that’s lighting up parent chats around the globe. And while Salish and Jordan Matter might be new toNetflixKids users,the father-daughter content creators are familiar to anyone who’s spent any time on the internet.Jordan Matter, who started his YouTube career in 2017 as a photography vlogger, pivoted to family content after his energetic preteen daughter, Salish – a competitive gymnast – brought viral traction to the channel in2019 and 2020.(Famously, hisYouTube bioreads, “My daughter has taken over my channel!”)After amassing more than 42 million YouTube subscribers, the duo signed a landmark deal withNetflix in February,constituting remixed content from the Matters’ YouTube archives. Soon an exclusive, original series starring the now 16-year-old Salish and her dad will be out as part of a broad trend of Netflix poachingYouTubecreators to attract younger audiences. (YouTube is trying to stem the flow withexclusivity contracts.)I’m a psychoanalyst. Social media is damaging children’s inner lives in ways we don’t fully understand | Robin KirmanRead moreThink gamified family life challenges such as “I Went On a Fake Date To Prank My Dad” and “I Can’t Sleep Until I Find a Rare Glitter Dumpling” in the style popularised by the world’s most famous YouTuber, Mr Beast. It’s the kind of frantic, shouty, hyper-stimulating unscripted kids’ content shaped in part by an obsessive, second-by-second eye on YouTube Studio’s audience retention graphs. There are a lot of pop-up graphics and fast cuts – a style known asretention editingthat has developed specifically around YouTube’s algorithm. Like Mr Beast, Jordan Matter optimises for views with aggressivelyA/B/C-tested, aggressively colour-saturated thumbnails.“It’s our responsibility to ensure that we save our kids from this grey matter-destroying nonsense as they won’t do it themselves,” Hooper says. “The strength of the addiction is too strong.”More than 3,900 comments underneath the post heartily agree, with a few exceptions. “This is super easy. You parent. That’s it. You own the house, the TV etc. Enough said.”View image in fullscreenThe banner on Jordan Matter’s YouTube page states: ‘Subscribe or my daughter will punch you’‘It’s exhausting’Michelle Yates has a long-running “no YouTube” policy in her home but a few months ago she started to notice Netflix Kids was “suddenly more shouty, more gamified and more focused on dares”. Her eight-year-old son had discovered Salish and Jordan Matter. About the same time, she says, people on her parents’ group chat started exchanging tips on how to blockYouTubecreators on Netflix. Plus, she started noticing promotion for YouTuber Mark Rober’s Roblox game on his Netflix CrunchLabs show, on top of the usual promo for his educational CrunchLab science boxes.“The advertising thing is such a grey area,” Yates says. “I don’t mind the CrunchLab kits so much but I don’t want my kid anywhere near Roblox … and the Salish Matter show is awful. I’m thinking of cancelling the subscription because I don’t want to have to monitor every show … it’s exhausting.”It started with Cocomelon – the mesmerisingsmooth-brain channelfor toddlers – which moved over to Netflix in 2020. In a concerted push Netflix have now scooped up favourites including Ms Rachel, Blippi, Danny Go!, the Stokes Twins and now the Stem educator Mark Rober of CrunchLabs.View image in fullscreenA still from CocomelonThis is entertainment of varying style, educational ambition and target age group but, crucially for Netflix, these creators have all brought prebuilt audiences and pre-honed retention knowhow to the streaming service. (Cocomelon’s parent company has notoriously tested retention of focus-group children with a sinisterDistractatron.)‘Mum, where did my Robux go?’ The Roblox scam targeting childrenRead moreThe content boon for Netflix is part of a larger pattern of changing content presentation and consumption for kids that’s also reflected on Amazon Prime and Disney+. Digital whack-a-mole has become the ultimate gamified family life challenge. But unlike the Matter family, it doesn’t take place inside theme parks or between the candy-coloured aisles of Sephora. It’s a repetitive quest that happens inside the settings menus of digital interfaces.“We’re going to see more of this sort of thing where … all of the streamers are going to start feeling like each other,” says Prof Tama Leaver, an internet studies researcher at Curtin University. In addition, “we’re going to see a lot of entry-level tiers where advertising comes back through streaming platforms”.Many parents don’t see a problem or a distinction between traditional programs and those with their genesis on YouTube but for those who do, and want to limit the content, Leaver says the challenges are immense.“Defaults are very, very powerful and streaming companies could make it much easier for parents,” he says. “Your experience as a parent of your child’s life should not be sitting in a command and control centre trying to read the thousand dashboards and apply them to their digital experiences.”The ‘dopamine-crash effect’Sasha Giocondo’s two kids, aged eight and 13, stream videos on both Netflix and YouTube but she has always kept a much closer eye on YouTube. “I have noticed something like a ‘dopamine-crash effect’ after they watch this kind of thing on YouTube … Before, I could rely on Netflix not to produce that effect. Now I can’t.”Parents often talk about this “crash effect” but, given the limited research, it’s not possible to draw firm conclusions on the impacts of specific media types – including on-demand streaming. Alarge-scale umbrella studypublished last week, examining data across 64 countries, linked higher childhood screen use to lower academic achievement and language development issues. But there is a growing body of correlational research about the negative impacts offast-paced mediaon kids.double quotation markChildren are developing more self-awareness and critical literacies with how algorithms and platforms feed contentJessica BalanzateguiThis year the American Academy of Pediatrics updated its guidelines in line with research. The new guidelines step back from recommended daily limits on broadly defined “screen time”. Instead, the academy is now mapping some of its recommendations to specificcontent design types, including caution around media platforms with “engagement-prolonging design” that displaces other off-screen activity.Demanding and rewarding attentionGiocondo is among those who are troubled by the blurring of social media and long-form entertainment. “I can’t fully separate it from a broader unease about the kidfluencer industry, the pressure on young creators, and the open question of who’s really benefiting from all of it.”Parents have solid reasons for discomfort around the treatment of kids on YouTube family channels. In an interview, Jordan Matter acknowledged thedark historyand stressed that his daughter’s wellbeing wastop of mindwhen striking the Netflix deal.View image in fullscreenSalish and Jordan Matter.Photograph: Monica Schipper/Getty ImagesWhen it comes to YouTube, the medium is truly the message. The YouTube star is an avatar, compressed, commodified and optimised to compete in a ruthless attention economy. There are endless feedback loops, demanding and rewarding attention, for both the star and the viewer. For some parents watching their six-year-old daughters mimic Salish’s multi-step skincare routine, there’s something more at play.Last year the Matters co-founded a skincare brand for teens,Sincerely Yours, available exclusively at Sephora, after claiming that a generation of teens were feeling “equally unseen” by the skincare industry. Jordan Matter has seemed very open toSincerely Yours brand tie-inson Netflix. And why wouldn’t he be? Mark Rober enjoyed a massive CrunchLabs sales boost when he moved to the streaming platform last year and Ted Sarandos, the Netflix co-chief executive, has been happy topublicise the fact.‘They’re so smart these days!’Hooper’s video ultimately shows viewers how to block Salish and Jordan using Netflix parental controls. It has racked up more than 60,000 likes, presumably because parental controls are far from user friendly. In the comments section parents rail that they are constantly blocking apps and channels across their devices, only to see blocked features pop up elsewhere, with YouTube and Netflix pre-installed into most smart TVs without the option to delete them. If parents do manage to restrict YouTube on their smart TV, their kid might stream it on the PlayStation instead, or watch videos made by YouTube creators through the Spotify app.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueNetflix declined to comment for this story but provided links toits parental-control instructions, with cute tips such as “Lock your profile (and other profiles on your account) with a PIN, which helps prevent your kid from disabling or overriding your parental controls. (They’re so smart these days!)”But, as Leaver points out, you can’t block Netflix shows using the app on your TV. “You’ll need to go to another device and go to the settings in the web browser.” (Streaming companies are smart too!)High screen time can hurt children’s learning and language skills, study suggestsRead moreUltimately, Leaver suggests that parents talking to their “kids about their media experiences is perhaps more valuable than trying to block everything that might be a little bit iffy”.Jessica Balanzategui, an associate professor in media at RMIT University, tracks children’s streaming habits as part of an Australian Research Council project entitled Children’s Content in the Streaming Era. She says the data suggests kids are wising up.“Our current research with tween children aged seven to 13 is demonstrating that children are developing more self-awareness and critical literacies with how algorithms and platforms feed content to them than we saw in our research in 2023. For instance, children … often tell us that YouTube is to be treated with care as it is full of ‘dodgy’ or ‘slop’ content, or even that it is ‘full of lies’.“This indicates that families are developing some effective strategies and having robust conversations around YouTube at home.”Good luck to any families attempting to embark on this ultimate gamified challenge. And don’t forget to like and subscribe to see if parents turn the mole-whacking mallets on their own heads as the great streaming convergence charges ahead.Explore more on these topicsChildren's TVYouTubeTelevision (Television & radio)Television (Technology)NetflixSocial mediafeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Our town is making jeans again’: meet the firm reviving jobs and skills in Wales | Retail industry | The Guardian
description: In the first article in a series on high end British manufacturing, we visit the Hiut Denim factory in Cardigan
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: In the first article in a series on high end British manufacturing, we visit the Hiut Denim factory in Cardigan
Content: Hiut Denim has kept its manufacturing in the UK while many rivals make their products abroad.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/Athena PicturesView image in fullscreenHiut Denim has kept its manufacturing in the UK while many rivals make their products abroad.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty Images/Athena PicturesRetail industry‘Our town is making jeans again’: meet the firm reviving jobs and skills in WalesIn the first article in a series on high end British manufacturing, we visit the Hiut Denim factory in CardiganJoanna Partridgein CardiganSat 10 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWorn on the streets of London’s Soho, San Francisco or Sydney, every pair of high-end jeans made by Hiut Denim comes from the rather unlikely location of a small coastal town in west Wales.Cardigan, with a population of just 4,200, has a proud history of denim production and was once home to Britain’s largest jeans factory, even if the town’s name recalls a different garment entirely.When jeans manufacturing in Wales was moved abroad at the start of the century, hundreds of local people lost their jobs and were forced to find work elsewhere.Hiut Denim was founded by David and Clare Hieatt in Cardigan in 2011. The couple, both originally from Wales, previously ran the ethical fashion brand Howies. They set up Hiut – the brand name blends their surname with the word utility – with the goal of reviving denim-making skills in the town and training up the next generation of skilled craftspeople.Elin Evans was one of those “grand masters”, as they are known in the company, with a lifetime’s experience of making jeans. Now 59, Evans is Hiut’s factory manager and has been in the trade since 1983, when she was 16.“I’ve done a full loop, because this is where I started,” she says, from her seat behind a sewing machine on the factory floor. Deftly handling the indigo fabric, she moves individual pieces through the machine and a pair of jeans begins to take shape.View image in fullscreenFactory manager Elin Evans has been in the jeans trade since 1983, when she was 16.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/Athena PicturesIn its heyday, the Dewhirst factory in Cardigan where Evans once worked employed about 400 people, representing about 10% of the town’s population, and cranked out 35,000 pairs of jeans each week for Marks & Spencer.When Dewhirst decided to outsource production to Morocco, Evans was given the opportunity to move to Tangier. But the founding of Hiut led to her returning home to Wales and to a sewing machine. “I hoped it was like riding a bike,” she says, “but you never forget and the rest is history”.As Hiut took off, the company moved into what was once part of the Dewhirst factory, taking Evans back to the place she began her career. A slogan painted on the factory wall proclaims “Our town is making jeans again” and Welsh flag bunting flutters above the sewing machines, in celebration of the annualcultural festival, held this year in early August just a miles south of Cardigan.View image in fullscreenThe Hiut Denim factory in Cardigan features the slogan ‘Our town is making jeans again’.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/Athena PicturesEvans and the other grand masters who joined Hiut have spent decades cutting pieces of fabric, creating pockets and stitching denim.The brand’s production levels are far removed from the mass manufacturing which previously took place in Cardigan – Hiut employs 20 people, who make 120 pairs a week.The company insists its product is no ordinary wardrobe staple. Each pair is made by hand from 17 pieces of fabric, with a “made in Wales” label inside the waistband and another label signed by the member of staff who stitched the jeans. Hiut also offers lifetime repairs.“The majority of the time, you know the name of the person that’s bought your jeans. You know your customer and the customer gets to know us as well,” says Evans. “We’re very proud of what we’re doing and the quality is top notch.”Indeed,online fashion reviewspraise Hiut’s attention to detail, such as neat seams and how all of the rivets featuring the brand’s name or owl logo are added by hand to ensure they face the same way.View image in fullscreenHiut Denim jeans cost about 10 times more than the price of a high-street pair.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/Athena PicturesSuch premium jeans come with a suitably premium price tag – about 10 times higher than the cost of a high-street pair – starting at £245 for men’s and women’s slim-fit styles, made from organic cotton from Turkey, and rising to £350 for pairs made from premium Japanese selvedge.Hiut customers includes TV personalities Ant and Dec and the brand got a big boost whenthe Duchess of Sussex wore a pairduring her first official visit to Wales in 2018, resulting in a three-month backlog of orders.Despite such endorsements, the company hit financial difficulties in the wake of the Covid pandemic, when the founders approached some of their top customers to ask if they wanted to invest in the company.One of these was the German von Loeper family. They initially became minority shareholders in late 2024, before taking over the company in September 2025. Johann von Loeper, 26, became the company’s chief executive, leaving a career in finance in London to move to Cardigan.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe says his father, Philipp, was a loyal customer first, which prompted the family-owned investment group to take a stake in a firm beyond its usual investments in life sciences or agricultural companies.“We don’t do anything in retail or fashion really, this is more of a passion project,” von Loeper says. “My father sort of became obsessed with the product … I think he bought more than 30 pairs.”View image in fullscreenJohann von Loeper, the chief executive, left a career in finance in London to move to Cardigan.Photograph: Dimitris Legakis/Athena PicturesThe family has committed to keeping the manufacturing in Cardigan, although von Loeper adds that the factory’s west Wales location creates logistical challenges when moving finished garments or bringing in photographers and models for photoshoots.He adds: “The thing that attracted all of us to Hiut was the purpose of making jeans again, and not just for the sake of making jeans, but to have the jobs, to have to craft, to have skills remain here.”Some high-profile visitors have tried out the craft. A framed photo and letter from Kensington palace hangs on the factory wall, commemorating the March visit of Catherine, the Princess of Wales, where she had a go on a sewing machine.Walking past huge rolls of fabric from some of the most prestigious denim mills in the world – in Japan, Italy and Turkey – von Loeper says he faced a big decision shortly after taking over running the company. A key Japanese denim supplier warned Hiut and other long-term customers that operational pressures meant it was about to close its order books until 2027.“We bought £100,000 worth of selvedge in my first few weeks here because I said ‘let’s get it now before we run out’ and that was one of the better things I did,” he says.When the von Loeper family took over, they said Hiut was “losing a lot of money every month”, but they believed that with investment and a new strategy, the brand could become profitable again.View image in fullscreenLoyal customer Paul Tomlin bought two pairs of jeans when he went to the Hiut factory during a visit to Wales.Photograph: Joanna Partridge/The GuardianThe new owners soon got to work updating the entire jeans collection, and are hoping to take on more staff so they can increase production. Von Loeper is aware that Evans and other grand masters are fast approaching retirement age and believes the company has a “five-year window” to hire and adequately train new employees. He also wants to broaden Hiut’s appeal, and as part of that has secured new stockists, including Liberty department store in London.“Our customer age group has always been 35-55,” says von Loeper. “Our jeans were worn to the office even before Covid, but we can definitely see that customers and what they are buying for has changed and we are trying to adapt to that.”At the shop located just metres away from where jeans are being made, customers come to try on different denims. One customer, Paul Tomlin, has made a purpose journey to Hiut during a visit to Wales to buy more of his favourite jeans.“I came to make sure I got the right fit. I tried on three pairs and found a style that suits me,” says Tomlin, holding a branded bag containing two new pairs. He says he likes the firm’s ethos as well as its clothing: “It’s a good story and has a good feel as a company”Explore more on these topicsRetail industryJeansfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Juliet Stevenson: ‘Do I have a nemesis? Where do we start? Putin, Musk, Trump, Erdoğan, Modi, Netanyahu’ | Culture | The Guardian
description: The British actor on the genius of Bend It Like Beckham, the role she lost to Emma Thompson and why some actors get worse with age
Author: Sian Cain
