Headline: The British actor on the genius of Bend It Like Beckham, the role she lost to Emma Thompson and why some actors get worse with age
Content: Juliet Stevenson: ‘Most of the work we do is ephemeral and that’s OK. But Truly Madly Deeply goes on having a life and I’m so thrilled by that.’Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The ObserverView image in fullscreenJuliet Stevenson: ‘Most of the work we do is ephemeral and that’s OK. But Truly Madly Deeply goes on having a life and I’m so thrilled by that.’Photograph: Antonio Olmos/The Observer10 Chaotic QuestionsCultureJuliet Stevenson: ‘Do I have a nemesis? Where do we start? Putin, Musk, Trump, Erdoğan, Modi, Netanyahu’The British actor on the genius of Bend It Like Beckham, the role she lost to  Emma Thompson and why some actors get worse with ageSian CainSat 10 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 19.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhat was the most Australian thing that you experienced while you were in the country filming Dustfall?Working with a python? We don’t tend to work with snakes in the UK. I’m absolutely snake phobic but the python was very professional. Behaved better than I did.Also, the phenomenal openness which I associate with Australian people – the lack of class pretension, the glass half-full approach. That seems to me a very Australian quality. It’s like the landscape: big, open and generous.In Dustfall you play the mother of Anna Torv’s character. I understand you seek roles specifically that pull you out of your comfort zone – was Olivia one of them?I do, because it’s very boring playing characters who are close to myself. I didn’t become an actor because I wanted to play me! On the contrary – as a kid I was always dreaming of being a very different person. Unfortunately our industry is pushing back on that. You’re supposed to be playing nearer and nearer your own lived experience and you’re not allowed to play other people’s lived experience. Well – what’s the word “act” mean, then?As you get older, if you’re not careful, you get worse as an actor. Because you get too comfortable, too safe. You know how to do things, you’ve got a lot of technique. So you need to be pushed out of your comfort zone.I’m certainly not like Olivia. There are overlaps. She’s a feminist and she’s my age, so we were brought up in the same culture in terms of attitudes to sexuality. But I’m a very hands-on mum, and Olivia handed over a lot of parenting to her own mother. She comes breezing back in, flirts a lot, gets drunk and stoned. She’s pretty insensitive. But it’s fun to play all that. I hope my kids would say that wasn’t like me.Drunk and stoned acting is quite hard to do convincingly, isn’t it?Yes. I think I’ve only ever been stoned once in my life. It just didn’t appeal to me. That was probably 40 years ago.How often do millennial women want to talk to you about Bend It Like Beckham?A lot, and it thrills me! I was filming a big film in Australia when that script arrived, and I thought, “Oh my god, I have not got time to read this, and what a rubbish title!” Then I opened it late one night and by page three I was roaring with laughter.It was brilliant not just because it’s very funny but because it was touching on two really important things: women’s football, obviously, but also what it means to be a British Asian girl. There’s one reality inside your family home, shaped by your mum and dad’s values and codes of conduct and so on. And then they step out the front door and they’re in the street or they’re at school and they have to cope with a completely different set of values and a completely different culture.These young kids are negotiating all that and I hadn’t ever given that enough thought. It was a really beautiful film. Lots of young Asian girls still come up to me to talk about it. Which is great, because most of our work dies away.Juliet Stevenson: ‘I didn’t read Alan Rickman’s diaries ... I know what my relationship with him was like’Read moreWhich role has been most personally fulfilling for you and why?I’ve never felt so free as I do on stage. Nobody can stop you. Nobody can edit you. There’s a freedom in that which, on a good night, is incomparable. It’s intoxicating. There’s also nights when you’re out there and you think, “Shit, I’m so bad.” But when it’s good, it’s so intoxicating. You have this power over 1,000 people and you’re just holding them. It is hard to pin just one down, but perhaps The Doctor, the Robert Icke play we brought to the Adelaide festival in 2020, just before Covid lockdowns.Film-wise, I would sayTruly Madly Deeply. That’s had such a legacy. As I said, most of the work we do is ephemeral and that’s OK. But Truly Madly Deeply goes on having a life and I’m so thrilled by that. I think it speaks to people’s need for their grief to be recognised.Grief is so often glamorised in film but there’s nothing glamorous when you’re in grief. You feel like shit, you feel ugly and angry, you hate the rest of the world, you hate happy people. The elegant single tear rolling down the perfect cheek, which is so often what you see in cinema – we had all the snot! I think people were grateful for that.That was a blissful collaboration – [director] Anthony Minghella wrote that part for me and we knew each other very well by that time, so it felt very liberating on set in a way you don’t often feel.View image in fullscreenJuliet Stevenson and Alan Rickman in the 1990 film Truly Madly Deeply.Photograph: Bbc/AllstarWhat are you secretly really good at?I’m a good driver! What else … I’m a rubbish cook. I love to draw and paint – I’m not really good at it but I really love it. I think I’m quite a good parent. I hope that’s not too secret! And I’m a really good cleaner. If you want a cleaner, call me! I have that skill if the career goes wrong.Is there a role that you really wanted that you didn’t end up getting?When Merchant Ivory made Howards End, I desperately wanted to play Emma Thompson’s role [Margaret] because I just felt Iwasher. I loved that book so, so much. When I heard they were making a film of it, I thought, I can’t bear this. I did go up for it but it was just after my dad died and I was sort of in pieces. He died quite suddenly and I’d been nursing him, so that was my first job interview in that sort of state of skinlessness. I had an interview with James Ivory in London and I messed up so badly.I think I’ve never got a job that I desperately wanted from an audition. Because you go into the room slightly desperate, which in my case probably looks a bit mad. Luckily most things get sent to me now. I didn’t watch the film, not out of pique I don’t think. I hope not. I know Emma and she’s wonderful.Do you have a nemesis?So many. Most of the men running most of the world. Where do we start? Putin, Musk, Trump, Erdoğan, Modi, Netanyahu … I’m quite politically active and I’m very preoccupied at the moment with the fact that most of the world is run by authoritarian men who are terrifyingly rolling back women’s rights, human rights, progress, civil rights, generating racism and homophobia. It’s just terrifying.I’ve been politically engaged since I was about 16. I’m in my late 60s now, and to see everything that we have marched for and fought for being rolled back by these horrendous men is inconceivable. That we have someone like Trump in a position of power like that – a man so uneducated, so corrupt, so evidently, blatantly stupid … yes, I have plenty of those kinds of nemeses.What has been your most memorable interaction with a fan?Until I made Truly Madly Deeply, I hadn’t got that sort of recognition. Suddenly I had people coming up to me on the street. I was in a flower shop in London and I was in a hurry buying some flowers for a friend when this woman came in. I became aware that she was staring at me. I never imagined that she was staring at me because I was an actor; I was even getting a little angry about it, thinking, what the hell? Then she came up and said, “Please, can I talk to you?”Artist or activist? For Juliet Stevenson and her husband, Gaza leaves them with no choiceRead moreHer daughter had died, in her late teens, maybe her early adulthood. I think it hadn’t been very long ago. She’d seen Truly Madly Deeply and she just desperately wanted to talk about her loss. For her, the film had been an incredible catharsis. I think it was the first time she felt anybody understood what she was going through.I really had to get somewhere, I had an appointment or an interview or something. But I could not leave her. I think our conversation went for about 45 minutes. We ended up on the pavement outside and I found it impossible to pull away. I didn’t really want to. It was memorable because I’d been doing a lot of theatre until then and you don’t really get to talk to the audience after. The impact of Truly Madly Deeply had been so huge for her and she was trusting me with so much. It was the most extraordinarily huge conversation between two complete strangers on a street in London. I still think about her.What is the strangest thing you have done for love?I’m married to an anthropologist – the love of my life isHugh Brody, who has worked largely in the field with the Inuit and First Nations people in the high Arctic. We once found ourselves staying in a chief’s ranch in a remote part of Canada. I was incredibly excited about it – I mean how glamorous, how did my life bring me to this thrilling point? The chief and his wife were very keen on horse riding. I’ve always been terrified of riding, I had a bad experience when I was a kid. But there was this big expedition planned to go bareback riding and I couldn’t really say no. So there we were, galloping bareback across the Canadian landscape! I was completely terrified.Hugh’s work is so interesting and it has taken me to thrilling places. But there have been occasions where I thought, “I like to be out of my comfort zone, but this is a little too far out!”Dustfall airs 8.20pm on ABC TV on Sundays, with all episodes available to stream on ABC iview. It will air in the UK on the BBC at a later dateExplore more on these topicsCulture10 Chaotic QuestionsJuliet StevensonTelevisionAustralian televisionAustralian Broadcasting CorporationBereavementTruly Madly DeeplyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Despair after 200-year-old ‘grandmother’ tree toppled for Trump’s border wall: ‘It crushes your heart’  | US immigration | The Guardian
description: Protesters spent months occupying an ancient cottonwood. Then a tense standoff with US border patrol came to a head
Author: Douglas Main
Headline: Protesters spent months occupying an ancient cottonwood. Then a tense standoff with US border patrol came to a head
Content: A drone view shows the mangled remains of the ancient cottonwood tree where activists staged a tree-sit to protest the construction of the US-Mexico border fence, in Lochiel, Arizona.Photograph: Rebecca Noble/ReutersView image in fullscreenA drone view shows the mangled remains of the ancient cottonwood tree where activists staged a tree-sit to protest the construction of the US-Mexico border fence, in Lochiel, Arizona.Photograph: Rebecca Noble/ReutersUS immigrationDespair after 200-year-old ‘grandmother’ tree toppled for Trump’s border wall: ‘It crushes your heart’Protesters spent months occupying an ancient cottonwood. Then a tense standoff with US border patrol came to a headDouglas MainSat 10 Oct 2026 16.57 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 16.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA200-year-old cottonwood tree near theUS-Mexico border, known as the “grandmother”, has been destroyed to make way for the construction ofDonald Trump’s border wall, despite a months-long effort by protesters trying to save it.In late July, land defenders begana tree-sitin the ghost town of Lochiel,Arizona, taking turns occupying a platform high in the tree’s canopy. The group remained there for more than 70 days.Protesters occupy 200-year-old tree at US-Mexico border to stop its destruction: ‘She’s our Statue of Liberty’Read moreThen, on Monday at dawn, more than 80 federal agentsswarmedthe protesters’ camp, which is located on private land, making arrests and preventing people from reaching the cottonwood. Some agents in a steel basket on an extendable crane lift forcibly removed the person in the tree platform, according to videos andphotosshared on social mediaand descriptions of people there at the time. Others were shoved and tackled as they tried to rush toward the tree to prevent its destruction, according to witnesses.Contractors with Fisher Sand & Gravel, a company building this section of wall, then used an excavator topush over the tree, which cracked and crashed to the earth. Land defenders shrieked, cried and yelled at the federal agents.“Seeing that – it crushes your heart,” said Erick Meza, the Sierra Club’s Borderlands coordinator who has been working to save the trees for months, beginning with a series of letters to US Customs and Border Protection (CBP).“That tree brought a lot of people together,” he said. Now, he added, “there’s a community response of outrage. People are pissed off.”The cottonwood’s toppling was filmed by a team fromTurning Point USA, the far-right political group, who appeared to be embedded with border patrol andallowed free access to roamthroughout the closed off public road.View image in fullscreenA tree-sitter on 29 July 2026 in the ancient cottonwood tree at the US-Mexico border in Lochiel, Arizona.Photograph: Rebecca Noble/ReutersOne of the land defenders had scaled another ancient cottonwood tree situated right on the border with Mexico. On Thursday, CBP and Mexican police, who have been present for several days and visibly working with American authorities,removedthe tree-sitter’s platform, food and water supplies, according to Alex Chabbott, a land defender who has been present at the camp on and off for over a month.Late on Friday, the tree-sitter came down on their own volition after not being resupplied for several days.double quotation markWe’re not going anywhere. We are rooted, like the grandmothersKate Scott, a tree-sit leaderThe agents involved include border patrol officers, part of CBP, and a special forces tactical unit calledBortac, whose self-described purpose is to “respond to terrorist threats”.The tree-sit began shortly after contractors knocked over and killed three other ancient cottonwood trees nearby on 27 July.Two 30ft-tall walls are being built throughout this area, known as the San Rafael valley, a remote and once idyllic high elevation prairie where the movie Oklahoma was filmed. The valley, and the Patagonia and Huachuca mountains on either side of it, form one of the most important regional wildlife corridors between the US and Mexico,providingpassagetoanimals includingjaguars, ocelots, bears and even beavers and porcupines in recent years.Already, government contractors have finished 88 miles (140km) of secondary wall, which is a second 30ft fence set at some distance from a primary wall of the same height. Another 444 miles of secondary wall are under construction,according to DHS, much of that in Arizona, using billions of dollars allocated by Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.View image in fullscreenMembers of the Nogales fire department use a cherrypicker to remove a platform from another tree on the border with Mexico, leaving a protester stranded.Photograph: Rebecca Noble/ReutersProtesters say that construction in the area is progressing rapidly, 24 hours a day. In recent days, Fisher Sand & Gravel has completed the secondary wall, which includes placing 30ft steel panels within a trench filled with rebar and cement, along a part of the private property where the camp is located, including up to the point where the tree stood.These trees, which depend on a regular supply of water underground, are a hallmark of riparian forests, an endangered ecotype throughoutArizonaand the south-west, said Russ McSpadden, an advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity. The ecological importance of these trees is one of the animating factors behind the land defenders.Water usefor wall construction hasdepletedwells throughout the south-west, threatening natural featuressuch as Quitobaquito Springs. CBP does not say how much current construction uses, but in 2008 itestimateda smaller wall nearby could use up to 710,00 gallons per mile for construction; the current project likely uses more, as it is larger.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines USGet the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘We are starting a movement’Since Monday, dozens of land defenders have beenarrested, many for entering the road between the private property and the border, which wasordered closedby federal authorities in late September due to wall construction. Protesters have been doingprayersin the road near the tree every morning.Some of those arrested were physically hit and came back with bruises and black eyes, Chabbott claimed.Several more people attemptedto use nonviolent tacticsto halt or delay construction, including one woman wholocked herselfto a cement truck on 7 August, according tovideos sharedon social media.View image in fullscreenProtesters face off with US border patrol as Fisher Sand & Gravel construction crews work on 8 October 2026.Photograph: Rebecca Noble/ReutersThe protester was sprayed in the face with mace and wrestled by several agents, and her limbs forced into painful positions, according to witnesses and social media videos.The truck was later drivenawaywhile the land defender was still attached, and cut from the vehicle later that evening, according to witnesses. She is now in custody, according to what authorities have told the land defenders’ lawyers.double quotation markThat tree brought a lot of people together. People are pissed offErick Meza, Sierra ClubJulia Butterfly Hill,whospent two yearsliving in a redwood in California’s Humboldt county in the late 1990s, said she was horrified to see how roughly border patrol treated this woman on a livestreamed video, she said.This land defender’s courage and commitment to nonviolent resistance in the face of brutality “brought tears to my eyes”, Butterfly Hill said. “She’s a hero of the highest order.”CBP did not respond to a request for comment about this and other clashes, but has previously said that walls in areas like this will help combat unauthorized immigration. The sheriff of Santa Cruz county, David Hathaway, who did not respond to a request for comment for this story, haspreviously saida wall in this area is senseless since this remote valley has no history of significant illegal activity. Fisher Sand & Gravel did not respond to a request for comment.View image in fullscreenA drone view shows the remains of two other ancient cottonwood trees in Lochiel, Arizona, on 27 July.Photograph: Rebecca Noble/ReutersIn a press conference on 8 October, Adelita Grijalva, a congresswoman who represents the area, said she was “heartbroken” about the loss of the “grandmother” trees, and said she plans to try to introduce a bill that will revoke the DHS’s ability to waive any and all laws in building border infrastructure.The tree-sit began shortly after contractorsknocked over and killedtwo other ancient cottonwood trees nearby on 27 July.In felling the tree, the contractors and federal agents “try to break us, but we are not broken”, said Kate Scott, one of the leaders of the tree-sit. “We are starting a movement, and we’re not going anywhere. We are rooted, like the grandmothers.”Explore more on these topicsUS immigrationArizonaUS-Mexico borderTrump administrationDonald TrumpUS politicsTrees and forestsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘A proud loaf with a deep, caramel crust’: the best (and worst) supermarket sliced wholemeal bread, tasted and rated | Bread | The Guardian
description: Our wholegrain hero sorts the wheat from the chaff in the search for a simple pleasure: a satisfying sandwich loaf
Author: Tom Hunt
Headline: Our wholegrain hero sorts the wheat from the chaff in the search for a simple pleasure: a satisfying sandwich loaf
Content: All rise …Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert Billington.View image in fullscreenAll rise …Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food styling: Robert Billington.Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterBreadReview‘A proud loaf with a deep, caramel crust’: the best (and worst) supermarket sliced wholemeal bread, tasted and ratedOur wholegrain hero sorts the wheat from the chaff in the search for a simple pleasure: a satisfying sandwich loafThe best supermarket sourdoughTom HuntSat 10 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI’ve broken my strict, like-for-like approach this week in the interests of just finding a really good sliced wholemeal sandwich loaf. Alas, most of these are made to the standard Chorleywood process, with each one a cardboard replica of the other and with only nuanced differences. However, I did find two with exceptional flavour and one with a notably good, firm texture that’s ideal for spreading stuff on; to my surprise, several have an impressive lack of additives, too, and they all score well on value.The Chorleywood processis an industrial method for making bread in just three and a half hours using high-speed mechanical processes and chemical additives. It was developed in the 1960s, and now accounts for about 80% of the bread made in the UK. If you’re looking for palm oil-free loaves with zero additives, emulsifiers or preservatives, sandwich loaves are hard to navigate, but there are some that fit the bill – just check the label.The best supermarket sliced wholemeal breadBest overall:Jason’s sourdough wholemeal ciabattinView image in fullscreen£2.20 for 580g at Morrisons (38p/100g)£2.35 for 580g at Waitrose (41p/100g)★★★★☆A small, round-topped tin loaf with a closed crumb, a dense texture (perfect for spreading) and an evenly glazed crust. A sweet, wheatgrass aroma, medium-firm bite and simple flavour profile. A sweet, nutty taste without any bitterness. A simple ingredients list (wholemeal wheat flour, water, wheat gluten, fermented wheat flour, salt), zero additives and palm oil-free.Best bargain:Aldi Specially Selected wholemeal seeded loafView image in fullscreen99p for 800g at Aldi (13p/100g), in store only★★★☆☆A soft loaf speckled with millet, sunflower and other seeds and with a fresh and wholesome malty aroma. Yielding to the bite, with good texture from the seeds and the chewy crust. Three additives (two emulsifiers, one preservative), but palm oil-free.And the rest …Wildfarmed regenerative sliced seededView image in fullscreen£2.25 for 550g at Ocado (41p/100g)£2.25 for 550g at Tesco (41p/100g)★★★★☆A soft and seedy loaf (loads of millet, sunflower seeds, linseeds and others) with a roasted barley and fermented yeast aroma. A sweet flavour with a complex nuttiness and toasted bran finish, and extra texture from the sheer quantity of seeds. Made with flour from cereals grown by Wildfarmed’s regenerative farming project. B Corp-certified, zero additives, and palm oil-free.Exceptional by Asda wholemeal superseeded sliced loafView image in fullscreen£1.60 for 800g at Asda (20p/100g)★★★☆☆A thick slice with a medium closed crumb and an appetising, sweet, nutty aroma. A bit gummy, but with substance and a good and textural bite from all the seeds (sunflower, pumpkin, linseed). A well-balanced flavour profile, too, with zero additives. Contains palm oil and palm fat, though.Sainsbury’s Taste the Difference multiseed wholemeal farmhouse loafView image in fullscreen£1.60 for 800g at Sainsbury’s (20p/100g)★★★☆☆A proud loaf with a deep, caramel-glazed crust. A sweet, malty but sour aroma, and a dense, firm crumb with mixed seeds throughout (mainly millet and sunflower). Firm and crunchy with a sweet, nutty flavour and no bitterness. Zero additives, but contains palm oil.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe FilterGet the best shopping advice from the Filter team straight to your inbox. The Guardian’s journalism is independent. We will earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTesco Finest wholemeal seeds and grainsView image in fullscreen£1.75 for 800g at Tesco (22p/100g)★★★☆☆A soft, seedy loaf topped with wheat flakes. A rich, bran-forward aroma, and a simple flavour, with a savoury, nutty finish and a decent bite. Zero additives, and palm oil-free.M&S medium wholemeal super soft loafView image in fullscreen75p for 800g at Ocado (10p/100g)★★☆☆☆A soft loaf with a closed crumb and gummy texture. A sweet, nutty aroma with a bitter, burnt finish. Sweet at first, with a nice, nutty middle. A good everyday loaf with zero additives, but does contain palm oil. Exceptional value, too.Allinson’s The Champion wholemealView image in fullscreen£1.50 for 650g at Asda (24p/100g)£1.80 for 650g at Ocado (28p/100g)★★☆☆☆A dark, round-topped sandwich loaf with a closed crumb and soft, gluey texture. An acrid, over-toasted bran aroma and distinctive malty but bitter bran flavour. Zero additives or labelled artificial preservatives, and emulsifier-free. Contains certified “sustainable” palm oil.Hovis granary wholemealView image in fullscreen£1.95 for 800g at Tesco (25p/100g)£2 for 800g at Waitrose (25p/100g)★★☆☆☆A rich, tanned loaf topped with wheat flakes. A sweet, nutty aroma and a soft texture. Simple, bran-forward flavour with a bitter aftertaste. Three additives (one preservative, two emulsifiers), but palm oil-free.Co-op Bakery farmhouse wholemealView image in fullscreen£1.30 for 800g at Co-op (17p/100g)★☆☆☆☆A standard soft wholemeal loaf with a closed crumb, a sweet but mildly synthetic aroma and a gummy texture. A sweet-forward flavour with subtle, nutty notes and a pleasant aftertaste. Three additives (two emulsifiers, one preservative), plus palm oil and palm fat.For more, read our roundup of thebest sourdoughand thebest brioche bunsExplore more on these topicsBreadThe FilterFoodfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Six men on how they plan to stand up against rape culture | Sexual consent | The Guardian
description: While most of the crowd at a Stop Sexual Violence rally in New York City was mostly women, men of all ages were in attendance too
Author: Iris Kim
Headline: While most of the crowd at a Stop Sexual Violence rally in New York City was mostly women, men of all ages were in attendance too
Content: Demonstrators rally in Foley Square outside the New York state supreme court building in lower Manhattan to demand justice in the Cornell gang-rape case.Photograph: Gina M Randazzo/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenDemonstrators rally in Foley Square outside the New York state supreme court building in lower Manhattan to demand justice in the Cornell gang-rape case.Photograph: Gina M Randazzo/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockBuilding powerSexual consentSix men on how they plan to stand up against rape cultureWhile most of the crowd at a Stop Sexual Violence rally in New York City was mostly women, men of all ages were in attendance tooBuilding power is supported byAbout this contentIris KimSat 10 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 09.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTens of thousands of protestersgathered at city halls and college campuses across the country on Thursday to demand an end to sexual violence. The nationwide rallies followed weeks of public outcry over the mishandling of campus sexual assault cases atCornell UniversityandLouisiana State University.The protest organizers – including Women’s March, Feminist Generation and Me Too International – demanded justice forJane Doe, who said she was drugged and gang-raped by seven students at a Cornell frat party; Kendall Francis, who said she was raped by an LSU football player; and all survivors harmed “from the frat house to the White House”. They also called for reform of Title IX, a set of protections for sexual misconduct victims and LGBTQ+ students that the Trump administration has slowlystripped away.The latest cases have outraged college students and their families over the pervasiveness of rape culture; 81% of women and 43% of men in the US said they have experienced sexual harassment or assault, according to theNational Sexual Violence Resource Center. Parents online are questioninghow to raise sonswho will stand up to sexual violenceinstead of being bystanders.Women, survivors and longtime advocates say theonus has often been on themto use the momentum in moments like these to educate others and demand concrete change.While the demographic makeup of the crowd at the Stop Sexual Violence rally inNew YorkCity was majority women, men of all ages were there, too, holding “I Am Jane Doe” signs and yelling to end rape culture. We asked six of them how they are personally taking a stand against rape culture.Speak up against toxicity in the chatKaif Gilani, 29Too often, we see that after a big uproar and high-profile news, that the only people standing up and attending protests are women or female-identifying folks. It’s really important for men to step up and say: “Hey, I need to put an end to this in any way that I can in my day-to-day life.” We need to try to make a difference in our own communities, whether that’s speaking up against frat brothers who say something toxic or misogynistic in the chat, or going out and attending events like the Women’s March.Pass legislation for consent educationBen Tee, 42There’s some really important legislation in the New York state legislature to make consent education a mandatory part of the school curriculum. I’m in Democratic party leadership, and we just passed a resolution last week supporting a framework for teaching consent. I actually think that’s the most important thing that we can do.People are talking about increasing penalties and closing the voluntary intoxication loophole, which is super important. But the reality is that we don’t get [sexual assault] convictions, the police don’t take [sexual assault] seriously and DAs do not prosecute.We need to be doing a lot more in prevention. After the assault is just too late. There have been really good studies that show that consent education can have a huge impact on reducing the rate of victimization and perpetration, and nobody talks about it at all. It’s a real, real shame.‘Men need to do more teaching’Peter Walsh, 64I know from my own experiences as a man that many boys need to be taught what is appropriate, and when consent means consent. Men need to do more teaching.Be aware if someone is uncomfortableNicola Francia, 21It really starts with reconsidering your own position and understanding where it isnearyou, andinyou.I’m from Italy, and there was a girl from my high school who was killed by her ex. In my home country, there has been a lot ofmobilizing around this issue.It’s very evident that [rape culture] is near us, all across the country, in our society.There were cases in my social life where I wish I had been more present for the women I know. They have felt uncomfortable in social situations with guys being creepy when they were intoxicated. We all have to be very aware of whether someone is feeling uncomfortable or whether you are making someone uncomfortable.Take a stand against victim blamingShalin Upadhyay, 27I see rape culture as something that starts from little moments – how people talk, how women are treated. The language that we use when we talk to women or talk about them is objectifying. Those things are normalized, and then that’s what turns into something bigger, like rape. And when rape happens, it’s also not seriously considered. It always turns into victim-blaming. I’ve seen that, and I want to stand against that.When you see something happen, take actionDaniel Olivier, 37I grew up in the punk rock scene, and when things happened, we took action. You got your head kicked in if you did something bad. I wish that would happen more often. I know that’s not the right thing to say, and I don’t stand for violence. But the violence that [abusers] are doing to us is so much worse.In my current life, just being in New York, it’s constant. You can’t sit at a bar without overhearing people saying disgusting things about women. I worked in the music industry and the alcohol industry, and I’ve been surrounded by it my entire life. I’ve spent my whole life fighting against this stuff.Explore more on these topicsSexual consentBuilding powerRelationships and sex educationRape and sexual assault#MeToo movementProtest (US)New YorkSchoolsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A replica of Donald Trump’s Oval Office goes for the gold in Washington DC | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: The tourist attraction just unveiled an elaborate, full-scale overhaul to match Trump’s second-term aesthetic
Author: David Smith
Headline: The tourist attraction just unveiled an elaborate, full-scale overhaul to match Trump’s second-term aesthetic
Content: A replica of the Oval Office being updated to Donald Trump’s current decor, at The People’s House: A White House Experience in Washington DC, on 2 October.Photograph: APView image in fullscreenA replica of the Oval Office being updated to Donald Trump’s current decor, at The People’s House: A White House Experience in Washington DC, on 2 October.Photograph: APDonald TrumpA replica of Donald Trump’s Oval Office goes for the gold in Washington DCThe tourist attraction just unveiled an elaborate, full-scale overhaul to match Trump’s second-term aestheticDavid Smithin WashingtonSat 10 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 11.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSitting behind a replica Resolute Desk, nine-year-old Sydney Wright posed for the camera like a future US president. “I love it,” she smiled. And what about the dazzling gold appliqués, gold leaf and gold trim surrounding her? “It’s cool.”Sydney was among a steady stream of visitors on Thursday toThe People’s House: A White House Experience, an interactive museum – with an orientation film narrated by The West Wing star Martin Sheen – at 1700 Pennsylvania Avenue, just 150 yards from the real thing.Run by theWhite House Historical Association, the tourist attraction has just unveiled an elaborate overhaul of its full-scale Oval Office to match Donald Trump’s second-term aesthetic, described by the New York Times as a “gilded rococo nightmare”.Gone is the understated, plain decor of Joe Biden and his predecessors. In its place is a spectacle of two dozen portraits in heavy carved frames, swirling wall onlays, gleaming brass vases and decorative knickknacks crowding nearly every available surface.Barack Obama had pictures oftwo former presidentson the wall; Biden put up a total of seven paintings. Trump has stacked the walls with historical figures including George Washington, Andrew Jackson and Benjamin Franklin.Ronald Reaganappears twice, while there is only one woman on display: former first lady Jackie Kennedy.A bust of former president Theodore Rooseveltby James Earle Fraserglowers from a bookshelf, flanked by bound volumes of the 26th president’s works. Other books on display include Hawthorne’s Works and Writings of Washington. There are two mirrors and a copy of the Declaration of Independence.But for all the detail, the people’s house cannot recreate the experience of former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, whoreportedly entered the Oval Officeone day to find Trump in DIY mode, using superglue in an effort to stick gold ornaments to the fireplace.View image in fullscreenA replica of Trump’s Oval Office, on 2 October.Photograph: APStill, for many tourists arriving in the nation’s capital, this is as close as they will get to the heart of presidential power, especially with the White House currently undergoing extensive demolition and construction work.Sydney’s father, Drew Wright, a 36-year-old firefighter from Athens, Georgia, said he viewed the room’s additions as “paying homage to the people who laid the pathway that we have to raise our children in this great nation”.Asked aboutthe goldening, Wright, who voted for Trump twice, replied: “There’s always going to be critics. There’s always going to be haters. Just because they’re the loudest ones in the room doesn’t mean they’re right. I don’t know what it looked like before but I think it’s a pretty classic look.”Cheri Lujan Hamilton, 54, the chief clerk of the New Mexico state senate, also likes what Trump has done with the place. “I’m kind of in awe,” she said. “I was disappointed we couldn’t get into the White House for a tour so this is the next best thing.”Taking in all the gold, Hamilton remarked: “It’s grand. I like everything that’s grand.I do think all the gold around the doors is maybe a little too much. But I like it on the top.”Pedro Robles, 50, a police officer from Nashville, Tennessee, called the replica “pretty cool” and disputed the notion that the gilding crosses into bad taste. “I don’t think so,” he said. “I don’t think it looks tacky.”Such opinions would be music to the ears of Trump who, whenasked by Time magazinewhat he would miss most about the White House after he leaves, answered: “This beautiful room that nobody should be allowed to rip down. The Oval Office.”View image in fullscreenThe replica of Trump’s Oval Office being updated by workers, on 2 October.Photograph: J Scott Applewhite/APA team of specialised designers visited Trump’s actual office while he was away to ensure authenticity. They used 3D scanning in Indianapolis and crafted hand-carved gold frames in California, while teams in Canada and Virginia worked on replicas of vases and other tabletop pieces.The replica transition took one week with more than 25 crew members onsite. They used laser levels and temporary adhesive to fix items to the walls, checking their work for accuracy against renderings of the actual office before nailing many adornments to the walls.Matthew Costello,chief education officer at the White House Historical Association, said in an email: “As we have seen throughout White House history, each president transitions the Oval Office according to his own tastes. It is our hope that through the evolutions of our Oval Office replica, people will be inspired to learn more about and even see themselves in White House history.”There is, however, one key difference between the real Oval Office and its imitator. While the actual workspace relies on gilded gold leaf, the museum opted for a specialised gold paint solution to protect against chipping or other wear and tear from visitors.The transformation provides a microcosm of an aggressive campaign by Trump to remakeWashington DCin his own image.Beyond the Oval Office makeover, Trump knocked down the East Wing tobuild a $400m ballroom, paved over the Rose Garden’s traditional grass lawn to build a white stone patio reminiscent of his Mar-a-Lago resort in Florida, added a row of presidential portraits that replace Biden with an autopen and constructed a granite helipad on the south lawn.He also initiated a troubled overhaul of the Lincoln Memorial reflecting pool, proposed a towering 250ft triumphal arch near Arlington national cemetery andthreatened to tear downthe John F Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts if it does not bear his name.Washington purists and architecture critics have recoiled at Trump’s ostentatious tastes. But Carl Wilkerson, 73, a retired marine wearing a US Marine Corps T-shirt, offered an impassioned defense of presidential swagger, saying: “We need to have a little bling-bling, man. This is the United States of America. This is the greatest country on the planet, so we need to show it off.”Drawing on his time overseas, Wilkerson, from Hereford, Arizona, argued that US presidential architecture had fallen behind the competition, saying: “You go over there in the east. He’s walked in their palaces and it’s like, boom. It pops. Their palaces outdid the White House 10 to one. We need to step up our game a little bit. We are the greatest country on the planet. So you need to act like it – and look like it.”Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpWashington DCUS politicsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Ray Gunn review – Brad Bird’s animated film-noir sci-fi caper is an old-school family classic | Movies | The Guardian
description: Sam Rockwell voices the gumshoe who becomes embroiled with Scarlett Johansson’s femme fatale in this big-hearted and beautifully designed fantasy spectacular
Author: Peter Bradshaw
Headline: Sam Rockwell voices the gumshoe who becomes embroiled with Scarlett Johansson’s femme fatale in this big-hearted and beautifully designed fantasy spectacular
Content: Mean streets … Ray Gunn voiced by Sam Rockwell.Photograph: Skydance AnimationView image in fullscreenMean streets … Ray Gunn voiced by Sam Rockwell.Photograph: Skydance AnimationMoviesReviewRay Gunn review – Brad Bird’s animated film-noir sci-fi caper is an old-school family classicSam Rockwell voices the gumshoe who becomes embroiled with Scarlett Johansson’s femme fatale in this big-hearted and beautifully designed fantasy spectacularPeter BradshawSat 10 Oct 2026 09.45 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 09.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrad Bird, the Spielberg of animation, applies his masterly authorial touch to a terrific family film that retrieves the genre from the doldrums of dull, AI-formulaic stories and visuals. This animation is smart, witty, humane: a fantasy spectacular with old-fashioned entertainment values and some amazing cityscape design showcasing a beguiling and sweet romance.The setting is a city of marvels in a world to come, a retro-futurist urban landscape with hints of Metropolis and Blade Runner; there are plenty of regulation moving walkways, flying cars and eerie hologram billboards, yes, but a light touch to put the fun back into what could be just cliche. Here is where an old-school noir thriller is to take place with tough private detectives and bad guys wielding state-of-the-art laser-particle firearms (this explains the title, though I’d hoped that it might also include some reference to 1980s Republican politics). There are careworn cops, cynical club owners and alluring shady ladies with touches of Lana Turner and Veronica Lake. The airborne automobiles also have the bulbous lines of a previous century, and the TV monitors show black-and-white images; plasma flatscreens have evidently been disinvented.Sam Rockwell voices the role of Raymond Gunn, an ex-cop turned gumshoe who left the police after covering up for the misdeeds of a female detective with whom he’d been poignantly in love; his tough persona covers a gallant softie. He lives in a world of racist bigotry towards aliens, and Ray takes some heat for working with Eyera (voiced by Tom Waits), an alien who, at the end of one bruising incident, is not admitted to a humans-only hospital. Ray’s path crosses with that of sultry singing superstar Venus Nova (voiced by Scarlett Johansson) whose creepy nogoodnik fourth husband Arnold (Bobby Cannavale) is having an affair with Venus’s stand-in double; he tries using this woman to fabricate bogus evidence of an affair which would lead to a lucrative divorce. (The divorce laws are a bit retro in this world as well.)When Venus discovers his planned scam, she threatens to kill Arnold in front of witnesses, creating a murderous cloud over her reputation – but malevolent Arnold has something on her too. It all leads to a scary plot, involving Venus’s smoothie manager and first husband Barry (Alan Tudyk) and fez-wearing nightclub proprietor and mob boss Slugsy (Matt Berry), who comes on like a cross between Sydney Greenstreet and Jabba the Hutt.There are some lovely set piece scenes – especially when Ray and Venus take to the floor at a club which offers a “zero gravity” interlude allowing its dancers and lovers the chance to float surreally around as if in space. We also get a bizarre interlude when a gun turns out to be – temporarily – capable of scrambling the limbs of those in its sights. And on top of all that, the film has something to say about algorithmic ads and data privacy. It’s a charming, very enjoyable movie with a big heart.Ray Gunn screened at the London film festival; it is in Australian cinemas from 3 December, UK and US cinemas from 4 December, and on Netflix from 18 December.Explore more on these topicsFilmAnimation in filmFamily filmsScience fiction and fantasy filmsCrime filmsThrillersBrad BirdreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The moment I knew: We were babysitting my younger siblings and he wore a tutu to make them laugh | Australian lifestyle | The Guardian
description: When Sarah Maloney’s primary school crush danced back into her life, she braced for a ‘teenage whirlwind romance’. Then one night, she realised they were both all in
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: When Sarah Maloney’s primary school crush danced back into her life, she braced for a ‘teenage whirlwind romance’. Then one night, she realised they were both all in
Content: Jake and Sarah Maloney, both 16, at the debutante ball in 2017: ‘While everyone else hit the dancefloor, Jake and I hit the couch in the foyer and stayed there all night talking’View image in fullscreenJake and Sarah Maloney, both 16, at the debutante ball in 2017: ‘While everyone else hit the dancefloor, Jake and I hit the couch in the foyer and stayed there all night talking’The moment I knewAustralian lifestyleThe moment I knew: We were babysitting my younger siblings and he wore a tutu to make them laughWhenSarah Maloney’s primary school crush danced back into her life, she braced for a ‘teenage whirlwind romance’. Then one night, she realised they were both all inFind more stories fromthe moment I knew seriesSarah MaloneySat 10 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 19.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2017 I was 16, went to an all-girls Catholic school in Melbourne and had zero tolerance for teenage boys and their nonsense. Instead I spent a lot of gossip time lamenting Jake, who broke my tiny heart in primary school and then moved hours away.The moment I knew: after their first meeting, my young son hugged him goodbye – and didn’t want to let goRead moreAdebutante ballwas coming up. It was an expensive tradition that was fundamentally at odds with my values but I couldn’t say no to a pretty dress and dancing – I was a teenage girl, after all. Some friends asked cousins or co-workers from our part-time jobs to be partners. I got knocked back by everyone. When I complained to my mother, she let me know Jake had moved back to town, and did she want me to ask his mum if he would be willing?Jake accepted and we spent weeks rehearsing. My mum would pick him up on the way to the dance hall and we would sit in the back seat, catching up on the last five years and laughing at our juvenile romance. It felt as though we just clicked again, and our giggly behaviour during dance rehearsals earned us more than one disapproving look from the teacher.I was done for. I frantically asked my friends: did they think he might like me too? Should I ask him to my year 11 formal? Should I kiss him on deb night?The ball was wonderful. While everyone else hit the dancefloor, Jake and I hit the couch in the foyer and stayed there all night talking. We missed dessert and I couldn’t find the courage to kiss him but he asked me to see a movie with him the next day.double quotation markOn our first date I had my first kiss. I almost chipped my toothOn our first date – where we were dropped off at the local cinema with a curfew – I had my first kiss. I almost chipped my tooth.The first months of our relationship were full of nonstop texting during the day and after-school visits with my bedroom door wide open.I was surprised at how earnest he was; I felt as though I didn’t have to pretend to be a cooler version of myself. I wrote in my diary about how excited I was to finally have my “ill-fated teenage whirlwind romance”. I figured if I held on to the idea that we’d break up, then I wouldn’t get hurt.About two months into our relationship, my mother tasked Jake and I with babysitting my younger siblings. We weren’t technicallyallowedto spend the evening in my room with the door closed but that didn’t stop us. After a few hours of laughing at YouTube videos, I went to have a shower and heard a crash down the hallway. My little sister had dropped a plate and it had shattered all over the tiles. I rushed out to help before she started crying. But when I got there, she and Jake were already cleaning up together and giggling. I snuck back to the bathroom with relief. Jake was good with my siblings and that was important to me.View image in fullscreen‘Jake and I make each other laugh more than anything else’: Jake and Sarah in 2024Later that night I wandered into our lounge room to find Jake elbow-deep in our dress-up box and wearing a bright-orange tutu. My sister was beside him wearing a white wig. They ran around the room, Jake spinning like a ballerina to make her laugh. Neither of them noticed me. I stood and watched as I came to terms with the sudden feeling of certainty in my chest.Lying in the dark that night, I told Jake I loved him. It flew out of my mouth before I could stop myself. I remember my heart playing jazz while I waited for his response. He whispered, “I love you too” and hearing him sound so sure made me cry.Nine years on, my “ill-fated teenage whirlwind romance” has turned into a loving, long-term relationship.Jake and I make each other laugh more than anything else. Life might throw a curveball but one of us is sure to make a joke about it. We often fall into comedic improv bits when we’re together, and I’m sure our neighbours think we are completely nuts when they hear us bicker like old people for the fun of it. But it’s safe. And it’s home.Being with the same person since age 16 might seem crazy but I always say that kids are dumb, not stupid. I knew back then what I know now – that the right person will show up even if it seems too early. You just grow together. Jake may have broken my little heart once but I’m willing to have him hold it now for good.Tell us the moment you knewShare your experienceShare your love storyDo you have a romantic realisation you'd like to share? title: From The Social Reckoning to Harriet Kemsley: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead | Culture | The Guardian
description: Jeremy Strong plays Mark Zuckerberg in Aaron Sorkin’s sequel to The Social Network, and the Last One Laughing star reckons with divorce in her new standup tour
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Jeremy Strong plays Mark Zuckerberg in Aaron Sorkin’s sequel to The Social Network, and the Last One Laughing star reckons with divorce in her new standup tour
Content: Zucker punch … Jeremy Strong in The Social Reckoning.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyView image in fullscreenZucker punch … Jeremy Strong in The Social Reckoning.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyGoing out, staying inCultureFrom The Social Reckoning to Harriet Kemsley: your complete entertainment guide to the week aheadJeremy Strong plays Mark Zuckerberg in Aaron Sorkin’s sequel to The Social Network, and the Last One Laughing star reckons with divorce in her new standup tourSat 10 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleContents1Going out: Cinema2Going out: Gigs3Going out: Art4Going out: Stage5Staying in: Streaming6Staying in: Games7Staying in: Albums8Staying in: Brain foodView image in fullscreenGoing out:CinemaThe Social ReckoningOut nowThe David Fincher-directed The Social Network has only come to seem more canny over time, with the site co-founded by Mark Zuckerberg being held responsible for all manner of social ills. In this sequel from Aaron Sorkin (this time directing and writing) based on the incidents around the 2021 leak of internal Facebook memos, Zuck is embodied not by Jesse Eisenberg but Jeremy Strong.The UprisingOut nowPaul Greengrass (United 93) tackles the 1381 peasants’ revolt, a fracas caused partly by the decision to introduce a new tax of four pence per person, regardless of whether you were in the greedy elite or a worker who might make about £2 in a whole year. Heading up the rebels with a cause are Andrew Garfield and Cosmo Jarvis.The Lost Children of TuamOut nowIn 2017, the New York Times chronicled the efforts of amateur local historian Catherine Corless’s campaign to expose the abuse by Irish nuns that led to almost 800 child and infant deaths in Ireland. This dramatisation of the scandal stars Monica Dolan as Corless and is produced by Liam Neeson.Other MommyOut nowJessica Chastain stars as both regular mom Ursula and her supernatural doppelganger, creeping around the house interacting with eight-year-old Bela (Arabella Olivia Clark) in this Blumhouse horror directed by Rob Savage (Dashcam). An adaptation of Josh Malerman’s creepy 2024 novel, Incidents Around the House.Catherine BrayGoing out:GigsView image in fullscreenBig weekend … Arab Strap.Photograph: Luke BovillArab Strap12 to 17 October, tour starts EdinburghThe Scottish duo returned last month with their ninth album Half-Told Tales. A 14-song collection of strangely danceable odes to ageing (You You You), angry warnings about masturbation (I Get Noise), and an overarching sense of black humour, it should make for a fun night out.Michael CraggManifestWembley Arena, London, 16 OctoberLike their girl group contemporaries Katseye, this Turkish sextet were created via a TV singing competition. They also share some of their musical DNA, with Manifest’s brightly hued songs bubbling like a sugary soft drink. Support on this debut arena show comes from UK girl band newcomers XO.MC606 Club 50th anniversary festival606 Club, London, 12 to 25 OctoberWest London’s much-loved 606 Club celebrates its 50th anniversary over a fortnight, with star guests including Jamie Cullum (13 Oct), Gwilym Simcock (15 Oct), and many trailblazers of UK jazz. Founded and run by saxophonist Steve Rubie, “The Six” is as devoted to good music as it’s ever been.John FordhamOxford international song festivalVarious venues, 10 to 24 OctoberAn ambitious local event turned major international fixture, this festival celebrates 25 seasons with big-name performances on the theme of love. Highlights include baritone Matthias Goerne and pianist Tamara Stefanovich in Schubert’s Winterreise (10 Oct), and songs by György Kurtág from baritone Benjamin Appl and pianist James Baillieu (Mon).Flora WillsonGoing out:ArtView image in fullscreenGood night sweet prints … Madame Yevonde’s Edith Hart-Davis (Wallace), later Lady Brougham and Vaux (‘Mrs Richard Hart-Davis as Ariel’) 1935.Photograph: National Portrait Gallery, LondonLight and Magic: The Birth ofArtPhotographyTate Modern, London, 14 October to 21 FebruaryThe Tate’s big autumn show takes a global look at the more conceptual, artier side of photography, with 200 prints by 80 artists from across the world, including Madame Yevonde, who saw the camera as more than a documentary tool.Prem Sahib, Gordon Matta-ClarkDe La Warr Pavilion, Bexhill-on-Sea, 10 October to 4 JanuaryPrem Sahib has been making some of the most interesting art in the UK over the past few years, all about queer intimacy and clubbing, and he is getting some well-deserved institutional attention here alongside the brilliant late American conceptualist Gordon Matta-Clark.Julia IsídrezNottingham Contemporary, to 10 JanuaryUK museums’ fascination with indigenous art continues unabated with this show of ceramics by Paraguayan Guaraní artist Julia Isídrez, filled with mythical creatures and multi-headed amphibians.Frieze art fairRegent’s Park, London, 14 to 19 OctoberEvery autumn, Frieze shows up in a massive tent in Regent’s Park and plays host to the best art galleries in the world. It is a cultural phenomenon, and well worth visiting if you can stomach the price of entry.Eddy FrankelGoing out:StageView image in fullscreenLolly pop star … Harriet Kemsley.Photograph: Pål Hansen/The GuardianHarriet KemsleyBrighton, 11 October; Hull, 14 October; Leeds, 15 October; touring to 26 FebruaryOn stage, the Last One Laughing star comes across as a giggly, chaotic oversharer – but you don’t become a successful standup without serious finesse and focus. Kemsley’s current show Floozy sees the 39-year-old relate her experiences of post-divorce dating in deceptively daffy style.Rachel AroestiThe Cherry OrchardHarold Pinter theatre, London, to 9 JanuaryAutumn is the season when all the stage stars come to play in the West End – and there are none bigger than Kristin Scott Thomas, who stars alongside Stephen Mangan in Chekhov’s richly rewarding final play.Miriam GillinsonMiddlemarch Parts 1 & 2Swan theatre, Stratford-upon-Avon, to 16 JanuaryNina Raine has adapted George Eliot’s exquisite novel into a play in two parts, directed by Jeremy Herrin – who is so good at injecting ambitious shows with shape and purpose. Nia Towle plays Dorothea Brooke alongside Amanda Root, playing both George Eliot and matchmaker Mrs Cadwallader.MGEnglish National BalletLiverpool Empire, 15 to 17 October; touring to 25 OctoberThere are two ways to watch the ENB this week: see them live in Rudolf Nureyev’s staging of Romeo & Juliet, with one of the best ballet scores ever written. Or settle down with some popcorn for their sumptuous production of Sleeping Beauty, recorded at the Royal Albert Hall in cinemas (13 to 18 October).Lyndsey Winshipskip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenStaying in:StreamingView image in fullscreenSimply the chest … Treasure Island.Photograph: Paramount Plus (UK)Treasure IslandParamount+, 12 OctoberRobert Louis Stevenson’s 1883 novel – responsible for creating the pirate caricature of the popular imagination – was first adapted for television 75 years ago. This new version stars David Oyelowo, Jack Huston, and Hayley Atwell as Bess Hawkins, who helps her son Jim in his hunt for fabled riches.VisionQuestDisney+, 14 OctoberIt can be juvenile, but Marvel lore has also powered some of the cleverest TV of recent times. This mind-boggling spin-off of 2021’s WandaVision rejoins Paul Bettany’s ex-Avenger Vision as he tries to understand what it means to be an android. James Spader co-stars as his maker, the villainous AI Ultron.TimeiPlayer & BBC One, 11 October, 9pmThe bracing, brutal prison drama returns for series three, this time shifting focus to disturbed teens locked up in a young offenders institute. Siobhan Finneran reprises her role as a disenchanted chaplain, while David Tennant joins the cast as a custodial manager at the end of his tether.Killing AnnaChannel 4, 12 October, 11pmAn expat Syrian academic sees a video of a civilian massacre in Damascus and uses social media to track down the chief perpetrator; she then poses as Anna, a regime sympathiser, to encourage him to reveal details about his work in this remarkable documentary about vigilantism in the digital age.RAStaying in:GamesView image in fullscreenTrunk cost fallacy … Planet Zoo 2.Photograph: Frontier DevelopmentsPlanet Zoo 2PC, PS5, Xbox; out 14 OctoberThe popular zoo management sim returns, letting players build their animal kingdoms from a vast toolset of detailed habitats. The addition of aquariums and bird sanctuaries bring in new animals to observe and care for.Valor MortisPC, PS5, Xbox; out 14 OctoberA dead soldier of Napoleon’s army finds himself reanimated in an alternate 19th century filled with plague-ridden monsters. An epic fantasy adventure crammed with gutsy combat and supernatural peril are his certain fate.Keith StuartStaying in:AlbumsView image in fullscreenTough mudder … Remi Wolf.Photograph: Zachary GrayRemi Wolf – MudOut nowThe Californian genre alchemist returns with her third album of sideways pop. Less eccentric and neon-splattered than her previous outings, here Wolf contemplates heartbreak on the contemplative Bottle, while the stuttering Twiggy spins through memories via an earworm melody.MCDawn Richard – Creole CultureOut nowAfter two albums with avant-garde multi-instrumentalist Spencer Zahn, girlband member turned experimental art-pop practitioner Dawn Richard returns to more solo endeavours with this seventh album. Influenced by her heritage as a Black and Native American woman, songs such as the single Chuuuuurch are relentlessly thrilling.Troye Sivan – She’s the BestOut nowAfter the commercial highs of 2023’s Something to Give Each Other, there is a palpable sense of confidence on Australian banger merchant Sivan’s follow-up. Its title track is an experimental melange of spoken word and 90s trip-hop, while sugar rush banger Party contorts Madonna’s Music into new shapes.Jamie T – Ghosts (100 Days of Morning)Out nowFour years after scoring his first No 1 album, south Londoner Jamie T is back with this sixth record featuring a collaboration with Damon Albarn. As the title suggests, its lyrical focus is on various spectres of his past, with the nostalgia motherlode being the galloping lead single 3310.Staying in:Brain foodView image in fullscreen13 MinutesPodcastThe BBC’s space podcast returns with a new series on the Hubble telescope touching on its delayed and over-budget launch and the discovery of a fatal flaw in the build. We hear how scientists salvaged the operation.@DictionarycomInstagramManaging to make the mundane functionality of the dictionary more interesting, dictionary.com’s Insta account posts unusual “word of the day” picks, as well as analysis on the linguistic choices of artists such as Taylor Swift.The Last First: Winter K2Apple TV, out nowThis vertigo-inducing film follows the extreme climbers who in 2021 attempted to be the first to summit the Pakistani‑Chinese K2 mountain in winter. During the gruelling expedition they exposed how dangerously commercialised modern climbing has become.Ammar KaliaExplore more on these topicsCultureGoing out, staying inDanceTheatreTelevisionArtGamesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Five Great Reads: unmarked graves, Happy Mondays, and a childhood without sugar |  | The Guardian
description: The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Miles Herbert
Author: Miles Herbert
Headline: The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Miles Herbert
Content: Composite: Guardian design/Drew Leventhal/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian design/Drew Leventhal/Getty ImagesFive Great Reads newsletterFive Great Reads: unmarked graves, Happy Mondays, and a childhood without sugarThe Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected byMiles HerbertGet this in your inbox every weekend.Sign up for Five Great Reads hereMiles HerbertSat 10 Oct 2026 00.24 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 00.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHello and welcome to the weekend.This selection of reads from across the Guardian has chronicles of evolution, investigations and interviews which ask us to think about how we remember our loved ones when they are gone, and – of course – stories that leave you with a little something sweet.Enjoy.1. Unmarked gravesView image in fullscreenElaine Grady was a friend of Peter Giesel, whose remains were sent to a communal, unmarked grave in Sydney in June.Photograph: Drew Leventhal/The GuardianPeter Giesel was buried inan unmarked communal grave. The state government laid Giesel to rest in a cemetery on the outskirts of Sydney in a single plot with three others. This week, a Guardian Australia investigation found there are more than 100 cases like his across New South Wales. The Guardian revealed Vietnam veterans, rough sleepers and other impoverished Australians are being buried in graves often holding four or more people, a practice relatives such as Giesel’s sister, Nicole, have described as “unspeakable” and “a disgrace”.Persons without means:This is the designation the state gives to those who are unable to afford their own funerals. Over the course of the investigation, the Guardian discovered at least 18 individuals known to homelessness services in Sydney who have been placed in unmarked graves in the last 10 years.Notable quote:“How could such a heartless thing happen to someone who gave so much of his heart to others,” asks Giesel’s friend Elaine Grady (pictured).An immediate response:When asked about the revelations, NSW Health delivered an apology to the dead and their loved ones, acknowledging they had not always been treated with the dignity and respect they deserved.How long will it take to read:Less than seven minutes.Further reading:Shared gravesand stories such asJayne and Barbara’s, have brought this issue tonational attention.2. A new ‘Lonely Generation’View image in fullscreenIn the book The Lonely Generation, Dr Michelle Lim seeks to dispel myths around loneliness.Photograph: Yutthana Gaetgeaw/Getty ImagesYoung people around the world arelonelier than ever, and examples of this are not hard to find. In online forums, users ask: “How do you deal with touch starvation?” Another asks: “The loneliness is unbearable, is anyone else experiencing this?” The answer to the latter question is yes. FromGermanytoAustraliatothe UK, studies show teenagers and young adults are finding social connections harder to form.Why?The list is long. In her new book, the loneliness researcher and clinical psychologist Dr Michelle Lim examines why young people have turned toward solitude. She cites a long list of overlapping factors, including hyper-competitive education culture, social media, shifting family dynamics, the cost-of-living crisis, the grief many are still feeling from the Covid pandemic, and the rise of automation, “which means a trip to the supermarket can be conducted entirely without speaking to another human”. Young adults are simply not being offered the opportunities to form meaningful connections, Lim says.“People are getting used to being alone”:Lim’s biggest fear is what she calls “social atrophy”. Young people, she writes, can fall into what she calls the “loneliness loop”. When you experience loneliness, it can cause you to run away from further social interaction out of fear, making connections harder to come by.How long will it take to read:Five minutes of solitude.Further reading:Community-maxxing, and makingnew friends and connectionsas adults.3. Drugs, drink and dancing with Bez from the Happy MondaysView image in fullscreenBez at home in Herefordshire with his sausage dogs, Snoop and Yoko.Photograph: Francesca Jones/The GuardianTaking drugs, drinking heavily and dancing to the tunes of the Happy Mondays on stage made Bez famous. The story goes, as the Manchester music scene was exploding, band member Shaun Ryder urged Bez (whose real name is Mark Berry) to jump on stage with the band when they were supporting New Order. His “wild-eyed dancing” is now synonymous with the music itself, and as the band celebrate the 35th anniversary of their landmark album Pills ‘n’ Thrills and Bellyaches,Bez is back at itas the Happy Mondays go on a global tour.A change for the good:After decades of partying, one might expect Bez to show signs of wear from his life on the road with a rock band. But when interviewer Emine Saner showed up at “his lovely cottage, down a rural track in Herefordshire”, Bez appeared unscathed by the years of drugs and drinking. Having given up cocaine and sugar, the former24 hour party personnow “juices every day, eats only organic food, drinks filtered water and works out with weights in his garden”.Notable quote:“There’s sheep everywhere now,” Bez told Saner. At first, Saner took it as “a reference to our zombified society”, but he meant “actual sheep in the field” they just entered.How long will it take to read:Just over five minutes, giving you enough time toStep On.Further reading:Which isthe bestHappy Mondays song?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toFive Great ReadsEach week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion4. My sister Nicole married OJ SimpsonView image in fullscreen‘When you are in a cycle like Nicole … you are the only one who realises how dangerous that situation can be,’ says Denise Brown.Photograph: Mikaela Martin/The GuardianDenise Brown’s sister Nicole wasmurdered by OJ Simpson. On the last night the two sisters spent together, Nicole looked out the window to see Simpson driving by. “He’s constantly following me,” she told Brown. After her sister’s murder and the evidence of long-term abuse that emerged during the trial, Brown became a campaigner against domestic violence. She sat down with the Guardian to discuss what she wishes she had known before her sister’s death, and how she hopes her new book can save lives.It’s rarely simple to leave:Brown says she told her sister all the wrong things. “You’ve got to leave him. You’ve got to get out of this situation. What are you doing?” she told Nicole. Brown now realises she was being unsupportive at the time, and has learned it is often not easy for a victim to leave. “Batterers usually threaten to take children away, threaten family members. When you are in a cycle like Nicole – like a lot of victims of domestic violence – was in, you are the only one who realises how dangerous that situation can be.”The car chase:The day after Nicole’s funeral, Simpson was scheduled to turn himself in to the police, but elected to go on the run. While millions watched on TV, Brown says she joined in the chase. “We were out of our minds. We got on the road, but he was so far ahead of us. I mean, come on, really?” She laughs at herself, but says: “It was a time of our lives that was insane.”How long will it take to read:Five minutes.Further reading:Morestories of survival.In Australia,domestic and family violence counsellingis available from Full Stop Australia on 1800 385 578. In the UK, call the nationaldomestic abuse helplineon 0808 2000 247, or visitWomen’s Aid. In the US, the domestic violence hotline is 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). Other international helplines may be found viawww.befrienders.org5. The generation raised on sugar rationsView image in fullscreenChildren enjoy a portable, healthy snack – carrot on a stick – amid wartime rationing in July 1941.Photograph: Ashwood/Getty ImagesIn the dark days after the second world war in Britain, many foods, including sugar, remained rationed. Adults had just 3 tbsp (40g) a day to stretch between cups of tea and desserts. Children were offered even less, with the very young expected to have no sugar at all. But then the brakes came off, and sugar consumption in the UK almost doubled. Now scientists arelooking back on this erato study the impact of sugar on our health.Notable quote: “History created an experiment that we could never deliberately run over a human lifetime,” says Dr Jiazhen Zheng at Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.What have they learned?Using data from theUK Biobankto compare the health of people born shortly before and after sugar rationing ended in the UK, scientists from the University of Southern California found that the longer people had spent under rationing, the lower their risk of developing type 2 diabetes and high blood pressure in mid- to later life. Another study, this one led by Zheng in Hong Kong, found reduced sugar exposure was associated with a lower risk of a growing list of health conditions. “In our work,” Zheng says, “we have seen associations with cardiovascular disease, liver disease, respiratory health, dementia and, more recently, broader measures of ageing.”How long will it take to read:A sweet three-and-a-half minutes.Further reading:Everythingyou need to knowabout sugar.Sign upIf you would like to receive these Five Great Reads to your email inbox every weekend,sign up here. And check out outthe full list of our local and international newsletters.Explore more on these topicsFive Great Reads newsletternewslettersShareReuse this content

title: From Carrie to Olivia Dean: the week in rave reviews | Culture | The Guardian
description: Stephen King’s high-school scare-’em-up is reinvented for 2026, and the pop superstar brings the love in her feelgood live extravaganza. Here’s the pick of the week’s culture, taken from the Guardian’s best-rated reviews
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Stephen King’s high-school scare-’em-up is reinvented for 2026, and the pop superstar brings the love in her feelgood live extravaganza. Here’s the pick of the week’s culture, taken from the Guardian’s best-rated reviews
Content: Scream queen … Carrie.Photograph: Courtesy of PrimeView image in fullscreenScream queen … Carrie.Photograph: Courtesy of PrimeThe week in reviewsCultureFrom Carrie to Olivia Dean: the week in rave reviewsStephen King’s high-school scare-’em-up is reinvented for 2026, and the pop superstar brings the love in her feelgood live extravaganza. Here’s the pick of the week’s culture, taken from the Guardian’s best-rated reviewsSat 10 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTVIf you only watch one, make it …Damilola: The Untold StoryBBC iPlayer; available nowSummed up in a sentenceJohn Boyega opens up for the first time about being with childhood friend Damilola Taylor on the night he was murdered.What our reviewer said“Damilola: The Untold Story swerves true-crime cliches of graphic reconstructions and psychological profiling. Instead, the scenes it chooses to recreate are stylised but disquieting.”Lucy ManganRead the full reviewFurther readingStar Wars actor John Boyega on the day his 10-year-old school friend Damilola Taylor was killed: ‘It kept me up at night because I was just with the guy’Pick of the restCarriePrime Video; available nowSummed up in a sentenceA witty, smart remake of the classic horror movie based on Stephen King’s terrifying debut.What our reviewer said“It has intelligence, wit and things to say about the fathomless potential for good and ill in the teenage heart.”Lucy ManganRead the full reviewBelBBC iPlayer; available nowSummed up in a sentenceA tender, grief-stricken documentary about singer-songwriter Beldina Odenyo, who took her own life in 2021, featuring her sister trying to finish her album.What our reviewer said“A sensitively drawn portrait of a visionary artist haunted by trauma.”Lucy ManganRead the full reviewPierreChannel 4; available nowSummed up in a sentenceDavid Harewood stars in a noirish series that feels like a milestone for Black British crime drama.What our reviewer said“Establishes itself with confident concision, which is largely down to Harewood’s performance.”Ellen E JonesRead the full reviewYou may have missed …My Brilliant CareerNetflix; available nowView image in fullscreenAussie rules … Phillipa Northeast as Sybylla Melvin and Jake Dunn as Frank.Photograph: Netflix/PASummed up in a sentenceA joyous, witty and beautiful adaptation of the classic feminist novel about a young woman in 1890s Australia who rebels against society’s expectations.What our reviewer said“Sybylla, the charmingly irrepressible and irrepressibly charming heroine, is played utterly convincingly and with vim, vigour and joy by Philippa Northeast. Creator Liz Doran must have wept with happiness when they found an actor capable of bringing so much to an already glorious script – and who embodies the joie de vivre upon which so much of the plot, as everyone she meets becomes part of her orbit, depends.”Lucy ManganRead the full reviewFilmIf you only watch one, make it …The Social ReckoningIn cinemas nowView image in fullscreenHitting the Mark … Jeremy Strong in The Social Reckoning.Photograph: SonySummed up in a sentenceAaron Sorkin’s jittery sequel, with Jeremy Strong as Facebook founder Mark Zuckerberg, is the background to a thriller about whistleblower Frances Haugen (Mikey Madison).What our reviewer said“Mikey Madison sympathetically plays the unhappy, principled, supersmart Haugen, who is dismissed as a ‘disrupter’ – and Sorkin leaves it to us to notice that this in other circumstances is what oligarchs smugly call themselves.”Peter BradshawRead the full reviewFurther readingBig tech goes to Hollywood: is Silicon Valley ready for a silver-screen reckoning?Pick of the restThe Lost Children of TuamIn cinemas nowView image in fullscreenMonica Dolan in The Lost Children of Tuam.Photograph: Enda Bowe/PASummed up in a sentenceDeeply serious retelling of Ireland’s devastating tragedy, with Monica Dolan superb as the amateur historian who uncovered the horror of mass graves at a mother and baby home.What our reviewer said“It is usual to say that a film like The Lost Children of Tuam is a difficult watch – but in fact it’s the opposite: hard to look away.”Cath ClarkeRead the full reviewFurther reading‘She never accepted no’: Liam Neeson on dogged heroine behind Tuam mass baby grave film24 Hour Party PeopleIn cinemas nowSummed up in a sentenceMichael Winterbottom’s freewheeling 2002 film about the Manchester music scene stars Steve Coogan as post-punk champion Tony Wilson in a daring metatextual paean.What our reviewer said“The music itself is not used in the jukebox slam way that another director might have chosen, to direct mood and atmosphere and help create the light and shade of narrative. It always seems to stay diegetically in the background as the story just rolls onward, all its crazy episodes and incidents apparently not having any real emotional effect on Wilson, even as his empire collapses financially.”Peter BradshawRead the full reviewThe CraftIn cinemas nowSummed up in a sentenceCult high-school witch horror rereleased for its 30th anniversary, starring Robin Tunney and Neve Campbell, tackles the sensitivities of teenage anxiety with energy and confidence.What our reviewer said“It’s a movie to compare to Heathers or Mean Girls but with a supernatural edge, a flourish of scariness where the comedy or sexiness might otherwise go.”Peter BradshawRead the full reviewNow streaming …InterceptedTrue Story;
