title: Carrick ‘massively disappointed’ after United drop points against 10-man Spurs | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: After a 1-1 draw that left Roberto De Zerbi praising 10-man Spurs’ character, his Manchester United counterpart reflected on the club’s worst start since 1986
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: After a 1-1 draw that left Roberto De Zerbi praising 10-man Spurs’ character, his Manchester United counterpart reflected on the club’s worst start since 1986
Content: Michael Carrick had a lot to reflect on after Manchester United conceded a late equaliser to a team with 10 men.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersView image in fullscreenMichael Carrick had a lot to reflect on after Manchester United conceded a late equaliser to a team with 10 men.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersManchester UnitedCarrick ‘massively disappointed’ after United drop points against 10-man SpursSix points from six games is worst start since 1986De Zerbi praises Spurs’ character after late equaliserJamie Jacksonat Old TraffordSat 10 Oct 2026 16.19 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 16.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Carrick was left “massively disappointed” by Manchester United’s 1-1 draw with Tottenham at Old Trafford and admitted they need more points after managing six from their opening six league games.This is United’s poorest start to the season since 1986, Saturday’s draw coming when concedingDominic Solanke’s added-time equaliserfor 10-man Spurs, following Rodrigo Bentancur’s 78th-minute red card. The midfielder was sent off five minutes after Bryan Mbeumo’s opener had left United heading for only a second league victory.Solanke strikes late as 10-man Spurs salvage point at Manchester UnitedRead moreCarrick said: “I am massively disappointed with the result, for sure. A mixed performance. I’m not happy with the amount of points that we’ve had so far. There’s no hiding from that. I think it could have been different for a couple of little things here or there, but the reality is the reality, we’ve got to accept it, you know. We need to put things in a direction, in a positive direction quite quickly, that’s pretty plain.”United were disjointed throughout. The manager was asked if he felt let down by the players. “I don’t feel let down, because you can make mistakes. You can make mistakes, things go against you,” said Carrick. “I’ve made mistakes in games, and it’s not so much letting everyone down. We’ve all got standards, we’ve all got levels, the players have got levels and standards, and they hold their hands up at times when something goes against them.”United’s fans jeered at times during the game. “When things aren’t quite going to plan, I understand the reaction at times,” said the manager. “Obviously, it hurts a lot. It’s not nice to go through, but sometimes you have to go through it, that’s how it is.“I care as much as anybody about this place, so sometimes you could say too much because then it overspills. But it’s coming from a good place, really, and so I understand it.”View image in fullscreenLuke Shaw (right) clashes with Rodrigo Bentancur (centre) and other Tottenham players.Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesBentancur might have caused a serious injury had a scissors-challenge on Shaw connected.Roberto De Zerbibacked his midfielder, who was sent off for a head-butt in the resulting melee.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I kiss Rodrigo and say thanks,” said the Spurs manager. “It is clear it is a mistake from Rodrigo, it is not the right reaction in football but in that moment maybe with 10 players we played with more courage, more energy and for a long time Tottenham played without this blood this character. I am the coach and I want to see this character every game.”While Spurs have only three points and remain winless, they are now off the bottom though remain in the relegation zone. “Today has been the game where for the first time this season we showed we are a team, we played for the teammates, we played together,” said De Zerbi.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedMichael CarrickTottenham HotspurRoberto De ZerbinewsShareReuse this content

title: Henderson and João Pedro lead Chelsea charge against Bournemouth | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Jordan Henderson scored his first two goals for Chelsea in a 5-1 thrashing of Bournemouth at Stamford Bridge
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Jordan Henderson scored his first two goals for Chelsea in a 5-1 thrashing of Bournemouth at Stamford Bridge
Content: Jordan Henderson celebrates with Cole Palmer (right) after scoring his second goal, and Chelsea’s fifth, against Bournemouth.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenJordan Henderson celebrates with Cole Palmer (right) after scoring his second goal, and Chelsea’s fifth, against Bournemouth.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersPremier LeagueHenderson and João Pedro lead Chelsea charge against BournemouthJacob Steinbergat Stamford BridgeSat 10 Oct 2026 12.18 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 16.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWatch and learn, kids. The day began with one for the youth audience, Cole Palmer appearing on a live stream to explain the thinking behind his latest contract extension. It finished with the oldest player to joinChelseaduring the BlueCo era stealing the show with an all-action midfield display.Even Palmer was happy to step aside as Jordan Henderson used his right foot to curl home a free-kick that drew comparisons with one of David Beckham’s specials. It was Henderson’s second spectacular strike – he marked his home debut by opening the scoring with a bending effort from 20 yards and also laid on an assist for Morgan Rogers to make it 2-0 – although it is fair to assume that Xabi Alonso did not bring the veteran to Stamford Bridge for his goalscoring prowess.The idea was more to lift standards in the dressing room. Chelsea needed experience and are surely better off now a 36-year-old starting for them in midfield is no longer a laughable notion.Aston Villa’s wait for home win goes on after Ajer hits back for BrentfordRead more“We signed him for everything,” Alonso said of Henderson. “If he’s able to score two beauties as today, we are more than happy for him. But apart from the goals he’s done many good things. He’s always involved in the action, always giving solutions to teammates.”Henderson set the tone for Chelsea, driving into tackles and raising the tempo with the urgency of his passing. He joined from Brentford in the summer and is keen to do more than make up the numbers. Chelsea, up to fifth after their first win in four league games, were more stable with Henderson alongside Moisés Caicedo, who lasted 72 minutes on his long-awaited return from a calf injury.View image in fullscreenMoisés Caicedo (left) returned to the Chelsea team after a spell on the sidelines due to injury.Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesAlonso, who was without Reece James after the captain picked up a knee injury in training on Friday, was still disappointed his side have now gone 22 league games without a clean sheet. They were 3-0 up when Evanilson pulled a goal back forBournemouth, who are finding the transition from Andoni Iraola to Marco Rose trickier than anticipated and must manage games better.Even so, Alonso was pleased with Chelsea’s level. They have scored in the first 10 minutes in five of their six league games this season and are a match for anyone when the front three of Palmer, Rogers and João Pedro take full flight.Palmer had a point to prove after having his desire to play for England questioned by Thomas Tuchel last month. His impact was immediate, although it owed much to Bournemouth’s naivety. The visitors lined up in a flat 4-4-2 formation and gave Palmer far too much space when he sauntered down the right in the first minute.It was encouraging to see Palmer moving freely, especially after Alonso’s admission that the playmaker’s decision to sit out the international break was related to last season’s groin pain, but Bournemouth were a soft touch. There was no challenge on the 24-year-old, who has displayed his commitment to Chelsea by signing on until 2034.Palmer floated into the area, turned and rolled the ball to Henderson, who hit it first time with the inside of his right foot and saw his bending effort go in off the inside of the right post.View image in fullscreenJordan Henderson (centre) give Chelsea an early lead with a fine finish.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersThere were 68 seconds on the clock when Henderson became Chelsea’s oldest scorer in thePremier Leaguesince John Terry in May 2017. “We knew Chelsea are a team that starts well,” Rose said. “It was our responsibility that we didn’t react the right way with this information.”Bournemouth were overwhelmed. Chelsea pushed again in the third minute, Palmer’s flick freeing Pedro Neto to test Djordje Petrovic. The ball broke loose and Henderson swept a pass to Rogers, who cut in from the left and his shot flew in via a deflection off Antonio Silva.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIpswich’s O’Shea and Ouattara stun Fulham with last-gasp comeback winRead moreThe focus switched to Bournemouth’s long list of absentees. Justin Kluivert and Eli Junior Kroupi are big losses in attack. Alex Scott, the subject of multiple bids from Chelsea in the summer,exacerbated a thigh problemduringa scintillating displayforEngland against Croatia last Saturday.These are worrying times for Bournemouth, who are winless after six league games. Goal difference is keeping them out of the bottom three and they struggled without Scott’s energy and quality in midfield. Ryan Christie and Tyler Adams were overrun and Silva had a nightmare at the back, his error at the start of the second half allowing Neto to nip in and set up João Pedro to make it 3-0 with an emphatic shot.Bournemouth had chances during the first half, Christie, Rayan and Silva drawing saves from Emiliano Martínez, but it suited Chelsea for a basketball game to develop.View image in fullscreenA tidy finish from close range gave João Pedro a second goal of the game and Chelsea a fourth.Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesThere were echoes of past battles between Alonso and Rose in the Bundesliga. Rose, who ended Alonso’s 35-game unbeaten run with Bayer Leverkusen when he was RB Leipzig’s manager, was a distinct second-best this time. Evanilson bundled in from a corner, but Chelsea were rampant.The fourth goal arrived when Rogers found the overlapping Pep Chavarria, whose low cross was gobbled up by João Pedro. Alonso, who had become increasingly frantic on the touchline, relaxed. He was a great midfielder in his day and will have appreciated the technique when Henderson’s free-kick flew beyond the reach of Petrovic.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueChelseaBournemouthmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Sleightholme hat-trick fires up Northampton in 11-try blast of Bath  | Prem Rugby | The Guardian
description: Ollie Sleightholme helped himself to a hat-trick and Tommy Freeman two of Northampton’s 11 aginst Bath in the second-highest scoring match in the league’s history
Author: Gerard Meagher
Headline: Ollie Sleightholme helped himself to a hat-trick and Tommy Freeman two of Northampton’s 11 aginst Bath in the second-highest scoring match in the league’s history
Content: Fin Smith starts the Saints rolling, diving over to score the first of their 11 tries against Bath.Photograph: David Rogers/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFin Smith starts the Saints rolling, diving over to score the first of their 11 tries against Bath.Photograph: David Rogers/Getty ImagesPrem RugbySleightholme hat-trick fires up Northampton in 11-try blast of BathPrem Rugby: Northampton 71-48 BathSecond-highest scoring match in league’s historyGerard Meagherat DPD Stadium at Franklin's GardensSat 10 Oct 2026 12.22 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 14.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleChalk this up as a victory for theNorthamptonKnicks. In a remarkable match with 18 tries, 119 points were racked up and defence relegated to the merest of afterthoughts, the defending Prem champions romped home.Ollie Sleightholme helped himself to a hat-trick and Tommy Freeman two of Northampton’s 11, in the second-highest scoring match in the league’s history, behindSaints’ 94-33 win over Bristolin May.The Spurs of Prem Rugby: how Harlequins lost their swaggerRead moreBath, for their part, scored seven tries but ended up comfortably beaten. For it was a contest that left us questioning much of what we thought we knew about the sport. Tries are supposed to come at a premium, not as an inevitability.Some wonderful ones were scored, the fly-halves Fin Smith and Finn Russell showcased their array of tricks, but when 69 defenders are beaten in 80 minutes, you are left wondering quite what you have witnessed.A penny for the thoughts of the England head coach, Steve Borthwick. If England try to play with this sort of abandon at next year’s World Cup they are in for a rude awakening. Knockout international rugby does not give out tries for free.Quick GuideCaluori and Itoje lead Saracens past BristolShowNoah Caluori [pictured] made a try-scoring return forSaracensasBristolsaw their bright start to the Gallagher Prem hit the buffers in a comprehensive 30-7 away defeat. Making his first appearance of the season after undergoing wrist surgery, the England wing  produced the opening touch down to continue the blistering form that catapulted him to fame inn 2025-26.Alex O’Driscoll and Jack Bracken also crossed on top of a penalty try as Saracens reacted to their disappointing loss to Sale  by taking Bristol apart in the second half with Ben Earl and Maro Itoje particularly influential. Two penalties and a conversion from Owen Farrell helped ensure the Bears are still searching for a first win at StoneX Stadium in eight visits.The Saracens head coach, Joe Shaw, said Itoje’s summer break has given him a 'new lease of life' after watching the England captain star at blindside flanker, rather than his customary position of second-row.'Maro was unbelievable,' Shaw said. 'England and the club have given him a new lease of life by giving him the summer off. It’s the first one he’s had since he was 19. He had a full pre-season with us. He’s as fresh as a daisy. He’s training so well.'His body’s in good nick,' Shaw added. It’ll benefit not just us, but it’ll benefit England in the long run going into next year’s World Cup.'Press AssociationPhotograph: Gaspafotos/Getty Images EuropeWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.It was, however, entertaining. The comparison with basketball is often held up as a criticism by purists who love nothing more than an arm-wrestle, but not for nothing are the Harlem Globetrotters one of the hottest tickets in town. It is just that we are having to recalibrate what we thought we knew about the domestic game. A number of directors of rugby are convinced that while we arewitnessing an attacking boom, defence will soon be back in vogue. On this evidence we are still waiting.Maybe it is too curmudgeonly to complain. The skills showcased by both sides in their ability to capitalise on turnover ball took the breath away at times. Most neutrals would agree that it beats a 9-6 dogfight in the mud. But you are still left with a feeling that you have watched an 80-minute highlights reel rather than a match that ebbs and flows. It is a dream for marketing departments, but it feels like sport for the instant gratification generation.“I know people will say it is too easy to score, but you’re not going to please everybody,” said Northampton’s director of rugby Phil Dowson. “I think there’s a balance. We don’t want it to be 99-88. It’s not basketball, but we also don’t want a 9-3.“I used to have a coach called Mike Friday and one of his sayings was that ‘you can’t defend good rugby’ and there’s lots of good rugby being played.“I have no doubt there will be some games this season that will be tough, ugly, horrible and nasty. But we want to be able to enjoy and reward great rugby. And, by the way, basketball is selling loads of tickets to sold out arenas.”Northampton drew first blood with Smith cruising through a gap after a lovely show and go, but not to be outdone Russell replied with a moment of magic of his own, offloading to Arthur Green, who fed Tom Carr-Smith to score. Bath’s ascendancy was soon rewarded again with Charlie Griffin squeezing over on the left.Saints responded with Sleightholme finishing a glorious move – showcasing the kind of dexteritythe All Blacks had showna few hours earlier – before James Pater put his winger clear.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe BreakdownThe latest rugby union news and analysis, plus all the week's action reviewedEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenOllie Sleightholme breaks clear before scoring the second of his three tries in a high-scoring collision with Bath.Photograph: David Rogers/Getty ImagesFreeman was soon in on the act before Bath came again when Archie Griffin barrelled over and Green went over on the left once more. The young hooker, Kepu Tuipulotu, played eye-catching roles in both. Fraser Dingwall then dummied his way over for the eighth try of the first half.Two tries apiece inside 11 minutes of the second half kept Bath’s noses ahead. Green forced his way over on the left soon after the restart before Pater scampered clear after Santi Carreras had spilled a long pass near halfway. The Argentina full-back made amends by waltzing over before Josh Kemeny was released on the left.Alex Mitchell broke away for Northampton’s seventh try to restore the lead at 45-41. Bath introduced their Bomb Squad, but proceeded to be blown away and by the end of the third quarter Northampton were further ahead.Quick GuideNorthampton 71-48 Bath: teams and scorersShowNorthampton:Pater (Belleau 75); Freeman, Hutchinson, Dingwall (capt), Sleightholme; Smith, Mitchell (McParland 62); Iyogun (Fischetti 57), Langdon (Smith 57), Kundiona (Neculai 57), Coles, Van der Mescht (Prowse 46), Kemeny (Lockett 72), Pollock (Taylor 57), Chick.TriesSmith, Sleightholme 3, Freeman 2, Dingwall, Pater, Kemeny, Mitchell, ColesConsSmith 8.Bath:Carreras; Cokanasiga, Ojomoh, Redpath, C Griffin (Davies 71); Russell, Carr-Smith; Kirk (Obano 54), Tuipulotu (Dunn 54), A Griffin (Stuart 54), Jeanes (Coetzee 54), Molony (Ewels 54), Bayliss, Reid (capt; Reid 23), Green.TriesCarr-Smith, C Griffin, A Griffin, Green 2, Carreras, BaylissConsRussell 5PenRussellSin-binBayliss 27, Lawrence 63.RefereeMatthew Carley.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Freeman began a flowing move inside his own 22 before Sleightholme had the pace to finish in the corner. Sleightholme was in the mood by this point and, after Ollie Lawrence had been sent to the sin-bin, he wriggled his way through the defence to complete his hat-trick.Bayliss kept Bath in the hunt, but scores for Alex Coles and another for Freeman gave Northampton a comfortable ride to the finish line.“Maybe 50 is not the margin any more,” said Bath’s Johann van Graan. “To get 50 was at some stage a big achievement, now we score 48 away from home. But I would say that is a big positive in the game of rugby. Maybe it evens out as the season goes.”Explore more on these topicsPrem RugbyRugby unionNorthamptonBathmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Real Madrid’s Vinícius Júnior sent off for hair-pulling in victory over Villarreal | La Liga | The Guardian
description: Vinícius Júnior’s goal was disallowed and the substitute was dismissed after a VAR review showed he had pulled Nathan Saliba’s hair
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Vinícius Júnior’s goal was disallowed and the substitute was dismissed after a VAR review showed he had pulled Nathan Saliba’s hair
Content: Real Madrid’s Vinícius Júnior is held back by Antonio Rüdiger after being sent off.Photograph: Ángel Martínez/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenReal Madrid’s Vinícius Júnior is held back by Antonio Rüdiger after being sent off.Photograph: Ángel Martínez/Getty ImagesLa LigaReal Madrid’s Vinícius Júnior sent off for hair-pulling in victory over VillarrealAFPSat 10 Oct 2026 17.38 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 18.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYan Diomandé earned Real Madrid a tight 1-0 victory over Villarreal to keep them six points behind La Liga leaders Barcelona, even though wingerVinícius Júniorwas sent off for hair pulling.Vinícius, on as a substitute, scored but his goal was disallowed and then he was dismissed after a VAR review showed he had pulled the hair of Villarreal’s Nathan Saliba.European football: Gordon boosts Barcelona and Bayern battle backRead moreJosé Mourinho’s side battled through the final stages with 10 men, holding on to win and provisionally going third. But the red card left a bitter taste for Real, with Vinícius running the risk of a potential ban which could keep him out of El Clásico on 25 October.“I don’t know what’s going on with the referees, with this red card, I don’t understand,” said the Madrid midfielder Aurélien Tchouaméni. “But the most important thing is the victory.”Kylian Mbappé was fit to start the match for Madrid after suffering a knee problem playing for France during the international break. There were a smattering of whistles for the superstar forward, with some fans believing he has been unprofessional in recent weeks, but also applause from others.Mbappé, acandidate for the Ballon d’Ortrophy later this month, was Madrid’s most threatening player in the first half, although he had little competition.View image in fullscreenPlayers react as the referee, Isidro Díaz de Mera Escuderos, sends off Vinícius Júnior.Photograph: Denis Doyle/Getty ImagesMourinho started with out-of-form Vinícius on the bench, following his trips to Australia and India with Brazil during the international break.Madrid improved defensively, giving Villarreal few chances of note, but struggled to build much in attack themselves in a drab opening half.Mbappé struck the post from Álvaro Carreras’s lay-off as Madrid pushed Villarreal back early on. Villarreal soon gained a foothold and restricted Madrid’s opportunities, until Mbappé forced a good save from Peter Gulacsi.There was some more mild whistling for Madrid’s display from their fans at half-time, but soon they were able tocelebrate summer arrival Diomandé’s first goal for the club. The Ivorian winger, Madrid’s record signing, produced a sharp low finish into the far corner after good work from Federico Valverde to play him in.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenYan Diomandé scores the only goal of the game at the Bernabéu.Photograph: Óscar del Pozo/AFP/Getty ImagesVinícius thought he had doubled Madrid’s lead after Jude Bellingham charged in down the left and cut the ball back for him. However the winger’s joy turned to anger after the referee, Isidro Díaz de Mera Escuderos, was called to watch Vinícius’s hair pull on Saliba in the buildup by VAR and sent off the Brazilian, disallowing his goal.Madrid’s Belgian goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois, who had made a couple of smart saves earlier in the half, then produced an acrobatic stop to thwart Carlos Romero.Mbappé was denied again by the Hungarian goalkeeper Gulasci as the forward left the Bernabéu frustrated in his hunt for goals, although his team were able to clinch three important points to stay on Barcelona’s trail.Explore more on these topicsLa LigaReal MadridVinícius JúniorVillarrealmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Why we’re stuck with a Premier League in the clutches of the global mega-rich  | Premier League | The Guardian
description: There’s little prospect of a troubled model changing in a country that welcomes wealthy international owners with open arms
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: There’s little prospect of a troubled model changing in a country that welcomes wealthy international owners with open arms
Content: The Etihad Stadium at sunset. Manchester City’s Gulf-based owners are a world away from the local businessmen who once coveted English clubs.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe Etihad Stadium at sunset. Manchester City’s Gulf-based owners are a world away from the local businessmen who once coveted English clubs.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersInside footballPremier LeagueWhy we’re stuck with a Premier League in the clutches of the global mega-richJonathan WilsonThere’s little prospect of the model changing in a country that welcomes wealthy international owners with open armsSat 10 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTShareFootball, the world’s most popular sport, played by laws drawn up in London in 1863. ThePremier Leagueis the UK’s greatest soft power export. Premier League clubs are owned by a deputy prime minister of Abu Dhabi, the public investment fund of Saudi Arabia, a billionaire based in Monaco for tax reasons and a disappointing assortment of investors and private equity funds. And what, really, could be more British than that? Football truly is the national game.Whatthe Manchester City casehas exposed is just how difficult it is to regulate some of the richest and most powerful bodies in the world. While the wait for the verdict was frustrating, it’s perhaps unavoidable given the possibility of legal objection at every turn when a leaked email from City’s in-house lawyer during Uefa’s action against the club had threatened to “spend 30 million on the 50 best lawyersin the world to sue them for the next 10 years”. You didn’t get that with Albert Alexander Sr or Peter Swales.Everton owner The Friedkin Group exploring sale of club after two yearsRead moreFootball clubs in England and Wales still represent their communities, a relationship that may be strained in certain cases by the pressures of a globalised entertainment economy, but remains broadly true. Arsenal can feel like the club of choice for the nouveau fan from across the world, butthe scenes of celebrationwhen they ended their 22-year wait for the league title last season were an undeniable expression of local pride.The idea that there was ever an idyll when clubs were run by benevolent potentates for the good of those communities is romantic nonsense. But just because there was no golden age is not to say that the situation has always been as bleak as this.How did we get into a situation in which clubs are flotsam on the swirling currents of geopolitics and the world economy? Chelsea alone in the past four years have had aRussian oligarch forced to sell the clubafter falling under UK government sanctions, while a subsequent American co-owner has been forced to sell his minority stake after his insurance business came under federal investigation in the US. It’s a curious world in which the professional gamblers feel like a welcome breath of fresh air.View image in fullscreenChelsea fans hold banner during a peaceful, fan-led protest calling for accountability and structural change at Chelsea Football Club in January. Fans criticised the club’s ownership model, recruitment strategy, and overall leadership since the takeover, urging an end to micromanagement and a return to long-term ambition at the top level of English and European football.Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty ImagesThe days of the local businessmen, the owners of mines, shipyards and factories, the hauliers and scrap-metal dealers, are gone. Some invested because they genuinely wanted to give back to their communities or liked the sport. Others did so because it was easier to fund a local football club than to improve working conditions or pay a proper wage. And some did so because, wrongly in most cases, they thought there may be money to be made.But nobody should think those were days of purity. The decrepitude of English stadiums in the 1980s should caution anybody who thinks football was uncomplicatedly better then.The contradiction has always lain at the heart of English football. Clubs represent their communities and for fans support becomes an aspect of identity, a link to family and place and past, a role that has only become more significant as the influence of traditional institutions – the church, the workplace, the social club – has faded. Yet fans in England have almost never owned their club, which in part underlies the present crisis.That is not to say fan ownership is a panacea. There is much to be admired about the German 50+1 model which, to oversimplify, ensures outside investors can never own a majority of the club. But it has not prevented Bayern Munich from winning 13 of the past 14 Bundesliga titles. Some sort of recognition that a club is not just a business, that it has a community function might, though, have prevented the free-for-all that has led to this mess.At least when most owners were local, there was some understanding of what the club meant to its area, and a recognition that exploitation or neglect could have direct consequences. No owner wanted demonstrations at the directors’ entrance, or to be jeered as he drove the streets in his Rolls-Royce, or to have his car showroom boycotted because he put up ticket prices then sold a popular centre-forward at a knockdown price. The distant majority shareholder in his boardroom in Los Angeles, his penthouse in Monte Carlo or his luxury villa on the Gulf feels the sting less keenly.Richard Scudamore, the former chief executive of the Premier League, who did more to shape the modern competition, for good and for ill, than any other individual always spoke of being “neutral about ownership models”. Essentially that meant taking the money without worrying too much about where it came from. The current Premier League is the consequence: a gleaming, world-leading edifice, but built on what?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPerhaps it’s not fair to be too harsh on the Premier League. This is not just modern football; it is modern Britain. As Miguel Delaney and Jack Pitt-Brookeargued on the Libero podcast this week, the Premier League is a direct outcome of Blairite economic policy, a point made clear inOliver Bullough’s Butler to the WorldIn the book he described the classic New Labour approach as “allowing something, making money from it and attempting to solve the problems it causes after they’ve occurred”.Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekendRead moreBut how do you solve those problems in football? How can football extricate itself from the clutches of the mega-rich? Regulation, up to a point, helps – and there may at least now be a sense that there can be enforcement. Whatever the flaws of theprofitability and sustainability rules, or thesquad cost ratiothat has replaced them, it may be useful if football could accept the basic premise that the game shouldn’t just be about how rich your owner happens to be. But that can only go so far; a door open to the world has admitted a world of problems.Short of some sort of financial crash in football, the sort of apocalyptic event that would make the sport unappealing to big finance and require the game to be built anew, with a fresh spirit that might recategorise football clubs as community assets rather than simple businesses, we’re probably stuck with it.How, after all, could football ever escape the society that produced it?Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueInside footballBusinessManchester CityChelseacommentShareReuse this content

title: Max Verstappen takes F1 Singapore GP pole from Leclerc after sprint win | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Max Verstappen’s good weekend in Singapore continued on a day when George Russell crashed out of the sprint from the lead
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Max Verstappen’s good weekend in Singapore continued on a day when George Russell crashed out of the sprint from the lead
Content: Max Verstappen enjoys his pole, flanked by second-placed Charles Leclerc (right) and Lewis Hamilton.Photograph: Mark Thompson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMax Verstappen enjoys his pole, flanked by second-placed Charles Leclerc (right) and Lewis Hamilton.Photograph: Mark Thompson/Getty ImagesFormula One 2026Max Verstappen takes F1 Singapore GP pole from Leclerc after sprint winHamilton qualifies third with Antonelli fourthRussell crashed out of sprint when leading on lap oneGiles RichardsSat 10 Oct 2026 11.17 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 14.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile Red Bull andMax Verstappenwere very much on a roll at the Singapore Grand Prix with victory in the sprint and then pole position, Britain’s George Russell was left having to roll with the punches. His vanishingly slight title hopes took another blow after he crashed out of the sprint race on the streets of the Marina Bay circuit.Verstappen’s pole was a mighty lap to beat the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc into second by five-hundredths of a second as the Dutchman enjoys his best form of the season. A 50th pole, his first in Singapore coming on theback of a pole and win at the last round in Malaysiaand pole and victory in the sprint at Marina Bay.Singapore Formula One Grand Prix – updates as Verstappen adds pole to sprint victoryRead moreBehind him, the title is edging close to being decided. The championship leader, Kimi Antonelli, was fourth in qualifying for Mercedes, a decent return after he has struggled with the car over the weekend and of greater import given Russell, his teammate and title rival, will start from the back of the grid on Sunday.Russell qualified in sixth – in the process saving soft tyres for use on Sunday – but will be opening at the back of the field because of the penalties applied for taking a new engine this weekend. He had no control over the reliability issues that saw his engine fail at the last round in Malaysia but his weekend in Singapore was compromised on Saturday after he made an error in the sprint and crashed out from the lead of the race.He had taken the lead, passing Verstappen into the first corner but put his wheels on to the white lines at the final corner at the end of the opening lap. In the wet conditions, he lost the rear, spun and went into the barriers, out of the race and the team had to work fast just to repair the car before qualifying. Russell held his hands up for the mistake and it once more played into Antonelli’s hands.“Miscalculation,” Russell said. “Came through the corner had more battery deployment than I thought, pushed me a little bit wider than I hoped and went onto the white line. Silly mistake. Big consequences.”View image in fullscreenGeorge Russell crashes out of the sprint race in Singapore.Photograph: Mark Sutton/Formula 1/Getty ImagesBig consequences indeed. Antonelli’s advantage over his teammate is now 89 points. If he leaves Singapore with a lead of 101 points, he can seal his first championship at the next round in Austin.Verstappen was all but flawless in Singapore. Having thrown himself into the lap on the absolute edge, he found the limit with precision, his time of 1min 31.373sec on his first run in Q3 could not be matched. Lewis Hamilton chased him hard and then Leclerc edged into second place, but no one could better Verstappen’s effort. Hamilton finished third for Ferrari, with Lando Norris in fifth for McLaren.It was another demonstration of how the recent upgrades have improved the Red Bull and how much more comfortable Verstappen was with the car in Singapore. It is a track where he has yet to win a GP and one of two, along with the Madring, on the current calendar where he has yet to take victory.Verstappen won the sprint, which had been delayed because of heavy rain, with complete control from the front once he had inherited the lead after Russell’s crash. He had enough pace to comfortably see off Hamilton in second, who had made a superb start to move from sixth to third off the line. It was very much a processional affair, with overtaking all but impossible as drivers managed their tyres to the flag.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe short-form dash was enlivened by late drama when Norris made a move on his teammate, Oscar Piastri, on the final lap, the pair clashed, taking the Australian out and dropping Norris to eighth, to the consternation of his McLaren team.“Seeing two McLarens making contact like that is simply not acceptable,” said the team principal, Andrea Stella. “Something we will discuss with out drivers, we will iterate that the team interest is far bigger than any of us.”That moved Antonelli up from sixth to fourth place, another indication that simply everything seems to be going the Italian’s way, even when he is just keeping his head down and grinding out a result.The track was holding a sprint for the first time as F1 looks to enliven some of the more processional circuits, including having Monaco host a sprint next season. However, it was not welcomed with any enthusiasm by the drivers. “If it was dry that would probably have been the most boring race to have watched,” said Hamilton. An opinion echoed by his teammate Leclerc, who was third in the race.“I don’t think it makes sense to have any sprint races on city tracks in general,” he said. “Here or Monaco, I don’t think it adds anything to the weekend.”Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportMax VerstappennewsShareReuse this content

title: Wallabies mugged at their own game to leave coach Kiss mulling hard lessons | Bledisloe Cup | The Guardian
description: Old habits resurface as Australia fritter away advantage and allow All Blacks to mount aerial assault at Eden Park
Author: Angus Fontaine
Headline: Old habits resurface as Australia fritter away advantage and allow All Blacks to mount aerial assault at Eden Park
Content: Wallabies coach Les Kiss speaks to his players after a chastening defeat by their old foes to end Australia’s six-game unbeaten streak.Photograph: Fiona Goodall/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWallabies coach Les Kiss speaks to his players after a chastening defeat by their old foes to end Australia’s six-game unbeaten streak.Photograph: Fiona Goodall/Getty ImagesBledisloe CupAnalysisWallabies mugged at their own game to leave coach Kiss mulling hard lessonsAngus Fontaineat Eden ParkOld habits resurface as Australia fritter away advantage and allow All Blacks to mount aerial assault at Eden ParkSat 10 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 20.20 EDTShareLes Kiss stood forlornly in the middle of Eden Park wearing a thousand-yard stare. The past 10 Wallabies coaches had all been where he was now, shaking their heads and cursing after a failed attempt to storm the fortress of New Zealand rugby. This was Kiss’s first loss as Australia coach and the little bloke was nursing a big hurt.His side had arrived on a six-game unbeaten streak, fresh fromstomping the world champions South Africa a fortnight before. Conversely, their old enemy were facing a fourth consecutive defeat after falling three times to that same Springboks side. After 25 years of Trans-Tasman pain, the Bledisloe Cup finally looked within reach.Wallabies blown away by All Blacks blitz as Bledisloe Cup misery extends to 24th yearRead moreEven the Kiwi supporters sensed it. All over town, Wallabies fans were being treated with respect rather than pity. They had seen what Australia had done against the Boks – the aerial majesty of Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii and Max Jorgensen, the courage to hang on with 11 men at the death. This time the threat was genuine.After the anthems, in the calm before the kick-off, a large bloke in a faded gold jersey and three sheets to the wind, stood up and did his very best Gladiator impersonation. “Today is the day!” he bellowed. “Today we finally give it back to these Kiwi bastards.” The tiny fires of Australian support in an otherwise roiling sea of more than 48,000 black jerseys at the 105-year stronghold roared in unity.The dream was alive when Ben Donaldson’s deft tap-on pass sent Tom Wright slicing into space after seven minutes to ignite the Kiss Army’s march into history. The All Blacks knew it too and botched the kick-off, surrendering to another attack. But then a traditional failure reared its ugly head: the Wallabies’ ability to self-immolate.Donaldson had delivered a diamond, now he coughed up a rock, wasting the halfway scrum not by feeding his weapons out wide to get them deeper into the enemy lines but instead reefing a mindless, maddening kick for touch. The ball duly plonked out on the full and the reprieved All Blacks suddenly remembered who they were playing.Peter Lakai scored in a sizzling piece of counterattack for seven-all, then Tupou Vaa’i crossed shortly after for 14-7 and then, with a penalty kick, Australia were down by 10. They cut the margin when Donaldson’s cut-and-run sent Wilson over before half-time, but the usually reliable RyanLonergan shanked an easy conversion.View image in fullscreenHarry Wilson feels the full force of a crunching tackle by New Zealand’s Anton Segner.Photograph: Michael Bradley/AFP/Getty ImagesBehind 17-14, Kiss must have launched a piece of half-time oratory to rival that of dusty Rusty in the crowd because he kept the home side waiting long minutes after the break. When the Wallabies finally emerged, they exploded, jagging a daring kick to the corner which Jorgensen hared after and almost collected to take the lead.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toAustralia SportGet a daily roundup of the latest sports news, features and comment from our Australian sports deskEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNew Zealand 50-19 Australia: Bledisloe Cup rugby union international – as it happenedRead moreBut again Australia frittered their enterprise by botching the killing stroke, giving away an idiotic obstruction penalty in their haste to maul the final metres. Spared, the All Blacks went berserk, scoring twice in six minutes before icing a 54th straight Eden Park win. The big mug was paraded around the old ground, touched by fans across the fence but out of reach for Kiss’s players, who could only watch it roll by.Australia had been beaten at their own game, the aerial assault they used to defeat South Africa. Jordie Barrett and Will Jordan outjumped the Wallabies flyers, and Dave Rennie outcoached Kiss. “The lessons are there,” said Kiss. “If you can’t get your strengths going and their strengths grow, it becomes a difficult game.”Cam Roigard’s kicking game scrambled Australia’s attacking shape, a move that paid extra dividends after Australia’s midfield spearhead Len Ikitau left early for an HIA. “[It] allowed us to put a lot of pressure on,” said Rennie. “Receiving those kicks is difficult and our guys did an excellent job winning it in the air or picking up scraps.”Len Ikitau’s likely absence for next week’s rematch in Sydney compounds the cruelty of partner Hunter Paisami’s suspension after an innocuous head clash tackle against South Africa. His replacement, Isaac Henry, made 15 tackles on Saturday, but offered little in attack. Kiss will have to shuffle his backline again or inject yet more rookies.The Wallabies have returned to earth with a thud. They have a week to lick wounds and reset. TheBledisloe Cupis gone for another year but there’s still the chance to beat the All Blacks for the first time since 2020 and snap the Kiwis’ 12-Test dominance. “When you get a knockback, you find out more about yourself,” a defiant Kiss said.His heroic captain, Wilson, called this Test defeat “a step back” but Kiss sees glimmers of gold even in a 41st year of mud, blood and tears at Eden Park. “Belief is created and sustained not by just wins and losses,” he said. “These boys have a strong culture, a strong belief in themselves and a confidence about what they can do. We’ll go back to work and turn the dial in the right areas so we can go to Sydney and return fire.”Explore more on these topicsBledisloe CupNew Zealand rugby union teamAustralia rugby union teamAustralia sportRugby unionanalysisShareReuse this content

title: USWNT exposed by ruthless Spain as early goals settle heavyweight friendly | USA women's football team | The Guardian
description: The world champions scored twice in the opening 14 minutes before saving a second-half penalty to secure a 2-0 win over Emma Hayes’s side in Washington
Author: Ella Brockway
Headline: The world champions scored twice in the opening 14 minutes before saving a second-half penalty to secure a 2-0 win over Emma Hayes’s side in Washington
Content: USA midfielder Lindsey Heaps challenges Spain’s Eva Navarro for the ball during Saturday’s international friendly at Audi Field in Washington DC.Photograph: Patrick Smith/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUSA midfielder Lindsey Heaps challenges Spain’s Eva Navarro for the ball during Saturday’s international friendly at Audi Field in Washington DC.Photograph: Patrick Smith/Getty ImagesUSA women's football teamUSWNT exposed by ruthless Spain as early goals settle heavyweight friendlyGuijarro and Navarro score in opening 14 minutesUS midfield and defensive lapses exposed by SpainYohannes misses penalty as US fightback falls shortElla Brockwayat Audi FieldSat 10 Oct 2026 16.53 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 19.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn less than a year’s time, the United States and Spain will almost certainly arrive in Brazil as the top two contenders to win the Women’s World Cup. Spain, holders of the top spot in Fifa’s rankings for the past 60 weeks, are the defending champions; the second-ranked US won gold at the 2024 Paris Olympics.This month’s pair of friendlies between the two sides are taking place with caveats. Both sides are missing several of their most important players to injuries. The opening match in Brazil is 258 days away. Spain have booked their place, but the US still have to actuallyqualifyfor the World Cup, through a regional tournament that begins next month.‘A lot of people counted me out’: Ashley Sanchez on goal records, grit and potential USWNT returnRead moreEven without full-strength rosters, a meeting between these two teams is a compelling bill. And in their first of two friendlies, on Saturday in Washington DC, Spain had the upper hand, scoring twice in the first 14 minutes of a 2-0 win.“You can’t afford to go 2-0 down against the best team in the world, especially the way we conceded those goals,” US coachEmma Hayessaid. “That’s the learning.”In just the fifth meeting between the two sides and the first since 11 October 2022 – before Spain broke through to win the 2023 World Cup – the reigning champions took advantage of defensive lapses and the US midfield’s struggles. After trailing by two goals for the first time under Emma Hayes, the Americans played a much-improved second half, but failures to convert chances and a stopped penalty kept them scoreless.In many ways, Saturday’s game and the rematch on Tuesday in Chester, Pennsylvania, are more stress tests than clashes of titans – or causes for alarm bells. Hayes has intentionally crafted this year’s calendar to pit the US against elite competition. The Americans played Japan three times in April, winning twice and losing once, and split a pair of away friendlies against Brazil in June. Saturday was the first time the US ever played the world No 1 in Fifa’s rankings on home soil.“There’s going to be games like that, and I’m happy it’s not the World Cup right now,” forward Trinity Rodman said. “You take what you can from this game and go into the next game.”View image in fullscreenTrinity Rodman controls the ball during the United States’ international friendly against Spain at Audi Field in Washington DC on Saturday.Photograph: Patrick Smith/Getty ImagesA matchup with both sides closer to full strength would have perhaps been more instructive as a preview of a potential World Cup meeting, but such a clash had been ruled out this week. Center-back Naomi Girma and midfielder Sam Coffey, the two players most vital to the US defensive spine, are out with injuries. Spain are missing two-time Ballon d’Or winner Aitana Bonmatí, Vicky Lopez, Mariona Caldentey and Cata Coll with injuries; Clàudia Pina and Mapi León withdrew from camp on Friday.If the lengthy list of absentees affected Spain, it didn’t show. They went ahead in the third minute on a 20-yard screamer by Patri Guijarro. The US struggled to assemble their shape after a turnover and left the Barcelona midfielder with significant space.The second goal came just 11 minutes later, the result of another defensive breakdown. Salma Paralluelo isolated Tierna Davidson on the left side and sent a cross to a wide-open Eva Navarro, who fired it for a one-touch finish on the run. All 11 US players huddled above the box for several minutes after conceding.The US’s connections looked off throughout the first half, from giveaways to overhit clearances. Rose Lavelle attempted to lay off a forward pass with Sophia Wilson and Alyssa Thompson on the break, but both players mistimed their runs and the ball rolled out of bounds to a groan from the Audi Field crowd. Wilson’s best attempts of the half hit the post and rolled wide. The issues in themidfield– for the first 65 minutes, Lavelle, Lily Yohannes and Lindsey Heaps – that predate the Hayes era were evident again.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSpain’s Natalia Ramos reacts during Saturday’s international friendly against the United States at Audi Field.Photograph: Patrick Smith/Getty ImagesThe Americans looked improved and composed in the second half after adjusting their high press. Spain did not produce a shot on target in the second half, and the US outshot them 13-6 on the day. Wilson thought she had scored the US’s first goal in the 53rd minute, but it was waved for offside after video review.The US earned a penalty in the 67th minute after Wilson drew a foul by Natalia Ramos in the box. The taker was Yohannes – a surprise choice, given the 19-year-old has never attempted a penalty in four seasons at Ajax and OL Lyonnes. Wilson, a regular taker for the Portland Thorns, is a perfect 11 for 11 on penalties in the NWSL. (Yohannes told reporters after the game she was second on the US’s list of takers, behind Heaps.) Adriana Nanclares saved Yohannes’s stutter-step attempt and the Americans remained off the board.Forward Mallory Swanson and midfielder Ashley Sanchez were among the second-half substitutes. Swanson, who was out for all of 2025 on maternity leave, made her first game appearance in 710 days. Sanchez was recalled to the national team amida strong NWSL seasonwith the North Carolina Courage and earned her first US minutes since October 2023. She nearly scored off a cross in the 88th minute but slid as her foot connected with the ball.Spain increased the physicality for the final quarter-hour. They committed 12 fouls to the US’s four and went down to 10 players in stoppage time after Athenea del Castillo saw red for a hair pull.The US will have a chance to remedy their finishing issues in Tuesday’s rematch in Pennsylvania. They have not gone consecutive games without scoring since the 2023 World Cup.Explore more on these topicsUSA women's football teamSpain women's football teamUS sportsWomen's footballEmma HayesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Matt Renshaw’s epic 190 helps Australia turn tables on South Africa in Durban | Australia cricket team | The Guardian
description: Matt Renshaw scored his first century in Tests for nine years and 280 days as Australia notched 390 with a second highest ninth wicket partnership of 134
Author: Geoff Lemon
Headline: Matt Renshaw scored his first century in Tests for nine years and 280 days as Australia notched 390 with a second highest ninth wicket partnership of 134
Content: Australia's Matt Renshaw acknowledges the crowd after his dismissal having scored 190 runs.Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAustralia's Matt Renshaw acknowledges the crowd after his dismissal having scored 190 runs.Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty ImagesAustralia cricket teamMatt Renshaw’s epic 190 helps Australia turn tables on South Africa in DurbanRenshaw’s century was his first in Tests for nine yearsLyon helps build second-highest ninth-wicket partnershipGeoff LemonSat 10 Oct 2026 11.51 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 20.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf the choice to ask Nic Maddinson to open in Durban was a bust, the upside for Australia was that it pushed Matthew Renshaw down to number five. From there, the Queenslander returned from 10 years on the periphery to the centre of the spotlight in the first Test against South Africa, with an innings of 190 that saved Australia from peril, settled them into stability, then lifted them to dominance.Staunch support from the lower order was the other part of the equation, as Renshaw batted through two extended sessions until he was last man out, just after tea, with Australia’s 390 followed by South Africa’s 27 for one before stumps.South Africa v Australia: first men’s cricket Test, day two – liveRead moreImagine the likelihood, with the score at 124 for six on the first day, that Renshaw might go on, not just to score his second Test century, but to exceed that career high of 184? His secret was that there was no secret, just the most common formula known to the game: patience, concentration and pacing. Continuing in the style of his unbeaten 46 from day one, Renshaw defended calmly, kept the score moving with singles and picked off the odd poor ball.He was aided by an often passive approach to fielding, despite some tough spells of bowling from Marco Jansen and Anrich Nortje. Resuming after 65 overs, they had a morning burst with the old ball, then a short rest before the new one, often dropping short and hitting gloves or body. But it was the more modest velocity and bounce of Wiaan Mulder in between times that reaped rewards.Pat Cummins carried on the previous day’s partnership to 86, but lost concentration eight overs into the morning to poke the old ball to slip for 43. With the slightest bit of inswing from the new ball, Mulder bowled Mitchell Starc an unplayable that pitched on leg stump before seaming away to take middle and off.At 230 for eight, South Africa would have imagined a quick finish, but Temba Bavuma let things drift by spreading the field for Renshaw. Against players with the right temperament, this tactic often backfires, and so it was here. Renshaw happily defended or added a few runs early in each over, turned over strike from the fourth or fifth ball, and watched Nathan Lyon defend what was left.Lyon did not score for 16 overs either side of lunch, facing 24 balls. When Renshaw for once failed to farm the strike, Nortje immediately came back on to target Lyon, Australia’s spinner flicked him for four.By the second session the pitch had gone to sleep and with it went the South African bowling. Even with two specialist spinners in the side, part-timer Aiden Markram was called upon. Lyon had never been part of a century stand, but up that landmark came: no cricketer has played more Tests than his 144 before achieving that feat.When Jansen finally ended his team’s pain by dishing some out, smashing Lyon in the foot with a fierce yorker from around the wicket, the partnership was 134, Australia’s second-highest for the ninth wicket.View image in fullscreenSouth Africa’s Marco Jansen (centre) celebrates the wicket of Australia’s Nathan Lyon (right) who helped notch up the second highest ninth wicket partnership of 134 runs.Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty ImagesLyon made 27 from 92 balls and Renshaw was up to 169. He went up a gear, uppercutting Nortje for six and nailing a pull for four. Josh Hazlewood was able to help him bat through a monster session, ending up at two hours and 45 minutes after one extension to make up lost overs and a second one for being nine wickets down.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRenshaw fell two balls after the resumption, driving the off-spinner Simon Harmer to slip, but it had been a flawless innings otherwise. It set records for Durban: the highest score by an Australian, past the Phil Hughes 160 that is part of folklore; and the highest score by any batter at five or below, past the 2019 Kusal Perera epic that was Ben Stokes at Headingley before Ben Stokes went to Headingley.Australia bowled fewer than nine overs in the last session before bad light once again stopped play, although that was enough time for Hazlewood to have Ryan Rickelton edge a drive to slip from a ball that was not full enough. South Africa will start the third day 363 runs behind.For Renshaw, though, the day was eventful enough. Treated as a prodigy at 20 years old, then discarded summarily by 21, he has loitered on the sidelines with occasional nibbles at a Test return. Now he will get a proper second chance.His century celebration was chiefly a smile of vast relief. At nine years and 280 days, the only Australians to have waited longer between hundreds are monochrome memories, Bob Simpson and Warren Bardsley.Where Renshaw bats next may still be an open question, as the shuttle continues between number five and opening. Usman Khawaja went from five to the top, then Travis Head did the same to replace him. Renshaw was just shunted from opening to five, but may soon have to go back to accommodate Cam Green, who was the most convincing batter in Australia’s previous series but is injured. That will be next week’s problem. Renshaw is this week’s solution.Explore more on these topicsAustralia cricket teamSouth Africa cricket teamCricketAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: In three years, Israel’s war on Gaza hasn’t just changed the Middle East, it’s changed the world | Steve Bloomfield | The Guardian
description: A whirlpool of violence has engulfed everywhere from Lebanon to Yemen. Meanwhile, the west has destroyed any political authority it once had, says Steve Bloomfield, former international editor of the Observer
Author: Steve Bloomfield
Headline: A whirlpool of violence has engulfed everywhere from Lebanon to Yemen. Meanwhile, the west has destroyed any political authority it once had, says Steve Bloomfield, former international editor of the Observer
Content: Palestinians inspect the damage to an apartment block on Friday after an Israeli strike on Khan Younis.Photograph: Tariq Mohammad/APAImages/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenPalestinians inspect the damage to an apartment block on Friday after an Israeli strike on Khan Younis.Photograph: Tariq Mohammad/APAImages/ShutterstockOpinionIsrael-Gaza warIn three years, Israel’s war on Gaza hasn’t just changed the Middle East, it’s changed the worldSteve BloomfieldA whirlpool of violence has engulfed everywhere from Lebanon to Yemen. Meanwhile, the west has destroyed any political authority it once hadSat 10 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 09.20 EDTShareThere was a world before 7 October, 2023, and now there is a world after. For Gaza, forIsrael, for the wider Middle East, and for everyone else too. Not all hinge points in history are obvious at the time. Three years on from the day it began, and precisely one year since a supposed ceasefire was agreed, this one is now impossible to ignore.The before-and-after pictures tell part of the story. An update to Google Maps,released last week, underscores just what three years of relentless Israeli military onslaught has done to Gaza. Satellite images show how entire towns have been reduced to rubble. Mosques and hospitals, visible three years ago, have now disappeared. Meanwhile the once-empty shoreline is now crammed with tents. This is what it looks like when an attempt has been made to destroy a people.For Israel, too, there has been a before and after. Prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu had cultivated a sense of security, even of impregnability. The ease with whichHamascarried out its terrorist attack, killing 1,200 Israelis, including hundreds of young people at a music festival, destroyed that belief for ever.Three years on from 7 October, both Israel and Gaza have changed beyond recognition.But the consequences of Hamas’s attack and Israel’s brutal response, which has killed more than 73,000 Palestinians, including 21,000 children, have spread far wider.Under the pretext of protecting its own borders, Israel has launched wars and military offensives across the region, sending troops into Syria; effectively annexing parts of southern Lebanon, deploying the same tactics there that it used in Gaza; and starting, with the US, an unwinnable war with Iran that has spiralled into a regional conflict affecting all six Gulf states.The Iran war has sparked a new conflict between the Houthis in Yemen and Saudi Arabia, which this week triggered a mutual defence pact with Pakistan and Turkey, dragging two other countries into the maelstrom. Across the Red Sea, some of the same combatants are involved in the war in Sudan anda fresh conflict inside Ethiopia.More than a dozen countries across two continents are now entangled in a rising number of wars, with overlapping participants and numerous competing interests.But there is something else, more insidious, that has changed. The rule of international law, tenuous as it was, has been openly replaced by military might. In 2022, western leaders – building a coalition rightly opposed to Vladimir Putin’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine – made moral appeals based on the violation of international law. In Gaza, they encouraged and supported Israel, even when it was clear that the rules were being broken. That hypocrisy has not gone unnoticed, not just in the global south but among many millions of citizens in the west.We have watched this happen in real time. Despite the ban on international journalists, anyone with a phone knew what was happening in Gaza from the early days of Israel’s response. Hundreds of Palestinian journalists have reported on the bombing of hospitals and schools, the bombing of cafes and wells, the killings at food distribution points, the deaths of children and babies. War crimes have never before been broadcast in real time, relentlessly, every hour of every day, around the world.Gaza has also changed how wars are fought. Israel has pioneered the use of AI to select targets, accelerating our descent into a future for which we are unprepared.All of this was allowed to take place in a time when the west could still argue that the “international rules-based order” existed. It may have been destroyed by Donald Trump, but we cannot forget that the dismantling began under Joe Biden. It was Biden who ensured the flow of weapons to Israel continued uninterrupted, Biden who insisted that every United Nations security council resolution calling for a ceasefire wasvetoed, and Biden whoattackedthe international criminal court when it sought to indict Netanyahu for war crimes.US support for Israel has always been strong and, on the whole, unquestioned. But even Republican presidents have understood they have influence over Israel’s actions and have been prepared to use it.Ronald Reagansuspended an arms deal in 1981after Israel annexed the Golan Heights. A year later, his administrationstopped supplying cluster weapons to Israelafter Menachem Begin’s government used them in populated areas during its invasion of Lebanon. In 2002, the killing of 15 Palestinians in Gaza was enough for Colin Powell, the then secretary of state, toannounce a review of Israel’s use of American arms.Israel was also given a free pass by every other member of the G7, including those run by centrists or centre-left politicians. French president Emmanuel Macron, German chancellor Olaf Scholz, Justin Trudeau in Canada and Australia’s Anthony Albanese all initially gave Israel their backing.Only António Guterres, the much-maligned UN secretary general, emerges with a modicum of credit. Less than three weeks after 7 October, he called Israel’s response “collective punishment of the Palestinian people” and demanded an immediate ceasefire.The one ray of hope for the future is that our shared understanding of what has happened over the past three years means that in many countries the political winds have shifted.Before Andy Burnham even entered Number 10, he apologised for how Labour had handled the early days of the conflict. The UK now has a prime minister who was one of the few western politicians to call for a ceasefire just weeks after 7 October. Ed Miliband’s willingness toaccurately describe Israel’s actions in the West Bank as “ethnic cleansing”indicate a change in attitude that could lead to more concerted international action against Israel.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the US, support for Israel has fallen through the floor. For a Democrat who wants to be president in 2028 there is no credible path to the White House that doesn’t involve support for the Palestinian cause. And yet, we cannot simply close our eyes and hope that a change in America will magically restore the world to how it was on 6 October 2023.Nor should we pretend that the previous era was one we should wish to return to. Did we enter a new world on 7 October, or did we just notice where we were? In the three years before the Hamas attack, the wars in Tigray and Sudan saw many of the same trends play out.In Tigray, the northernmost part ofEthiopia, a war between the central government and the Tigray People’s Liberation Front killed 600,000 people. There were brutal massacres, forced starvation, widespread use of drones – and absolutely no accountability. In Sudan, too, hospitals have been hit by drones, women have been raped, children have been shot dead. Again, we could see it happen. Again, there were no consequences.Gaza, though, has undoubtedly accelerated the trend, normalising the immoral. The wars that have begun, that have spiralled out of control and pulled more countries and more actors into their orbit, cannot easily be stopped. There is a momentum to this conflict, a hardening of positions, as each new outrage leads to a response. When there is impunity, when there is no price that those responsible will ever pay, there are terrifyingly few levers to pull. If war crimes go unpunished, they only escalate.And so a family in Addis Ababa fears the sound of a drone crashing into their home. A village in Lebanon is evacuated, destroyed and the land made uninhabitable. A mundane job at Riyadh airport becomes a dailydeadly gamble. A crew of badly paid seafarers pray to their gods as they cross through the strait of Hormuz. The dreams of millions of children shrink from university, fame or fortune, to the brute reality of survival.And in Gaza, crammed into tents, deprived of enough food and water, two million Palestinians are still living under the brutal rule of Hamas and the daily threat of death from a military force that fears no consequences.This is our world now. We need to recognise that, if anything is going to change.Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the ObserverDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
