title: Four dead as Isaias weakens to post-tropical cyclone after striking Florida panhandle | Hurricane Isaias | The Guardian
description: Some of deaths came from falling trees as half a million people without power and rain and flooding still a concern
Author: Alba Asenjo Domínguez
Headline: Some of deaths came from falling trees as half a million people without power and rain and flooding still a concern
Content: A home damaged by Hurricane Isaias in Milton, Florida, on 10 October 2026.Photograph: Dan Anderson/EPAView image in fullscreenA home damaged by Hurricane Isaias in Milton, Florida, on 10 October 2026.Photograph: Dan Anderson/EPAHurricane IsaiasFour dead as Isaias weakens to post-tropical cyclone after striking Florida panhandleSome of deaths came from falling trees as half a million people without power and rain and flooding still a concernAlba Asenjo Domínguezand agenciesSat 10 Oct 2026 19.20 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 10.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least four people were reported dead on Saturday amidIsaiasafter itmade landfalllate on Friday on Florida’s panhandle as a category 2 hurricane, according to authorities.The storm also took down trees, knocked out electricity for hundreds of thousands and flooded highways – but as Saturday evening approached, the region was reopening.Key things to know about Hurricane Isaias as millions under evacuation ordersRead moreDespite warnings of storm surges ahead of the storm, several major routes along the coast were open by daybreak on Saturday and free of downed trees and power lines typically seen after major hurricanes.Two of the deaths reported during Isaias occurred in Escambia county,Florida, and two others were reported inAlabama, as the storm moved inland, local officials said. Of those deaths, one each occurred in Escambia and Birmingham, Alabama, when trees fell on homes.Another person whose death was linked to Isaias was found in a closed garage with a running generator in Escambia county. Four members of that person’s family have been transported to the hospital with carbon monoxide poisoning, the Escambia sheriff’s office said.“Don’t run any generators inside your home, it can be very, very hazardous,”Floridagovernor Ron DeSantis said in a press conference.View image in fullscreenPeople retrieve belongings from a collapsed boat house in the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias in Destin, Florida, on Saturday.Photograph: Gerald Herbert/APInAlabama, governor Kay Ivey said Isaias – predicted to dissipate on Sunday – “cannot clear fast enough”.Meanwhile, though it had weakened on Saturday to a post-tropical cyclone as it passed through central Alabama, Isaias still posed flooding and tornado threats as it moved inland, forecasters and officials warned.Hurricane-force winds in the Florida panhandle blew the roof off a Pensacola hotel, and the city’s mayor said the airport “took some damage”. The storm flattened a boathouse in Destin and ripped away part of the facade of a high-rise in Panama City Beach.A worker in a condominium parking lot swept piles of the building’s insulation while others put back beach chairs that had been tossed about.View image in fullscreenLee Glessner begins to remove tree limbs from a fallen tree block a road after the landfall of Hurricane Isaias in Milton, Florida, on 10 October.Photograph: Dan Anderson/EPA“Remember, there can still be flooding from rising rivers,” Jared W Perdue, the secretary of Florida’s state transportation department, said at a news conference. “I’m just going to remind all of you – please, if there’s standing water or flowing water on top of a road, please do not drive through it.“It does not have to be that deep, and it can wash away your car, it can wash away a human, it can become very dangerous very quickly.”Nearly 550,000 customers were still without power across Florida, Alabama and Georgia on Saturday afternoon as those in the path of the storm began the cleanup process, according toPowerOutage.us. Though still high, the number of outages was down from more than 900,000 earlier on Saturday.View image in fullscreenDark clouds loom over a historic Catholic church on Friday in Mobile, Alabama.Photograph: Octavio Jones/APStorm surge and tropical storm warnings associated with Isaias by then had been discontinued, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) warned there would still likely be “considerable impacts” associated with Isaias across much of southern Alabama, Florida’s panhandle and south-westernGeorgia.“Flash, urban and river flooding is possible across the region,” the NHC said in a Saturday-morning advisory, adding that there was a considerable potential for flash flooding and landslides across the southern Appalachians. “A risk for tornadoes will persist … through [Saturday] afternoon across parts of the eastern Florida panhandle, Georgia and the Carolinas.”Isaias through Sunday is expected to produce rainfall amounts of 4-8in across southern Alabama, Florida’s panhandle and Big Bend regions, and south-west Georgia. Localized totals up to 15in are possible, particularly within rain bands across the Florida panhandle and Big Bend.View image in fullscreenIn an aerial view, an apartment complex is seen after the roof was blown off when Hurricane Isaias passed through the area on Saturday in Milton, Florida.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesAcross much of the remainder of the south-east US, rainfall amounts of 2-5in are expected, and localized higher amounts up to 10in are possible, especially across the southern Appalachians and coastal Carolinas.The hurricane’s maximum sustained winds were 105mph (169km/h). That was intense enough to sound like “a train whistle”, Tim Mowrytoldthe Associated Press after enduring the storm as his home in Pensacola, Florida.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida and hammers Gulf coastRead moreMowry described losing power on Friday afternoon but said could rely on a generator. He said his son tried to drive to his home after his place about 15 minutes away lost power but had to turn around because downed trees and power lines blocked the road.All things considered, Mowry said he was “really fortunate” with respect to how he fared during Isaias.Along Alabama’s Gulf coast, authorities in Mobile reported numerous downed trees and power lines.Maranie Adams, who rode out the storm with her family and their chickens in Gulf Shores, Alabama, said the winds rocked their home, but it was nothing like Hurricane Sally, which left water under their elevated house.“I feel very much more relieved today,” she said.Donald Trump has allowed the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) to provide resources to Georgia to help grapple with the ongoing storm, including possible tornadoes, the agency said on Saturday.Several roads have already been blocked by fallen trees around Atlanta, local outlets have reported.View image in fullscreenPeople line up for gas at one of the few open stations after the landfall of Isaias in Milton, Florida, on Saturday.Photograph: Dan Anderson/EPATrump previously approved emergency declarations for Florida and Alabama ahead of the landfall ofHurricane Isaias.While the stronger El Niño seemed to limit the number of hurricanes in the Atlantic for the year so far, Isaias forming in October with maximum sustained winds of 105mph marked a stark contrast from historical trends.The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) predicted a quiet year in terms of hurricanes at the beginning of a season that officially begins annually on 1 June. Noaa anticipated between three and six hurricanes, well below the average of seven. An August forecast from Noaa cut the expected number to between two and six.Isais is one of the twolatest-forming Atlantic hurricaneson record, tying a record set on 8 October 1905. Otherwise, the second-latest date for the first Atlantic hurricane was 11 September – in 2002 and 2013.None of the eight previous named storms of the 2026 Atlantic season intensified above tropical storm status.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsHurricane IsaiasFloridaAlabamaGeorgiaHurricanesExtreme weatherUS weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: Candidate named Hitler Mussolini elected mayor in Peru | Peru | The Guardian
description: Leftwing Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores beats far-right candidate in election in remote district of Andes
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Leftwing Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores beats far-right candidate in election in remote district of Andes
Content: Benito Mussolini with Adolf Hitler at a meeting in Florence, Italy, in 1940.Photograph: Everett Collection Historical/AlamyView image in fullscreenBenito Mussolini with Adolf Hitler at a meeting in Florence, Italy, in 1940.Photograph: Everett Collection Historical/AlamyPeruCandidate named Hitler Mussolini elected mayor in PeruLeftwing Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores beats far-right candidate in election in remote district of AndesAgence France-PresseSat 10 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 06.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA businessman called Hitler Mussolini Simeon Flores has been elected the mayor of a remote district in the Peruvian Andes, according to local election data.The 45-year-old, who shares two of his names with the notorious European dictators, won the race for mayor of Queropalca, in Peru’s central Huánuco region, and will take office on 1 January.The candidate from the leftwing Ahora Nación party won 229 out of a total of 663 votes in elections on 4 October, according to the national office of electoral processes.His closest rival, the far-right candidate Gaspar Osorio, received 204 votes.Flores, who works in freight transportation, had belonged to Popular Force, the party of Peru’s rightwing president, Keiko Fujimori, until 2025, according to electoral authorities.Despite the name being associated with Germany’s Nazi leader Adolf Hitler, several candidates with the name have won elections in Peru.In 2021, the doctor Hitler Saavedra Casternoque was elected to parliament for the centrist party Somos Peru.In 2018, Hitler Alba Sánchez was voted in as mayor of the Andean district of Yungar, saying during his campaign that he was “the good Hitler”.Explore more on these topicsPeruAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Man with gun kills one Philadelphia police officer and injures another | Philadelphia | The Guardian
description: 10-year police veteran Shane Seiber was killed after responding to a report of a man with a gun
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: 10-year police veteran Shane Seiber was killed after responding to a report of a man with a gun
Content: A suspect has been taken into custody, according to the Philadelphia police commissioner.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA suspect has been taken into custody, according to the Philadelphia police commissioner.Photograph: Anadolu/Getty ImagesPhiladelphiaMan with gun kills one Philadelphia police officer and injures another10-year police veteran Shane Seiber was killed after responding to a report of a man with a gunAssociated Press and Guardian staffSat 10 Oct 2026 16.12 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 19.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAPhiladelphiapolice officer was fatally shot and another was wounded on Saturday after responding to a report of a man with a gun, authorities said.Shane Seiber, 40, was killed early on Saturday morning in WestPhiladelphia, according to the city’s police commissioner, Kevin Bethel.Seiber, a 10-year veteran of the Philadelphia police department, and the other officer were transported to the Penn Presbyterian medical center, where the surviving officer underwent surgery. He was listed in stable condition, Bethel said.Bethel also said a suspect was in custody.Citing law enforcements sources, the Philadelphia Inquireridentifiedthat suspect as Eric Lewis. The Inquirer also reported that Lewis, 35, was employed by Philadelphia’s municipal water department.Pennsylvania’s governor, Josh Shapiro, said he ordered flags to fly at half-mast for Seiber. He is survived by his wife and two children: a boy, age seven, and a girl, three.Seiber was at least the 376th Philadelphia police department officer to die in the line of duty since 1851, according to theOfficer Down Memorial Page, which honors US law enforcement personnel who died while on the job. He was the 129th of those officers to die from gunfire, the memorial page said.Explore more on these topicsPhiladelphiaUS policingGun crimeUS crimePennsylvanianewsShareReuse this content

title: Greens must avoid ‘capture by extremists and racists’, says party MP | Green party | The Guardian
description: Ellie Chowns says vote for ‘Zionism is racism’ policy by 0.4% of members shows party processes are not working
Author: Geneva Abdul
Headline: Ellie Chowns says vote for ‘Zionism is racism’ policy by 0.4% of members shows party processes are not working
Content: Ellie Chowns is the Green party’s leader in the House of Commons.Photograph: House of CommonsView image in fullscreenEllie Chowns is the Green party’s leader in the House of Commons.Photograph: House of CommonsGreen partyGreens must avoid ‘capture by extremists and racists’, says party MPEllie Chowns says vote for ‘Zionism is racism’ policy by 0.4% of members shows party processes are not workingGeneva AbdulSat 10 Oct 2026 07.46 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 06.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA Green Party MP has said she wants to make sure her party is not “vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists” amid the continuing fallout from the “Zionism is racism” vote.The party faces a political maelstrom over its policy decision last weekto treat Zionism, the movement for a Jewish state, as any other form of racism,and to back a single Palestinian state over a two-state solution. The motion was passed at the annual party conference with just over 1,000 votes, approximately 0.4% of the total membership.What is Zionism and why do some critics describe it as racist?Read moreEllie Chowns, the party leader in the House of Commons, said the ability to pass such a “significant and damaging policy” in that way made it clear the party’s structures and policymaking processes were not working.“I don’t think that policy, ‘Zionism is racism’, represents the large majority ofGreen partymembers, nor of people in the country,” Chowns told BBC’s Radio 4 Today Programme on Saturday.“We don’t want to be in debates about the meaning of contested terms, we want to be united and focusing in contesting and criticising the horrific actions of the Israeli government,” said Chowns, who lost a co-leadership run againstZack Polanskiin 2025.The debate over whether the Greens’ decentralised policymaking structures remain suitable for a party whose membership has expanded rapidly comes hours after the party’s leader for England and Wales wasdefeated by Labour in the Holborn and St Pancras byelection.Polanksi, who received just under 33% of the vote on Friday, insisted he intended to remain as Green leader, despitecalls to stand down, including from the chair of the Jewish Greens. The party normally holds leadership elections every two years, meaning the next election would be in the summer of 2027.Does Polanski have to go? Greens at the crossroads after Holborn and St PancrasRead moreChowns said Polanksi’s “clear” lack of leadership over the Zionisim motion was “disappointing”, but that he had an opportunity to unite the party, having recognised the flaws in the motion.Tensions were heightened between the UK and Israel after the Labour government imposed sanctions on illegal settlements in occupied Palestine, and Israel retaliated by trying to close the British consulate in Jerusalem.Research carried out before the motion was passed found thatJewish people who vote for the Greens felt their attachment to Israel had weakened, even as the percentage of British Jews who identified as Zionist rose more broadly between 2022 and 2025.When asked about extremism and racism within the party – not only in relation to the motion but comments made by the deputy leader, Mothin Ali, after the Hamas attacks on 7 October 2023 in which he called for an end to “white supremacist European settler colonialism” – Chowns stressed the importance of the party’s internal processes.“I don’t know if there are extremists and racists in my party but I want to make sure that my party isn’t vulnerable to capture by extremists and racists, I want to make sure my party’s policies represent the views of the majority of members of the Green party who absolutely are not that sort of person at all,” she said.“Of course its legitimate to have difference of opinions including on many of the matters that this motion covers,” she added.Polanski has been accused of abdicating leadership after he missed the debate and the vote at the conference to instead campaign in the byelection, and for giving no clear message about whether or not he backed it.In interviews after the byelection loss, Polanski said he would have voted against the motion had he attended, given that two amendments he supported, both saying any future structure of a Palestinian state should be decided by Palestinians rather than a one-state system being imposed, were voted down.On Friday,Vivien Lichtenstein, the chair of the Jewish Greens, said Polanski, who is Jewish, made a “big mistake” by avoiding the vote. Asked if he should continue in his role, she told Times Radio: “No, I think he should resign.”However, other members of Jewish Greens said Lichtenstein’s comments did not reflect the majority view in the group, and that a vote of no confidence in her had been tabled.Explore more on these topicsGreen partyZack PolanskiJudaismnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Cockroach’ leader among thousands detained in Delhi protest crackdown | Delhi | The Guardian
description: Authorities impose strict lockdown in capital to try to stop rally against removal of 130m names from electoral roll
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Authorities impose strict lockdown in capital to try to stop rally against removal of 130m names from electoral roll
Content: 1:34Police detain anti-government 'Cockroach' party leader amid Delhi protests – videoDelhi‘Cockroach’ leader among thousands detained in Delhi protest crackdownAuthorities impose strict lockdown in capital to try to stop rally against removal of 130m names from electoral rollHannah Ellis-PetersenandAakash Hassanin DelhiSat 10 Oct 2026 07.17 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 01.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndian authorities have placed Delhi under a severe lockdown and detained tens of thousands of people, including the leader of the youth-led “Cockroach” movement, in an attempt to stop an anti-government protest.Thousands of people from across India were blocked from attending the demonstration, which had been called by the “Cockroach Janata party” (CJP) to protest against an exercise that has stripped 130m names from India’s electoral roll.TheCockroach movement, as well as opposition parties, civil society and student groups, have alleged that the process of “purifying” India’s voter roll was done toentrench the power of Narendra Modi‘s government, and have called for India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who oversaw the exercise, to resign.View image in fullscreenPolice detain and carry a protester away in Delhi.Photograph: Manish Swarup/APDelhi police denied permission for the protest to take place in the centre of the capital, and in the days leading up to Saturday, officials began to barricade roads throughoutDelhi. More than 25,000 police and security personnel were deployed across the city, many pulled from other states.Abhijeet Dipke, the founder and leader of the CJP, accused the government of being scared of the young people who were rising up in protest. “The mass crackdown on protesters and the shutdown of Delhi are not signs of strength but of a leader terrified of his own people,” said Dipke.Millions in India stripped of vote before critical state election, as government seeks to ‘purify’ electoral rollRead moreOn Saturday morning, police boarded Dipke’s plane as it landed at Delhi airport and detained him, alongside several other senior figures in the Cockroach movement. In a video recorded just before police detained him, Dipke said: “If you think you can stop us by threatening us with jail, then you have it wrong. Put us in jail if you want … but we will keep fighting to protect the democracy of this country.”View image in fullscreenA protester being detained by security personnel.Photograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersOthers in the CJP movement were detained across India, with arrests and detentions reported to be in the tens of thousands. One of India’s most popular YouTubers, Dhruv Rathee, who has 33m followers and has become a supporter of the CJP, was among those put under house arrest, while Delhi’s former chief minister Arvind Kejriwal was detained at the protest site.Student groups, who have also been calling for Kumar to resign, had described the march as India’s “second freedom struggle”, akin to Gandhi’s fight for independence. As police began mass detentions on Friday night, Neha Bora, a student leader at the forefront of the protests, said: “History is repeating itself. Just like in 1942, the arrest of leaders could not stop the Quit India movement; this movement will also not stop.” By Saturday afternoon, Bora had been detained.Over its 14 years in power, the Modi government has been rigidly intolerant of dissent. However, few protests have prompted such a draconian nationwide crackdown, signalling the government’s concern that this unrest could present a serious political challenge.In major disruption to travel, all trains arriving into Delhi’s two main stations on Saturday were cancelled for 10 hours and almost 50 metro stations were shut. Delhi’s schools and courtrooms were instructed to go online for the day and hotel owners were told to turn away customers.View image in fullscreenSecurity personnel chase a protester.Photograph: Manish Swarup/APTraffic diversions were in place across Delhi and police checkpoints were set up along the main highways from neighbouring states into the capital, with passengers being stopped and interrogated about their final destination. Delhi police told Uber drivers not to drop people near the protest area and said they were “tracking and stopping” bulk orders on food delivery services to Jantar Mantar.In Mumbai, housing societies sent out mass WhatsApp messages, telling parents to “mind your kids” and make sure they didn’t attempt to travel to join the protest.Around Jantar Mantar, which had previously been Delhi’s designated protest site and where the Cockroach supporters had hoped to gather, most of the main thoroughfares were shuttered and barricaded, surrounded by police and paramilitary officers. Riot-control vehicles and trucks fitted with water cannon stood nearby.View image in fullscreenPolie try to stop a detained protester escaping from a bus.Photograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersBuses were used to transport more than 6,000 people who were detained while attempting to reach Jantar Mantar. Paravin Singhal, a 75-year-old lawyer, said he had left home at 5am and shown his court identity card at checkpoints along the way, only to be stopped about 200 metres from Jantar Mantar.Singhal said he had come to stand with young people fighting to save the country from a “lawless regime playing with the constitution”. He accused Modi’s government and the election commission of using the revision of electoral rolls to influence future votes.After voting in elections for 50 years, he said, he had recently been told that his name had been removed from the rolls. “How can this happen to someone who has been voting for 50 years? What is even more disturbing is that the government is taking away our most fundamental right – the right to vote.”Singhal said he would stay put in the hope that more protesters would arrive. “The government is afraid because young people in this country are awake. They know their rights and are fighting for them. That is why the government is behaving like a dictatorship.”View image in fullscreenPolice patrol the streets of Delhi.Photograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersAmina Minnath, an undergraduate student at Delhi University, had also travelled to the area with friends. They had left before sunrise and navigated the checkpoints. The police barricading of Delhi, she said, had only strengthened her determination to protest.“These restrictions show that the government does not care about people’s rights,” she said. “This will not stop us. We may be detained, but we will come back in greater numbers. This will not end in a single day.”The revision of electoral rolls, in a process known as “special intensive revision (SIR), began last year and attracted criticism from civil society groups and the opposition alliance after it emerged that millions of names were being deleted.The backlash grew when SIR was held in the state of West Bengal and it became clear that Muslims and other minorities, who traditionally do not vote for Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP), were being disproportionately stripped of their vote.View image in fullscreenA protester is detained.Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPAYet it didn’t become an issue of national outrage until late last month, when the Indian Express newspaper published an investigation that exposed multiple irregularities in the SIR process, which had been flagged in more than a dozen internal objections but had been unilaterally overruled by Kumar.Opposition parties, the Cockroach movement and student groups began to call for the resignation of Kumar, who was appointed by a committee led by Modi. This week, India’s main opposition Congress party, also tried to reach Jantar Mantar to protest but were blocked by police, and the Congress leader, Rahul Gandhi, was detained twice.This week,the supreme courtordered the Modi government and the election commission to respond to the allegations. A BJP spokesperson said they had “no base, not an iota of evidence” and accused them of being driven by “an irresponsible, anarchist opposition”.Saturday’s protest follows the triumph of the Cockroach movement in July, when it led mass protests that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister. Since then, India’s youth have proved more willing to criticise the Modi regime and have expressed mounting anger at the obstruction of their freedom to protest.By Saturday evening, young people continued to gather in central Delhi neighbourhoods as the police continued pick up protesters en masse. Many, such as Prakhar Vashishth, who is in his early 20s, remained defiant despite the aggression of Delhi police. He had recently been asked to submit additional documents to establish his eligibility to remain on the electoral rolls.“We are living in extraordinary times, and young people in this country must come out to defend their future,” he said, as he stood near the police barricades around Jantar Mantar.“This government will go to any lengths to stay in power, even changing election rules or removing people it believes will not vote for it. But they cannot keep us away for ever.”Explore more on these topicsDelhiIndiaNarendra ModiSouth and central AsiaProtestActivismCivil liberties - internationalnewsShareReuse this content

title: Tourism expansion v turtle nests: the dispute dividing communities in one Tobago resort | Trinidad and Tobago | The Guardian
description: Plans for a 200-room project on an unspoiled beach have pitted developers against the conservationists fighting for smaller-scale schemes to protect the island’s habitat
Author: Jewel Fraser
Headline: Plans for a 200-room project on an unspoiled beach have pitted developers against the conservationists fighting for smaller-scale schemes to protect the island’s habitat
Content: Rocky Point and Pleasant Prospect, Tobago, where plans for a 200-room hotel have become a thorny issue. Photograph: Mark Meredith/Getty ImagesPlans for a 200-room project on an unspoiled beach have pitted developers against the conservationists fighting for smaller-scale schemes to protect the island’s habitatByJewel Fraserin Rocky Point, TobagoSupported byAbout this contentSat 10 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVisitors to Rocky Point in south-westTobagoare drawn to its sandy beach, fringed by coral reefs and dark rock formations and carpeted with the fruit-bearing trees found on Caribbean coastlines – almonds, sea grapes, coconuts, and the poisonous manchineel. The beach is part of Back Bay, a 500-metre swathe of land, and trekking through its undulating terrain, thickly covered in bush and shrubs, feels akin to walking through a rainforest.But this still relatively unspoiled location is at the centre of a struggle between two opposing interests – those who see large-scale development as the most profitable path and those who believe smaller, incremental developments owned by the community would be best.As elsewhere in the Caribbean, the need for economic growth has led to growing interest in tourism development. Rene Seepersadsingh, the first vice-president of theTobago Hotel and Tourism Association, says: “Tobago is very focused on attracting private partnership investment because our tourism product is now in that evolution stage, where we’re looking to upgrade the offering that we have.“There are great opportunities for participation and development within the sector,” he adds.View image in fullscreenThe eastern end of Back Bay, which houses multiple swimming areas and rock pools.Photograph: Theon Graham/The GuardianWith that goal in mind, the 12 hectares (30 acres) of Rocky Point became the subject of a request for expressions of interest in 2021 from the governmentagency Eteck, which manages and develops economic zones.Eteck invited proposals from qualified firms to design and manage a premier hotel and property development on the site. Superior Hotels, a locally owned company, ultimately won. It received a 99-year lease to develop a $500m (£378m), 200-room property on the site, which also includes plans for a number of privately owned villas.Since then, the project has sparked a struggle that has been going on for the past four years, led by environmentalists, Tobagonians and others who believe the development will ruin Rocky Point.Duane Kenny, a founding member of the Rocky Point Foundation – one of several entities that submitted an expression of interest to Eteck – is now advocating for increased accountability. A former hotel manager, he is an avid surfer at Back Bay and owns tourism-related businesses in Tobago.View image in fullscreenDuane Kenny, a founding member of the Rocky Point Foundation and avid surfer, at Rocky Point.Photograph: Theon Graham/The Guardian“Our focus is to make sure that whatever is done on that site is done in an environmentally sound way, in a way that preserves it for Tobago and for future generations,” he says.He says he and his associates replied to the expression of interest with a proposal for a small eco-resort featuring nature trails, turtle watching and a wax museum showcasing Amerindian artefacts discovered at Rocky Point. He also highlighted the remains of Fort Monck, a distinctive fort with well-preserved masonry.Kenny says the winning project’s initial design raised concerns about it seemingly ignoring many archaeological and ecological features at Rocky Point, and that the subsequent amendments still do not adequately address many of the issues raised.“The amount of concrete development on this site, at least in the current model, makes us worry that the impact on the environment will be significant,” he says, adding that in his view a 200-room hotel has little chance of success in Tobago, where most large hotels struggle to achieve sustainable occupancy levels.View image in fullscreenThe distinct rock formations that line the beach along the western end of Back Bay, Rocky Point.Photograph: Theon Graham/The GuardianMichelle Cazabon-Mannette, an environmental biologist anddirector at the NGO SpeSeas, says more than 100 people submitted written objections to theEnvironmental Management Authority(EMA) as part of the environmental impact assessment, which the project needs to obtain a certificate of environmental clearance (CEC). She says that after widespread objections at town hall meetings and in written submissions, the project holder made only minor design adjustments.After the adjustments, theEMA granted Superior Hotels a CEC, with about 20 pages of mitigation measures attached that the project must follow.Kirkland Brathwaite, principal at Katalyst Solutions, an environmental and project management firm, says a CEC often includes several environmental impact mitigation measures, adding that a quality assurance project plan is mandatory to ensure proper monitoring.View image in fullscreenThe dense tree canopy that sits above large sections of Rocky Point.Photograph: Theon Graham/The GuardianCazabon-Mannette says the mitigation measures listed in the CEC are insufficient, though she acknowledges that “the project designs provided – on which the CEC is based – were conceptual and (Superior Hotels) made it clear these were not final designs”.Whatever form the final designs take, Cazabon-Mannette and Kenny say a 200-room hotel and numerous villas will probably mean removing many of the trees on Rocky Point. “A major concern is having an appropriate scale of development that would minimise the footprint in terms of the coastal vegetation that would need to be cleared,” Cazabon-Mannette says.View image in fullscreenTree roots form natural steps leading down to the beach, which also protect the cliff from erosion.Photograph: Theon Graham/The GuardianShe adds that the trees provide shade and help protect the beach from coastal erosion, and their removal would harm one of Tobago’s most important turtle nesting sites. “At Back Bay, the shade keeps the sand cool,” she says, making it a choice for hawksbill turtles and leatherback turtles laying their eggs.Cazabon-Mannette says that sediment runoff from development could also threaten the unique coral reef that makes it a surfer’s paradise. The developer has promised to set up silt fences during construction to control sediment runoff, but “these things fail all the time”, Kenny says.‘A defining moment’: Trinidad and Tobago at a crossroads as oil runs outRead moreWhen questioned about the concerns of environmentalists, John Aboud, chairman of Superior Hotels T&T, replied to the Guardian by forwarding the CEC, without further comment.While the EMA approval has been issued, final approvals from Tobago’s Town and Country Planning Division and the assembly, its legislative body, remain under review.Marriott International, the company reportedly in talks to manage the resort, says it is not involved in the proposed development at Rocky Point and that it has not executed any agreement with Superior Hotels for the site.The EMA and Eteck were also approached for comment.Brathwaite says that expecting a developer to make significant changes to designs after an environmental impact assessment is completed would be unrealistic. “There is a general resistance to making any modifications because they have already spent quite a lot of money.”View image in fullscreenJemma’s Treehouse in Speyside, Tobago, a restaurant built around a tree.Photograph: PBH Images/AlamyHe believes that once the EMA grants a CEC and the accompanying mitigation measures are followed, there should be no real concerns about its environmental impact.“The CEC codifies the conditions that have to be met … and the monitoring requirements scale with the likely risk and severity posed to the environment in which the activities are proposed to be carried out,” he says. “So they become progressively more stringent for areas that are more environmentally sensitive.”Yet many local people believe a development thatneeds so many mitigation measures, which they consider to carry extensive risks, is not the way forward for Tobago.TheCaribbean Natural Resources Institute(Canari) has been advocating a different approach, called community-based tourism, in other areas of Tobago, such asSpeyside, about an hour’s drive north of Rocky Point.Dylis McDonald, Canari’s senior technical officer, says projects such as the one at Speyside are usually small-scale and rooted in community members’ own vision for their future. “In the community-based tourism space, very often conservation, restoration and protection are core to what the enterprises are doing,” she says. “There is a particular type of ownership and understanding and connection to the areas where those activities are implemented.”View image in fullscreenKenny among the nature-rich site of Fort Monk on the western end of the cliffs overlooking Rocky Point.Photograph: Theon Graham/The GuardianCampaigners and experts acknowledge that while small hotels succeed in Tobago, other small-scale eco-tourism sites may still not consistently provide steady income. Turtle nesting patrols, for instance, employ people to protect the hatchling turtles and eggs, but it is seasonal work that offers only a stipend when funds are available.Yet, Kenny says, a development that is in harmony with nature and a sustainable business model is possible. “You can have your cake and eat it, too.”Explore more on these topicsSouthern frontlines: Latin America and the CaribbeanTrinidad and TobagoCoralEndangered habitatsLogging and land-clearingTravel & leisureCaribbeanfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Climate crisis is coming to crush many of world’s best surf breaks, study warns | Coastlines | The Guardian
description: Changing tide levels, shifting sands and hardened shorelines put waves at risk, affecting more than just surfers
Author: Damian Carrington
Headline: Changing tide levels, shifting sands and hardened shorelines put waves at risk, affecting more than just surfers
Content: A surfer rides a tube at Oriente-Salvaje, El Salvador, one of the most at-risk surf breaks in the study.Photograph: Angelo PicardoView image in fullscreenA surfer rides a tube at Oriente-Salvaje, El Salvador, one of the most at-risk surf breaks in the study.Photograph: Angelo PicardoCoastlinesClimate crisis is coming to crush many of world’s best surf breaks, study warnsChanging tide levels, shifting sands and hardened shorelines put waves at risk, affecting more than just surfersDamian CarringtonEnvironment editorFri 9 Oct 2026 23.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe climate crisis is coming for some of the world’s greatest surf breaks, submerging some as sea level rises and wiping out others as classic breaks get crushed against coastal developments.Analysis of dozens of famous waves inworld surfing reserves(WSR) found more than three-quarters were at high risk because of changing tide levels, hardened shorelines and shifting sands.The impacts matter not only to the surfers catching the waves but also to the communities that depend on the multibillion-dollar surf economy, often located in places with little else.The waves rated at most risk in the study include the “bombing barrels”of Croyde beach in north Devon, UK, the point breaks at Noosa in Australia and Oriente Salvaje, El Salvador, and Santa Cruz reefs of California such as Sewer Peak and Wind and Sea.View image in fullscreenCroyde’s heavy wave is considered the best beach break in the UK.Photograph: Rob TibblesThe best surfing waves are created by intricate combinations of sea-floor shape, swell direction and tide. “Surf breaks are incredibly unique oceanographic phenomena – a confluence of all these factors that fit together just right to make the wave happen – and so those processes are really sensitive,” said Dan Reineman, an associate professor at California State University Channel Islands and a co-author of the study.Global heating is pushing upsea leveland changing rainfall patterns that affect sediment movement, which can upset the delicate balance and destroy the wave. However, the researchers said the expert local knowledge of surfers could be tapped to help protect the waves.Trent Hodges, a co-author of the study and a senior programmes manager at Save the Waves Coalition, which launched the WSR programme in 2009, said: “Climate change will impact surf breaks all over the world in different ways, depending on their unique geographies. We learned directly from the local surfers how they are seeing their waves change. It’s a canary in the coalmine too – when a wave changes, that often means the beach is changing, and everybody enjoys the beach.”View image in fullscreenThe point breaks at Noosa in Australia are among those at most at risk.Photograph: Luke SorensenThe study,published in the journal Climatic Change, concludes: “Climate change and coastal management both have significant negative implications for the future viability of multiple surf breaks of global significance and, therefore, the myriad distinct local communities, cultures and economies they support.”Almost 200 local experts analysed 57 surf breaks in all but two of the 13 WSRs, spread across eight countries. The researchers said thousands of other surf waves around the world faced similar peril.A key finding was that where coastlines were more natural, they could adapt better to the changes brought by the climate crisis, by shifting inland and relocating sediments. Development such as sea walls, jetties and groynes made the beaches and waves less resilient, Reineman said.View image in fullscreenSaunton Sands in north Devon has a world-renowned longboard wave.Photograph: Rob TibblesAdam Hall, a co-founder of the North Devon WSR, was one of the local surfers who contributed to the study. He said: “North Devon is so special. We have Saunton Sands, a world-renowned longboarding wave with really long, mellow rides, and the UK’s best beach break at Croyde. We’ve got left- and right-hand point breaks and a sheltered spot for when it gets too windy and too big. Whatever you want to do, we’ve got it.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toDown to EarthThe planet's most important stories. Get all the week's environment news - the good, the bad and the essentialEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe said surfing was very important for the local economy, and not just in summer. “Surfers will come throughout the year. They fill up the pubs, restaurants and car parks when the swells are good in January, February and March, where if you go to any other tourist destination that doesn’t have surf, they’re dead on their knees.”The researchers want more local surfers to use the tools developed to assess their own breaks and work with local authorities and other groups to protect waves from coastal development and climate change.View image in fullscreenSurfing brings in about $200m a year to Santa Cruz, according to Save the Waves Coalition’s Trent Hodges.Photograph: Ryan Chachi CraigSome places already do this, such as the city of Gold Coast in Australia, which has put surf protection in planning law; New Zealand, which designates surf breaks of “national significance”; and Peru’sLey derompientes(law of the breakers) that protects listed surf breaks.“Surfing is a huge driver of local economies,” Hodges said. “So whether you’re a surfer or not, that money supports local businesses, hotels, lodgings and so on.”In Santa Cruz, surfing brings in about $200m (£151m) a year, he said.“In the east of El Salvador, you have some of the most perfect point break waves you will find, and the entire economy there is pretty much dependent on surfing,” Hodges added.Explore more on these topicsCoastlinesClimate crisisOceansSurfingTravel & leisurenewsShareReuse this content

title: Country diary: The house martins are gone for another year. But they’re not forgotten | Birds | The Guardian
description: Lockerbrook, Derbyshire: Last week they were here, now they are not. Yet the details of their epic migration are still a mystery to us
Author: Ed Douglas
Headline: Lockerbrook, Derbyshire: Last week they were here, now they are not. Yet the details of their epic migration are still a mystery to us
Content: A common house martin, which breeds in Europe and winters in sub-Saharan Africa.Photograph: AlamyView image in fullscreenA common house martin, which breeds in Europe and winters in sub-Saharan Africa.Photograph: AlamyCountry diaryBirdsCountry diary: The house martins are gone for another year. But they’re not forgottenLockerbrook, Derbyshire:Last week they were here, now they are not. Yet the details of their epic migration are still a mystery to usEd DouglasSat 10 Oct 2026 00.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 02.21 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe sudden absence of something, even though you know it’s coming, can dent the heart a little. The Japanese, inevitably, have a phrase for it:mono no aware, the pathos of things – and by things, in this case, I mean house martins.Last week I had stood in the same spot, looking across the same valley. The weather then was much the same as it was today, low‑angled sunlight through patchy cloud lighting up the yellowing birch leaves and bronzing moors on the north-eastern slopes ofKinder Scout. It had picked out the spread wings of a buzzard a little below my eyeline, along with a haze of large insects, which in fact, I quickly realised, were house martins.Such fecundity was thrilling to see, especially as dwindling numbers have put house martins on the red list of threatened species. Dozens swooped and turned just in front of me, and as I looked through this cloud of acrobatic mayhem, dozens more were doing the same in the middle distance, gorging on insects before the long flight south.Country diary: where did house martins live before there were houses?Read moreToday, though, they were gone, the sky empty save for a kestrel quartering her patch, head dropped between her shoulders like a jeweller over her loupe. I wondered where these brave little travellers were now and how many would survive to return.The mere fact of such migrations is astounding, made more so by the mystery that still surrounds them. These birds will winter somewhere in sub-Saharan Africa, but exactly where is unknown. Dutch researchers looked at isotopes in the feathers of their returning birds and could onlynarrow it down to west Africa. Researchers have also found microplastics trapped in house martin feathers, tiny fragments swept up into the air, where they linger among the martin’s insect food.We blunder through these gossamer systems, brushing them aside almost unseen with every turn around the sun. It’s revealing, too, how those who find it politically expedient to mention natural variation in climate are much less interested in discussing the evolved instinct of many species, including our own, to migrate for survival.Under the Changing Skies: The Best of the Guardian’s Country Diary, 2018-2024, is available now atguardianbookshop.comExplore more on these topicsBirdsCountry diaryRural affairsAnimalsWildlifeAnimal behaviourfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Recruitment boss accused of being behind ‘doxxing’ campaign against RNLI and anti-racism activists | RNLI | The Guardian
description: Tom Watson, of Worcester, alleged to be behind Big Time Charlie X account that created so-called Traitorbase
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Tom Watson, of Worcester, alleged to be behind Big Time Charlie X account that created so-called Traitorbase
Content: Tom Watson is accused of being behind the X account Big Time Charlie.Photograph: FacebookView image in fullscreenTom Watson is accused of being behind the X account Big Time Charlie.Photograph: FacebookRNLIRecruitment boss accused of being behind ‘doxxing’ campaign against RNLI and anti-racism activistsTom Watson, of Worcester, alleged to be behind Big Time Charlie X account that created so-called TraitorbaseBen QuinnPolitical correspondentSat 10 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 03.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe owner of a recruitment firm has been accused of being at the centre of a so-called “doxxing” campaign against the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), anti-racism activists and business executives who recruit black, Asian and minority ethnic workers.Tom Watson, from Worcester, is alleged to be behind anXaccount calling itself “Big Time Charlie”, which was deactivated shortly after he was named by the campaign group Hope Not Hate.The account had almost 50,000 followers and had become increasingly prominent in recent weeks as RNLI staff found themselves being harassed and attacked online as far-right activists targeted them over their involvement in rescuing people trying to cross the Channel in small boats.The account, which has a history of racist comments, appears to have been using AI to scrape data from LinkedIn and other sites to build a so-called Traitorbase. The Big Time Charlie account was removed almost immediately after Hope Not Hate alleged that Watson was behind it, and after the Guardian approached him for comment.Like the posts on Watson’s LinkedIn account, the X account has frequently praised the hard-right MP Rupert Lowe. It also claimed to have donated £2,500 to Lowe’sRestore Britainparty and joined its “Cromwell Club” for those activists who pay a certain level of donation.Targets of doxxing by the Big Time Charlie account told the Guardian of the impact.They included Chantelle Lunt, a Green party councillor in Merseyside who has already been targeted by the far right, and who made a report to the police after details about her were published online by the account.She said: “Someone told me that I had been doxxed and when I went to look I saw that details about me appeared to be on a spreadsheet which included reference to other people who were involved in Stand Up to Racism.“The climate at the moment is horrendous and I’m no stranger to people targeting me and my family, but there’s a big concern when this information is actively put out there. You can see people engaging with it and actively encouraging each other.”A spokesperson for a charity that was targeted told the Guardian: “This is another example of a cynical attempt to spread misinformation that has unfortunately gone unchecked on social media platforms.“This is an attempt to sow discord and division among communities and prevent organisations trying to help the most vulnerable communities in this country from operating at their full potential.“Time spent combating misinformation and bigotry is a distraction from these organisations’ programme work here at home, which actually makes a difference in the ordinary lives of people in the UK.Social mediacompanies, the media and politicians have a responsibility to clamp down on misinformation and the division it causes.”RNLI warns supporters their personal information may have been hackedRead moreA number of businesses, big and small, were also doxxed on the account, which posted the photographs and names of executives who were said to have been involved in hiring minority ethnic staff.A businessperson who was also targeted described their doxxing by the account as “bizarre”.“Thankfully it doesn’t seem to have led to any problems, but it’s not something that you expect to have to contend with. It’s a pretty unpleasant thing to do, especially if it’s someone who is involved in their own business,” they added.Watson divides his time between the UK and US and founded the recruitment firm Futura Energy Group, which describes itself as “a specialist recruitment and build-with talent partner for companies operating across AI”.Archived online records show that the Big Time Charlie account originally bore the name Tom Watson, while a range of other evidence links him to it.That included regular references by the account to being in Puerto Rico, where Futura is based according to its LinkedIn account, and references to working in recruitment for technical roles.The Big Time Charlie account posted on 20 July that they were in Zurich and shared a photo taken in the grounds of the Vitznauerhof hotel. Two days later, Watson posted on his LinkedIn profile that he was in Switzerland and shared another image taken from the Vitznauerhof hotel.Watson was approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsRNLIRupert LoweRestore BritainAI (artificial intelligence)XSocial medianewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘If voters aren’t better off by the next election, we’re screwed’: Labour insiders voice fears over budget | Budget | The Guardian
description: Some say party risks ‘looking twee’ by focusing on small fixes amid growing nervousness that budget lacks ambition
Author: Pippa Crerar
Headline: Some say party risks ‘looking twee’ by focusing on small fixes amid growing nervousness that budget lacks ambition
Content: Andy Burnham set out a big vision at conference, but some  Labour figures fear ‘low-key’ budget could underwhelm voters.Photograph: Zeynep Demir Aslim/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham set out a big vision at conference, but some  Labour figures fear ‘low-key’ budget could underwhelm voters.Photograph: Zeynep Demir Aslim/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockBudget‘If voters aren’t better off by the next election, we’re screwed’: Labour insiders voice fears over budgetSome say party risks ‘looking twee’ by focusing on small fixes amid growing nervousness that budget lacks ambitionPippa CrerarandJessica ElgotSat 10 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the days since Labour’s annual conference, party insiders have been sharing a word cloud produced by the pollsters More in Common, which shows the phrases voters most associate withAndy Burnham.Such polling is rarely flattering for politicians, and the prime minister’s version had its fair share of negatives. But one of the most prominent words inthe cloud– and the one that has caught the imagination of Labour strategists – was “trying”.At a cabinet away day at Chequers on Monday and a meeting for special advisers on Thursday, the idea that the government was doing its best to improve people’s lives – despite the difficult economic backdrop – was a golden thread.“The public think the only person that can reach those levers is you,” said a government insider. “They justifiably ask, can you do it or not? And if not, they’ll look for an alternative. We have to avoid the sense of things being out of our control.”A party strategist said: “Voters don’t want us to put our hands up in despair; they want us to roll our sleeves up. They don’t want us to be helpless in the face of global stuff; they want answers.” But will this prime minister be able to provide them?View image in fullscreenNo 10, Andy’s den? Burnham plays bingo with Brenda Ficociello, 88, during a visit to the Humphrey Booth Resource Centre in Salford.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/ReutersAt conference, Burnham set out his big vision for the future – on social care and the pensions triple lock, the EU and electoral reform. The party faithful lapped it up and polling suggested the “Burnham bounce” had continued.But whileLabourMPs are relieved to have a leader with a clear political direction, many worry that offering big promises for after the next general election will not be enough to scratch the itch for dramatic change.Downing Street believes part of the answer is what it describes as “everyday fixes” – cost of living measures that might not, on their own, amount to very much, but added up can make a difference and show the government is trying.Overseen by the No 10 policy unit and the Cabinet Office’s cost of living taskforce, each department has “incubators” where proposals are dreamed up. Many are in the works, such as rules around car-parking apps and unbranded school uniforms.They might not grab the media headlines, but strategists say they pick up engagement online, with 85m views across all social platforms last week alone. There will be more announced in the two-and-a-bit weeks running up to John Healey’s first budget on 28 October.“We want to show we can tackle the everyday frustrations that people assume are part of life,” one adviser said. But several admitted they had some qualms about the drumbeat of small interventions.“We risk looking twee, frankly, if we aren’t successfully thinking about how to tie it to the bigger picture of structural change. Public control, tax, that is what we want to be able to point to as well as the everyday things.”Another added: “We need to tread carefully. We have very small interventions now and huge ambitions for three years’ time. We also need medium-scale changes in the medium term, and that is what is missing at the moment.”View image in fullscreenA news screen announces Burnham’s £2 bus fares cap in Warrington town centre.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThe government faces a difficult budget, with inflation and soaring borrowing costs as a result of the Iran war thought to have blown a £12bn hole in the public finances, forcing the chancellor to consider tax rises and spending cuts to fund plans to ease the cost of living.The statement, which is expected to be “low key”, will focus on fiscal devolution, with a household support package centred on cutting energy bills and more help for small businesses. Next year’s spending review would require more revenue, sources said, but details would have to wait.A No 10 aide said: “The budget is a moment of peak attention and potentially peak peril. We’re not able to do everything we want to, so we have to level with people and say we can’t fix everything all at once, but we’re trying.”But for some MPs, there is a growing nervousness at the low level of ambition at this budget, especially on cost of living measures, which the Burnham government has made its main test.One said: “If voters aren’t better off by the next election, we are screwed. As things stand, this looks like a Reeves budget with better vibes. I hope this isn’t all there is. But I really fear that actually it is.”View image in fullscreenJohn Healey, then the defence secretary, with the former chancellor Rachel Reeves in March 2025.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live NewsTreasury insiders acknowledge the need to “kickstart” longer-term changes at the budget – and that a “low-key” statement with the big decisions put off until next year may not be enough for the public. “The budget will be our first punch in the face moment,” a government aide said.There was a “bit of friction” between the prime minister’s office and the Treasury over balancing fiscal responsibility with hope, the source added. “No 10 wants to signal intent: that we won’t get everything immediately, but we’ll get there.”There were lingering questions about “how this all adds up when we’re under grey skies”, another adviser added. “It’s impossible to see how anyone can square the additional spending we need given the tightness of the fiscal envelope.”Ministers and advisers are expecting a barrage of attacks from the Tories and Reform UK on welfare. But they believe the Milburn and Timms reviews, which will be published shortly after the budget – will help them fight back.Downing Street expects the days after the budget to be “bumpy” but is optimistic that Burnham’s communication skills will help to make the case, and that the public will continue – for now – to give him the benefit of the doubt.A source said: “We’ll take a bit of a hit over the budget. It’s going to be a tough couple of weeks. But then we have a run to the 10-year plan. If we get that right, we can potentially go into next year with people saying: ‘Yes, it’s difficult, but we trust this guy.’”At the cabinet away day, Burnham told ministers: “Politics has become too suffocating. We need greater ambition. The country is not where it should be and nothing simple gets us out of that. We need to show a journey and a longer-term plan.”Ministers were presented with polling that showed support for Labour’s social care policy, including adjusting the pensions triple lock, went up by a quarter after voters were shown a video of the prime minister explaining his plan.A party strategist told them: “On social care and the triple lock we need to continually make the case, time after time. When we make the case we have the power to persuade.”There is a political axiom that if you’re explaining, you’re losing. But Labour strategists are pushing back on that idea. The prevailing view inside government is that Burnham is the only one who can go out and make the case – on all of his big promises – to the country.Not everybody inside the party thinks it will work. “I don’t know how convinced I am about giving people essentially the same message as before: we want to do more but we’re constrained,” one insider said.But ministers hope that by focusing on policies which signal intent, they can get through these difficult months. “We need more time to lean into the big things we can do, like public control, but we need to be honest with voters. We set ourselves a target of tackling the cost of living, but so many things are out of our control.”No 10 insight work shows that people were still prepared to accept the Iran conflict as an explanation for why things are so tough, rather than viewing it as an excuse. At the away day, Healey told his colleagues: “We are recognising those pressures, being honest about what we can do and taking practical action wherever possible to give people some breathing space at the budget.”When parliament returns after conference recess on Monday, Burnham will give a statement, updating MPs on the past few weeks and taking questions. Throughout, he will aim to show the public he is on their side.But one senior Labour figure cautioned: “We all hope that he has a plan for what comes next. The sense that he gets it and that he’ll keep trying won’t last for ever.”On Tuesday 1 December, join John Crace and Pippa Crerar as they skewer the biggest stories from Westminster and beyond, as part of theGuardian’s year in review event. Joined by fellow Guardian writers, expect candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as they look back on the year-defining stories of 2026.
