title: Study explores links between 19th-century Manchester workers and enslaved Africans in Caribbean | Peterloo massacre | The Guardian
description: Global Threads research project reveals how slavery hung ‘like a spectre’ over the Peterloo massacre and other Mancunian struggles for equality
Author: Chris Osuh
Headline: Global Threads research project reveals how slavery hung ‘like a spectre’ over the Peterloo massacre and other Mancunian struggles for equality
Content: The Global Threads project is part of research into the history of the Portico Library.Photograph: Richard Saker/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Global Threads project is part of research into the history of the Portico Library.Photograph: Richard Saker/The GuardianCotton Capital: ongoing seriesPeterloo massacreStudy explores links between 19th-century Manchester workers and enslaved Africans in CaribbeanGlobal Threads research project reveals how slavery hung ‘like a spectre’ over the Peterloo massacre and other Mancunian struggles for equalityChris OsuhCommunity affairs correspondentSat 10 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 08.03 EDTShareThey were the killings that changed Britain, paving the way for working-class people’s right to vote, as well as leading to the founding of the Manchester Guardian. In thePeterloo massacreof 1819, peaceful protesters were shot and trampled to death by the Manchester and Salford Yeomanry at St Peter’s Field in the city.A study byGlobal Threads, a public history project, has examined how the exploitation of Africans enslaved in the Caribbean was linked with the struggles of cotton workers at Peterloo. Though these workers were divided by thousands of miles and led different lives, they were exploited by the same forces – asRobert Wedderburn, a Black abolitionist in London, said at the time.As well as looking atWedderburn’s story, Global Threads’ research looks at the life of Hugh Hornby Birley, the yeomanry commander who led the fatal charge on the crowd at Peterloo. It found Birley’s family fortune was intimately linked with transatlantic enslavement.View image in fullscreenRobert Wedderburn, a Black abolitionist based in London.Photograph: History and Art Collection/AlamyMeanwhile, the story ofSir George Philips, also examined in the project, reflects the contradictions of 19th-century liberal politics. While Philips helped fund the Manchester Guardian as a liberal reaction to Peterloo, he was personally invested in the exploitation of enslaved Africans in the Caribbean, as owner of theSuccessplantation in Hanover, Jamaica.Birley and Philips weremembers of the Portico Library, Manchester’s historic members’ library. In the 19th century it was a centre of information exchange for Manchester’s business elite, helping ensure their place at the apex of global capitalism. The Global Threads project is part of research into the history of the Portico, which stands a few yards from where the Peterloo massacre took place.Introducing the study, Global Threads said: “Drawing together just three of the thousands of threads connecting Peterloo with Africa and the Americas, we can see how the leaders of each wing of Manchester’s elite – Hugh Hornby Birley and Sir George Philips – owed their positions and power to their family and business activities drawing on colonialism and slavery.“They actively described the system they had created as a transatlantic one. It was not just profit that connected Peterloo … Birley and his reactionary colleagues brought colonial-style coercion more akin to the putting down of uprisings of enslaved people, working people themselves were connected to transatlantic people and places, and slavery hung like a spectre over the Mancunian struggles for justice and equality.”On 16 August 1819, 60,000 people converged in the centre of Manchester to campaign for political representation. Conditions for those workers were better than those endured by the trafficked and enslaved African workers at the other end of the transatlantic commodity boom, who were classed as property. But Britain’s working class were disenfranchised. Only 10% of men in the country could vote, and while landowners were enriched by the tariffs placed on foreign grain by the Corn Laws, workers could barely afford bread.The protest at St Peter’s Field ended in tragedy when the yeomanry – a militia of Tory businessmen – charged the crowd. In the aftermath, the authorities blamed protesters. But Wedderburn, a Jamaican-born Unitarian preacher, was quick to challenge the official narrative.In September 1819, at a meeting at his Soho chapel, he described Peterloo as “an act of murder … committed by the magistrates and yeoman”. In his preaching and writings, Wedderburn had long argued Africans and English labourers were being denied by the same forces.View image in fullscreenThe Peterloo tapestry in Albert Square, Manchester.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThe backstory ofBirleyshows how. Ella Sinclair, writing for Global Threads, found Birley’s family’s business financially benefited from the estate of Daniel Backhouse, an enslaver whofunded and profited from 103 voyages that set out from Liverpool between 1773 and 1807, trafficking more than 27,000 Africans.In the late 18th century, three of those voyages exported people to St Lucia, where Backhouse’s company funded and profited from the Rabot sugar estate. Early 19th-century records reveal that workers there included families trafficked from Guinea and Cape Verde.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |MonthlySign up toCotton CapitalStarting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter the emancipation of enslaved Africans in the British empire in the 1830s, the Birley family supported the enslaving US confederacy, which was integral to their cotton interests. Birley was closely involved with the development of Manchester institutions, including “the Liverpool and Manchester Railway – designed to more easily transport slave-produced cotton”, Sinclair found.Wedderburn’s family was also embedded in the plantation economy. His uncle, John Wedderburn, owned the Blackheath, Blackness, Bluecastle and Glen Islay plantations in Westmoreland, Jamaica. Workers on those plantations included people trafficked from Old Calabar, in modern-day Nigeria, to Montego Bay in 1773, on a ship carrying textiles woven in Manchester.Robert Wedderburn’s mother was an enslaved woman called Rosanne, while his father was the plantation owner who raped her. Raised in Jamaica by his African grandmother, Talky Amee, Wedderburn served in the Royal Navy and sailed to London, settling in multicultural St Giles and became a leading radical.Global Threads found that the Dreadnought, the ship that trafficked some enslaved workers to Wedderburn plantations, had also trafficked workers to Success, the plantation later owned by Philips.At the time of Peterloo, Wedderburn was in prison, accused of inciting slaves to kill their masters. He believed in armed struggle against enslavement across the Caribbean, and that a revolution had begun at Peterloo.Around the same time as Peterloo, hundreds ofabolitionists who had escaped slaverywere staging raids on plantations in St Catherine, Jamaica. The British governor at the time was, coincidentally, titled the Duke of Manchester.In a paper on Wedderburn, Global Threads historians write: “In the weeks following the [Peterloo] massacre, Wedderburn gave the most clear contemporary articulation of a transatlantic understanding of liberation and justice. He drew direct parallels for his followers … showing that the oligarchy profiting from the labour of working people in Manchester – while denying their rights to representation and improved working and living conditions – were part of the same elite and system that imposed the violence and coercion of slavery upon enslaved Africans.”Explore more on these topicsPeterloo massacreCotton Capital: ongoing seriesManchesterSlaveryColonialismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Telegraph owner poised to make newsroom job cuts in investment promise U-turn | Telegraph Media Group | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: German media group Axel Springer said to be planning between 50 and 100 editorial redundancies
Author: Michael Savage
Headline: Exclusive: German media group Axel Springer said to be planning between 50 and 100 editorial redundancies
Content: The German media group, Axel Springer, had said it would invest in the Telegraph to make it the ‘leading centre-right media outlet in the English-speaking world’.Photograph: Yui Mok/PAView image in fullscreenThe German media group, Axel Springer, had said it would invest in the Telegraph to make it the ‘leading centre-right media outlet in the English-speaking world’.Photograph: Yui Mok/PATelegraph Media GroupTelegraph owner poised to make newsroom job cuts in investment promise U-turnExclusive: German media group Axel Springer said to be planning between 50 and 100 editorial redundanciesMichael SavageMedia editorSat 10 Oct 2026 06.31 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 06.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe new owner of theTelegraphis preparing to make significant job cuts to its newsroom, just months after stating it would invest in the title to make it the “leading centre-right media outlet in the English-speaking world”.Axel Springer, the German media company overseen by its billionaire chief executive, Mathias Döpfner, is understood to be examining proposals that would make between 50 and 100 journalists redundant.A source familiar with the plans said a forthcoming consultation was likely to propose cutting a “significant proportion” of editorial staff, possibly before Christmas.They said such proposals called into question Axel Springer’s promise to “back an investment programme in [the Telegraph Media Group] to grow and expand the business”.A spokesperson for the Telegraph Media Group declined to comment. No redundancies have been announced to staff so far.View image in fullscreenAxel Springer’s chief executive, Mathias Döpfner, is understood to have said previously the Telegraph could not cut its way to growth.Photograph: Dpa Picture Alliance/AlamyIt would mark the first big intervention by Axel Springer since its £575m purchase of the Telegraph earlier this year. The sale endedthree tortuous yearsfor the Telegraph and its staff, during which potential owners were blocked, fell through or faced fierce internal opposition.The proposed cuts have confused some Telegraph figures, who are struggling to understand how it aligns with Döpfner’s pledge to “bring that uncertainty to an end”.At a recent Axel Springer leadership summit held in London, Döpfner is also said to have stated that the company could not cut its way to growth.Axel Springer, which also owns Politico and the German titles Bild and Die Welt, recently brought in consultants to examine the financial health of the Telegraph titles, which include the Daily Telegraph, the Sunday Telegraph and its online news operation.Döpfner has made no secret of his desire to boost theTelegraph’s US operation, with senior editors already deployed to the US to develop those plans.However, consultants are understood to have drawn up potential cuts to the existing news operation at the 171-year-old titles.Sources said consultants had also recommended that the Telegraph set up side projects to support its journalism, such as price comparison sites and healthcare. Some insiders were said to be baffled by some of the suggestions.A source familiar with the proposals said they would anger Telegraph staff, who had hoped Axel Springer’s ownership would mark the arrival of “sunny uplands” after three years of being “starved of any form of investment, pay rises or management changes that could move us on”.“The path to growth is not to cut jobs,” they said. “They’re still going to need to hire people in the States if they’re going to make any sort of push there, but staff haven’t been told where that money is going to come from.”The Telegraph Media Group’s latest accounts showed that it had slumped to a £4m loss last year as a result of legal fees connected to its ownership saga and the revaluing of assets. Its revenue had also fallen slightly from 2024 to £273.2m.However, the accounts of Telegraph Media Group Holdings also revealed it had made an underlying pre-tax operating profit of about £48m.Explore more on these topicsTelegraph Media GroupAxel SpringerNational newspapersNewspapersNewspapers & magazinesMedia downturnMedia businessnewsShareReuse this content

title: Alleged abuse victims at British military school in Germany tell of agonising fight for justice | Violence against women and girls | The Guardian
description: Two women, now in their 50s, say MoD refuses to take responsibility for abuse they suffered as children
Author: Hannah Al-Othman
Headline: Two women, now in their 50s, say MoD refuses to take responsibility for abuse they suffered as children
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesViolence against women and girlsAlleged abuse victims at British military school in Germany tell of agonising fight for justiceTwo women, now in their 50s, say MoD refuses to take responsibility for abuse they suffered as childrenHannah Al-OthmanSat 10 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnne and Jane* were 10 years old when a member of staff connected with their British military school in Bünde,Germanyis alleged to have singled them out and sexually abused them.Now in their 50s, the women say he coerced them into keeping silent, and for decades they had only discussed their experiences with one another. “He said if we ever told anybody, then our fathers would lose their jobs and they would be kicked out of the army,” Jane said. “Being two young 10-year-old girls who basically followed their fathers around the world, their jobs were our lives.”But five years ago, with her father retired from military service, Anne found out the man was still alive and decided to come forward to report the alleged abuse. She said she did so in the hope that she and Jane would finally see justice.More than 40 years later, they are affected by what they allege happened to them.“He was my first sexual encounter at the age of 10,” Jane said. “I struggled with relationships at an early age … I’ve never ever been able to be in a loving relationship.”Similarly, Anne said that from a young age “there was a spiral of self-destruction” and she had been left traumatised. As a school governor, she said smells from her childhood brought back memories of the alleged abuse. “I remember walking through the school corridor, and I just felt sick,” she said.But despite their efforts to bring their alleged abuser to justice,a joint investigation by the Guardian and openDemocracy has found that he cannot be prosecuted, because although he was a British citizen, employed by theBritish army, incomplete records of his employment have repeatedly halted investigations into the allegations.Nato rules state that countries with armed forces abroad can apply their laws to people who fall under their jurisdiction, including serving members of the military and civilian employees. But the absence of the man’s employment contract, along with no proof that he paid tax to the British crown, meant the police could not prove he was employed on aMinistry of Defence(MoD) London contract rather than a locally employed contract.The women say the MoD refuses to take responsibility for the abuse they allege they suffered while under its care._____Anne and Jane believe their alleged abuser deliberately targeted them because they were isolated from other children at the school.“I was shy, very, very shy and introverted, and also struggled with all the moving,” Anne said. “I was in quite a bad place anyway by the time I got to Germany.”She said it initially felt “so exciting to be singled out by this incredibly charismatic man. Everyone sort of swooned in his presence, adults and children alike.”She added: “When he did turn his gaze very singly on me, I absolutely fell for it.”The man’s interactions with the girls became sexual, they said, with much of the alleged abuse taking place in his office.“Once we’d get into that room, he’d lock the door from the inside,” Jane said, “and then it went very, very dark very quickly.”Jane can still remember the number plate of his car, reciting it effortlessly. “My stomach used to sink when I saw that car,” she said, “because I knew he was in there and I knew what the day was going to entail for both of us.”The alleged abuse, which took place in the 1980s, began to affect the girls straight away. Anne said she “went into a state of terror” at the time.“I was having night terrors, I was sleepwalking, I believed someone was outside looking into my bedroom. I hated getting changed at night, I’d go to bed in my clothes.”_________Anne and Jane kept in contact for a few years after they left the school, writing letters to each other in which they would reference the alleged abuse – and which Anne still has.But later they lost touch. It was only when they were in their 50s that they reconnected on Facebook, after Anne had come forward in 2018 to disclose what had happened as part of the Truth Project, run by the Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse in England and Wales.As part of her disclosure, Anne said she would be willing for the police to be notified, and the case was passed to the RoyalMilitaryPolice (RMP).The force told her that it would only be able to proceed with the case if it was able to track down Jane to corroborate her story.Around the time the pair connected online, detectives also found Jane, after the police knocked on her parents’ door and told them that the RMP needed to speak to her as an “important witness” in a case – leading her to disclose to her parents for the first time what had happened to her.With the RMP now able to investigate, Anne believed her alleged abuser would be brought to justice.“I thought they could arrest him and make him go to court and go to prison,” she said.Her hopes were shattered when the RMP said it was unable to progress the case because they did not have jurisdiction.She was told that her alleged abuser could not be prosecuted in the UK because they could not find evidence that he had paid tax to HMRC, meaning that the case would have to be prosecuted in Germany – where the statute of limitations had expired.The women were also told the RMP had been unable to find any evidence of his tax contributions in Germany.Although the RMP was passed some evidenceof his employment at the school, including staff lists, witness accounts and photographs, a lack of more formal evidence about his employment or tax status stalled all progress in their case.After the women complained about the outcome, they received a written apology from a senior officer, who said: “The handling of your case fell below the professional standards you had every right to expect.”The MoD’s then newly formed Defence Serious Crime Unit (DSCU) launched a second investigation, but it reached the same conclusion. Army records for the school from the time had been destroyed, and without evidence of his employment contract, which may have indicated his tax status, they were told there was no way forward.Jane said it felt like “another door slamming in your face” when the second investigation ended.__________________While Anne and Jane want justice for themselves, they are also telling their story in the hope that it may resonate with others and expose the jurisdiction issues that have denied them resolution.Emma Norton, a lawyer from the Centre for Military Justice, said: “To be told after so long, and after having taken the incredibly brave step of reporting the abuse, that nothing now can be done because they appear to have fallen into a ‘jurisdictional gap’ is devastating.”She added: “Given the number of overseas military schools, there is a serious risk that this gap is likely to affect other victims too.”Jess Phillips, a former safeguarding minister, said the case “exposes a cultural issue within the MoD”.“The MoD needs to treat these two women as people who have been wrongfully treated while under their care,” she said. “We do not have to continue the cultural failing of the past – we can make the future better.”Jane said: “The MoD had a duty of care to us. They were our caregivers.”She added: “We need somebody to stand up and say: ‘We failed you.’”While they are losing hope that their alleged abuser may be prosecuted, they are still fighting for an acknowledgment of, and accountability for, the alleged childhood abuse they say they suffered and that has affected their whole lives.“We should not have had to go through that,” Anne said. “I want public accountability.”But she feels increasingly pessimistic that anyone will be held responsible for what she and Jane experienced. “Hope feels like a very stupid act right now for me,” she added.A spokesperson for the Defence Serious Crime Command, which the DSCU is part of, said: “Every child has the right to be safe at school, and our thoughts remain with the victims.“We deeply regret that the initial handling of the case fell below the standards we expect and have formally apologised to the victims. A new investigation launched earlier this year concluded the Defence Serious Crime Command does not have jurisdiction to pursue charges.“We have taken a number of steps to strengthen investigative practices across defence and remain committed to ensuring every case is fully and thoroughly investigated to deliver justice for victims.”*Names have been changedIn the UK, theNSPCCoffers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In the US, call or text theChildhelpabuse hotline on 800-422-4453. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact theKids Helplineon 1800 55 1800, orBraveheartson 1800 272 831, and adult survivors can contactBlue Knot Foundationon 1300 657 380. Other sources of help can be found atChild Helplines InternationalExplore more on these topicsViolence against women and girlsRape and sexual assaultBritish armyMinistry of DefenceChild protectionPoliceMilitaryShareReuse this content

title: Don’t rebuild the dam: Ukrainian experts urge Unesco to protect site uncovered by Russian sabotage | Ukraine | The Guardian
description: As archaeologists find treasure trove along new floodplain, conservationists say another Nova Kakhovka would be ecocide
Author: Charlotte Higgins
Headline: As archaeologists find treasure trove along new floodplain, conservationists say another Nova Kakhovka would be ecocide
Content: Andriy Denysenko, hydroarchaeologist, restorer and senior research fellow at Khortytsia national reserve.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAndriy Denysenko, hydroarchaeologist, restorer and senior research fellow at Khortytsia national reserve.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianUkraineDon’t rebuild the dam: Ukrainian experts urge Unesco to protect site uncovered by Russian sabotageAs archaeologists find treasure trove along new floodplain, conservationists say another Nova Kakhovka would be ecocideCharlotte Higginsand Mariana Matveichuk in KhortytsiaSat 10 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a warm September day, a group of underwater archaeologists and researchers were boiling water for tea on their campfire on the banks of the Dnipro River, tents pitched on the sandy shoreline. They were three weeks into an archaeological expedition of the waters around Khortytsia – a rocky island 12.5km long and 2.5km wide that lies just downstream of the city of Zaporizhzhia, in south-easternUkraine.High above the island, a Shahed drone whined on its way. A Ukrainian interceptor, and small-arms fire from the ground, tried, unsuccessfully, to bring it down. The archaeologists ignored it. This is life as normal, 28 miles (45km) from the combat zone in Russia’s war on Ukraine.Olena Dzneladze, senior research fellow at Ukraine’s national Institute ofArchaeology, showed off their remarkable finds: a bronze-age deer antler, its tip shaped into a tool to press patterns into pottery or leather; a shard of ceramic most likely made by the Scythians, an ancient nomadic people of the steppe; a chunk of a Byzantine amphora; an 18th-century anchor.Most spectacular, though was an entire boat, hollowed out of a single tree trunk and beautifully preserved by a millennium’s river immersion – one of many remarkable vessels, including 18th-century warships, that have been discovered in this part of the Dnipro. The team was planning to lift it from the river the following day.MapWith its neighbouring, smaller islands, Khortytsia comprises a natural and historical reserve – a place of profound symbolic importance to Ukraine’s national narrative as the first stronghold of the Zaporizhzhian Cossacks, and with traces of human life stretching back to the Mesolithic era.Khortytsia lies at the head of a vast landscape known as the “great meadow”. This 2,155 sq km area was, between the building of the Nova Kakhovka dam in the 1950s until 6 June 2023, covered by a reservoir. That was the day the 30-metre high, 3km-long structurewas blown up– by the Russians, according to most analysts.Unchecked by the dam, the waters of the reservoir – 18 cubic km of it – drained out of its bed and roared downstream, creating an acute humanitarian crisis as its waters inundated towns and villages on both sides of the river, and both sides of the frontline.View image in fullscreenArcheologists move a boat hollowed out from a single tree trunk, which was found underwater just off Khortytsia island.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianNow, however, a vocal group of historians, naturalists, ecologists and archaeologists want to see this territory of the “great meadow” protected as a Unesco world heritage site for its value as a natural and a cultural environment. The former reservoir bed has, with startling speed, regenerated itself into something like its pre-dam self: ahabitat of wetlands, grassland and islands, richly populated with the traces of thousands of years of human life. The dam, say the experts, must never be rebuilt.Over 100 Ukrainian NGOs areformally supporting the bid. A letter of intent has been sent to Unesco, and cooperation sought from the Ukrainian government’s culture ministry. But other interests will want to see the dam replaced and the reservoir remade, to irrigate Ukraine’s southern farmlands. Soon after its destruction, the Ukrainian governmentset upa pilot project with the state-owned hydroelectric company Ukrhydroenergo to prepare the groundwork for its reconstruction after the end of the war.Map of Ukraine, with pre-June 2023 Russian controlled areas markedValeriy Nefedov, leading the team of archaeologists on the island, is one of those pressing for the preservation of the “unique historical and natural environment” that has re-emerged. In 1999 the underwater archaeologist an early-18th-century warship in these waters, now in the island’s Museum of Navigation. And, in the summer of 2023, he was one of the first to set foot on to the 2,155 sq kilometre territory revealed by the drained Kakhovka reservoir.View image in fullscreenOlexandr Tsegelnyk, head of the development and planning sector at the Khortytsia national reserve, in Khortytsia.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianNefedov was serving in the army on 6 June 2023, in the Donetsk region, and quickly heard the news of the destruction of the Nova Kakhovka dam. For him, there was a certain irony: since the 1990s, he had been pressing for the dam’s gradual dismantling, the draining of the reservoir and the restitution of the “great meadow” with its mosaic of grassland ecosystems and marshes, reed beds, scrub and sandy mounds.But not like this, in one single, catastrophic event. “The first crime was building the dam in the first place,” he said. “The second was blowing it up.”Later that month, he was asked to join a newly formed military unit consisting of experts – historians, ecologists, scientists and other researchers – to investigate the reservoir bed.View image in fullscreenOlena Dzneladze and Andriy Denysenko at the Chaika Maritime Museum on Khortytsia island.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian“Of course, I had some expectations about what I might see. But when we reached the area, it is impossible to describe the impressions and emotions I felt. The consequences were staggering: what had been a reservoir had, within a very short time, turned into the exposed bottom of the body of water. On the other hand, there was a sense of danger.”This was the grey zone, no man’s land, “extremely tense”, he said. There was constant shelling. Though Ukrainian reconnaissance units had been there ahead of them, Russian sabotage groups were also on the prowl. And they could see the occupied Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant, where the Russians were positioned. “It was a very strange feeling,” he said, “being between the positions of our Ukrainian forces and those of our Russian enemies.”Life returns to Ukrainian reservoir drained by Russian strike on damRead moreIt was more than that, though: a watery territory, that he knew intimately as a diver, was now dry land, and he was walking across it. “It felt like terra incognita, unknown land – as if we were the first people to set foot on it,” he said. “Everything we saw and found there made us feel like explorers or discoverers.“Very unusual, almost fantastical landscapes appeared before us. Ancient channels, straits and islands had been revealed.View image in fullscreenA disused boat as seen from Khortytsia island in Zaporizhzhia.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The Guardian“We saw the remains of settlements, the foundations of houses, roads. We also found archaeological material lying directly on the surface, from the neolithic right through into the 20th century.”There were alsotoxic heavy metalsrevealed on the reservoir bed, which biologist Pavlo Oliinyk, one of the research team at Khortytsia, is involved in monitoring. But, he said, the rapid growth of vegetation in the drained “great meadow” area may provide a “green shield”. Trees, he said, had already grown up to as much as 7 metres high in the reservoir area, in just three years.“Building the dam was ecocide, destroying the dam was ecocide, and the third ecocide would be rebuilding it,” he said.The “great meadow”, this vast area of the Dnipro floodplain – which remains a grey zone between the opposing armies – has always had huge significance owing to its unique topography; its first surviving mention in the written record is by Herodotus, the fifth-century BCE Greek historian. This section of the Dnipro was the last easily navigable stretch of the river north of the Black Sea, before the rapids upstream at Zaporizhzhia rendered the river unmanageable by all but the most knowledgable.View image in fullscreenA fire at the archaeology camp on Khortytsia island.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianThis protective geography created a safe haven for the Cossacks, who, fleeing persecution in the 16th century, established a free, quasi-democratic polity here. This Cossack state became a important reference for the19th-century intellectuals, including national poet Taras Shevchenko, who led the modern Ukrainian national project.The area’s significance goes back even deeper. Also working on the island of Khortytsia in September was archaeologist Anatoliy Volkov, who, inland from the group of underwater archaeologists, was excavating one of a series of bronze-age stone enclosures. “We are in a frontline area,” he said of continuing his work during the full-scale invasion of Ukraine. “We are potentially threatened. There is always a chance a missile or rocket will land here, and so the more we research and preserve, the better.”The urgency of the research and monitoring was even more acute on the shoreline and riverbed, according to archaeologist Olena Dzneladze. After the blowing of the dam, she said, thousands of tons of sand started to move down the river, “with artefacts appearing in the moving sand”.View image in fullscreenAnatoliy Volkov, research fellow at Khortytsia national reserve, showing the archaeology site on the island.Photograph: Julia Kochetova/The GuardianAmid this volatile military and geographical situation, the Dnipro is settling into something like its old course, before the Nova Kakhovka dam was completed in 1956. Between Khortytsia and the next great dam upstream, at Zaporizhzhia, further rocky islands and sandy spits have been revealed as the water level has sunk 6-8 metres, transforming the landscape.Serhii Plokhii, Harvard’s professor of Ukrainian history, grew up in Zaporizhzhia hearing his grandfather’s stories of hunting in the wetlands of the “great meadow” before the dam was built. He recalled his emotions seeing the newly emerging landscape of the famous Zaporizhzhia rapids for the first time – though most of the rocky outcrops lie upstream, still submerged thanks to the Zaporizhzhia dam.“It was something that I read about and was part of history, but I had never seen before. And I thought: ‘Whatever happens with the Nova Kakhovka dam, whether they will rebuild it or not, I at least have had this chance to see this piece of history that was there, but was always invisible.’”Explore more on these topicsUkraineEuropeConservationArchaeologyWetlandsRiversHeritagefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Geordie Greep denies sexual assault allegations from stage in Vancouver | Canada | The Guardian
description: While some heard the former Black Midi frontman out, others made for the exit as he addressed accusations
Author: George Francis Lee
Headline: While some heard the former Black Midi frontman out, others made for the exit as he addressed accusations
Content: 2:09Geordie Greep addresses allegation of sexual misconduct - videoCanadaGeordie Greep denies sexual assault allegations from stage in VancouverWhile some heard the former Black Midi frontman out, others made for the exit as he addressed accusationsGeorge Francis LeeSat 10 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 08.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Geordie Greep finally took to the stage in Vancouver this week, noticeably without his band, the crowd was hushed and the atmosphere tense. His lateness, however was the least of his problems.Greep, a Brit school graduate and the former frontman ofBlack Midi, had been accused of sexually assaulting a woman while on tour. Flyers had been handed out outside the venue spelling out the allegation against him. “Let him know what Vancouver thinks of rapists,” they read.What followed was an astonishing speech by Greep, who dealt with the accusations head on. While some of his fans inside the Pearl heard him out, others made for the exit.“This is a very serious matter that I must talk about,” he said. “Someone out front is handing out flyers saying I’m this, saying I’m that … and it needs to be talked about.” He added: “I would never rape a woman. I’m not a rapist. It’s not how that went down.”The flyers, which fans posted images of online, were detailed in their allegations. “You know what you did this morning Oct 8th,” it read, and: “He thinks he can do whatever he wants because he’s gone tomorrow.” Greep’s response was even more so.He said: “Essentially what happened last night … me and some of the band, we went out to some bars. We went around, we met people. And it ended up in a situation where really late at a house party I got the wrong end of the stick with someone that was there.”“I made a move and it didn’t come off,” he said, “and I really quickly of course apologised. It was a complete misunderstanding on my part. It felt extremely bad and I feel extremely sorry and extremely upset about the whole situation.”He added: “Basically I just wanted to be transparent with you about what happened. Very very sorry to someone … I made someone feel uncomfortable without meaning to. It’s not a good thing … and it’s not good.”Greep went on to explain the absence of his usual backing band, saying: “I didn’t want to force them to still play a show in the light of that happening. We were unsure what would, kind of, be the response in all of this. I can only tell you that it’s OK if people want a refund, if they want to leave it’s fine.”The 27-year-old added that proceeds from the evening’s event would be donated to a violence against women charity in British Columbia. Afterwards, Greep said that he would continue the show alone if the crowd wished. “It’s just gonna be me,” he said, “just like the old days.” Reports from fans online show that the musician continued with a solo set. Some members of the crowd could be heard cheering.Alex Lacidos witnessed the “jarring” speech. “The crowd was really confused, we had been waiting for more than two hours,” he said. “After his talk he started his performance by himself, the vibes were awful and it looked like he was about to burst into tears.“Many people left before it was over.”Reddit user wreeum – who recorded the concert – said he felt “conflicted” about the incident and that it was “a huge allegation to make on the same day it happened, especially to print out several dozen flyers”. He added: “Sexual assault shouldn’t be taken lightly.”Another fan who was present at the gig wrote on X: “Went to the Geordie Greep concert tonight, left after his little speech. I really don’t know what to think.”Greep is on tour in North America with his debut solo album, The New Sound.His previous band Black Midi released their albumSchlagenheimin 2019, and it was shortlisted for the Mercury prize. After speculation around the band’s breakup, the group was disbanded in 2024 following a live-streamed announcement by Greep on Instagram.Greep and his current backing band were still down to play a show in Boise, Idaho on Friday as they continue a series of gigs in the US before a European leg in November.Greep’s team has been approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsCanadaPop and rockBlack MidinewsShareReuse this content

title: UK must not be beholden to foreign AI, says head of Alan Turing Institute | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: George Williamson says ‘national resilience’ is key focus of ATI amid US and China’s runaway leadership in field
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: George Williamson says ‘national resilience’ is key focus of ATI amid US and China’s runaway leadership in field
Content: George Williamson: ‘As AI becomes more embedded in domains like defence, national security, critical infrastructure and healthcare we shouldn’t depend solely on systems we can’t inspect or control.’Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGeorge Williamson: ‘As AI becomes more embedded in domains like defence, national security, critical infrastructure and healthcare we shouldn’t depend solely on systems we can’t inspect or control.’Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianAI (artificial intelligence)UK must not be beholden to foreign AI, says head of Alan Turing InstituteGeorge Williamson says ‘national resilience’ is key focus of ATI amid US and China’s runaway leadership in fieldDan MilmoGlobal technology editorSat 10 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK must not become dependent on foreign AI systems that can be switched off at short notice and must develop its own versions of the technology, according to the head of the Alan Turing Institute.The country needs a stronger domestic position in AI in response to the US and China’s runaway leadership in the field, with “national resilience” a key focus for ATI said George Williamson.The institute is the UK’s leading AI research body and isunder new leadershipafter the government, its main source of funding, demanded a strategic shift.Palantir’s Tom Watson says ‘mob rule’ must not dictate awarding of government contractsRead more“As AI becomes more embedded in critical services, in domains like defence, national security, critical infrastructure and healthcare we shouldn’t depend solely on systems we can’t inspect or control, or that could be restricted or even switched off,” said Williamson.In June Washington temporarily blocked the release outside the US of Anthropic’s latest models, and has reportedly asked leading AI labs to withhold their models from being tested by the UK’s AI Security Institute until they have been examined by AISI’s US counterpart.“We’ve seen now that both political and commercial pressures mean we may not have access [to AI] in all the circumstances when we want it. That is not a place where a nation wants to be,” he said.Williamson added: “There’s a set of circumstances where it would be a good idea for us to have something that we don’t have to ask other people’s permission to use.”He said national resilience would be a focus of ATI’s work amid concern about the geopolitical situation and the risk posed by increasingly powerful AI systems.Those concerns were highlighted last month by the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, announcing a new national centre to tacklestate-backed disinformation, and Anthropic predicting the technology had agreater than 10% chance of wiping out humanity by 2030.“It’s a moment when national resilience is definitely what the country needs and it’s definitely a thing I think the Turing institute can help with,” he said.“We are facing a more adversarial world, more frequent shocks to our critical infrastructure and now powerful AI amplifying these threats. To strengthen national resilience, the Turing will focus on securing critical systems against disruption, countering threats from AI itself and helping to shape the right strategic AI capability for the UK.”Williamson said the institute could assist in building such resilience by helping produce uses for AI “for the public good”, working on areas from weather forecasting to farming, as well as helping spot disinformation. Referring to state-led disinformation campaigns, he said: “It’s very dangerous for the state of democracy and it’s an area that we can monitor.”Williamson is the former head of His Majesty’s Government Communications Centre, a secretive government body that makes gadgets for UK spy agencies and counts Alan Turing – the second world war codebreaker and AI pioneer after which ATI is named – among its former staff.Williamson said it had become clear in recent months that the UK needed “more agency on access to technology” and a stronger sovereign position in AI. “It feels pretty uncomfortable if you don’t have some control or ability to use technologies when you want them, and also harder to imagine how you build an economy on the top of stuff that can disappear,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn recent weeks Christine Lagarde, the president of the European Central Bank, and Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, have urged Europe to be more self-sufficient in AI, withLagarde speaking about the threat of being “cut off”from US and Chinese technology.Williamson cited China as another reason for boosting domestic AI, amid concerns that Chinese-made systems might not “coincide with our values”. He said: “Try asking some of these models about some events in the recent past in China and you’re not going to get an answer that’s particularly helpful if you’re doing GCSE history.”“This is the defining technology of our time. We want to be able to shape that technology … in a way that accords with who we are and our values,” he said, adding that while ATI and the UK probably could not match the financial resources of major AI labs, they could still produce “nationally owned IP” or smaller models that could be made available to startups.“We can be ambitious here without trying to copy what frontier labs are doing,” he said.Williamson said ATI, a registered charity, could be an “objective and helpful” arbiter of concerns about AI, including existential threat. “A national institute should be an active partner to government and the public more generally in helping to navigate some of this stuff.”He said there was a “a lot of stuff being tossed around” on the existential threat risk that “is not always well grounded in science”. Referring to the penchant among some in the sector for expressing the risk of AI-triggered extinction in percentage terms, he said: “I’m not sure it’s helpful trying to assign particular percentages to it because I have not seen anyone show me a convincing evidence of how they’ve arrived at the number they then start throwing around.”Williamson indicated that the focus on national resilience would enable ATI to keep doing work on the environment that Keir Starmer’s government had wanted to sideline. In 2025 the then technology secretary, Peter Kyle, wrote to ATI’s chair demanding the institute switch its main focus to defence and security. Williamson’s predecessor Jean Innesresigned soon afterwards.“For me climate is as much a national security issue as defence. For me, it [national resilience] is a frame that enables us to cover the range of threats and opportunities to the UK,” he said.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Defence policyUK security and counter-terrorismComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK savings: 5% interest rate deals may not last, say experts | Savings rates | The Guardian
description: Competition is hotting up, with National Savings & Investments lifting rates to the highest in years
Author: Rupert Jones
Headline: Competition is hotting up, with National Savings & Investments lifting rates to the highest in years
Content: NS&I has upped the rates on its ‘British savings bonds’. They now offer a fixed interest rates between 4.99% and 5.17% over their one-, two-, three- or five-year bonds.Photograph: Russell Hart/AlamyView image in fullscreenNS&I has upped the rates on its ‘British savings bonds’. They now offer a fixed interest rates between 4.99% and 5.17% over their one-, two-, three- or five-year bonds.Photograph: Russell Hart/AlamySavings ratesUK savings: 5% interest rate deals may not last, say expertsCompetition is hotting up, with National Savings & Investments lifting rates to the highest in yearsRupert JonesSat 10 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNational Savings andInvestments(NS&I) has increased the returns on some of its accounts, with many now paying more than 5% for the first time in nearly three years.Competition in the savings market has been growing,leading to some of the highest interest rates for years.However, in the current climate, attractive deals do not always hang around for long, says Rachel Springall at the financial data website Moneyfactscompare.co.uk. If a provider attracts enough savings cash it will pull a product from sale.View image in fullscreenNS&I has rebadged versions of its guaranteed growth bonds and guaranteed income bonds as ‘British savings bonds’.Photograph: Tetiana Chernykova/AlamyNS&I has upped the rates on its “British savings bonds”, which are rebadged versions of its guaranteed growth bonds and guaranteed income bonds. They offer a fixed interest rate over their one-, two-, three- or five-year bonds.The deals are available to new customers and those with existing accounts that are maturing. With the growth version, interest is added each year and paid when the bond matures, while with the income version, interest is paid monthly.Looking at the growth bonds, the new interest rate on the one-year product is 4.99% (up from 4.82%), while the two-year rate has risen to 5.07% (was 4.81%). The three-year rate has gone up from 4.83% to 5.1%, while the five-year rate has been increased to 5.17% (was 4.85%).Premium bonds: more chance of win as NS&I ups prize fund rate againRead moreThose are pretty competitive rates, though as Sarah Coles, the head of personal finance at the advice firm AJ Bell, says, “you can still make more money elsewhere”.At the time of writing, the top-paying one-year fixed-rate bond was paying 5.12%, while the highest-paying five-year fixed bond was offering 5.37%. But getting the very highest rates sometimes means signing up with less-well-known names. The one-year deal is from Union Bank of India (UK), while the five-year version hails from GB Bank.If you have a very large sum that you need to stash somewhere – for example, the proceeds of a house sale or an inheritance – these NS&I bonds have one big thing in their favour: you can invest up to £1m per person in each bond issue. The minimum investment is £500.View image in fullscreenThe savings provider Marcus by Goldman Sachs this week upped the interest rate on its one-year fixed-rate savings account from 4.3% to 4.75%.Photograph: True Images/AlamyAs NS&I says, “most banks only guarantee your savings up to £120,000,” whereas it is backed by the Treasury and is “the only provider that secures 100% of your savings above this amount”.Also, it means you are putting your money into the government’s savings bank, and “your savings will be invested back into supporting the UK”.Money invested in NS&I’s British savings bonds cannot be withdrawn before the end of the fixed term.That will not suit everyone, and it is a good idea to keep some money in a high-paying easy access account to cover things such as unexpected bills. Earlier this month the digital bank Starling announced that people who sign up for its Easy Saver account will enjoy a table-topping 5% interest rate. This account offers unlimited penalty-free withdrawals, but that rate (made up of a 2.5% variable standard rate, plus a 2.5% fixed interest bonus lasting for six months) only applies to those who open, or have opened, a Starling current account on or after 1 October. The rate applies on balances of up to £25,000.Starling customers who signed up before then can benefit from a 4% rate when opening a new Easy Saver. That includes a 1.5% fixed interest bonus for six months.Meanwhile, the savings provider Marcus by Goldman Sachs this week upped the interest rate on its one-year fixed-rate savings account from 4.3% to 4.75%.Explore more on these topicsSavings ratesBanks and building societiesSavingsBondsInvestmentsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Create new pre-apprenticeship scheme to close youth unemployment gap, says Milburn | Apprenticeships | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Former minister’s review warns that dramatic action is needed over huge drop in youth apprenticeship starts
Author: Richard Partington
Headline: Exclusive: Former minister’s review warns that dramatic action is needed over huge drop in youth apprenticeship starts
Content: The number of under-19s enrolling on an apprenticeship has also almost halved in a decade.Photograph: Monty Rakusen/Getty Images/Image SourceView image in fullscreenThe number of under-19s enrolling on an apprenticeship has also almost halved in a decade.Photograph: Monty Rakusen/Getty Images/Image SourceApprenticeshipsCreate new pre-apprenticeship scheme to close youth unemployment gap, says MilburnExclusive: Former minister’s review warns that dramatic action is needed over huge drop in youth apprenticeship startsRichard PartingtonSenior economics correspondentSat 10 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA national apprenticeship readiness scheme should be introduced in England to close the gap for young people between leaving school and starting work, the government is to be told.Alan Milburn, who is leading a majorreview into Britain’s youth jobs crisis, will call for a new “national pre-apprenticeship route” to offer young people further education, training and work experience.Setting out the recommendation from his highly awaited final report – which has been delayed until after this month’s budget – the former Labour cabinet minister warned action was required to address a dramatic plunge in the number of youth apprenticeship starts over the past decade.Against a backdrop of soaringyouth unemployment, as few as one in five apprenticeship starts currently go to a 16- to 18-year-old. The number of under-19s enrolling on an apprenticeship has also almost halved in a decade.The detail comes as Andy Burnham’s government delays Milburn’s full recommendations until at least November, amid concerns in Downing Street that his report could sit uneasily alongside the 28 October budget.A former minister in Tony Blair’s cabinet, Milburn has signalled that a shake-up of Britain’s benefits system would form a central plank of his report, alongside measures to boost job support, training and apprenticeships.In response, ministers are exploring plans for sweeping welfare changes, includingscrapping a critical disability benefitfor under-25s and replacing it with a multibillion-pound package of support to get into work.Burnham and his chancellor, John Healey, have signalled readiness to stem the government’s rising benefits bill. Other senior Labour figures, including the work and pensions secretary, Pat McFadden, have said there is botha moral caseand an economic one to overhaul the welfare system, as the war in the Middle East rattles the public finances.However, the government is taking a cautious approach to avoid provoking a repeat of thewelfare rebellionwhich forced Keir Starmer and Rachel Reeves into an embarrassing and costly U-turn.View image in fullscreenAlan MilburnPhotograph: Owen Humphreys/PAMilburn’s review had been scheduled for launch next week.Sources close to the review confirmed the delay, although downplayed its significance. One said that Downing Street was working to decide how to present the report alongside several other big reviews, including the Timms review into disability benefits, as well as the budget and the prime minister’s 10-year plan for government.Burnham has promised to tackle the rise in the number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) to almost 1 million at the top of his agenda for power, including sweeping changes toretool technical education and apprenticeships.Currently, as few as 2% of people starting apprenticeships were previously Neet.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPresenting the details of his pre-apprenticeship plan, Milburn said his call for a new programme in England would be targeted at young people who lack the qualifications, confidence, workplace experience or routines needed to secure and sustain a full apprenticeship.Delivered mainly through further education colleges, it would combine English and maths with technical learning and hands-on experience with an employer. The proposal would be similar to a one-year pre-vocational pathway in Austria that is designed to prepare young people for progression into apprenticeships.Other countries with much lower Neet rates than the UK have placed much greater emphasis on vocational routes, including the Netherlands and Austria, where more than half of 15- to 19-year olds in upper-secondary education enrol in vocational programmes.This month, the government announced an expansion in local apprenticeship services, backed by £100m of funding, in a programme delivered by regional mayors, across two years, to double the number of areas matching young people with local businesses.Milburn said young people had been told for years to go and get an apprenticeship. “But for many young people there is a gap between leaving school and being ready for a full apprenticeship,” he added.“They may need to improve their English or maths or get more experience of a workplace. And employers understandably want to know that someone is ready to turn up, learn the job and stick at it.“I want a new national pre-apprenticeship route. A course done through colleges, combining English and maths, technical training and proper experience with an employer. Geared towards one thing: getting a young person into work.”Explore more on these topicsApprenticeshipsVocational educationYoung peopleEducation policyFurther educationYouth unemploymentUnemploymentnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Jelliness is my life motto’: jackpot theatre prize winner Jaha Koo on kimchi, K-pop and his robotic eel | Stage | The Guardian
description: Feted for cooking up shows that can be mouthwatering as well as thought-provoking, the artist discusses his fusion of South Korean and European culture
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Feted for cooking up shows that can be mouthwatering as well as thought-provoking, the artist discusses his fusion of South Korean and European culture
Content: ‘Did you have a good meal?’ … Jaha Koo.Photograph: Bea BorgersView image in fullscreen‘Did you have a good meal?’ … Jaha Koo.Photograph: Bea BorgersStageInterview‘Jelliness is my life motto’: jackpot theatre prize winner Jaha Koo on kimchi, K-pop and his robotic eelChris WiegandFeted for cooking up shows that can be mouthwatering as well as thought-provoking, the artist discusses his fusion of South Korean and European cultureSat 10 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 08.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I meet Jaha Koo in Oslo, where he has just been honoured with the prestigious International Ibsen award, I hand him a congratulatory packet of Haribo. The alternative would be a jar of kimchi but one of the many things you learn from Koo’s captivating theatre shows is that air travel and fermented vegetables can be a disastrous combo. When he moved to Berlin fromSouth Koreawith 10kg of his grandma’s finest kimchi, it became “bloated like a dead whale” and exploded on his balcony. His new neighbours were unimpressed.In Koo’s current touring production,Haribo Kimchi, he examines how this unlikely fusion of two foods represents his cultural identity. He does so while preparing an onstage banquet for two lucky audience members. Despite spending many years in Europe, where Haribo gummies originated around a century ago, Koo still finds himself considered foremost as Korean by Europeans. But when he returns to his original homeland he is not always seen as Korean either.We meet the day after the ceremony for the Ibsen award, founded by the Norwegian government and rewarding the winner with a huge 2.5m kroner (£200,000). Its past recipients include Lola Arias, Taylor Mac and Forced Entertainment. Koo cheerfully packs away my sweets for the next day’s flight to Belgium, where he is now based, and outlines his life motto of “jelliness”. It was only when he arrived in Europe that he started to eat gummy bears. “When you push jelly, it can shrink and change form but after a few seconds, it recovers its shape,” he says. “That is the same resilience I need to improve when I live outside Korea.” In the show, he explains how the bears’ smiley faces cheer him up when he’s feeling down.View image in fullscreenA kimchi diaspora … Jaha Koo cooks for theatregoers while he performs at the Edinburgh international festival 2026.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianIf Haribo was a new discovery, kimchi “was there before I was born and it was waiting for me”. As a Korean, he says, it is impossible to think about food without this quintessential side dish and he is part of “a kimchi diaspora”. The exact ingredients may differ around the world, depending on what’s available, but that doesn’t make any recipe inauthentic, he says: “Kimchi can be very diverse.” When he prepares the dish in Belgium, it sums up how he is true to his roots yet adapting to a new environment – “a kind of cultural assimilation”.Koo is an artist adept at setting out his stall – literally so in the case of Haribo Kimchi, where the set is a Korean snack cart called apojangmacha.It’s a movable feast, typically frequented by hungry customers of all backgrounds and generations – “kind of like a soul place,” he says. “They want to find comfort, eat quite humble food.” The roof of Koo’s bar has a Haribo-red glow that is translucent – a signifier, he suggests, of in-between states, much as thepojangmachassuggest lives in transit. “They are movable. There is no address. They appear in the evening and then disappear.” He draws a parallel with the country’s pop-up shop culture, which can transform a street over night, and Korea’s rapid pace of change which, viewed from Europe, makes him feel far behind as well as far away.A simple kimchi pancake is on the menu for Haribo Kimchi, its aroma filling the room in a show where Koo’s narrative is often sensory – such as the persimmon fruit trees he remembers from his youth. The theatregoers who take a seat at his bar are first given asomaek, a cocktail made with soju and beer, then several dishes including cold seaweed soup. As you’d expect from the theatrical cookery genre, which has included productions as different asTravis Alabanza’s BurgerzandHannah Khalil’s My English Persian Kitchen, each item on the menu has a different emotional resonance – Koo likens it to a score of carefully chosen compositions. Seaweed, for example, has links with birthday traditions in Korea and with ocean myths.View image in fullscreenA movable feast … the set for Haribo Kimchi with projected scenes from South Korea.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThat brings us to Koo’s unusual co-star: a robotic eel who slithers around the stage and even delivers a ballad. (A giant gummy bear and a snail break out in song too.) It’s not as random as it sounds – Koo says he was drawn to the way eels leave their birth home, journey afar, but “then go back to their home before they die”.Haribo Kimchi, designed by Eunkyung Jeong (who is married to Koo) and with dramaturgy by their regular collaborator Dries Douibi, had its UK premiere at this summer’s Edinburgh international festival, where the audience invaded the stage for his end-of-show buffet. It’s not the first time Koo has found that mealtimes can make perfect metaphors for a show. In Korea, he says, “When we say hello, we always ask: ‘Did you have a good meal?’ Korean people call familysikku,which means ‘people who eat together’.” His earlier productionCuckoo, which he revived in Oslo, uses rice cookers as a symbol of both “economic imperialism and the pressure upon society”.Cuckoo delves into the longterm impact of Korea’s late 90s financial crisis and its neoliberal shift after the International Monetary Fund intervened with a $58bn rescue package. The part played by US treasury secretary Robert Rubin in what Koo calls “economic imperialism” is given a catchy electro-pop tune to rivalBo Burnham’s Jeff Bezostakedown. Koo describes, in a show as angry and raw as Haribo Kimchi is gentle and warm, a severe spike in unemployment, inequality and isolation – “a generation without a future”, including an account of his close friend’s suicide.View image in fullscreenAngry and raw … Jaha Koo’s Cuckoo, 2019.Photograph: Eunkyung JEONGCuckoo is the name of Korea’s brand of ubiquitous talking rice cookers – Koo appears on stage with three of them which have been hacked so that they gripe at each other and even sing. Listening to an answerphone message from his father, Koo cradles one cooker as if it’s his own child. The show also has much of the poppy melancholy of Haribo Kimchi and blurs with performance art: in the climax, he tips a mound of rice from the cooker, steam rises, and he feverishly prepares it in portions – an act of control and division as much as cheffing.His other shows take in linguistic colonisation: Lolling and Rolling is about the tongue surgery some South Koreans pursue in order to pronounce the English “R”. The History of Korean WesternTheatreexamines what you could call theatrical imperialism. “I studied at university in Korea and it was quite a conservative environment in terms of what theatre can be,” he says. In this classical western definition of drama, there was no room for a robotic eel or a chatty rice cooker and Koo is intent on putting tech on stage. “When we think about our contemporary world, it’s impossible to think and understand only with a human perspective. If we want to understand our time, then we have to think about different perspectives – nature, animals – and also technology like robotics.”In his Oslo ceremony speech, Koo duly reflected on the irony of receiving an award named after a canonical figure such as Ibsen: “But he was also an artist who questioned the theatre and society of his own time.” His next project will grapple with another artform that has become “a force for change”:K-pop, whose fans have wielded the genre’s bangers and glow sticks as a form of political protest, notably against former President Yoon’s martial law attempt in 2024. It will be the first of Koo’s shows where he will not perform; the cast will comprise singers. “I want to examine our global society through the lens of K-pop,” he says. “It has strong power as a new form of pop culture … On the other hand, the industry has a really dark side.”Theatre, for Koo, is an arena for us “to think together” he says. “This kind of solidarity is very important,” he adds. It’s drama as an act of breaking bread with the audience – or slurping cold seaweed soup.Haribo Kimchiis touring Europe until 21 November. Chris Wiegand’s trip to Oslo was provided by the International Ibsen award.Explore more on these topicsStageTheatreSouth KoreaAwards and prizesK-popFoodEdinburgh festival 2026interviewsShareReuse this content

title: Amélie allowed me to embrace my neurodivergence | Amelie | The Guardian
description: Watching a DVD of the French film alone in my room, I saw for the first time a character who moved through the world like I do
Author: Lillian Crawford
Headline: Watching a DVD of the French film alone in my room, I saw for the first time a character who moved through the world like I do
Content: ‘As my understanding of myself has evolved over the years, so has my understanding of Amélie.’Illustration: Martin O’Neill/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘As my understanding of myself has evolved over the years, so has my understanding of Amélie.’Illustration: Martin O’Neill/The GuardianMy cultural awakeningAmelieAmélie allowed me to embrace my neurodivergenceWatching a DVD of the French film alone in my room, I saw for the first time a character who moved through the world like I doLillian Crawford; as told toOlivia LadanyiSat 10 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmélie likes the sound of cracking creme brulee with a teaspoon, plunging her hand into a sack of grain, and turning around in the cinema to watch people’s faces in the dark. I like the smell of books and I love cinema, but I hate the sound of people eating popcorn.Amélie was not the first neurodivergent-coded woman I’d seen depicted in film. There had been Margot Tenenbaum in The Royal Tenenbaums and Suzy Bishop in Moonrise Kingdom – two Wes Anderson characters in whom I’d recognised myself. But Amélie was the first who was at the centre of the story; she’s the titular character and we see things through her eyes. It was the first time I’d seen a woman on screen move through the world as I did: overstimulated, a bit lonely and afraid of the unknown, comfortable in her own company, with firm likes and dislikes and a powerful sense of social justice.My parents suspected I was autistic as a child: I didn’t have any friends, preferring my own company or that of my parents, and I couldn’t understand why other children behaved the way they did. They thought I was odd. I had hyperfixations and obsessive special interests. Doctors were trained to look out for the stereotypical signs of autism in boys, and autism can show up differently in girls, who tend to mask (assimilate the behaviours of neurotypical people) a lot more. My sense of humour, empathy and interest in history and culture rather than maths or science meant I wasn’t formally diagnosed until my early 20s. But a diagnosis has never felt important to me. That’s what I love about Amélie: she’s never labelled as autistic in the film, yet it was clear to me, as a neurodivergent person, that she was, too.In the opening credits, young Amélie flaps her hands over her ears, spins a coin and runs a finger round the rim of a glass – behaviours I now recognise as “stimming” (repetitive movements, sounds or words that help process sensory input or manage emotions). Adult Amélie’s overwhelm is communicated not only through Audrey Tautou’s performance, but through the cinematography. When she takes the Paris Métro, the wide lens and intensified sound evoke the experience of sensory overload. When Amélie is happy, everything glows. When she is sad, she literally becomes a puddle on the floor.double quotation markI have the urge to help Amélie, as if by helping her I would also be helping the younger version of myselfTen years ago, I was in my second year at the University of Cambridge when I first watched Amélie, on a DVD player alone in my room. I fell in love with it. After watching it twice that night, I became scared to return to it in case I didn’t connect with it in the same way. But in the past year, I’ve watched Amélie five times in an effort to make up for lost time, and on every watch I see something different.As my understanding of myself has evolved over the years, so has my understanding of Amélie. Now I have the urge to help her, as if by helping her I would also be helping the younger version of myself. To have a conversation with her and say: don’t be so afraid of things that feel alien and new.I had a book launch in August and it made my parents emotional how many people were there from different parts of my life. They never thought having friendships like I do would be possible for me. I wish I could tell my 14-year-old self, locked away in a library, or the 19-year-old who watched Amélie on repeat alone in her room, that she had all of this ahead of her. That she would programme and organise neurodivergent film screenings and have a community of autistic people around her. That her bones aren’t made of glass, and she can take life’s knocks, as the Glass Man tells Amélie in the film. That she would overcome her fears and learn to take up space in her own life, as Amélie had shown her was possible all those years ago.The Mind of the Doctor by Lillian Crawford is published by Darton, Longman & Todd (£14.99).
