title: Time: David Tennant and Siobhan Finneran are stellar in this horrifying and exceptional TV drama | Television | The Guardian
description: Jimmy McGovern’s grab-you-by-the-throat prison show is back and it could hardly be more urgent, prescient or excellent. Brace yourself though … Bake Off it is not
Author: Frances Ryan
Headline: Jimmy McGovern’s grab-you-by-the-throat prison show is back and it could hardly be more urgent, prescient or excellent. Brace yourself though … Bake Off it is not
Content: Behind bars … Siobhan Finneran, Chukwubuikem Molokwu and David Tennant star in Time.Photograph: BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyView image in fullscreenBehind bars … Siobhan Finneran, Chukwubuikem Molokwu and David Tennant star in Time.Photograph: BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyThe watcherTelevisionTime: David Tennant and Siobhan Finneran are stellar in this horrifying and exceptional TV dramaJimmy McGovern’s grab-you-by-the-throat prison show is back and it could hardly be more urgent, prescient or excellent. Brace yourself though … Bake Off it is notFrances RyanSat 10 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt takes a lot to drag me away from comfort TV in the autumn. Blame the shrinking hours of light or the apocalyptic news cycle but the closest thing I like to get to televisual trauma in October is watching comedians get into their own graves in The Celebrity Traitors. I doubt I’m alone. I don’t want to psychoanalyse the British public but I’d take a punt that collectively we are just about capable right now of looking at Josh Widdicombe trying to find a purpose next to Emma Willis on the Strictly dancefloor (andreportedly, even that’s a struggle).Enter legendary Jimmy McGovern with a new series of the Bafta-winning prison drama Time (Sunday, 9pm, BBC One) to drag the nation out of its Bake Off-related coma. Having already covered the devastation of men’s and women’s prisons in the first two series, the good news is that McGovern and co-writer Samuel Bailey’s trilogy surely can’t get any more distressing. The new episodes will be set in*checks notes* a youth offending institution for boys. OK great. It’s about children in prison. Thank you, Jimmy! I hope you’re happy! No one else is going to be.Of course, McGovern – long known for tackling social realism and institutional injustice in iconic shows such as Cracker, The Lakes and Hillsborough – is not going to put the viewer through the wringer without proper reason. Asprison overcrowdingdominates the headlines, alongside themultifaceted crisisamongyoung men, Time series three is so urgent and prescient that you wonder if the BBC were tempted to change the title to Time(ly).Still, best brace yourself before going in. Within 90 seconds, a teenage boy is being dragged horizontally by five adult guards to his cell; a hand half-covering his jaw as he screams obscenities. That hand belongs toDavid Tennant, playing veteran prison officer Bobby Bailey. Tennant is an impressively blank slate as Bailey: a figure who is almost always on screen but has such sparse dialogue and emotion that at times he is – in classic McGovern fashion – defined by his ordinariness and hard to box as “goody” or “baddy.”He’s joined by Happy Valley’s Siobhan Finneran who returns as prison chaplain Marie-Louise – the only common thread through all three series and a rare merciful sign of, dare I say it, hope.Tennant and Finneran both give stellar performances but it’s the three young actors playing new offenders who will surely be stars of the future. There’s Peter (Ollie McNulty), caught between the death of an innocent man and loyalty to his community, and James (Louis McCartney), struggling to face his broken parents after a life-changing act of violence. Then there’s Christopher (a heartbreaking Chukwubuikem Molokwu) battling a stammer and reconnecting with his birth mother.‘Me and the lads would not survive a day in here’: inside TV’s utterly stunning, Bafta-winning prison dramaRead moreOne of Time’s strengths is its exceptional writing, but it is not afraid to say plenty without a word. The white vans that transport the boys to jail with tiny square black windows for pockets of light. The gates in D-wing that are rarely opened and keep its violent not-yet-men apart (“Gates are dangerous,” Tennant tells Finneran ominously). Cells named “Room 29”, as if the boys are on a hostel break for the week – an illusion that’s only broken when you realise there’s not a scene that takes place in the wing that’s not accompanied by the sound of screaming.The whole thing is a lesson in tension, each minute in the prison dragging the viewer further into the claustrophobia of dread and despair.I won’t give any spoilers but I will say you will be thinking about a moment in the first episode for days. This is not easy viewing but nor should it be. McGovern is not delivering content that plays in the background while you’re scrolling Instagram. It grabs you by the throat, asking you to question whether it’s possible to change or if the horrors of the human-made system dooms certain people – certain children – before they ever really get a chance. All of us should watch it, not least politicians across the political spectrum. Just maybe stick Bake Off on afterwards to decompress.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionThe watcherDavid TennantfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Richard Ayoade and Hannah Waddingham’s cartoon comedy | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Rick and Morty fans will love ancient Greece animation Krapopolis. Plus, Danny Dyer takes the SNL UK hosting reins. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Rick and Morty fans will love ancient Greece animation Krapopolis. Plus, Danny Dyer takes the SNL UK hosting reins. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Not your typical ruler … Krapopolis on BBC Three.Photograph: BBC/Fox MediaView image in fullscreenNot your typical ruler … Krapopolis on BBC Three.Photograph: BBC/Fox MediaTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: Richard Ayoade and Hannah Waddingham’s cartoon comedyRick and Morty fans will love ancient Greece animation Krapopolis. Plus, Danny Dyer takes the SNL UK hosting reins. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Ali Catterall,Jack Seale,Hannah J DaviesandSimon WardellSat 10 Oct 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 01.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKrapopolis11.40pm, BBC ThreeThis starry-voiced adult cartoon by Rick and Morty creator Dan Harmon quietly dropped on iPlayer last month. Set in ancient Greece, it follows benevolent Tyrannis (Richard Ayoade) – the mortal son of vain goddess Deliria (Hannah Waddingham) and husband Shlub (Matt Berry) – who uses modern ideas as he rules Krapopolis. Served up in fun 20-minute bites, this six-episode bill will race by.Hollie RichardsonStrictly Come Dancing6.15pm, BBC OneChris and Amy were the first couple to cha cha their way from the dancefloor (in their Baywatch gear, no less), which means 14 pairs are left in week three of the competition. Lacey and Vito confirmed one dance at the end of last week’s show: they’ll be getting lively with a samba to Bamboléo by the Gipsy Kings.HR40 Hits of 1976 at the BBC8.40pm, BBC TwoOdd year, 1976. Perhaps the record-breaking heat boiled record buyers’ brains. How else to explain the UK’s best-selling single and Eurovision winner, Save Your Kisses for Me? Or the Wurzels ploughing Combine Harvester to No 1? Thankfully, punk was also battering down the door – along with Abba and Dolly.Ali CatterallMarble Hall Murders9.20pm, BBC OneA classy cast and the lure of gossip among pampered literati are keeping Anthony Horowitz’s convoluted mystery drama going. Book editor Susan (Lesley Manville), working on a roman à clef set in Crete in 1955, now meets the family of the author, who alleges one of them murdered his grandmother. Everyone is wonderfully barbed.Jack SealeSaturday Night Live UK10pm, Sky OneOh, this is going to be a good one: while his daughter hotfoots it on Strictly, actor/geezer/emerging national treasure Danny Dyer is the host of this edition of the show, which is back after a week off. Music comes from south London singer-songwriter Sasha Keable.HRThree Women1.30am, Channel 4If 1.30am is a little late, this candid drama based on Lisa Taddeo’s nonfiction hit about sex and desire is also streamable. In an episode that’s all the more resonant given grim events at Cornell, Lina (Betty Gilpin) tells Gia (Shailene Woodley) about a disturbing event from her student past.Hannah J DaviesFilm choiceMatchbox the Movie, out now, Apple TVView image in fullscreen‘Amiable muscleman’ … Matchbox the Movie on Apple TV.Photograph: Jasin BolandIn the wake of the pink powerhouse that was Barbie, toy giant Mattel is going all-in on adaptations. Before we get the pleasure of Polly Pocket on screen, the line of tiny toy vehicles is given some dramatic spit and polish in Sam Hargrave’s breezy caper. Amiable muscleman Jon Cena plays CIA covert agent Sean, who returns to his home town for a funeral and reconnects with four childhood friends known as the Matchbox Gang, including Jessica Biel’s paramedic – and youthful crush – Aimee. Unfortunately, Sean is the fall guy after a nuclear warhead vanishes, so his mates are thrown into his globe-trotting world of spies, close-quarter violence and, naturally, shiny fast cars.Simon WardellAnimals, out now, NetflixBen Affleck’s knotty kidnap thriller was put on hold in 2024 after it clashed with Spike Lee’s similarly themed Highest 2 Lowest, itself a remake of a Kurosawa classic. It’s finally here, with Affleck casting himself (original pick Matt Damon was stuck on an island in the Med) as an attorney standing for LA mayor and Kerry Washington as his wife. The plot revolves round their son being taken for ransom, as moral and political calculations seriously muddy the waters. Gillian Anderson walks off with her scenes as a cool, collected English fixer called upon to help.SWPoor Things,10pm, Channel 4View image in fullscreenDeeply weird yarn … Poor Things on Channel 4.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyA risk-taking performance from Emma Stone is at the heart of this deeply weird yarn from Yorgos Lanthimos. She plays Bella, a young woman who died but was revived with the brain of her unborn baby by the Frankenstein-esque Godwin (Willem Dafoe). As she learns to walk and talk, she yearns to discover more about life. Lothario Duncan Wedderburn (a hilariously louche Mark Ruffalo) has designs on being her svengali – but Bella has a mind of her own. A delightful, disconcerting comedy adapted from Alasdair Gray’s novel, set in a stunning, not-quite-realistic Victorian era. SWRed Rooms, 11.20pm, Film4In Montreal, Canada, a man goes on trial for the murder of three teenage girls, the torture and killing of whom he had filmed for paying customers on the dark web. Pascal Plante’s increasingly disturbing psychological drama follows the proceedings – and the media frenzy surrounding it – through the eyes of model Kelly-Anne (Juliette Gariépy), who is a regular attendee at court. But why is she there? Is she a groupie of the (clearly guilty) accused? A true-crime obsessive? Or something darker? Gariépy’s enigmatic performance keeps us guessing almost to the end.SWLive sportPremier League Football: Arsenal v Leeds, 11am, TNT Sports 1Man Utd v Tottenham is at 5pm on Sky Sports Main Event.Prem Rugby Union: Northampton v Bath, 3pm, TNT Sports 1Saracens v Bristol follows at 5.15pm.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: 14th review – Ava DuVernay’s galvanizing documentary is a remarkable achievement | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: New York film festival: the director has made a fascinating and troubling companion piece to her Netflix documentary 13th, which takes a fiery look at American injustice
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: New York film festival: the director has made a fascinating and troubling companion piece to her Netflix documentary 13th, which takes a fiery look at American injustice
Content: Carla Hayden with Ava DuVernay on 14th.Photograph: Paul Garnes/NetflixView image in fullscreenCarla Hayden with Ava DuVernay on 14th.Photograph: Paul Garnes/NetflixFirst look reviewDocumentary filmsReview14th review – Ava DuVernay’s galvanizing documentary is a remarkable achievementNew York film festival:the director has made a fascinating and troubling companion piece to her Netflix documentary 13th, which takes a fiery look at American injusticeAdrian HortonFri 9 Oct 2026 21.00 EDTLast modified on Fri 9 Oct 2026 21.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt feels at once like the blink of an eye and an eternity since Ava DuVernay’s documentary13tharrived on Netflix, a month before the election of Donald Trump to his first term as president. The intervening decade has more or less borne out the film’s thesis on the enduring specter of white supremacy in American life: that a clause within the 13th amendment abolishing chattel slavery – that involuntary servitude could be used as punishment for a crime – was immediately and continually exploited to criminalize black people, mass incarceration thus being the modern incarnation of America’s original sin.Artificial review – Luca Guadagnino takes on OpenAI in muddled tech satireRead moreThe Oscar-nominated film, which saw a surge in viewership during the protests of 2020, has remained both a time capsule of late Obama-era moral clarity and, arguably, the acclaimed director’s best picture. At least, until now – 14th, DuVernay’s sequel, of sorts, soon also to arrive onNetflix, is just as lucid and galvanizing as its predecessor, with an updated, more pressing urgency befitting a democracy in distress.The new film focuses its brisk 110 minutes on the 14th amendment, adopted in the aftermath of the civil war, in a moment of profound political destabilization. The five-point statute may be lesser-known and not widely understood, but the film summarily makes the case for its status as the “workhorse amendment”, the “magnum opus of American democracy”, to quote several of the film’s illustrious figures. Once again, DuVernay marshals a murderers’ row of constitutional experts and political figures, from Stacey Abrams to Hasan Piker, Equal Justice Initiative founder Bryan Stevenson to Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (and also, for some token Republican context, the former “Never Trumper” senator Jeff Flake and current anti-birthright citizenship Florida congresswoman Anna Paulina Luna, who gets ruthlessly factchecked by some title cards). DuVernay stages her largely persuasive cast – lawyers, politicians, civil rights organizers and more – in striking, stately tableaux, before marble and monuments, underscoring the argument for the amendment’s status as the epitome of humanist sophistication: government by the people, forallthe people.View image in fullscreenAva DuVernay with Dr David Blight.Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixThe heavy lifting in this argument is cogently provided by Sherrilyn Ifill, the former president of the NAACP Legal Defense Fund and a law professor at Howard University, where she founded the 14th Amendment Center for Law and Democracy; Ifill is a warm yet precise narrator, masterfully laying out the case that the verbose, multi-pronged amendment is actually the scaffolding upon which hang our hopes for a true multi-racial, multi-faith democracy. It is the 14th amendment that guarantees birthright citizenship as well as voting rights, that bars insurrectionists from again holding public office (you know what awful, infuriating footage is coming, though it is necessary) and, through numerous legal defenses, allowed interracial couples to marry and women to obtain credit cards.To summarily stamp down its importance and radical historical context, DuVernay employs many of the same techniques as 13th to arguably greater effect: trenchant illustrations, blistering through the Trump years as a literal desecration of the 14th amendment’s five-pointed star; needle-drops from Kendrick Lamar to Fleetwood Mac to James Brown. And, most potently, adding dimension and movement to archival photographs of both the Black flourishing in the immediate aftermath of the civil war – formerly enslaved people in the halls of Congress, churches, universities and other institutions – as well as the swift backlash to Reconstruction in the form of terroristic vigilante violence, penal colonies and Jim Crow segregation.It’s a bracing, riveting torrent dense with facts and figures – the 4,400 known lynchings of Black Americans between the civil war and the second world war, the 2,629 monuments to the Confederate slave republic erected in the same period, the galling visual evidence of it all – as well as some jittery timeline hopping. Some tangents, such as time with Devon Henry, the Black contractor tasked with dismantling several Confederate monuments in Virginia, are admirable but a bit afield, threatening to dilute the film’s tight, punchy focus on the amendment’s oft-challenged fortitude.Still, it paints a damning portrait of the Trump administration and the larger Maga movement, with its explicit invocation of a different, better past, as a continuation of the “Lost Cause” mythology of the Confederacy – a false narrative of historical memory that constitutes, to quote the southern historian Karen Cox, the “most successful propaganda campaign in the history of the United States”.The film’s final section, on the Trump administration’s all-out assault on every article of the amendment, is nothing any follower of US news doesn’t already know, but still burns with righteous anger and alarm. What was the insurrection clause if not an attempt to prevent, and then punish, the January 6 rioters who Trump wanted US taxpayers to compensate? What are masked ICE arrests and killings, played in one extremely effective if difficult montage, if not a direct violation of due process?Quibbles aside, 14th is a rare feat, at once informative, infuriating and undeniable. That DuVernay may too often repeat the same clip or phrase is largely outweighed by the import of the statement, such as one written by Frederick Douglass and delivered by Ifill: the spirit of white supremacy will not die out in a year; it will not die out in an age. As 14th illustrates, that legacy is the one we’ve all inherited, and it is ignored or underestimated at our peril.14th is premiering at the New York film festival and will be released in cinemas on 27 November and available on Netflix on 4 DecemberExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsFirst look reviewNew York film festival 2026FestivalsNetflixAva DuVernayreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I just wasn’t going to give up’: the fight to free the longest-serving political prisoner in the US | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: Leonard Peltier was imprisoned for 49 years before his sentence was commuted. A new Netflix documentary exposes the ‘corrupt’ system that allowed it to happen
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: Leonard Peltier was imprisoned for 49 years before his sentence was commuted. A new Netflix documentary exposes the ‘corrupt’ system that allowed it to happen
Content: Leonard Peltier in Coleman, Florida, on 18 February 2025 after his release from prison.Photograph: Angel White Eyes/NDN Collective/ReutersView image in fullscreenLeonard Peltier in Coleman, Florida, on 18 February 2025 after his release from prison.Photograph: Angel White Eyes/NDN Collective/ReutersDocumentary films‘I just wasn’t going to give up’: the fight to free the longest-serving political prisoner in the USLeonard Peltier was imprisoned for 49 years before his sentence was commuted. A new Netflix documentary exposes the ‘corrupt’ system that allowed it to happenAdrian HortonSat 10 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn 20 January 2025, with 14 minutes remaining in his term as president, Joe Bidencommutedthe life sentence ofLeonard Peltier, after years of pressure to release a figure seen by many as the longest-serving political prisoner in the US. The Indigenous activist, a leader within the American Indian Movement (Aim) and an icon of Native American resistance, served nearly 50 years in prison for allegedly killing two FBI agents during a shootout on the Pine Ridge reservation in South Dakota, in 1975 – killings he has always denied, prosecuted in a railroaded trial widely seen as corrupt.‘He’s going home’: new film documents the fight to free Leonard PeltierRead moreOutside the Florida prison where Peltier was being held that morning were several of the many activists and lawyers who fought for his release, as well as film-makers David France and Jesse Short Bull. The two directors’ long-gestating documentary on Peltier’s fight for justice was set topremierejust a week later at the Sundance film festival with a very different ending, the octogenarian still awaiting a chance to return home to the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa reservation in North Dakota. That morning, there was “a sinking feeling that it wasn’t going to happen”, France said.When it did, while the cameras rolled, the line of supporters erupted in joy for a commutation that allowed Peltier to serve the rest of his consecutive life sentences on house arrest, though it did not pardon him – not quite justice, but a victory so uncertain and so hard-fought, over more than half a lifetime, that I have cried every time I’ve rewatched it.Free Leonard Peltier, out on Netflix for Indigenous Peoples’ Day in the US, makes clear why, as Peltier put it to me over Zoom from his new home, “I just wasn’t going to give up.” Over 110 minutes, Short Bull and France retrace not only what happened that day at Pine Ridge, but the long arc of Indigenous activism in the US, from Peltier’s childhood resistingNative boarding schools, the government-run institutions used to forcibly separate Native families and force assimilation, to Aim’s occupation of the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) in 1972 and the many decades of work to free Peltier. For years, as more evidence of railroaded justice emerged, Peltier’s name became synonymous with Indigenous resistance, another abuse in a long chain of abuses by the US federal government. “His name was definitely said on the daily,” Short Bull, who is Oglala Lakota, told me. “It was just like, the sky is blue.” Still, “it wasn’t until I started gaining access to the history where I started to understand that this was a bad deal.”‘We’re not going to go away’: the mom fighting for social media reform after her son’s suicideRead moreMuch of the first half of the film relies on archival material and interviews with the now-elderly former members of Aim, introducing a new audience to the movement’s origins, in response to the crisis of boarding schools, forced evictions and the steady encroachment on tribal territory. Peltier joined the movement in the 1960s, after experiencing anti-Native police brutality while working at a power plant on the Navajo Nation, and participated on Aim’s “trail of broken treaties” caravan to Washington. He served as a security guard when Aim members occupied the BIA building, where things devolved after the discovery of paperwork confirming future plans to use tribal lands for mining.Such tribal lands included Pine Ridge, which held some of the richest uranium deposits in the United States. Peltier arrived on the reservation during a tense and dangerous time, as a corrupt tribal government, led by Dick Wilson and enforced by his BIA-backed private “goons” (Guardians of the Oglala Nation), clashed with tribal members and Aim, sent to help defend residents from routine violence; one former resident recalls in the film that there were 68 murders in Pine Ridge during that time, and no arrests. The day of the shootout, in which a militarized FBI – archival footage shows dozens of tanks and military-style assault weapons – traded fire with a handful of Aim security members, Wilson unilaterally ceded one-eighth of the reservation to the federal government.View image in fullscreenLeonard Peltier and Holly Cook Macarro in Free Leonard Peltier.Photograph: Courtesy of Netflix“We took this on as historians, really,” said France. “Our job wasn’t to do a whodunnit. We weren’t going to try to solve the case. It wasn’t our job to figure out who pulled the trigger – we know it wasn’t Leonard.” What became clear through extensive archival research was that “people knewthenthat this was all about land. And none of that had been brought out before in the telling of Leonard’s story or the telling of the American Indian Movement. It’s all about the land.”Almost every film participant, as well as France, Short Bull and Peltier himself, assert that given the land deal, the FBI at minimum escalated the violence that day, which killed agents Jack Coler and Ronald Williams, as well as Aim member Joe Stuntz, if not outright staged it. (No arrest was ever made in Stuntz’s death.)The ICE documentary as chilling as a horror movie: ‘We’re trying to put the audience in a position of terror’Read moreThe film’s second half details the numerous miscarriages of justice after Peltier, who escaped that day and hid out for a time in an RV loaned by Marlon Brando, was arrested in Canada. The litany of dubious maneuvers used to incarcerate Peltier plays like a who’s-who of prosecutorial misconduct on every level: Peltier’s extradition was secured via fabricated testimony from a “girlfriend” he had never met, and who later recanted, citing coercion; he was tried separately from his co-defendants Dino Butler and Bob Robideau, who were allowed to argue self-defense and acquitted, in a court presided over by a known racist judge in North Dakota; the FBI’s limited evidence, claiming with certainty that Peltier shot the two agents at point-blank range, was later revealed to be unreliable. “They had no evidence to even indict us,” Peltier told me. “That was not a trial.” Nevertheless, Peltier was sentenced to life in prison in 1977.In 1984, at a hearing prompted by international activism toward Peltier’s release, the defense presented a firing pin test conducted by the FBI demonstrating that Peltier’s AR-15 was not used to shoot the agents that day. Still, the case was not overturned. By the mid-1990s, Peltier was running out of options for a verdict reversal. At times, he was presented the option to plead guilty or admit wrongdoing for clemency, but refused. “I said, ‘they’ve been saying for 46 years I’ve been found guilty beyond a reasonable doubt, beyond a shadow of a doubt, that there’s overwhelming proof against me, and now they want me to plead guilty? No, that’s not going to happen,’” he recalled.View image in fullscreenLeonard Peltier while imprisoned in 1999.Photograph: Joe Ledford/Associated Press“We’re not the guilty party here,” he added. “We weren’t killing them. We weren’t trying to exterminate them.” During his half-century of prison, Peltier remained acutely engaged with politics – “he’s the Nelson Mandela of the movement,” said France. “He spent his time in prison still organizing” – so he speaks with conviction: “We’re still in danger right now.” Just this summer, the Trump administrationwent aheadwith its court-contested plan to build 62 miles of its border wall through Tohono O’odham Nation without the tribe’s consent. “There’s the same type of president in there, the fascists who are talking about doing away with our treaties,” he said. “If we do away with our treaties, that means the end of us as a race of people.“And people will say, ‘Why are people doing that?’ Well, as long as we’re alive, as long as we’re still living as a race of people, they could never legitimately claim to be the only and true Americans.”The film ends on an upbeat note – Peltier, at long last, at home, surrounded by friends and family, though he is quick to note that house arrest is not freedom. “I’m still battling for total freedom,” he said, including the ability to travel and meet many of his supporters. “I would like to have my total freedom before I pass, or at least what freedom I could have in America.”But Free Leonard Peltier argues that his legacy is not forgotten. “I’m a beneficiary of the sacrifice that that generation made,” Short Bull said. “Leonard reminds me of so many people here on the Pine Ridge reservation. Even today, young people that are willing to make the sacrifice … hopefully history doesn’t have to ever repeat itself ever again.”Free Leonard Peltier is released onNetflixon 12 OctoberExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsUS justice systemSouth DakotaJoe BidenIndigenous peoplesNative AmericansNetflixdocumentariesShareReuse this content

title: ‘People forgot I existed’: Audrey Niffenegger on taking 14 years to write a sequel to The Time Traveler’s Wife | Audrey Niffenegger | The Guardian
description: Her debut made her a global star. Now she has finally written a follow-up – and this time, it’s political. She talks about impostor syndrome, screen adaptations and becoming radicalised
Author: Sophie McBain
Headline: Her debut made her a global star. Now she has finally written a follow-up – and this time, it’s political. She talks about impostor syndrome, screen adaptations and becoming radicalised
Content: Audrey Neffenegger at her home in Chicago.Photograph: Lucy Hewett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAudrey Neffenegger at her home in Chicago.Photograph: Lucy Hewett/The GuardianAudrey NiffeneggerInterview‘People forgot I existed’: Audrey Niffenegger on taking 14 years to write a sequel to The Time Traveler’s WifeSophie McBainHer debut made her a global star. Now she has finally written a follow-up – and this time, it’s political. She talks about impostor syndrome, screen adaptations and becoming radicalisedSat 10 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 10.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe artist and novelistAudrey Niffeneggerbegan writing the long-awaited sequel to her bestselling debut, The Time Traveler’s Wife, in 2012, just after Obama’s re-election. It was a “rosy” time in American politics, “as good as it gets over here”, she says now, but her new novel required her to imagine what the world might look like in 20, 40, 60 years’ time. In the 14 years she spent exploring various dystopian futures, American politics moved on. And her imaginings began to look worryingly realistic.An early scene in the new book involves a group of neo-Nazis at a house party. When she was writing it, few people believed the US would witness a resurgence of neo-nazism. It’s not like she is “psychic or anything”, she tells me, the clues were all there. “The first thing I remember reading in the news was Watergate, and so I’ve grown up with Reagan, and the Republicans coming on stronger and stronger, so that every Republican president we get is more of a disaster. And I thought the logical progression of that would be fascism,” she says.Listen to an extract from the audiobook of Audrey Niffenegger’s Life Out of OrderSorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://uploads.guim.co.uk/2026/10/09/Life_Out_Of_Order_Chapter_1_Audio_Clip.mp300:00:0000:05:24The Time Traveler’s Wife – the 2003 novel so popular it became a cultural phenomenon – is about an artist named Clare who falls in love with Henry, a man who is forever disappearing on her because he has a rare genetic condition that causes him to lurch involuntarily forwards and backwards in time. Henry is condemned to keep revisiting the most painful chapters of his life, and knows – but cannot change – hardships that will happen in their shared future. Niffenegger’s sequel, Life Out of Order, tells the story of their daughter, Alba, who was born with the same condition, but has a little more control over her time travel, and a greater willingness to try to harness her special abilities to serve her personal and political ends.double quotation markYes, The Time Traveler’s Wife is romantic, but it’s also heavy. Things don’t all work outNiffenegger always saw The Time Traveler’s Wife as a much “darker book” than many of her readers. People would tell her the story was “so romantic” – “and I’m like yes, it’s so romantic. It’s also kind of heavy,” she says. “Because there’s a lot of inevitability, and they’re choosing to be happy in the moment, knowing that things are not going to work out so well.” With this new novel, there’s no missing the darkness.We meet in the book-filled Chicago home that she shares with the Scottish artist Eddie Campbell, her husband of just over a decade. The walls are hung with Niffenegger’s bold, dreamlike paintings, and she has an impressive taxidermy collection: a rhea in the front room, two doves in a bell jar, a pangolin on the coffee table (bought long ago, as an antique). She used to have much more taxidermy on display, but her three cats are “barbarians” and as kittens they started “interacting with it in weird ways”. She worried one would skewer itself on the huge porcupine that used to reside on the kitchen sideboard, which she has since sequestered upstairs.At 63, Niffenegger exudes a bookish bohemianism, with her cat-eye glasses, dangly earrings and cropped silver hair. She is softly spoken, but when she talks about politics, where the conversation keeps veering, she resorts to scathing sarcasm. She is currently recovering from a long and serious illness, something she doesn’t want to talk about, because she does not want it to detract from her work. People are always obsessed with how an artist’s life influences their work, she observes, and they forget how much art can change the person who made it. Every book she has written has transformed her life. The Time Traveler’s Wife opened up the world to her.When she started writing it, Niffenegger was working as an artist and a professor at the Columbia College Chicago’s Centre for Book and Paper Arts. She made her own hand-bound, hand-printed books, sumptuously illustrated gothic fairytales that she produced in editions of 10. She was sketching one day when the phrase “The Time Traveler’s Wife” popped into her head. “It’s a good title, because it gives you two people, their relationship with each other, and their situation,” she says. She imagined the novel, which was published in 2003 by MacAdam/Cage, a small independent press, might sell a few thousand copies. In fact it sold more than9m globally.She had a few lucky breaks, Niffenegger explains. At the time she didn’t know many other writers, but she gave the book to a fellow Chicago-based artist, Annette Turow, who liked it and passed it on to her husband, the novelist Scott Turow, who then recommended it during an interview with the US Today show. In the UK, the novel was picked for Richard and Judy’s Book Club. Quickly, it became apparent that the romance and tragedy of time travel struck a chord. She began receiving emails, often from people struggling in long-distance relationships. “A lot of the resonance comes from people having that absence in their lives. So, you know, my husband is in the military, my friend is in prison, my wife is in school far away … we’re both reading it together and talking about it over the phone,” she says. She received notes from young people who were sharing the novel with their boyfriends or girlfriends and knows of a “surprising number” of children who were subsequently named Henry or Clare.Becoming a sudden commercial success was “very odd”, she recalls: “all the running around and doing interviews and having people dig really deep into the novel and have very intricate questions was extraordinary”. The scrutiny didn’t trouble her too much – it reminded her of being critiqued at art school – but she struggled with “impostor syndrome”.For most of her life so far, Niffenegger had few opportunities to travel. She’d never been west of the Mississippi and, if she had a chance to leave Chicago, she tended to either go to New York or Europe. Suddenly, she went everywhere. Once, she visited a different American city every day for two weeks, which she found too much. At a literary festival in Australia, she knew almost no one – as was often the case back then – but the writer Neil Gaiman, who was interviewing her on stage, introduced her to a young journalist named Hayley Campbell. Hayley would eventually introduce her to her father, Eddie, and for many years the couple somehow made a long-distance relationship between Brisbane and Chicago work, meeting for dates all over the world.View image in fullscreenRose Leslie and Theo James in a scene from the HBO series of The Time Traveler’s Wife (2022).Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyMeanwhile, the ordinary Chicago restaurants she mentioned in The Time Traveler’s Wife got a lot of attention “which I’m sure confused them”. The city’s Newberry Library, where Henry works, had so many visitors that they had to print a Time Traveler’s Wife FAQ sheet for the front desk and an unremarkable stairwell, featured in the story, became a destination in itself. In 2009, The Time Traveler’s Wife was made into a Hollywood film, starring Rachel McAdams. The adaptation was panned by the critics. Niffenegger has never watched it. “I mean you can let people do their own thing, and not have anything to say about their thing, that’s OK,” she says. In 2022, it was also made into a series by HBO.Thanks to her runaway success, Niffenegger received a $5m advance for her second book,Her Fearful Symmetry(2009), a ghost story set in London. For her research, she moved to the city and became a tour guide in Highgate Cemetery. “I didn’t expect people to know about it,” she says when I ask her about the advance, her manner polite, her meaning very clear. “I didn’t understand that it was going to be news and that people would know about it and ask me about it. It was like ‘That’s just my finances. Why would anybody care what’s going on with my bank account?’.” And then she answers her own question: “People are kind of fascinated because it’s weird that I would make money – ever.”Her paintings were never very “fashionable”, she says, and in the art world she is relatively unknown. “Something where you kind of need a long explanation from the artist seems to be very in,” she observes, while her work has always been narrative and figurative. She paints self-portraits with butterflies, monkeys and birds, and skeletons are a recurring motif, a skeleton wearing a party hat, curled around a cat, skeletons intertwined with people, a child skeleton holding up his mother’s face like a giant inflatable balloon.The great advantage of earning money is that it buys you time to do creative work, she says: “Like if you own your day, that’s great.” Over the years she has cut back on teaching so that she can focus on her writing and art, and run a small nonprofit arts school, Artists Book House, which she founded in 2019. While she has been doing all this, in the many years since Her Fearful Symmetrywas published, something nice happened. “People just forgot I existed,” she says, which seems to suit her just fine.Niffenegger was raised in Evanston, a city north of Chicago and a short drive from where she lives now. “I think people imagine I had some baroque childhood. I actually just had a very American middle-class, suburban childhood,” she says. Her father was a civil engineer working for the department store chain JC Penney and her mother was a quiltmaker. Niffenegger studied at the School of Art Institute in Chicago, took a few years out to teach and work, mostly as a picture framer, and then did her MFA at Northwestern University. One of her graduate projects, the illustrated novel Three Incestuous Sisters, is currently being adapted as a silent film with a very illustrious cast: the novelist Ottessa Moshfegh worked on it alongside the director Alice Rohrwacher, and Dakota Johnson, Saoirse Ronan and Jessie Buckley will star as the sisters, whose suffocatingly close bond is ripped apart over their love for the lighthouse keeper’s son. Niffenegger has read the screenplay, and this time she plans to “watch the hell out of” the film. “It’s going to be wild,” she says approvingly. “It was just so over the top, I mean it’s far weirder than the book, and I can appreciate that.”double quotation markWhatever you can be doing, now’s the time. If all you can do is vote, then voteOver the decades, her artistic interests have not wavered: “Love and loss, death, rock and roll, sex and romance, to me those are the biggest issues,” she says. Except now, because she has been writing about the future, she’s been thinking much more about politics. Both Alba and Henry find it easier to move backward than forward in time, because the future is harder to imagine, but the more they do so, the more concrete the future becomes. Niffenegger realised this is true more generally. We find it hard to respond to the threat posed by, say, the climate crisis, because we find climate meltdown hard to visualise. In her book, she describes scenes in which whole cities are underwater, utilities no longer work, food is in short supply, and the weather is apocalyptically weird in an attempt to make extreme global warming feel less abstract. And she found the more time she spent trying to imagine 2040, the more jarring the disconnect with the US’s political discourse. “I’m just like OK, sure, build a bunker for yourself,” she says of Trump, oozing contempt. “Like OK, billionaires, go to Mars, that’s OK.”The current administration has radicalised her, she says. “Until the recent Trump debacle I was not a person who used to go to demonstrations. I was political in some ways, but I was not somebody who would drop everything and, you know, hit the street yelling. Now I am,” she says. She feels a sense of urgency. “I feel like whatever you can be doing, now’s the time. If what you can do is vote, vote. If that’s all you can do, cool. If you can give money to a cause, yay. If you can, go to a demonstration. Excellent. People should be paying attention and acting accordingly.”She says one advantage of being a slow writer is that she is able to respond to current events. It would have been strange, she realises now, if she’d published the book before the pandemic and the coronavirus lockdowns had not been mentioned at all. Part of the reason the writing took so long, she says, is that she was “waiting to find out the resolution to certain real world events”. Some outcomes felt predictable, others not at all. While imagining civil unrest in a fictitious future, she watched the protests over the police killing of George Floyd rock the US and felt sure something would finally change, “But no, it just seems to have been like a rock falling into a pond,” she says, sounding despondent.Niffenegger will leave on her book tour soon, though it will be a small one. There is art to make and new writing projects to get stuck into. She’s thinking of expanding her graphic novel, The Night Bookmobile, into a series of interlinked short stories. She’s also thinking about not doing too much at all. “After spending 14 years on one thing, I’m happy to have a little rest,” she says.Life Out of Order by Audrey Niffenegger is published by Jonathan Cape (£22). To support the Guardian order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Hear Audrey in conversation with Steven Moffat at Conway Hall London on 28 Oct.
