title: Blood of My Blood review – gripping ghost story is a reckoning with slavery | Theatre | The Guardian
description: A Black British woman traces her family’s enslaved past in Joy Nesbitt’s supernaturally charged play
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: A Black British woman traces her family’s enslaved past in Joy Nesbitt’s supernaturally charged play
Content: Such innovation … Karene Peter, Jodie Campbell, Ronkẹ Adékọluẹ́jọ in Blood of My Blood.Photograph: Marc BrennerView image in fullscreenSuch innovation … Karene Peter, Jodie Campbell, Ronkẹ Adékọluẹ́jọ in Blood of My Blood.Photograph: Marc BrennerTheatreReviewBlood of My Blood review – gripping ghost story is a reckoning with slaveryRoyal Court theatre, LondonA Black British woman traces her family’s enslaved past in Joy Nesbitt’s supernaturally charged playArifa AkbarSat 10 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJoy Nesbitt’s fantastically chilling play is both a ghost story and a reckoning with the undocumented history of enslaved people. It takes us from present-day America into the past, towards the exact moment when slavery was abolished.A white couple has turned their South Carolina plantation into a holiday rental. People come for celebrations and weddings, we hear. It is tantamount to slave-plantation tourism, says Talulah (Jodie Campbell), a Black British woman who has traced her family line to this spot. Talulah is trying to channel her descendant Ginnie (Ronkẹ Adékọluẹ́jọ) through the ritual practice of “conjuring” – making contact is a way to fill in the gaps of her family’s enslaved past.View image in fullscreenNot a traditional history lesson … Hannah Morrish, Patrick Vaill and Jodie Campbell in Blood of My Blood.Photograph: Marc BrennerUnder Tatenda Shamiso’s direction, the play never feels like a history lesson and deftly covers the uneasy waters between comedy, race drama and gothic horror, with passing similarities to Marlon James’s The Book of Night Women and Jordan Peele’s psychological terror. One world physically crosses another on stage as the unresolved past exerts itself in the present. As far-fetched as the central concept sounds – a meeting between a dead enslaved person and her living relative – it carries dramatic and emotional charge.The supernatural territory takes us back to the complicated reality of Ginnie’s life and how it is entwined with the Irish confederate enslaver John Good (Patrick Vaill). White liberal guilt is satirised through the over-accommodating figure of Nora (Hannah Morrish), who runs the plantation in the present day and tries to give it a homely decorative spin.Her husband, James (also Vaill), a direct descendent of Good and an academic of Irish history, is less comic, more defensive (“That was the way,” he says of his forefathers). Debates on confronting such a past come through prickly argument between James and Talulah.View image in fullscreenFilling gaps of the past … Ronkẹ Adékọluẹ́jọ.Photograph: Marc BrennerThe set comprises the cabin and tree outside it. Both cast shadows and gloom but also, it seems, sparks of magic. Simisola Majekodunmi’s lighting delineates the past and present; Kayodeine’s thudding, dread sounds raise suspense. The earthy tufts of plantation land extend across the auditorium, felt beneath our feet as we watch. It is a subtle way of suggesting that there is no clean cut-off point. This past is indeed nestling, alive, among us.The Hungry Ghost review – this sexy, juicily spooky romcom is a screamRead moreNesbitt’s gripping writing is accompanied by some excellent acting. Vaill’s doubling is demanding and navigated spectacularly. Adékọluẹ́jọ is excellent as Ginnie, full of quiet strength. Complicated plotting brings multiple pregnancies and family trees. There is an unconvincing scene in which James and Nora spend New Year’s Eve with Talulah, and a Black American character pops up briefly to deliver a clunky treatise on historical legacies. But these contrivances are forgivable in a play that treats its subject matter with such innovation. It grips, moves and raises hairs.AtRoyal Court theatre, London, until 7 NovemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreRoyal Court theatreSlaveryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: King Lear review – David Threlfall makes a moving Lear, but why is he playing the Fool too? | Theatre | The Guardian
description: Matthew Dunster’s disruptive reinvention of the tragedy merges two roles for its star and at times enters Game of Thrones territory
Author: Mark Lawson
Headline: Matthew Dunster’s disruptive reinvention of the tragedy merges two roles for its star and at times enters Game of Thrones territory
Content: Classic Lear … David Threlfall as the king.Photograph: Helen MurrayView image in fullscreenClassic Lear … David Threlfall as the king.Photograph: Helen MurrayTheatreReviewKing Lear review – David Threlfall makes a moving Lear, but why is he playing the Fool too?Royal Exchange theatre, ManchesterMatthew Dunster’s disruptive reinvention of the tragedy merges two roles for its star and at times enters Game of Thrones territoryMark LawsonSat 10 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe TV series Succession was partly modelled onKing Lear, the family name Roy derived from the monarchic Frenchroi.Returning the compliment,Matthew Dunster’s production centralises dynastic dynamics among the young as they plot around a splintering figurehead.The reading is supported by a modern setting – jeans, car keys and handguns for hessian, horses and swords – on an Anna Fleischle set of spangly strings variously dividing the stage into a nightclub, England and France, dungeons and, in the storm scene, serving as shower curtains to keep theatregoers dry.In a play notable for repeated words, versions of Lear are revealed through verbal italicisation.Titas Halder’s recent Sheffield staging with Ian McDiarmidstressednothingand other nihilisms, emphasising the end days of a man and society. Dunster underlines references to parenting and siblings – Jonathan Slinger’s unusually unpleasant Gloucester seems to have brought up Edmund and Edgar using Lear’s childcare manual – and, more conventionally, to senility, David Threlfall’s King feeling neurologically forensic.View image in fullscreenDynastic dynamics … l-r Jason Done (Kent), Jonathan Slinger (Gloucester), Tom Varey (Edgar) and David Threlfall (King Lear).Photograph: Helen MurrayOtherwise, Dunster is notably disruptive. Starting with Threlfall alone on stage delivering a speech from act III, he gives the younger generation introductory erotic dumb shows. The Mercury prize-nominated musician Nadine Shah becomes surely the first Goneril or composer for a staging of King Lear to mime sex to her own pulsing compositions. This accentuation of seduction as a power tactic and the implied significance of procreation to inheritance fits the brutal triangle of the final act – Paddy Stafford’s Edmund lasciviously tasting two glasses of wine as he juggles Lear’s daughters – but can feel like Succession becomingGame of Thrones.The most seismic rewrite removes a great Shakespearean character. Threlfall doubles as monarch and his Fool, doing both halves of their duologues like a ventriloquist whose mouth moves. When Jonathan Pryce’s Hamlet also played King Hamlet’s ghost, almost vomiting the lines, there was a sense of demonic possession. In this case, speaking to the unseen can be a dementia symptom but the change means we lose the one candid truth-teller to Lear. This could be an editorial point about the absolute insularity that destroys the powerful, but the casting-off adds another hole to a play that already bears one in the title character’s long act IV absence and makes the wonky trial scene even odder.View image in fullscreen‘May have inherited her dad’s wilful anger’ … Isobel Akuwudike as Cordelia.Photograph: Helen MurrayWithin this gimmickry, Threlfall delivers a fairly classic Lear, deeply affecting in the deathbed scenes but, having established the character’s nationalism, winning a big laugh with the usually nothing line, “Am I inFrance?” Isobel Akuwudikeintriguingly suggests Cordelia may have inherited her dad’s wilful anger.King Lear’s word reverberations include more than 40 uses of “letters” or “note”, and Dunster makes this unusually tangible: some correspondence generally only spoken of is delivered and opened; the kingdom of this Lear boasts an impressive Royal Mail. The director, you suspect, will get a lot of missives about the spectre jester. Lear without Fool is, in two senses, not funny.AtRoyal Exchange theatre, Manchester, until 15 NovemberExplore more on these topicsTheatreKing LearDavid ThrelfallRoyal ExchangereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Edge Control: the art exhibition using hidden camera images to explore race and beauty | Art | The Guardian
description: Artist Deana Lawson uses beauty supply store surveillance images to analyze power and personhood in her exhibition at the Gagosian in New York City
Author: Morgan Jerkins
Headline: Artist Deana Lawson uses beauty supply store surveillance images to analyze power and personhood in her exhibition at the Gagosian in New York City
Content: Edge Control – Deana LawsonPhotograph: Deana Lawson/Courtesy GagosianView image in fullscreenEdge Control – Deana LawsonPhotograph: Deana Lawson/Courtesy GagosianArtEdge Control: the art exhibition using hidden camera images to explore race and beautyArtist Deana Lawson uses beauty supply store surveillance images to analyze power and personhood in her exhibition at the Gagosian in New York CityMorgan JerkinsSat 10 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 08.03 EDTShareIn her essay The Oppositional Gaze: Black Female Spectators, writer and philosopher bell hooks explains that the relationship between Black people and the act of “looking” has been traumatic since slavery. Black people, many of whom are still subject to the constant surveillance that originated during enslavement, have historically been punished with severe consequences, such as lynching, for looking back at those who subjugate them. Despite these risks, hooks writes, they rebelled by secretly looking at white people, as well as their surroundings, rejecting the white gaze as the singular framework of reality. We can, as bell hooks writes, “interrogate the gaze of the Other but also look back, and at one another, naming what we see”.I thought of this analysis when I visited Edge Control, artist Deana Lawson’s latest photography exhibition at the Gagosian gallery inNew YorkCity. Edge control refers to the gels and pomades that slick the hairs along the edges of a Black woman’s hairline, but in Lawson’s exhibit, the phrase takes on an additional meaning. It’s at once a styling product for Black haircare devotees as well as a tool to examine the beauty industry, consumerism and how surveillance and race intersect.To explore these intersections, Lawson uses photos of alleged beauty supply store shoplifters, presented in large scale and outside their original contexts. As a warning to customers, many beauty supply stores post surveillance photos of alleged shoplifters caught in the act of stealing products. The stores, which almost exclusively sell Black haircare products within Black neighborhoods, are rarely owned by Black people. The small, indistinct images tend to fade in the background amid the various colors of shampoo bottles and hair accessories.View image in fullscreenDeana LawsonPhotograph: Courtesy the artist and GagosianLawson’s images, however, are large portraits framed by mirrors, forcing the onlooker to simultaneously see themselves looking at these shoplifters. The viewer is small and narrow while the shoplifters are life-size, and what was once quiet, passive spectatorship immediately becomes active participation. This evolution is further emphasized once a viewer moves to the middle of the gallery room where two holograms stand, revealing Black women’s bodies that shift depending on the viewer’s angle. These pieces demonstrate how Lawson manipulates perception: these alleged shoplifters are not frozen in time, they are in motion, just as the viewers are.The notion of wrongdoing is questionable as the exhibition becomes a house of mirrors exploring who is and is not being watched. Lawson accomplishes exactly what bell hooks wrote about – the rebellious gaze – by looking at her subjects, challenging viewers to evaluate them, and therefore exploring how perception functions within a space full of unequal power relations.The exhibit’s official description proclaims that Lawson does not intend to cast moral judgment over these images, but rather “foregrounds the implications of agency and transformative potential of beauty products within our late capitalist society”. Lawson is not trying to villainize or glorify these shoplifters, but she does protect them. The shoplifter photos are evasive – the original images are low resolution, some of the shoplifters are masked and a few of the photos are so blurry that the viewer is unable to make out the subject’s face. Lawson’s deliberate refusal to clarify these images causes the viewer to contemplate what or who they are looking at. Who is the regular customer and who is the criminal?She aims for neutrality in the depiction of her subjects by making the artistic decision to show them in stark contrast to other Black people whose images were not gathered from surveillance cameras. On the right wall opposite Lawson’s shoplifter images, the photographer’s signature style portraits hang: lush images of Black men and women in very private settings.In all these artworks, the subjects’ gaze always meets the viewers’, reinforcing their humanity and leveling the playing field. In fact, due to their size, the subjects seem to be looking down at you. In the early 20th century,Black photographers would immortalize their Black subjectsin suits, nuns’ habits or graduate gowns to usher in a new form of race pride – and respectability – into the mainstream. Lawson’s subjects are casually dressed – if at all. She’s not interested in a dignified kind of Blackness, but rather the beauty of Blackness within the mundane. By placing all of these images together within the same space, Lawson forces the viewers to view Blackness through a continuum of life in all of its contradictions, rather than a flat binary of good and bad behavior.The relationship between the Black subjects on both sides of the room is contingent upon the viewer’s own judgment. How different is the Black female shoplifter near the braid extensions aisle from the naked Black woman squatting with her knees apart? How different is the Black male shoplifter from the Black man with a busted eye posing with others in a living room? However the viewer judges these subjects reveals their own biases. But in this exhibition, one’s biases are not private, inconsequential flaws. They’re ideological constraints that must be confronted.Edge Control succeeds at capturing the extreme vulnerability of people who are being surveilled without their knowledge in active pursuit of beauty. At the same time, Lawson narrows the gap between spectator and participant as the viewer is confronted with multiple gazes–including their own–so that no one person is valued differently than the other. With power being briefly reassembled, parity is achieved.Edge Control is on view at the Gagosian in New York City until 24 October

title: ‘They looked like two curtain-twitchers, though not very subtle ones’: Peter Crome’s best phone picture | Photography | The Guardian
description: The photographer was walking home in London when he caught the attention of a pair of canine snoops
Author: Grace Holliday
Headline: The photographer was walking home in London when he caught the attention of a pair of canine snoops
Content: Neighbourhood Watch, 2026, shot on iPhone 14 Pro.Photograph: Peter CromeView image in fullscreenNeighbourhood Watch, 2026, shot on iPhone 14 Pro.Photograph: Peter CromeSmart shotPhotography‘They looked like two curtain-twitchers, though not very subtle ones’: Peter Crome’s best phone pictureThe photographer was walking home in London when he caught the attention of a pair of canine snoopsGrace HollidaySat 10 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘It reminds me of the love I felt for my faithful companion’: Tony Hertz’s best phone pictureRead moreWalking home after dropping his little girl at school, Peter Crome sensed he was being watched. A former professional ballet dancer now living in London, he had supplemented his income with photography work for 20 years. “But since having my daughter, my Nikon gear has sat idly by,” he says. “I got so used to lugging my heavy equipment around with me, it’s been quite refreshing to go somewhere just with a phone and still come back with wonderful pictures. My iPhone has also been a blessing for keeping in touch with family back home in Sydney,” Crome adds.The cause of his disquiet that day was, to his happy surprise, these two dogs. “It was such a comical moment,” he says. “They looked like two curtain-twitchers, though not very subtle ones. I liked how they were perfectly framed with the different layers of window frames, and the brickwork and hedge provided some pleasing textures, but it was the disapproving expression on their faces that made the photo for me.”Crome waited for a while as the dogs watched other passersby, turning their heads in unison. He crossed the road to draw their attention, then took a single photo on his iPhone 14 Pro. “This is the sort of picture I would have sent my mum before she passed away a couple of years ago. I think this one would have really tickled her,” Crome says.Explore more on these topicsPhotographySmart shotArtfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Remember Me review – narrow view of two photographic centuries is like a history of food in three ham sarnies | Photography | The Guardian
description: There are 700 works from François Pinault’s collection on display – more than half of them by Irving Penn – but it’s a blinkered selection and annoyingly didactic
Author: Charlotte Jansen
Headline: There are 700 works from François Pinault’s collection on display – more than half of them by Irving Penn – but it’s a blinkered selection and annoyingly didactic
Content: Extractive images … Irving Penn’s Cuzco Children, 1948.Photograph: © Irving Penn, Condé Nast Pinault CollectionView image in fullscreenExtractive images … Irving Penn’s Cuzco Children, 1948.Photograph: © Irving Penn, Condé Nast Pinault CollectionPhotographyReviewRemember Me review – narrow view of two photographic centuries is like a history of food in three ham sarniesBourse de Commerce, ParisThere are 700 works from François Pinault’s collection on display – more than half of them by Irving Penn – but it’s a blinkered selection and annoyingly didacticCharlotte JansenSat 10 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 00.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Beware … of assuming the sterile attitude of the spectator, for life is not a spectacle” scream the words of Aimé Césaire – writ large and bold by Barbara Kruger, in a giant installation, The History of Tears, that fills Bourse de Commerce’s spectacular Rotunda. Kruger’s angry, menacing, viscerally charged work – words as images, and large-scale video clips of people seething with self-hate – is a thrilling setup for Remember Me, an exhibition that promises a take on 200 years of photography through 700 works by more than 70 artists drawn from the collection of the French billionaire François Pinault. That excitement quickly dissipates as the exhibition moves on.This is the biggest photography show ever held at the Bourse de Commerce. Remember Me has two main problems: first, it tries to say too much with too few artists. For a start, nearly 450 of the 700 or so works are byIrving Penn. It leans heavily on classical, conventional approaches, styles and familiar names, and that creates a very obvious skew in the perception of what photography is, does, and how it is presented.View image in fullscreenLike waves … Remember MeThe organisation makes no real sense. There are two main spaces, in addition to Kruger’s installation, dedicated exclusively to one artist. Penn is one of them. The installation looks undeniably beautiful: following the curving Ando architecture, the works have been hung like waves, expanding in undulating lines across the walls, without chronology or theme, flowing freely into the space. However, when you look closely at the works themselves, this configuration becomes very problematic. There are a large number of colonial-style portraits taken in a temporary tent studio by Penn when he travelled in Cameroon and Benin. Many of the pictures depict men and women in traditional tribal dress, and were taken as a commission for Vogue. These nations were actively negotiating independence from France at that time. When you compare them with portraits byMalick SidibéorSeydou Keïtaof the same time, they look even more like anthropological, ethnographic, extractive images by a westerner who couldn’t even communicate with his subjects.“Primitive subjects respond more to tone than to obscure words,” Penn stated of how he directed the people who appear in these photographs. To me, that says everything about his perspective on African bodies and culture. Then you notice the rest of it: the glamorous white women who appear as pristine models of passive beauty, while all the men are mediocre-looking and wear suits. Still lifes are woven through – presumably to undo the idea of hierarchy between subjects. So, a man who looks at a vase or a plate of fruit the same way he looks at people. The camera has been instrumental in colonialism, and in cultural extraction and appropriation – including in the fashion industry, of which Penn was part. But there’s no attempt to tackle that here, to counter these visions with other perspectives.View image in fullscreenMan Ray’s Noire et Blanche, 1926.Photograph: © Man Ray Trust / Adagp, Paris 2018It’s not the last you’ll see of Penn, unfortunately – his works keep popping up through the upper floor, where various major names reappear in different sections that each try to heavy-handedly explain and demystify, in an annoyingly didactic way, what photography is and how it’s made. We jump between sections on composition, abstraction, portrait and seriality, to nudes – where the women have gorgeous bums and breasts turned alluringly to the camera, and the men are small and, so we’re told to think, weak and vulnerable, with very large penises. My biggest issue here was why the sumptuous, elegant nude portrait of Zanele Muholi (by the artist themself, but not technically a self-portrait) needed a lengthy wall text, justifying the work via the western painting tradition – where none of the nudes of white women seemed to warrant one. Yet a quirky series of small 1933 nude shots by Man Ray – an erotic performance featuring the younger artist Méret Oppenheim, unclothed, and Man Ray in a suit and bowler hat – are left with no explanation about the power dynamics of the camera and male surrealism’s issues with women.This is a show that’s too afraid to let people think for themselves. We’re told Richard Avedon’s trio of 1963 portraits of William Casby, a former enslaved person who was 106 when Avedon photographed him, elevate his subject, giving him back his dignity. They’re glaringly close and unflattering photographs that resemble mug shots. Compare them with Avedon’s smaller, slightly blurred, portrait of Malcolm X. Decide for yourself what Avedon felt, whose image is claimed and whose is handed to them.View image in fullscreenPerfect vision of a seascape … Gustave Le Gray’s Effet de soleil dans les nuages – Océan, 1856.Photograph: Pinault CollectionOnce the exhibition lets go of the binaries, the anxiety to overexplain, or to adhere to the techniques of photography, when it allows active participation or just to be with the work, it gets better. The looser, thematic unions between images are intelligible and interesting, such as sections on “hands” and a glorious room exploring photographs of the sea. These rooms make you feel something, and reflect photographic resonances through history in a more meaningful way. By the Sea, for example, moves seamlessly from the 19th century in Gustave Le Gray’s painterly wet collodion prints, where he spliced two negatives together, one for the sea and one for the sky, to create his perfect vision of a seascape, to Hiroshi Sugimoto and Wolfgang Tillmans’ elegiac and laconic black and white ruminations. I think about why artists keep returning to look at the sea, looking for the infinite, for continuity, for obliteration and enormity. This room captures the feeling of gazing out at the sea, the ocean’s soothing violence and impervious calm.Photography is an inherently accessible medium, and they take it seriously in France. This show feels fumbling, and an unnecessary dumbing-down. Trying to bend two centuries of one of the most prolific mediums around these particular artists is like trying to tell the history of food through three ham sandwiches. There are more than 8,000 photographs in the wider collection: perhaps it’s more varied in perspective than appears in this show – but as it is, it shirks the responsibility of retelling photography’s history with nuance and multiplicity. Remember Me forgets Kruger’s invocation at the start.Remember Meis at Bourse de Commerce, Paris, until 18 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsPhotographyArtExhibitionsParisFranceIrving PennreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Stacey Dooley: ‘My skirt fell down on the Strictly Live tour. I was wearing big borrowed stage briefs‘ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: The broadcaster on her days as a shoplifter, catastrophising, and a first kiss with her dance partner
Author: Rosanna Greenstreet
Headline: The broadcaster on her days as a shoplifter, catastrophising, and a first kiss with her dance partner
Content: Stacey Dooley: ‘If not myself, who would I most like to be? Katie Taylor, the Irish boxer. I am obsessed with her.’Photograph: BBC/Expectation EntertainmentView image in fullscreenStacey Dooley: ‘If not myself, who would I most like to be? Katie Taylor, the Irish boxer. I am obsessed with her.’Photograph: BBC/Expectation EntertainmentThe Q&ALife and styleInterviewStacey Dooley: ‘My skirt fell down on the Strictly Live tour. I was wearing big borrowed stage briefs‘Rosanna GreenstreetThe broadcaster on her days as a shoplifter, catastrophising, and a first kiss with her dance partnerSat 10 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBorn in Luton, Bedfordshire,Stacey Dooley, 39, left school at 15 and worked as a shop assistant. In 2007 she was selected to take part in the BBC reality series Blood, Sweat and T-Shirts. This led to the series Stacey Dooley Investigates and her career as presenter of hard‑hitting documentaries. In 2018, her face-to-face confrontation with an Islamic State soldier won her the One World Media award and she also received the MBE for services to broadcasting. She has made three new investigative films for the BBC and presents BBC series Clickbait Clinic. She met dancer Kevin Clifton when they were partnered on Strictly Come Dancing; they have a daughter and live in Merseyside.What is the trait you most deplore in yourself?I’m quite greedy. I achieve something or something’s feeling really brilliant and I’m, like, “Right, what are we doing next? What are we getting next?”What is the trait you most deplore in others?No manners.What was your most embarrassing moment?When I was doing the Strictly Live tour at the O2, my skirt fell down. So I am stood in the middle of the O2 in my knickers – and they weren’t even my knickers, they were big borrowed stage briefs.Would you choose fame or anonymity?Fame.Describe yourself in three wordsLucky, funnier than people think, unorganised.What would your superpower be?To be able to hear what people say when we’ve left the room.What makes you unhappy?I’ve become a lot more anxious since becoming a mum. Catastrophising about things is pretty grim.What do you most dislike about your appearance?When I know I’m going to be on the telly and I haven’t washed my hair the night before, I watch the edit and I’m, like, “Why didn’t I just get up and wash my hair?”If you could bring something extinct back to life, what would you choose?Dolly Parton.What is your most unappealing habit?Persistence – I can’t take no.What did you want to be when you were growing up?I wanted to run a hotel, work in a market, and run a dry cleaners.What does love feel like?Unconditional, unwavering, non‑negotiable. It’s the only thing that really matters.What was the best kiss of your life?Kevin Clifton. Our first kiss, in 2019.Which words or phrases do you most overuse?That’s showbiz.Dawn O’Porter: ‘My greatest fear? Clothes moths – and the imminent threat of world war three‘Read moreIf not yourself, who would you most like to be?Katie Taylor, the Irish boxer. I am obsessed with her.When’s the last time you changed your mind about something significant?I change my mind on political leaders all the time. I think it’s healthy to change your mind.How often do you have sex?If Kev’s on tour, never. If we’re at home and Minnie’s not in the bed, yeah, we’ll have sex.What has been your closest brush with the law?When I was younger I was shoplifting a lot – blue eyeliner, ice poles – all the necessities. And when I was older I was going around with a lot of questionable characters.What is the most important lesson life has taught you?Take important things seriously but don’t take yourself too seriously.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe Q&AStacey DooleyDocumentaryBBCTelevisionfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Squeezy olive oil bottles, Meghan’s pot filler tap and the rise of ‘cheffy’ kit in home kitchens | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Social media ‘chefluencers’ and open restaurant kitchens have made chefs more visible and inspired aspirational gadget-buying
Author: Ellie Violet Bramley
Headline: Social media ‘chefluencers’ and open restaurant kitchens have made chefs more visible and inspired aspirational gadget-buying
Content: The Duchess of Sussex appeared on Instagram this week at a hob with a special pot filler tap.Photograph: Netflix/PAView image in fullscreenThe Duchess of Sussex appeared on Instagram this week at a hob with a special pot filler tap.Photograph: Netflix/PAGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.Life and styleSqueezy olive oil bottles, Meghan’s pot filler tap and the rise of ‘cheffy’ kit in home kitchensSocial media ‘chefluencers’ and open restaurant kitchens have made chefs more visible and inspired aspirational gadget-buyingEllie Violet BramleySat 10 Oct 2026 07.49 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 09.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Duchess of Sussex is no ordinary home cook, but when Meghan appeared on Instagram this week at a hob presided over bya special pot filler tap, it spoke to a shift in the everyday kitchen – the rise of “cheffy” kit.While the pot filler is now most often found in luxury residential kitchens, it was reportedlyinvented in the early 20th centuryas a functional fixture for commercial kitchens. It joins a wealth of other restaurant equipment to have infiltrated our homes, fromsqueezy olive oil bottlestostainless steelmixing bowlsets.View image in fullscreenA pot filler tap by Harvey Jones over a large hob.Photograph: Box-PartnershipAt Sous Chef, a UK-based independent speciality food brand, sales of chef presses are up 26%, while sales of chef’s trays are booming, according to Holly Thomson, the company’s food editor.‘Hands down my favourite bit of kit’: 13 kitchen gadgets top chefs can’t live withoutRead moreFor Ella Risbridger, author ofThe Kitchen Book: Good Food for Every Day: “It’s an amazing thing, the blurring of lines between restaurant and home kitchens.” A byproduct of the increasing visibility we have of professional chefs at work, whether via open kitchens in restaurants or “chefluencers” on social media, the utilitarianism and gadgets of restaurant kitchens are increasingly aspirational. This week, in ahome tour with Architectural Digest, Julianne Mooreshowed off her Ikea industrial shelves.“People now can seewhat is happening in professional kitchens,” says Risbridger, “and likely, if they are watching The Bear or a lot of cheffy Instagrams, the algorithm knows that and knows what you might,might,want to buy for yourself.” From thewhite T-shirtto the JapaneseHasegawa chopping board, people want to channel Carmy and Syd as they make dinner midweek.Thomson suspects it might have something to do with the economic climate – people are thinking: “‘I’m not going to spend 90 quid on a meal, but I might invest in these products that are going to help me take eating at home a bit more seriously.’” According to James Lawless, a spokesperson at David Mellor, this shift links back to the pandemic, which “reignited interest in home cooking”.View image in fullscreenIndustrial-style dishware storage shelving unit.Photograph: San Francisco Chronicle/Hearst Newspapers/Getty Images“Professional chefs’ equipment may have specialist functions, but it isn’t special,” says Lawless. “They are first and foremost tools to perform a particular function.”For Thomson, they are “an extra piece of kit that adds a bit of ease, finesse, or streamlines the process”. Coming from a professional kitchen, where “you don’t have anything that takes up space that isn’t fully useful, used every day and has multiple purposes,” they’d have to be.Of course, one person’s useful can be another’s waste of space. In the case of the pot filler tap, in an ordinary small kitchen that might be unnecessary, but, according to Helen Parker, the creative director of deVOL Kitchens, it “has become the must-have addition to a larger kitchen”.Sometimes, you don’t know what you don’t know. As Thomson says of the squeezy olive oil bottle, which, at a few quid, is proof that this isn’t all about expensive equipment: “Precision squirting is just so useful, and once you’ve done it once, you’re like, ‘Oh, this is so much better than glugging oil out of a bottle.’”For Risbridger, “the trick is that it’s nice to buy something fancy for a hobby – it’s often a shortcut to taking yourself more seriously … you can now access a reasonably cheap version of something professionals use, and that makes you feel more like a professional. Which increases confidence. Which makes the thing you make better, whether or not you could have achieved it without the gadget.”Explore more on these topicsLife and styleChefsKitchen essentialsGadgetsMeghan, the Duchess of SussexfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Henry Harris’ recipe for tarte Vaudoise à la creme | Dessert | The Guardian
description: This Swiss cream tart is a minor miracle but only needs a few ingredients
Author: Henry Harris
Headline: This Swiss cream tart is a minor miracle but only needs a few ingredients
Content: Henry Harris’ tarte Vaudoise à la crème.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.View image in fullscreenHenry Harris’ tarte Vaudoise à la crème.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.DessertHenry Harris’ recipe for tarte Vaudoise à la cremeThis fantastic tart is a minor miracle invented by a legendary chef, yet it has very few ingredients and an intriguing technique for baking itHenry HarrisSat 10 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOften, the greatest dishes are made from very few ingredients and with pretty standard techniques, and this tart is one of them. It’s based on an oldFrédy Girardetrecipe that, despite his reputation as one of the all-time greats, calls only for a simple application of process to deliver a knockout result (which is one reason I put it in my latest book). A pastry case is spread with sugar and cream, then dotted with butter and sprinkled with cinnamon. The pastry is not blind baked, but filled and baked in a very hot oven. That sounds wrong, but it is not: a fierce heat is needed to bake the pastry under its filling and to meld the cream, sugar and butter. A pinch of flour is mixed with the sugar and, as it all boils up, that smidgen of flour holds everything together as it bubbles and reduces until it takes on the appearance of condensed milk while the pastry cooks and toasts at the edges. I still use Girardet’s quantities because, unsurprisingly, they work perfectly.Merci, chef.Tarte Vaudoise a la cremePrep10 minCook1 hr + coolingServes4-6For the pastry140g plain flour, plus extra for dusting5gbaking powder1 pinch salt1 generous pinchcaster sugar60g unsalted butter, at room temperature and cut into small pieces50ml cold whole milkFor the filling100g caster sugar1 generous pinchplain flour250mldouble cream50g cold unsalted butter, dicedA little ground cinnamon(freshly ground is worth the faff)Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7. To make the pastry, sift the flour into a large bowl, then mix in the baking powder, salt and sugar. Add the butter, then work it in with your fingertips until the mix resembles coarse breadcrumbs.Pour in the milk and mix with as light a hand as possible to bring the dough into a ball. Don’t rest the pastry, because that will activate the baking powder too soon and the pastry will puff up through the filling while it cooks. Roll out the pastry on a lightly floured surface into a circle big enough to line a 25cm tart tin, then lay it in the tin and prick the pastry all over with a fork.For the filling, mix the sugar and flour, then spread it in an even layer over the base of the pastry case. Pour in the cream, then scatter over the diced butter and a light sprinkling of ground cinnamon. Bake for about 25 minutes, until the edges of the pastry are a good biscuit colour and the cream has bubbled up and looks thick and almost about to split.Remove from the oven and transfer the tin to a rack to cool completely. To serve, carefully remove the tart from its tin and cut into slices.Henry Harris is chef/co-owner ofBouchon Racine, London EC1. His book, The Racine Effect, is published by Quadrille at £40. title: Spa bliss in the Alps: hot springs and hiking in the shadow of Mont Blanc | Spa breaks | The Guardian
description: An autumn break in the French mountain town of Saint-Gervais-Les-Bains offers thermal treatments and glorious walking trails before the winter ski crowds descend
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: An autumn break in the French mountain town of Saint-Gervais-Les-Bains offers thermal treatments and glorious walking trails before the winter ski crowds descend
Content: Les Thermes de Saint Gervais, which first opened its doors in 1806.Photograph: Saint-Gervais Mont Blanc tourist boardView image in fullscreenLes Thermes de Saint Gervais, which first opened its doors in 1806.Photograph: Saint-Gervais Mont Blanc tourist boardSpa breaksSpa bliss in the Alps: hot springs and hiking in the shadow of Mont BlancAn autumn break in the French mountain town of Saint-Gervais-Les-Bains offers thermal treatments and glorious walking trails before the winter ski crowds descendJane KnightSat 10 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 11.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMont Blanc is hiding behind the clouds, but the Aiguille du Midi spears the sky above a mountainside ablaze with russet, gold and tawny tones. The maples flare red; rowan trees are dusted with crimson berries.Our little group has trundled up to Mont Lachat station (altitude: 2,115 metres) on the Tramway du Mont Blanc, the century-old cog railway that climbs improbably steep slopes from the French alpine town of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains. Operational since 1909, the railway was once intended to reach the 4,809-metre summit of Mont Blanc, but war, glacial terrain and waning funds put an end to that ambition. But even from Mont Lachat, the view is a showstopper. On one side, the Bionnassay Glacier slips scenically down the slope, a buzzard soaring over the milky-green glacial lake at its base, while on the other the Chamonix valley basks in soft autumnal sunshine.View image in fullscreenAutumn is golden season in the Alps, when you can find quieter hiking trails, lower prices and air crisp enough to stir the senses without nipping your fingers. Once focused purely on winter sports, the region’s resorts have spent years building up their summer credentials to offer hiking and biking through flower-strewn meadows. Now they’re marketing their shoulder season, too, to meet a growing demand for off-peak escapes.The little spa town of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains, 50 minutes from Geneva and sandwiched between its glitzier neighbours Chamonix and Megève, is perfectly placed to take advantage of this trend. Unlike many resorts, the town of 5,800 doesn’t fall silent once the snow (or summer crowds) melts away, in large part thanks to its thermal waters, which were discovered at the beginning of the 19th century.double quotation markThe secret is that instead of thinking about tourists, you think about the people who live here. Then the tourists will be happy tooA year-round gondola called Le Valléen now links the train station in the village of Le Fayet, farther down the slope where the thermal spa is located, to Saint-Gervais proper. Opened in late 2024, it means you can arrive by rail from London via Paris and reach the heart of the resort without needing a car. “If you go to Megève in the shoulder season there’s no one there,” says long-serving mayor Jean-Marc Peillex. “That’s not the case here. The secret is that instead of thinking about tourists, you think about the people who live here. Then the tourists will be happy too.”View image in fullscreenA gondola heads up Aiguille du Midi.Photograph: KI Photography/AlamySaint-Gervais (850 metres) may lack Megève’s polish but it has its own quiet charm: a medieval fortified house, a 17th-century church with geometric stained glass windows, elegant belle époque buildings near the spa and a thriving market every Thursday. Several excellent restaurants stay open year round, and our hotel, the chocolate-box Coeur des Neiges, offers rooms at less than half the summer or winter rate, making it an ideal base for autumnal exploring.From here we take the Mont Blanc tramway one stop to Motivon, at 1,400 metres, then hike for an hour without seeing another soul; the only sound is the gentle clanging of cowbells. Our destination is the Distillerie Saint-Gervais Mont Blanc, one of Europe’s highest microdistilleries at 1,365m. It’s actually set in a converted donkey shed with windows framing pine forests and plunging valleys, shelves fashioned from old skis and two gleaming copper distillation stills.This is where Scotsman James Abbott, kilt and all, produces some 450 bottles a year of single malt whisky (in a Speyside style), along with vodka, the traditional herbal liqueurgénépiand a superb mountain gin infused with ingredients such as blueberries and wild herbs from the nearby slopes.View image in fullscreenThe Tramway du Mont Blanc, the century-old cog railway that climbs ‘improbably steep slopes’.Photograph: Hemis/Alamy“The locals noticed that when I went to parties, I took whisky, not wine,” James laughs. “They said: ‘Why don’t you make your own – you drink enough of it.’” It turns out he does it rather well: the whisky sells for €95, the gin for €50, and both go down beautifully after a day in the mountain air before we hop back on the tramway.Although the tramway stops running from the end of September, there’s no shortage of scenic hiking trails fanning straight out from town which are accessible later in the year, plus a free, year-round bus service linking the villages that make up the commune of St-Gervais. We’re due to take it the next morning for a walk from Saint-Nicolas-de-Véroce, whose baroque church is resplendent with blue-and-gold interiors and frescoed ceilings, but a heavy rainstorm postpones our plans.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markWe drift between pools of different temperatures, while the gondola glides silently overheadThat’s not a problem when just down the road (or a free cog lift ride down the mountainside) are Les Thermes de Saint-Gervais, which have been soothing weary bodies since 1806, when notary Joseph-Marie Gontard discovered the springs. The mineral-rich waters, packed with sulphur, magnesium, calcium and zinc, bubble up from underground at 39C, feeding a three‑hour wellness circuit.We drift between pools of different temperatures, move lazily from sauna to steam room, enjoy the rainforest spa and wallow outdoors as jets of water pummel our backs while the gondola glides silently overhead. Who cares about the rain?View image in fullscreenLes Thermes de Saint-Gervais.Photograph: Leblanc Catherine/AlamyBy the time we emerge, the storm has cleared, so we continue to Saint-Nicolas. From here, a steep two‑hour trail winds up to theRefuge du Mont-Joly, a century-old wooden inn that smells of woodsmoke and melting cheese. Normally there are sweeping views of Mont Blanc from the terrace, but today the peaks are shrouded in cloud.We might not be able to see the mountains but we can taste their produce, notably in the enormous portion of blueberry tart that follows a tartiflette big enough to satisfy a sumo wrestler. As I tuck in, snow begins to fall. By morning it will be gone, melted by the late-summer sun. But now it lies thick and soft outside, turning the world white, as if the Ice Queen from Narnia might step through the door at any moment. That’s autumn in the Alps for you.The trip was provided by theSaint-Gervais Mont Blanctourist board.Doubles at theCoeur des Neigesfrom €108 room-only, or from€76 room-only atPlan Bat Le Fayet. The Refuge du Mont-Joly is closed from the end of March to late May, and from November to mid-December.The Tramway du Mont Blanc now stops at theNid d’Aigle lookout (2,380 metres), after the line was extended in JulyExplore more on these topicsSpa breaksAlps holidaysRest and relaxationChamonix holidaysFrance holidaysEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Expert tips to make you a better runner - start slow, enlist a friend, choose strength over stretches | Running | The Guardian
description: Running is one of the easiest exercises to take up, but it can be easy to lose your mojo and get injured. Coaches give their advice on how to hit your stride
Author: Sarah Phillips
Headline: Running is one of the easiest exercises to take up, but it can be easy to lose your mojo and get injured. Coaches give their advice on how to hit your stride
Content: Composite: Guardian Design; Posed by models; Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design; Posed by models; Getty ImagesThe expertsRunningExpert tips to make you a better runner - start slow, enlist a friend, choose strength over stretchesRunning is one of the easiest exercises to take up, but it can be easy to lose your mojo and get injured. Coaches give their advice on how to hit your strideSarah PhillipsSat 10 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 00.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhether you have never been for a run or are building up to a marathon, sometimes the biggest challenge is just getting out the door. Here, running coaches share their tips on everything from mindset to avoiding injuries – but mainly how to find joy in running.Find your motivation“I absolutely hate getting out of bed and going for a run,” saysJo Wilkinson, a former GB and England athlete who has been a running coach for 10 years. “It takes me a good 20 minutes to get into a run, and then I quite enjoy it. Motivation ebbs and flows in all of us.” Wilkinson suggests arranging to run with someone to make yourself get out – “It’s much harder to let a friend down. There’s a sense of obligation to turn up” – or find a running club to sign up to.“If you’re running after work, my top tip is: do not sit down,” she says. “Walk in the front door and put your running clothes on. If you sit on your sofa, you will not get up again.”“There are going to be days when you don’t want to do it,” says Thomas Craggs, who leads the World Class Endurance Programme for UK Athletics, which includes Keely Hodgkinson and Emile Cairess. “People think these guys wake up every day and love what they do. They don’t. But they do it anyway.”double quotation markMost people would be less prone to injury if they took longer to build up their runningCraggs says he got into running as an “overweight, sedentary adult” and quickly became a mass participation marathon runner. For those who feel nervous about running in public for the first time, he says: “Being self-conscious is normal – you are not the exception. You are going to have to embrace a period of discomfort to reach the point where running feels comfortable. But one of the joys of being a new runner is that progression can be quite rapid, so you go from struggling to do 30 to 60 seconds’ worth of running to being able to run for 30 minutes.”Start slow“Couch to 5Kis probably your best bet to start, because then you have a little cheerleader on your phone,” saysAllie Bailey, an ultrarunner, coach and the author of31 Days: A Zero Bullsh*t Mindset Masterclass for the Modern Runner. The app involves a mixture of walking and running to get you going. “And when I say run,” says Bailey, “I mean run a bit faster than walking, because everybody goes off and sprints like they are at school – you don’t need to do that. If you can jog and hold a conversation, that’s a good pace to start.”Don’t be afraid to walk, agrees Wilkinson. “People think they have got to run continuously. I walk all the time,” she says. “Most people would be less prone to injury if they took longer to build up their running.” So don’t feel bad about taking your time to reach 5k.Wear sensible footwearView image in fullscreenChoose shoes that are comfortable rather than performance-enhancing.Photograph: Xavier Lorenzo/Getty ImagesEmma Kirk-Odunubi, a running coach and author ofFind Your Pace: How Running Changed My Life and How It Can Change Yours Too,recommends having your gait analysed, especially if you can get it done at an independent running store. “Then they can give you impartial advice on what shoes will work best for you.”“Find a pair of shoes that are comfortable rather than performance-enhancing,” says Bailey. Don’t forget: “You’re a hobby runner, not a professional athlete.”If you’re more of an experienced runner, is it worth buying those carbon-plated shoes – the kind favoured by record-breaking athletes – to get a PB (personal best)? “There is good evidence that they do make a significant difference,” says Wilkinson. “You just have to be aware that they don’t have much stability, so don’t wear them for every single run, as it could create problems down the line.”Prioritise comfortComfort is also key with what you wear, says Kirk-Odunubi. “We can get to the nitty-gritty of synthetic materials and the breathability later on, but to start with, the more comfortable you feel when you’re running, that’s already one barrier broken down – you feel good before you head out the door.”You don’t have to spend a fortune on kit, either. Bailey gets hers secondhand: “I buy from Preloved Sports. You can get everything – T-shirts, shorts, bras – really cheaply. The most sustainable kit you’ve got is the kit you’re already wearing.”Sign up to racesView image in fullscreenParkrun is for all ages and levels of fitness.Photograph: shapecharge/Getty ImagesWork out what your goal is. This could be, “I want to be able to run continuously to that lamp-post in six weeks’ time, or I want to go to a parkrun in six weeks’ time,” says Craggs. Signing up for a race or an event can be the best motivation you need to keep training, and there is perhaps no better place to start than parkrun. Although it can seem intimidating, says Wilkinson, “There are people of all shapes and sizes, ages and levels of fitness. Walking is encouraged as much as running.”Find a running routineHaving a routine will help you to commit, and Craggs says that frequency is the first thing to focus on.Runningthree times a week is a good starting point to “give your body what it likes, which is a managed stimulus, mixed with appropriate recovery time”. Build up the volume of continuous running slowly, so you don’t have to have more days off to recover, he adds. “The surefire way of stopping is by getting injured, and the most likely way you’ll get injured is by ramping up your training too hard.”It can help to use apps or training plans, but “always listen to your body”, says Kirk-Odunubi. “Sometimes an app can say ‘do this speed workout’, and you might be absolutely exhausted, but you do it anyway, and get a niggle or injury.”When you are running regularly, “There will come a point where those fitness gains slow down, and you start to plateau,” says Craggs. You can get through this by increasing the volume or intensity of your runs, or through adding interval training. “Runners can develop speed and endurance through managed doses of high intensity. This can stress your body beyond its comfort zone in a sustainable way.” The key, he says, is to “tailor the intensity and recovery to your ability and build progressively”.Use a watch, but don’t let it rule youView image in fullscreenLook away!Photograph: Jacob Ammentorp Lund/Getty Images/iStockphoto“Data is great if the watch is working for you and you’re not working for the watch,” says Bailey.“Don’t let yourself be emotionally abused by your watch,” agrees Wilkinson. “Is it going to make you fitter? No. What will is running and training.“One of the biggest skills you can develop as a runner is the ability to judge your pace, but not run with your eyes glued to your watch. It shouldn’t suck the fun out of it.”Load up on carbohydrates“Carbs are your friend,” says Wilkinson. “They are the most efficient source of energy physiologically. You need to focus on carbohydratesregularly throughout the day.”“Before we run, it is important to fuel ourselves,” says Kirk-Odunubi. “Whether it’s a piece of toast with honey, a bowl of porridge or even just a banana.”And the best thing to consume after a run? “A pint of cow’s milk,” says Wilkinson. “You want to have a mix of protein and carbohydrate, and cow’s milk is cheap, simple and highly effective.”Choose strength work over stretchingView image in fullscreenHamstring exercises give more benefits than random stretches.Photograph: Posed by models; FG Trade/Getty ImagesMany of us don’t bother to stretch. Is this a problem? “Stretching is good if it is done well,” says Wilkinson, “but often people don’t hold a stretch for long enough.” Ten seconds is pretty useless; there is better evidence that it will benefit you if you hold it for more like one minute. She says it is far better to do a short yoga or pilates routine than a few token stretches.What is more important, the experts agree, is strength and conditioning work. “Join a gym and do some lower leg and lower body strength work every week,” says Bailey. This is especially important as we get older, says Wilkinson, because “our muscle mass and bone density start to decline. The more strength work you can do, the more you’ll maintain that for longer” – and be able to keep running.What are the beststrength exercises for runners? “We run on one leg at a time,” says Kirk-Odunubi. “So go for any exercise that is unilateral, like lunges or split squats. And then look at things like single-leg calf raises, and some low-level plyometrics, like hops and pogo jumps. Adding those in will make a massive difference.”Take injuries seriously“If running caused your injury, more running will not make it better,” says Wilkinson. “So, if in doubt, stop. Even if you are a long way from home.”“Never run through pain,” says Kirk-Odunubi. “If your day-to-day activities are being interrupted by discomfort, there is no way that you should be running, and that is a sign to go and seek out some help from a physiotherapist or osteopath.” Without a proper diagnosis, you won’t know how to respond.Don’t overdo your marathon preparationView image in fullscreenRun consistently and continuously in the lead-up to your marathon.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianIf you’ve got a place in a spring marathon, start training now, says Craggs. “But also make sure you “don’t overcook it too early,” says Wilkinson. “It is better to have done less but run consistently and continuously over the whole period up to your marathon than it is to have put in some amazing long runs and then had three weeks off because you overdid it.”“I get people to think about nutrition, hydration and sleep,” says Kirk-Odunubi. “If life’s got in the way, and you’ve been working long hours and you are fatigued, skipping one session is probably going to be more beneficial for you than pushing through.”“You don’t have to get to 20 miles in training,” says Craggs. “Your job is to do enough, but not so much that you come into the marathon knackered. Loads of runners run great marathons off a longest run of 16-18 miles.” Doing a 10k or half-marathon first can help to rehearse race day logistics such as fuelling with gels and energy drinks.On the day itself, leave plenty of time to get there and queue for the toilets, says Wilkinson. “Nerves are good; they make you want to do well, and they give you adrenaline.” Then, when you set off, “however slowly you think you’ve started, start more slowly,” says Wilkinson. “Have a feeling for your first few miles, and do not exceed it. If you do, even if you feel amazing, you will regret it. That is the time when you really need to use your watch.”606 miles in six days: teacher Megan Eckert chases ultrarunning history – and a men’s recordRead moreTry to be philosophicalAs a coach, Wilkinson says she prides herself on predicting people’s times, but a lot of people aren’t as accurate about themselves. “Afterwards, ask yourself: was the time you hoped for realistic based on the training that you did and the fitness you had? Did you have a race plan that was sensible, and did you stick to it? Did you take gels at the right time? Did you keep yourself at the pace that you planned? Were you ill, injured, stressed or overcome by the whole experience? All of those things affect you.”Whatever happens, “It’s not the end of the world,” says Wilkinson. “And do you know what? Ninety-nine percent of people won’t judge you on your time, or won’t even know what it means. My PB was2 hours and 37 minutes.People think that is amazing. I tell them I ran 3 hours and 48 minuteslast year, and they think that’s equally amazing.”“It’s OK to be disappointed,” says Craggs, who advises focusing on other things that went well, such as spotting your family and friends in the crowd. “If sport was predictable, we wouldn’t do it.”Explore more on these topicsRunningThe expertsFitnessTraining programmesMarathon runningfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Tim Dowling: at last I join the ranks of competent people | Family | The Guardian
description: It’s not often I get the chance to admire my handiwork, but I have finally fixed a light switch
Author: Tim Dowling
Headline: It’s not often I get the chance to admire my handiwork, but I have finally fixed a light switch
Content: Illustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Selman Hosgor/The GuardianThe Tim Dowling columnFamilyTim Dowling: at last I join the ranks of competent peopleIt’s not often I get the chance to admire my handiwork, but I have finally fixed a light switchTim DowlingSat 10 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 11.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a single strange moment, everything appears to be in hand: the garden is tidy and free of dead branches, thanks toGardening Steve; the back door, which refused to close properly for most of the summer, has fixed itself in the cooler weather. I’ll take that as a win.The bathtub’s clawed feet are sitting on two long planks, safely spreading its enormous load evenly across the squishy,sinking bathroom floor. There are, theoretically, further repairs to be undertaken here, but I’ve reached an age where I’ve had to make sharp adjustments to my idea of what constitutes a permanent solution. If nothing else happens, this will do.The kitchen table has been sanded down and refinished, by me. At first the effect was a bit too orangey for my wife’s liking, but over the subsequent days the colour of the wood seemed to improve when contrasted with the prospect of doing the whole thing all over again.double quotation markA problem I had not foreseen arises: without any lights on, it’s hard to see what I’m doingAs the nights draw in, only one real job remains: the kitchen’s three-button dimmer switch wall plate is broken – one of the main lights simply won’t come on.“I can fix that,” I say, rashly.“Are you sure?” my wife says.“If you can find a like-for-like replacement for the switch plate, I can put it in,” I say, still more rashly.“Shouldn’t I get an electrician?” she says.“No,” I say. “I can manage.”My wife sources a new switch plate more quickly than I’d imagined possible. It arrives the next day. I open the box and consult the instructions.“This product should be installed by a competent person,” I read.“Uh-oh,” my wife says.“Eg, a qualified electrician,” I say.“We need to call someone,” she says.“A qualified electrician is just one example of a competent person,” I say, “Other examples include chartered accountants, or the Lord Mayor.”“It seems complicated,” my wife says, looking over my shoulder at the connection diagrams.“Don’t worry, I’m ignoring all that,” I say. “I’m just going to take the old switch off the wall, and copy exactly what I find behind it.”“I might not be here when that happens,” she says.I begin work the next morning, after my wife leaves to walk the dog. I start by turning off the electricity for the entire house – you can’t be too careful. Then I unscrew the broken switch plate and gently pull it away from the wall.A problem I had not foreseen arises: without any lights on, it’s hard to see what I’m doing – I have to shine my phone torch down on my work. At times, when the installation gets fiddly, I have to hold the phone between my teeth.double quotation markFinally, the time comes to turn the electricity back on. Gritting my teeth, I flip the switchThere are a lot more wires than I expected, but the new switch has the same basic arrangement as the old one. I don’t dare disconnect the old switch plate completely, because the wires aren’t labelled. Instead I undo each wire individually, immediately connecting it to the corresponding contact on the new switch plate. It’s exciting doing it this way – I feel as if I’m trying to bypass an alarm so I can rob a museum.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut it’s also frustrating. The wires are trimmed short, and the connecting screws are tiny. There’s no room to work. At the point when I have both the old and new plates hanging out of the wall, each half connected, my concentration falters: what am I doing? I bite down hard on my phone, and continue.Finally, the time comes to turn the electricity back on. Gritting my teeth, I flip the switch.“I wasn’t expecting this,” my wife says, rolling the leftmost button clockwise and watching the light over the kitchen table intensify. “I thought I’d find you sitting on the floor crying.”Tim Dowling: I’ve been replaced by a younger model … it’s a reliefRead more“You missed that bit,” I say.“And no problems?” she says.“At one point I got into a panic and had to pause for half an hour,” I say, “to educate myself about the difference between leading edge and trailing edge dimmers.”“Which is?” she says, rolling the button back.“Leading edge dimmers are cheap and cause problems with LED bulbs,” I say. “Trailing edge, or reverse phase dimmers, are the best choice for most premises.”“What do we have?” she says.“Ours can switch from one to the other,” I say, “but trailing edge is the default setting.”“So I didn’t really need to hear any of that, did I?” she says.“I learned it,” I say, “so it’s gotta come out somewhere.”“Anyway, it’s very satisfying,” she says, moving to the next button along.It’s more than satisfying for me. When I turn the kitchen lights on my heart skips a beat, every time.Explore more on these topicsFamilyThe Tim Dowling columnDIYfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Marina Silva on Flávio Bolsonaro: He will try to finish his father’s ‘perverse project’ to destroy the Amazon | Flávio Bolsonaro | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Former Brazilian environment minister warns of destruction as far-right scion favourite to become president
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Exclusive: Former Brazilian environment minister warns of destruction as far-right scion favourite to become president
Content: Marina Silva says a second Bolsonaro presidency will spell disaster for the globally crucial ecosystem, for its inhabitants and for the climate crisis.Photograph: Sérgio Lima/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMarina Silva says a second Bolsonaro presidency will spell disaster for the globally crucial ecosystem, for its inhabitants and for the climate crisis.Photograph: Sérgio Lima/AFP/Getty ImagesFlávio BolsonaroInterviewMarina Silva on Flávio Bolsonaro: He will try to finish his father’s ‘perverse project’ to destroy the AmazonTom Phillipsin Rio de JaneiroExclusive: Former Brazilian environment minister warns of destruction as far-right scion favourite to become presidentSat 10 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 18.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former Brazilian environment minister Marina Silva has said that ifFlávio Bolsonarobecomes president he will seek to finish the “perverse project” of rampant rainforest destruction initiated by his jailed far-right father.The Amazonwas thrown into chaosduring Jair Bolsonaro’s 2019-2022 presidency, when Brazil’s environment and Indigenous protection agencies were gutted and environmental criminals ran riot, causing surges indeforestationand violence.Despite that, Bolsonaro’s eldest son, Flávio, is the favourite to beat the leftwing incumbent,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, in the second round of the presidential election on 25 October. Flávio, 45, beat Lula, 80, by more than 2m votes in the first round last Sunday, amid a wave of anti-incumbency and anti-left sentiment that catapulted a record number of far-right politicians into an already conservative congress.Silva, a world-renowned environmentalist who was Lula’s environment minister until April, says a second Bolsonaro presidency will spell disaster for the globally crucial ecosystem, for its inhabitants and for the climate crisis.“I’ve no doubt that this time they will try to finish the perverse project they started with [Jair] Bolsonaro. If they are elected – and God, and the Brazilian people, willing they won’t be – they will use their time totry to speed up as much as possible all of the regressions they can, including to keep themselves in power,” says Silva, who was appointed after Lula beatJair Bolsonaroin the 2022 election.View image in fullscreenAerial view of an area of Amazon rainforest deforested by illegal fire in Amazonas state in 2024.Photograph: Evaristo Sa/AFP/Getty Images“The vision they have for the Amazon is the same vision they have for everything. They are denialists.Their vision is that the forest must be removed for economic activities,” she adds. “They will again encourage illegal mining, the invasion of Indigenous lands, and violence against Indigenous and Quilombola communities.”Silva fears aggressiveresource extractioncould be turbocharged by Donald Trump’s designs on Latin America, exemplified by the US commandeering Venezuela’s huge oil reserves after the capture of Nicolás Maduro. The Bolsonaros are long-term allies of Trump, who has called Venezuela’s oil “the spoils”of his brief war.“Brazil cannot [be governed by] a political group that wants to turn itself into an American protectorate, as is the case with Venezuela today,” says Silva, who believes a Flávio Bolsonaro administration would be “subservient” to the US.View image in fullscreenMarina Silva believes a Flávio Bolsonaro administration would be ‘subservient’ to the US.Photograph: Diego Herculano/ReutersSpeaking from São Paulo, Silva recalls the “scorched earth” she encountered when she took over a defanged and dispirited environment ministry in January 2023 and set about trying to control soaring Amazon destruction. One of Lula’s first acts was to send troops to expel thousands of illegal miners from the country’s largest Indigenous territory.Silva saysthe “Herculean effort” of environmental and security forceshas paid off. Amazon deforestation has fallen nearly 50% under Lula, with an estimated 2,600 sq km (1,004 sq miles) lost this year compared with almost 11,600 sq km during Jair Bolsonaro’s last year in office. Illegal miners and ranchers have been evicted from a succession of Indigenous territories. Tens of billions of dollars of international funding for rainforest protection have been restored after being frozen during Bolsonaro’s era of destruction.Now, Silva believes all those achievements are in jeopardy. “It’s deeply sad and troubling,” says the 68-year-old, who was born in the Amazon to a family of rubber tappers.View image in fullscreenEnvironmental special forces raid an illegal cassiterite mine near the Yanomami village of Xitei in 2023.Photograph: Tom Philips/The GuardianThe veteran activist pauses to compose herself as she considers the prospect that in just a few weeks all that work could be undone.“It’s just like the myth of Sisyphus. Rolling the boulder all the way up to the top and watching it fall back down. Except it won’t fall on open ground – it’s going to fall right on top of all of us,” Silva says of the consequences of allowing deforestation to again spiral out of control.“Paradoxically, just at the moment when we could be about to achieve the lowest rate of deforestation [in more than a decade] and hit a once unthinkable target of zero deforestation by 2030, we face the threat of a government which … would set all of this back to square one.”She adds: “It’s frightening, too, to think that [this is happening when] we’re living througha super El Niño, which will bring severe problems of drought and floods … during a government that has zero commitment to the prevention, adaptation and mitigation agenda.”View image in fullscreenPeople take part in Acampamento Terra Livre (Free Land) protest to demand the demarcation of Indigenous lands and defend constitutional and cultural rights in Brasília in April.Photograph: Adriano Machado/ReutersEven if Flávio Bolsonaro loses, congress’s shift to the far right means the coming years are likely to prove dire for the environment in the world’s most biodiverse country. In the recent election, Bolsonaro’s Liberal party (PL) won 19 of the 54 seats up for grabs in the 81-seat senate and 121 seats of the 513 lower house seats, making it easier for lawmakers to remove environmental and Indigenous protections.Silva sought a seat in the senate but was beaten by a former special forces police officer and another Bolsonarista politician. “Even with the current makeup [of congress] we’ve witnessed numerous setbacks,” says Silva, who fears lawmakers will move to “uncreate” conservation units and Indigenous territories.“It’s adevastating process. I’m worried not just about the Amazon but about all of our biomes, like the Atlantic Forest,the Cerrado,the Pantanal,the Pampa. All of Brazil’s biomes are equally threatened by this Trumpist vision.”Silva’s fears are not confined to the environment. She believed countless social advances achieved during Lula’s three terms as president would also be reversed, including the eradication of hunger and dramatically increased access to higher education.View image in fullscreenJair Bolsonaro, with his sons Eduardo (L) and Flavio (R), waves his supporters during a rally at Copacabana beach in April 2024.Photograph: Buda Mendes/Getty ImagesShe argues that Brazil’s democracy is at risk if the Bolsonaros reclaim power, with Jair, who is serving a 27-year sentence for plotting a coup after losing the 2022 election, expected to be released and made a minister.Those fears grew this week when Flávio Bolsonaro announcedhe would seek to “re-democratise”Brazil and change the constitution, possibly allowing longer presidential terms.“That is a very dangerous word, because to an authoritarian mindset, what does re-democratisation mean?” Silva says. “It means democracy for them to stay in power ad infinitum; riding roughshod over constitutional rules; interfering with the logic of the separation of powers; having the power to appoint supreme court justices to mould a supreme court in their own image and likeness. In reality, they are a sort of right-wing version of what was done in Venezuela [under Maduro].”“They are willing to erode our democracy from within,” she adds.View image in fullscreenMarina Silva hopes Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva can bounce back and win the presidential runoff on 25 October.Photograph: Andressa Anholete/Getty ImagesSilva voices hope that Lula can bounce back in the second round. “I believe deeply that it’s possible,” she says, vowing to spend the coming days battling to convincethe more than 30 million people who did not vote in the first round of the“incalculable damage” another Bolsonaro presidency could cause.On Thursday, a survey by the Datafolha polling institute gave Bolsonaro a 52% to 48% lead over Lula in the runoff.Silva, who has been defending the Amazon since the 80s, vows to fight on.“I draw my energy from insisting on living. I believe life means holding on, and the death impulse – strong as it may be – always loses to the life impulse. Look at us: we are here. Our parents and our grandparents are gone, but we made it. I truly believe this instinct to live will prevail. My hope is that it proves stronger right now, so Latin America isn’t consumed by this drive for death.”Explore more on these topicsFlávio BolsonaroAmazon rainforestDeforestationLogging and land-clearingBrazilLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaLand rightsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We’re not asking for luxury’: school protesters in Paris suburb feel abandoned by French state | France | The Guardian
description: Students say they are desperate to get back to class but conditions are so bad that the protests must continue
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Students say they are desperate to get back to class but conditions are so bad that the protests must continue
Content: A sign reading ‘Education in peril – angry youth’ on the gates of the Lycée Blaise-Cendrars in Sevran.Photograph: Ed Alcock/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA sign reading ‘Education in peril – angry youth’ on the gates of the Lycée Blaise-Cendrars in Sevran.Photograph: Ed Alcock/The GuardianFrance‘We’re not asking for luxury’: school protesters in Paris suburb feel abandoned by French stateStudents say they are desperate to get back to class but conditions are so bad that the protests must continueAngelique Chrisafisin SevranSat 10 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 05.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a normal school day, Mohammed, 17, wakes at 6am, cares for his younger siblings to help his single mother who works as a security guard, then takes two crowded buses and a local train to get to his high school in Sevran, a low-incomebanlieuetown in the suburbs north-east of Paris.“There aren’t enough chairs or desks to go round, so some students have to stand up,” Mohammed said. “Classes can be so packed you can’t interact with the teacher. In this year’s heatwaves, it felt like 40 degrees in overcrowded classrooms with no shade or curtains. It was so hot my brain couldn’t function.”The 17-year-old in his last year of high school wants to study management and digital communication at a Paris university. But he said conditions were so poor, he felt all odds were stacked against him and his classmates.“Some of us have to go months without teachers when absent staff aren’t replaced,” he said. “One class had no French teacher for several months just before the French baccalaureate, so they couldn’t even study all the set texts for their exam. Recently we needed a teacher for a subject taught through English, but when that teacher arrived they didn’t speak English.”Thebiggest youth protest movement in the country in decadesbrought hundreds of thousands on to the streets across France this week demonstrating againstinequality in the French education system, decrepit schools, a lack of teachers and large class sizes. Hundreds of schools were blockaded, thousands of teenagers were arrested, and rights groups warned ofalleged police brutality, with one child losing the use of eye and another losing a hand.View image in fullscreenGraffiti on a wall at the Lycée Blaise-Cendrars.Photograph: Ed Alcock/The GuardianMohammed and his classmates, often supported by their parents and teachers, have been at the frontline, barricading their school, the Lycée Blaise-Cendrars, which is in one of mainland France’s poorestdépartements, Seine-Saint-Denis. They have voted to continue their protests next week, taking theirgrievancesto the local mayor, elected officials and education representatives. Many local politicians have supported their demands. Even the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, conceded that teenagers had “legitimate” concerns.Photos on the Sevran students’ phones showed broken classroom chairs, holes in walls, holes in ceilings, mould, buckets to catch leaks, faulty lights. They said basic needs weren’t met, with some toilets broken, others with no doors and often no toilet paper or soap. Video projectors and science equipment were lacking.View image in fullscreenA student shows an example of conditions in the school on their phone.Photograph: Ed Alcock/The Guardian“We’re not asking for luxury, just the basics to learn in decent conditions,” Mohammed said. “And yet police on horseback charged us when we were gathered to protest outside our school, firing teargas at us and making arrests. It’s so dangerous to be charged by a horse, it could kill you. I just ran, I was trying to help my classmates.”The high schools of Seine-Saint-Denis, a suburban area nudging against northern Paris, have been a driving force in the protests. The area has the youngest population in mainlandFrance, one of the highest birthrates and the among the lowest average income.
