Instead, the additional money has been swallowed by childcare fees.“I did not want to go back full-time, it was purely because of the cost of living,” she says.“We went from paying around $175 a week for four days of care … to now paying $536 a week for five days, so any increase I got in my salary I’m basically now paying in day care.”Hill says her husband always wanted a bigger family. If raising children were more affordable, they may have considered having a third. But with only a small village around them, she says “it’s just not working”.“If our circumstances were different I might have had more reason to pursue more children, but financially it just wasn’t ever going to work for us.”The prime minister,Anthony Albanese, wants universal childcare to be his political legacy, his entry to the Labor hall of fame alongside Medicare and the National Disability Insurance Scheme. It should, he says, be “as natural as public school”.But the sector has been rocked by widespread allegations of child abuse and safety breaches, damaging public trust and forcing the government to tighten standards – all while trying to figure out what a universal system might look like and how to pay for it.It is working against a ticking clock: the2026 intergenerational report, released last month, showed deaths would outnumber births in Australia by the 2060s. Australia needs more babies, and Labor says universal childcare is key to making that happen.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailWhat is universal childcare?While many might presume universal childcare means free childcare – akin to public schools for older children – the government has defined it as care that is “available, quality and affordable”. Overseas examples point to provinces in Canada which offer $10 a day capped care, or Estonia, where fees are capped at low weekly or monthly rates tied to the minimum wage. Labor won’t yet say which model it would choose but has indicated it is likely to be means-tested.It has commissioned two consulting firms to produce separate work outlining the scope of the challenge. The biggest report is by Deloitte and aims to set out thecost of delivering childcare servicesin any part of the country – metropolitan, outer-suburban, regional or remote.The work requires the cooperation of about 1,000 childcare centres across that geographic spread but they have not been forthcoming. The low turnout of volunteers has led to the government compelling service providers to hand over the centres’ financial data. Deloitte is due to hand the report to government by the end of the year.The cabinet is also mulling over a report by KPMG which outlined the business case for the government owning and leasing childcare centres. The work – which the government has refused to release, citing cabinet in confidence rules – centres around the $1bnbuilding early education fund, which provides for state governments and not-for-profits to set up centres in childcare deserts.The first grant round from that fund was announced this month, with $17.3m split between three not-for-profit providers to build four childcare centres in outer metropolitan and regional areas. Dozens more are yet to be announced.It gives us a clear hint of where Labor believes it can make a mark. The government wants to see not-for-profits making up a bigger share of the childcare sector, with 70% of the sector currently privately run.View image in fullscreenChildcare is likely become a key election battleground, with Labor, the Coalition, One Nation and the Greens all clashing over how to best provide it.Photograph: Joel Carrett/AAP“Outer suburbs and regions where there are growing families, but not enough childcare places, we want to build more quality, not-for-profit early learning in those places that need it the most, and it is part of our journey towards universal early education,” the childcare minister, Jess Walsh, told Guardian Australia.That shift is starting to happen. In August, the for-profit provider Edge Early Learning went into administration, while competitor G8 has closed dozens of under-enrolled and underperforming centres. This week, Goodstart Early Learning, a not-for-profit provider and one of the recipients of the building early education fund, signed an agreement to investigate the potential take over of up to 31 of Edge Early Learning’s 64 centres.Goodstart’s head of advocacy, John Cherry, says there is “certainly an opportunity there for the not-for-profit sector to expand, but at the moment, not-for-profit providers around the country are running on very thin margins and very challenged by operational conditions”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNot-for-profit childcare providers are not necessarily cheaper for parents – comparison website childcare estimator says fees are about 8% cheaper at some not-for-profits – but they consistently have higher quality and safety ratings.Changing the subsidyAny reform would also have to tackle the childcare subsidy.A family with one child and a household income of up to $88,520 now receives a government subsidy covering 90% of childcare fees. That subsidy tapers off at a rate of 1% per additional $5,000 of income, running down to nothing when the household income reaches $538,520.Labor has consistently raised these subsidies since it came to power in 2022 and says a family with a household income of $168,000, with one child in care for 30 hours a week, is $7,440 a year better off than they would be without the higher subsidies. But the fees themselves have been rising quickly, jumping 7.3% in the 12 months to August – more than twice the inflation rate.The childcare subsidy was projected to cost the budget about $16.2bn last financial year and is slated to rise to $18.4bn by 2028-29.The government already has a blueprint for universal childcare sitting on its desk. In June 2024, the productivity commission looked at three options: the recommended option was free childcare for families with a household income under $90,000, then progressively dropping the subsidy down from 100% towards zero with every $5,000 increase in household income, tapering off at $580,000. For a household income of $168,000, mentioned above, that would be an 85% subsidy.The Productivity Commission also modelled a flat $10 a day or 90% subsidy option for all families but said the cost to the budget would be much higher and the benefit would disproportionately go to wealthier households.Parents have to wait until their children turn three to get further relief, when additional subsidies offered by state governments for preschool kick in. But preschools run on school terms and typically offer 15 hours a week, leaving considerable gaps for parents working full-time.The fees now faced by parents are comparable to private school fees, says Eshanee Collins, a Sydney-based mortgage broker. She says returning to work was part of her identity after having children but the cost of care made it a tough decision.“I work full-time, and in all honesty, our household would probably be better off if I didn’t work and [did] not pay that [childcare] money,” she says.Childcare is likely to become a key election battleground, with the Coalition looking at both the design of the childcare subsidy and paid parental leave settings, while One Nation has promoted income splitting and other policies that incentivise one parent staying home.The Greens, meanwhile, have commissioned parliamentary budget office modelling on the cost of providing 50 hours a week of free childcare, which could cost $127bn over a decade.Whichever way it’s sliced, childcare is expensive to run and public buy-in is essential. Labor is running out of time to decide what model of universal care it wants to pursue – and how to get voters on board.Explore more on these topicsChildcare AustraliaAustralian politicsAnthony AlbaneseLabor partyCost-of-living crisisAustralian economyWelfareanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Falling international student numbers create ‘massive problems’ for Australian universities, expert warns | Australian universities | The Guardian
description: Immigration debate and visa uncertainty are putting students off and increasing pressure on budgets
Author: Krishani Dhanji
Headline: Immigration debate and visa uncertainty are putting students off and increasing pressure on budgets
Content: On average Australian universities are filling just two-thirds of their allocated international student places.Photograph: Asanka Ratnayake/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOn average Australian universities are filling just two-thirds of their allocated international student places.Photograph: Asanka Ratnayake/Getty ImagesAustralian universitiesFalling international student numbers create ‘massive problems’ for Australian universities, expert warnsImmigration debate and visa uncertainty are putting students off and increasing pressure on budgetsGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastKrishani DhanjiSat 10 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 18.40 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUniversity leaders warn they’re struggling to fill international student places due to visa uncertainty and heated political debate on immigration, with regional areas hit the hardest amid concern that financial deficits could affect domestic students.The latest numbers from the Department of Education in October show on average universities are filling just two-thirds of their allocated places, and just five public universities have reached more than 80% capacity, all in capital cities.Mike Ferguson, pro vice-chancellor of international students at Charles Sturt University, which has campuses across regional New South Wales, said his institution has filled just 40% of its cap this year.Labor targets ‘visa hopping’ international students in crackdown on ‘permanently temporary’ migrationRead more“At the moment, we’re around 35% down on where we were last year, and we had expected to grow from last year,” Ferguson said. “Currently we only have 20% of the international student volume we had prior to the pandemic.”Charles Sturt has estimated the gap between international student recruitments pre-Covid and now is costing $35m, and the university has announced job cuts and restructuring in response.Ferguson attributed the fall to government policy, including hiking visa applications to $2,500, high refusal rates, and growing uncertainty from announcements by the Coalition and One Nation targeting international students.He said regional universities primarily recruited students from south Asian countries, which were experiencing higher visa refusal rates of about 53%.“It’s not only resulting in us losing what we believe to be largely genuine students … but it’s also creating a large deterrent from new students to come in and apply, knowing they’re having to pay world record visa fees with only a one in two chance of actually getting a visa,” Ferguson said.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailBut he said the university did support Labor’s decision to crack down on onshore student transfers and visa hopping to improve integrity in the system.Prof Andrew Norton, an expert in higher education, said the declining numbers were affecting all public universities because they cross-subsidise their teaching and research with international student fees.“It creates massive problems because international students are basically the only profitable aspect of university operations,” he said.Duncan Bentley, vice-chancellor of Federation University in regional Victoria, said he too supported those measures but that his university was also facing significant pressures with far fewer international students enrolling this year.The university has pushed the government for a special regional skills student visa that would prioritise international students wanting to do courses in critical areas such as allied health or teaching.“We endorse, and have been asking for a long time for, the 12-month ban on course hopping, apart from exceptional and genuine circumstances,” Bentley said.“The criteria for this regional visa would be any overseas student who wants to come and study in a regional university can have access to a special visa … the course should be on a regional skills shortage list, based on the premise that domestic regional graduates can’t meet the demand.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWestern Sydney University vice-chancellor, George Williams, said his university had also experienced significant declines in overseas students and warned the financial deficits could have an impact on domestic students.“It has an enormous impact on our budget and it means universities across the sector are asking where they can save money, where they can pull back,” Williams said.“In our case, international students heavily subsidise domestic students, and it puts real pressure on the services we can offer to domestic students.”Williams also said international students were being deterred by the heated political debate, “which would lead people to wonder whether they would be welcome in Australia”.Adelaide University told the ABC in September it had only reached 60% of its international student capacity, after its merger with the University of South Australia, creating a potential $90m revenue shortfall.The government’s 2026 planning level for international students was set at 295,000, and so far it’s tracking towards 250,000, which is just above the Coalition’s proposed level of 240,000.Labor will also reduce the number of international students eligible to bring family to Australia while they study, while the Coalition has promised to abolish temporary graduate visas.Phil Honeywood, chief executive of the International Education Association of Australia, said diminishing international student numbers in regional areas could also lead to critical skills shortages.“The high non-refundable visa cost makes the system more like a lottery ticket,” Honeywood said.“There’s not enough nurses, childcare workers, aged care workers or engineers in regional communities … so basically if you have diminishing numbers of international students in these regional areas and they’re not able to stay past their degrees, that creates a cascading skill shortage.”Explore more on these topicsAustralian universitiesAustralian educationAustralian politicsAustralian immigration and asylumnewsShareReuse this content

title: Trump says Ukraine needs a new leader after diesel deal with Russia | Volodymyr Zelenskyy | The Guardian
description: US president suggests Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has not done enough to end war
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: US president suggests Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has not done enough to end war
Content: Rescuers evacuate a wounded woman from under the debris of an apartment building hit by a Russian airstrike in Zaporizhzhia.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenRescuers evacuate a wounded woman from under the debris of an apartment building hit by a Russian airstrike in Zaporizhzhia.Photograph: ReutersVolodymyr ZelenskyyTrump says Ukraine needs a new leader after diesel deal with RussiaUS president suggests Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has not done enough to end warOliver HolmesSat 10 Oct 2026 16.42 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 10.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump has said Ukraine needs “a new leader”, a day after making a deal withVladimir Putinto buy large quantities of Russian diesel.The US president suggestedVolodymyr Zelenskyyhas not done enough to end the war with Russia and blamed him for high diesel prices in the US.“I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal because he could have made many deals and for some reason he never does,” Trump said.Trump made the comments as Russia launched deadly strikes on civilians inUkraine, which Zelenskyy said were a “thanks” to Trump for the diesel deal.The Ukrainian president has expressed outrage at theagreement announced by Trumpon Friday, which the US president said was needed to reduce diesel prices, and comes ahead of November’s midterm elections in which fuel costs are a key voter issue.The deal, which appeared to blindside Kyiv as it was announced while Ukrainian negotiators were in Miami for peace talks, was described by Zelenskyy as a “gift” to Russia’s president.He said Russia would use the money it raised from the fuel sales to invest in its war and that “any easing of sanctions” would play into Russia’s hands, “allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer”.That prediction was realised hours later, when Ukrainian officials announced that a barrage of Russian strikes on the country’s south-east early on Saturday had killed 20 people, including three children.View image in fullscreenRescuers working at the site of an apartment building damaged by a Russian strike in Zaporizhzhia.Photograph: Reuters“Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia,” Zelenskyy saidon social mediaon Saturday.“Last night confirmed once again that in Russia, they take any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed,” he said.There were also “large-scale power outages” in the capital, Kyiv, the country’s largest private energy provider said.Map of Russian-controlled territory in UkraineAndy Burnham reiterated his “complete solidarity” in a call with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and the leaders agreed to meet in person in the coming days to continue talks.The prime minister said he recognised the past day had been “difficult for Ukraine” and the two talked about the importance of keeping up pressure on Russia, No 10 said.In stark contrast to Zelenskyy’s open frustration with Trump, a Kremlin readout of Friday’s call between the US president and Putin was glowing, with the Russian ⁠news agency Interfax ⁠quoting ​an aide as saying it was “very substantive and friendly”.“Neither wanted to be the first to hang up,” the Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov said of the two leaders. “They hung up simultaneously, literally at the same time.”​Zelenskyy has previouslysaidPutin is playing games with Trump.The diesel deal disrupts four years of western financial pressure on Moscow and leaves Kyiv’s allies inEuropeand Nato scrambling to adapt their sanctions plan. The EU’s top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the diesel deal “provides Moscow with more revenues to wage war”.“This is not the time to ease pressure on Russia, and Europe won’t,” shesaidon Saturday. “On Monday, EU foreign ministers intend to approve the biggest set of sanctions listings targeting Russia’s war machine since the start of the war.” She was referring to plans to formally add 1,600 new individuals and entities to the EU’s sanctions blacklist.View image in fullscreenKaja Kallas with Volodymyr Zelenskyy at a summit in Copenhagen last year.Photograph: Piroschka Van De Wouw/ReutersMajor European governments have attempted to balance their diplomatic and trade relationships with a mercurial Trump and their support for Ukraine.The more Putin escalates his attacks on Europe, the more Europe should support Ukraine | Timothy Garton AshRead moreThe German government spokesperson Stefan Kornelius said Berlin “remains committed to the sanctions imposed on Russia and is working with its European partners on further sanctions”, adding that support for Ukraine “remains unwavering”.Ulf Kristersson, the Swedish prime minister, expressed “regret” at the US agreement, saying energy revenues were “a vital source of funding Russia’s war of aggression”.Zelenskyy said on Saturday that Russia “must feel its losses” and has promised to respond. In the Russian-occupied ‌Luhansk ‌region, Ukrainian attacks in the past 24 hours had killed four ⁠civilians and wounded ⁠five, the region’s ‌Russian-installed governor, Leonid Pasechnik, said ​on Saturday.Zelenskyy said that Ukraine was ready to take “de-escalatory steps” in the war but only if Russia did the same.Russia’s fuel production has become a key point of contention between Zelenskyy and Trump, who has attempted to stop Ukraine from bombing Russian refineries, which he says exacerbates a global diesel shortage. The Ukrainian leader has rejected such requests unless Russia stops attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.The Financial Timesreportedthat during the talks in Miami, Trump’s envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner raised the possibility that US intelligence sharing could be cut off if Kyiv did not halt the strikes.Explore more on these topicsVolodymyr ZelenskyyUkraineRussiaTrump administrationDonald TrumpVladimir PutinUS foreign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Dozens injured and buildings damaged as tornadoes hit Sicily  | Tornadoes | The Guardian
description: Marsala on island’s west coast badly affected after powerful storm approached from Mediterranean
Author: Lorenzo Tondo
Headline: Marsala on island’s west coast badly affected after powerful storm approached from Mediterranean
Content: 0:50Powerful tornado in western Sicily leaves trail of devastation – videoTornadoesDozens injured and buildings damaged as tornadoes hit SicilyMarsala on island’s west coast badly affected after powerful storm approached from MediterraneanLorenzo Tondoin PalermoSat 10 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 06.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo tornadoes have struck the coastal town of Marsala in western Sicily, injuring dozens of people, damaging buildings including a school, and overturning cars.A series of videos began to circulate on Friday morning showing two waterspouts approaching the Sicilian town from the sea as people braced for their arrival.Dozens of people were reported injured, with at least 11 taken to hospital after being struck by flying debris and shattered glass. Among the most seriously injured was a 70-year-old man admitted to Mazara del Vallo hospital in a critical condition with several fractures.A school was also hit by the powerful winds, leaving six children with minor cuts and abrasions. At the time the tornado struck, 273 pupils were inside the building, all of whom were safely evacuated. Drone footage showing the aftermath revealed extensive damage to the school, with windows shattered and desks and chairs overturned.View image in fullscreenExtensive damage to buildings and cars in Marsala after a tornado struck the west coast of Sicily on Friday.Photograph: Antonio Cascio/ReutersIn recent years, people in southernItalyhave been bracing for the arrival of a “medicane” – a rare Mediterranean storm with hurricane-like characteristics, capable of producing winds exceeding 60 miles an hour and waves reaching five metres in height.The weather system developed amid intense heat over north Africa and unusually warm Mediterranean waters. Scientists have warned that rising sea temperatures, driven by the climate emergency, can provide additional energy for powerful storms in the region.According to experts, record temperatures in the Mediterranean contributed to the freak storm that sank the Bayesian, a super yacht off the coast of Sicily, in August 2024, killing seven people including the tech tycoon Mike Lynch and his teenage daughter.Explore more on these topicsTornadoesItalyExtreme weatherNatural disastersClimate crisisEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Zelenskyy furious as Trump announces deal to buy Russian diesel | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: US president says agreement needed to lower fuel prices, but move likely to create fresh crisis with Ukraine and Nato allies
Author: Robert Tait
Headline: US president says agreement needed to lower fuel prices, but move likely to create fresh crisis with Ukraine and Nato allies
Content: Donald Trump said lower fuel prices for Americans was his ‘greatest priority’.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDonald Trump said lower fuel prices for Americans was his ‘greatest priority’.Photograph: Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty ImagesDonald TrumpZelenskyy furious as Trump announces deal to buy Russian dieselUS president says agreement needed to lower fuel prices, but move likely to create fresh crisis with Ukraine and Nato alliesRobert Taitin Washington, andOliver HolmesSat 10 Oct 2026 06.09 EDTFirst published on Fri 9 Oct 2026 19.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trump is on a fresh collision course withVolodymyr Zelenskyyand European allies after his stunning agreement to buy Russian diesel upended years of US and western pressure on the Kremlin to end its war against Ukraine.Zelenskyy reacted furiously to Trump’s announcement of the deal with Vladimir Putin on Friday,calling it“absolutely terrible” and “not fair and not honest”.The Ukrainian president said “back room deals” with the Russian leader would give Putin more chances on the battlefield. On Saturday morning, Ukrainian officials reported that a Russian attack had killed 12 people in the south-east, including three children, and Moscow claimed its troops were advancing in the east.View image in fullscreenRescuers free people trapped under rubble at the site of a Russian attack on a residential area in Zaporizhzhia.Photograph: Daryna Naumova/EPAIn a move likely to create a fresh crisis with Washington’sNatoallies, Trump announced the deal with Putin on his Truth Social network, saying it was essential to reduce fuel prices in the US, which have soared as a result of his decision to go to war against Iran.“I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with PresidentVladimir Putin, of Russia,” he said, to deliver millions of tonnes of diesel fuel over the next few months.He added: “Diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my greatest priority.”Fuel prices have soared since Iran closed the strait of Hormuz, a strategically sensitive choke point that was the passageway for 20% of global oil supplies before the war. While costs have risen for motorists – a gallon of regular fuel in the US is about $4.20 (£3.17) – it is the price of diesel, which last month hit a record high of $6.52, that has inflicted the most damage on Trump and the Republicans as November’s midterm elections approach.Diesel is the main supply chain fuel, and a rise in its costs feeds into consumer prices and also hurts US farmers, who need it to operate machinery.View image in fullscreenA person filling up at a gas station in Buda, Texas.Photograph: Brandon Bell/Getty ImagesDemocrats said the agreement undercut a lawTrump signed last monthallowing for a broad range of sanctions on Russian banks, officials and tankers, as well as directing him to impose steep tariffs on the top five importers of oil or natural gas from Russia. The law gave Trump wide discretion to make exceptions to its provisions.“This is what failure looks like. Failure for President Trump to live up to his promises to lower costs for Americans. Failure to protect America from its adversaries,” said a statement from the Senate Democratic leader, Chuck Schumer, Senator Jeanne Shaheen, who is the top Democrat on the foreign relations committee, and Senator Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the banking committee.Some Republicans also criticised the agreement.“Propping up Putin’s war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities,” congressman Don Bacon, a Nebraska Republican,wrote on X. “The President’s policies towards Russia and Ukraine are failures. We need moral clarity not moral ambiguity.”Zelenskyytold Axiosthat it “looks like a happy birthday present for Putin. It looks absolutely terrible.” The Russian leader turned 74 this week.View image in fullscreenVolodymyr Zelenskyy speaking with Donald Trump at the UN general assembly in September.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APIn a long social media post, Zelenskyy, who has had an uneasy relationship with Trump,saidthe deal amounted to “an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged”. Russia was likely to repay it with “further terror and perfidy”.“It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said.Referring on Saturday to the attack on the south-eastern city of Zaporizhzhia that killed 12 people, Zelenskyy wrote on X: “Today, Russia expressed its thanks for the lifting of sanctions on diesel exports by dropping five glide bombs on residential buildings in Zaporizhzhia.“Last night confirmed once again that in Russia, they take any easing of pressure to mean they can keep fighting, to mean they can keep dropping bombs on cities. Different signals are needed.”View image in fullscreenPolice officers standing next to the covered bodies of people killed by a Russian strike on a five-storey residential building in Zaporizhzhia.Photograph: Ukraine national police/AFP/Getty Images​Separately, Russian media cited the defence ⁠ministry ⁠​as saying its forces ⁠had ​captured ‌the ‌settlements of Lukashove ‌and Lobanivka in Ukraine’s​ eastern ‌Kharkiv region.​Zelenskyy previouslysaidPutin had been playing games with Trump, and on Saturday, a Kremlin spokesperson said the Russian leader had responded with “understanding” to Trump’s proposals to de-escalate the conflict.Trump announced the diesel deal as his envoys, Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner, met Ukrainian and European officials in Miami to discuss proposals to end the war.Zelenskyy, in a separate statement released by Ukraine’s embassy in Washington on Friday, said the Ukrainian negotiators had been “used as a smokescreen for the deal”, which he called “a weak decision by strong partners”.“That is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” he said.Trump recently criticized Ukraine for attacking Russian diesel refineries, calling on Zelenskyy to choose alternative targets. The Ukrainian leader rejected the request unless Russia stopped attacking Ukraine’s energy infrastructure.Tensions have been rising between Russia and European Nato members amid speculation that Moscow might be preparing military action intended to test the alliance’s resolve.The latest development is likely to worsen Zelenskyy’s relationship with theTrump administration. He was infamously ambushed by Trump and the vice-president, JD Vance, last year in an explosive White House encounter when the president told him: “You don’t have the cards.”But Trump has since reportedly grown disenchanted with Putin, expressing disappointment at his failure to reach a peace deal.Trump’s willingness to reach a fuel agreement with Putin comes despite Russia’s support for Iran in its war with the US. Russia is believed to have given Iran satellite intelligence and overhead surveillance data detailing the locations of US forces, ships, aircraft and military bases. It has also provided drone components and ammunition.Explore more on these topicsDonald TrumpVolodymyr ZelenskyyRussiaUS politicsEuropeNatoUkrainenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We’re not asking for luxury’: school protesters in Paris suburb feel abandoned by French state | France | The Guardian
description: Students say they are desperate to get back to class but conditions are so bad that the protests must continue
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Students say they are desperate to get back to class but conditions are so bad that the protests must continue
Content: A sign reading ‘Education in peril – angry youth’ on the gates of the Lycée Blaise-Cendrars in Sevran.Photograph: Ed Alcock/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA sign reading ‘Education in peril – angry youth’ on the gates of the Lycée Blaise-Cendrars in Sevran.Photograph: Ed Alcock/The GuardianFrance‘We’re not asking for luxury’: school protesters in Paris suburb feel abandoned by French stateStudents say they are desperate to get back to class but conditions are so bad that the protests must continueAngelique Chrisafisin SevranSat 10 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 05.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn a normal school day, Mohammed, 17, wakes at 6am, cares for his younger siblings to help his single mother who works as a security guard, then takes two crowded buses and a local train to get to his high school in Sevran, a low-incomebanlieuetown in the suburbs north-east of Paris.“There aren’t enough chairs or desks to go round, so some students have to stand up,” Mohammed said. “Classes can be so packed you can’t interact with the teacher. In this year’s heatwaves, it felt like 40 degrees in overcrowded classrooms with no shade or curtains. It was so hot my brain couldn’t function.”The 17-year-old in his last year of high school wants to study management and digital communication at a Paris university. But he said conditions were so poor, he felt all odds were stacked against him and his classmates.“Some of us have to go months without teachers when absent staff aren’t replaced,” he said. “One class had no French teacher for several months just before the French baccalaureate, so they couldn’t even study all the set texts for their exam. Recently we needed a teacher for a subject taught through English, but when that teacher arrived they didn’t speak English.”Thebiggest youth protest movement in the country in decadesbrought hundreds of thousands on to the streets across France this week demonstrating againstinequality in the French education system, decrepit schools, a lack of teachers and large class sizes. Hundreds of schools were blockaded, thousands of teenagers were arrested, and rights groups warned ofalleged police brutality, with one child losing the use of eye and another losing a hand.View image in fullscreenGraffiti on a wall at the Lycée Blaise-Cendrars.Photograph: Ed Alcock/The GuardianMohammed and his classmates, often supported by their parents and teachers, have been at the frontline, barricading their school, the Lycée Blaise-Cendrars, which is in one of mainland France’s poorestdépartements, Seine-Saint-Denis. They have voted to continue their protests next week, taking theirgrievancesto the local mayor, elected officials and education representatives. Many local politicians have supported their demands. Even the French prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, conceded that teenagers had “legitimate” concerns.Photos on the Sevran students’ phones showed broken classroom chairs, holes in walls, holes in ceilings, mould, buckets to catch leaks, faulty lights. They said basic needs weren’t met, with some toilets broken, others with no doors and often no toilet paper or soap. Video projectors and science equipment were lacking.View image in fullscreenA student shows an example of conditions in the school on their phone.Photograph: Ed Alcock/The Guardian“We’re not asking for luxury, just the basics to learn in decent conditions,” Mohammed said. “And yet police on horseback charged us when we were gathered to protest outside our school, firing teargas at us and making arrests. It’s so dangerous to be charged by a horse, it could kill you. I just ran, I was trying to help my classmates.”The high schools of Seine-Saint-Denis, a suburban area nudging against northern Paris, have been a driving force in the protests. The area has the youngest population in mainlandFrance, one of the highest birthrates and the among the lowest average income. Local high schools have a high turnover of young teachers.Despite co-hosting the2024 Paris Olympics, and numerous government plans to try to combat long-running problems of inequality and poverty, the area north-east of Paris is still disadvantaged compared with the capital.In 2005, Seine-Saint-Denis was the starting point for weeks of unrest on housing estates across France, leading to a state of national emergency being declared, after thedeath of two young boyshiding from police in an electricity substation. This week’s protests have shown that inequality and discrimination has not been addressed in the Paris suburbs and the mistrust between young people and police persists.Sevran’s Lycée Blaise-Cendrars, with more than 1,000 pupils, has been at the heart of protests about school conditions before. In 2024, students and teachers made a viral video about the state of classrooms, toilets and equipment. The local Île de France region said it had put in place a major refurbishment project for high school buildings. But the teenagers said key issues had not been addressed.View image in fullscreenLycée Blaise-Cendrars has been at the heart of protests about school conditions before.Photograph: Ed Alcock/The Guardian“We’re starting at an unfair advantage because our parents aren’t as rich as others, they can’t buy us books, they can’t take us to films,” said Ilian, 17, whose family has Moroccan roots and whose father is a traffic warden. “We’re missing school during these protests, we risk falling behind in an exam year, we’re desperate to get back into class to study, but the conditions we’re facing are so bad we can’t stop until the government promises action.”The education ministry this week promised 3,000 teachers to urgently fill gaps, but teachers’ unions expressed doubts and said longer-term plans and more funding was needed, even if the government argues there is little spare cash.Children’s mental health is also an issue in Seine-Saint-Denis. Ilian has been waiting to see a child psychiatrist for months. At the high school, there was no school nurse and a lack of support staff for children with disabilities, he said.“The police look down on us as if we’re animals”, Ilian said. “They talk to us with such cruelty.” He told local politicians that some teenagers alleged police had made racial insults against them during protests.Stéphane Troussel, the Socialist head of the Seine-Saint-Denisdépartementcouncil who met the pupils this week, said: “It’s intolerable that policing is causing part of the difficulties.” He called for the police to stop using a type of rubber-bullet launcher, after they suspended use of stun grenades following injuries. The French interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, has defended policing tactics.View image in fullscreenStéphane Blanchet, the local mayor, meets students at the town hall.Photograph: Ed Alcock/The GuardianStéphane Blanchet, the mayor of Sevran, said he supported the school protesters’ demands. He said many in his town of 52,000 people, with a higher than average poverty rate, felt “relegated” and forgotten by the state.Sarah, 17, who wanted to study at an elite Paris engineering faculty, and whose warehouse worker father was proud she was protesting and meeting the mayor, said teenagers in thebanlieue“really feel abandoned”.She said: “We’ve been surprised and so appreciative of other teenagers in better-off places in Francemarching in the streets to support usthis week. We know we’re disadvantaged and that we have to work 10 times as hard as others to escape discrimination against our postcode. But we can’t learn properly in these conditions when we’re not even guaranteed a chair to sit on in school.”Students’ names have been changedExplore more on these topicsFranceEuropefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Trump fumes over Nobel peace prize snub and criticizes Norway | Donald Trump | The Guardian
description: President complains about not winning prize in year he started war with Iran and says: ‘We will not forget, Norway’
Author: Robert Mackey
Headline: President complains about not winning prize in year he started war with Iran and says: ‘We will not forget, Norway’
Content: Trump at a campaign rally in Syracuse, New York, on Friday.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APView image in fullscreenTrump at a campaign rally in Syracuse, New York, on Friday.Photograph: Julia Demaree Nikhinson/APDonald TrumpTrump fumes over Nobel peace prize snub and criticizes NorwayPresident complains about not winning prize in year he started war with Iran and says: ‘We will not forget, Norway’Robert MackeyFri 9 Oct 2026 21.57 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 18.57 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDonald Trumpcomplained on Friday about not winning theNobel peace prizefor 2026, a year in which he started awar with Iran.At what was supposed to be a rally for other Republican candidates in Syracuse, New York, the US president devoted a long portion of his speech to airing his grievances with the Nobel committee.“The United States of America, represented by me as your president, should have received theNobel peace prize, but didn’t. And this is an indelible stain on the country of Norway, and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” Trump said.“The Nobel peace prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilization,” Trump went on. “We will not forget,Norway, that you didn’t give this prize.”ICJ judge Navi Pillay wins Nobel peace prize for promoting international lawRead moreTrump also recited a list of wars he claims to have settled, some of which were not wars and some that are still not settled, before adding: “I’m about to settle or win two more: Iran and Russia-Ukraine.”Trump said he would be ending both wars “quickly”.“I will tell you what,” he added, darkly. “Iran will be very quick one way or the other: that they give us everything or they don’t exist any longer.”“Additionally, I stopped Iran from having a nuclear weapon and blowing up the entire Middle East and ultimately far beyond the Middle East, including Europe, perhaps the US and I saved more lives than anyone in history,” Trump claimed, despite the fact that US intelligence agenciesreported to Congress in 2025that Iran had actually suspended its pursuit of nuclear weapons in 2003.“Despite all of this and all of these unbelievable accomplishments, the Nobel prize was given out today to a liberal person who works at the United Nations, who nobody has ever heard of,” Trump said ofNavi Pillay, the South African former UN human rights chief who chaired the UN commissionthat concluded Israel was guilty of genocidein Gaza.In Pillay’s first public comments after learning of the award,she jokedto colleagues at a conference of human rights lawyers in Nuremberg, Germany, on Friday: “If you clap a little bit more, I may share this prize with Trump.” She then burst out laughing.1:11Nobel peace prize winner Navi Pillay jokes about sharing award with Donald Trump – videoExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpNorwayNobel peace prizeUS politicsTrump administrationEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Twelve killed and hundreds injured in Houthi attack at Riyadh airport | Saudi Arabia | The Guardian
description: Donald Trump evaluating whether US should join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Yemeni rebels
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Donald Trump evaluating whether US should join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Yemeni rebels
Content: Thick black smoke and flames rising from a fire at King Khalid International airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, 9 October 2026.Photograph: UGC via APView image in fullscreenThick black smoke and flames rising from a fire at King Khalid International airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, 9 October 2026.Photograph: UGC via APSaudi ArabiaTwelve killed and hundreds injured in Houthi attack at Riyadh airportDonald Trump evaluating whether US should join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Yemeni rebelsPatrick WintourDiplomatic editor and agenciesSat 10 Oct 2026 19.37 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 11.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYemen’s Houthis have launched a missile attack on Riyadh’s international airport inSaudi Arabia, killing at least 12 people and leaving hundreds wounded, the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority has said.Operations at King Khalid international airport in Riyadh were suspended as ambulances rushed to the airport. More than 300 people were reported injured in the deadliest attack in any Gulf Arab country since the start of the Iran war.Donald Trump said he was evaluating whether the US should join Saudi strikes against the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighbouringYemen.“We may. We’re going to look at it,” Trump said. “We just found out about the recent attack. So we’ll make a decision. We move very quickly.”The US secretary of ⁠state, Marco ⁠Rubio, called the attacks “​reprehensible” and said “they must ​stop ‌now”.A Saudi government statement said the dead included four Saudi citizens, as well as two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a US citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese.One witness at the Riyadh airport reported hearing an explosion while waiting to board a flight, and another said they saw a strike that left people wounded.“I was on gate 403,” at the domestic terminal, the witness told the Agence France-Presse news agency. “I saw [gate] 401 hit, I saw injured [people] in front of my eyes. Everyone was running.”The relative of one injured person said they had been wounded in the shoulders and arms by shattered glass and taken to hospital.A missile struck an airport complex housing terminals 3 and 4 for domestic flights, a regional official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorised to speak to the media.Yemen civil war: what sparked latest escalation and who is involved?Read moreA projectile also fell near the King Fahd international airport in Dammam, according to the Saudi-led coalition fighting theHouthis. The Dammam airport has become an important alternative to Riyadh amid the recent spate of attacks.Saturday’s incident comes amid an escalation of missile strikes by Yemen’s Iran-aligned Houthis ⁠on the kingdom. The airport has already been attacked twice this ​week, leaving four people dead and ‌others wounded, and ‌badly damaging an aircraft.The Houthis have repeatedly attacked Saudi airports, oil facilities and tankers after a truce in their long-running war with Yemen’s Riyadh-backed government unravelled in July.The attack came as forces allied to the UN-recognised government in Yemen claim to have mounted a successful offensive to retake the Bab al-Mandab strait from Houthi rebels, but accounts vary as to whether the push has been repelled.View image in fullscreenFighters from the Southern Giants Brigades clash with Houthis near the Bab al-Mandab strait in Taiz province, 6 October.Photograph: Yemen Giants Brigades Media Centre/AFP/Getty ImagesA Houthi spokesperson said forces from the Saudi-backed government based in Aden “were targeted with a large number of ballistic missiles, artillery support and heavy weapons, resulting in the destruction of more than 22 armoured vehicles and the killing and wounding of dozens, including a number of commanders.“More than 30 ambulances arrived in Aden to transport the dead and wounded from the Saudi enemy’s mobilisations.”By contrast, the Saudi ambassador to Yemen, Mohammed al-Jaber, said: “Blessed Friday and victory for every Yemeni and Arab. Bab al-Mandab has been cleared of the remnants of the Houthi terrorist militia.”View image in fullscreenThe Southern Giants, linked to the STC, are the chief pro-government force fighting around the Bab al-Mandab strait.Photograph: Yemen Giants Brigades Media Centre/AFP/Getty ImagesThe exposed 5 sq mile (13 sq km) Perim Island straddles the strait, acting as a lookout point for all traffic from the Red Sea into the Gulf of Aden and towards the Indian Ocean. Aidarous al-Zubaidi, the president of the Southern Transitional Council (STC), one of the main political forces in the south of Yemen, claimed the island and coastal area had been recaptured from Houthi hands.An official military spokesperson for the UN-recognised government forces qualified the claim, saying only half the area had been recaptured so far. Waddah al-Dabish said newly established Houthi defensive lines had been broken on the land next to the strait, leading to the death of thousands of Houthi fighters.It is thought that as many as 500 Houthi fighters are stationed on the island, and Saudi Arabia is desperate to be able to report that the strait has been reclaimed to show thatthe land counteroffensive it launchedat the beginning of the week is advancing.View image in fullscreenSouthern Giants fighters fire at Houthis near the Bab al-Mandab strait in Taiz province, 6 October.Photograph: Yemen Giants Brigades Media Centre/AFP/Getty ImagesThe report came as the United Nations’ special envoy to Yemen, Hans Grundberg, admitted to the UN security council in New York that Yemen – one of the poorest countries in the world – had lapsed back into full-scale war and said the first victims would be women and children.The Houthis seized control of the strait two weeks ago and said no Saudi-linked commercial traffic would be permitted to go through the narrow waterway. The Houthis are waging a war to remove Saudi influence from Yemen, and have been mounting missile attacks on Riyadh in support of this objective.There have been previous prematurereports of military breakthroughsby the Saudi-backed Yemeni government since it launched its counteroffensive at the start of the week, but the recapture of the land by the strait and Perim Island (also known as Mayyun Island) is a military prize western governments desperately need.Explore more on these topicsSaudi ArabiaYemenHouthisUnited NationsMiddle East and north AfricaAir transportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Thousands gather in London to express support for Palestinians after three years of ‘genocide’ | Israel-Gaza war | The Guardian
description: Twenty arrested in first march since Ed Miliband declared UK’s position was that Israel’s occupation of West Bank was unlawful
Author: Sammy Gecsoyler
Headline: Twenty arrested in first march since Ed Miliband declared UK’s position was that Israel’s occupation of West Bank was unlawful
Content: Pro-Palestinian march in LondonIsrael-Gaza warThousands gather in London to express support for Palestinians after three years of ‘genocide’Twenty arrested in first march since Ed Miliband declared UK’s position was that Israel’s occupation of West Bank was unlawfulSammy GecsoylerSat 10 Oct 2026 12.52 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThousands of people have gathered in central London to express their support for Palestinians after three years of “genocide” carried out against them byIsrael.The demonstrators, many wearing keffiyehs and holding Palestine flags, gathered on the Embankment at midday on Saturday. Some carried placards reading “End the genocide” and “Free Palestine” as they marched towards parliament. A bride and groomappearedto be among those in attendance and a two-minute silence was held to reflect on the lives lost in Gaza.The Metropolitan police said 20 arrests had been made, including for criminal damage after demonstrators climbed on to the Battle of Britain memorial, havingPalestineAction placards, making a Nazi salute and assaulting police as officers made arrests.Protesters were calling for the UK government to stop supplying arms to Israel, which various bodies – including the UN, Amnesty International, B’Tselem and Physicians for Human Rights, the latter two of which are Israeli-based – have said is committing genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.View image in fullscreenProtesters at the National March For Palestine.Photograph: Guy Smallman/Getty ImagesA ceasefire was declared a year ago but Israeli airstrikes have continued in Gaza. In the last year, the overall death tollhas risenby a further 1,400 people. Settlers have also ramped up their attacks against Palestinians in the West Bank. According to UN figures, 230 Palestinians were killed in the West Bank by Israeli forces and settlers in 2025.Husam Zomlot, the Palestinian ambassador to the UK, shared a video from the march on social media. “Three years on, Israel’s atrocities in Gaza and the West Bank continue, and so does the solidarity of the British people. Louder, bigger and not going anywhere. Thank you all,” he said. By Saturday afternoon, organiserssaid250,000 people were at the march.‘Neither war nor peace’: Palestinians in Gaza on existing amid disease, despair and ruinsRead moreThe Met have imposed conditions on the event – which is organised by the Palestine Coalition, which has organised more than 30 mass demonstrations since October 2023, with a counter-protest by Stop The Hate – to “minimise the risk of serious disruption to communities”.The Met posted on X saying: “The front of the procession has now entered Whitehall where a rally will take place.“Several arrests have been made so far including a woman and a man with placards declaring support for proscribed organisation Palestine Action.“We have also arrested a number of protesters on suspicion of criminal damage after they climbed on to the Battle of Britain memorial on Victoria Embankment.”The national march is the first held since the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, announced sweeping sanctions on trade with Israeli settlements and declared the UK government would take the official position that Israel’s occupation of theWest Bankwas unlawful in its entirety. He also told the Commons that settler terrorists supported by Benjamin Netanyahu’s government are committing ethnic cleansing in the West Bank.View image in fullscreenA pile of placards at the end of the pro-Palestinian protest march through London to mark the third anniversary of the war in Gaza.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersAt Labour party conference last month,Miliband appeared to reference the marches, which at their peak regularly numbered hundreds and thousands of people, telling the audience in Liverpool: “I want to say to the millions of people in this country and indeed elsewhere who have been moved and outraged by the plight of the Palestinian people: we hear you, you were right.”Deputy assistant commissioner Carl Galvin said: “We know Saturday’s event, so close to the third anniversary of the terror attack on Israel, has the potential to have a greater impact on communities than the previous national marches.”Galvin, who is leading the policing operation this weekend, said the force’s presence on Saturday will be “significant”.“We will also be using powers under the Public Order Act requiring anyone in the protest area wearing face coverings to deliberately conceal their identity to remove them,” Galvin continued.The Met have imposed conditions on the march and require the group to travel via Westminster Bridge, York Road, Waterloo Bridge and The Strand on to Whitehall, with a rally concluding by 6.30pm. The force has said that any speeches and music must conclude by 5.30pm.British consulate in East Jerusalem will stay open as UK mission, says Ed MilibandRead moreA counter-protest by Stop The Hate is also taking place, with about 30 people gathered outside New Scotland Yard, some with flags.The force has also imposed conditions on the demonstration “to minimise the risk of serious disruption”. The demonstrators must remain within a designated area outside the Met’s headquarters, with the assembly concluding at 2.30pm.View image in fullscreenPeople clash with police officers during the pro-Palestine march in London.Photograph: Jordan Pettitt/PALast Saturday, on the third anniversary of the 7 October attacks, when Hamas militants broke across the Israeli border to launch a wave of attacks on kibbutzim, border towns, military bases and music festivals, killing at least 1,209 people, a small pro-Palestine student demonstration in centralLondonwas held.The Met publicly appealed to those behind the demonstration to “exercise [their] right to protest on a different date” and admitted that finding the organisers had been “frankly difficult”. In the end, it went ahead and about 100 people attended. Five people were arrested for breaching conditions imposed on the march.The Palestine Coalition organising the march includes Palestine Solidarity Campaign, Stop the War, CND, the Muslim Association of Britain, Friends of Al Aqsa and the Palestinian Forum in Britain.Explore more on these topicsIsrael-Gaza warLondonProtestFreedom of speechIsraelPalestineGazanewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Cockroach’ leader among thousands detained in Delhi protest crackdown | Delhi | The Guardian
description: Authorities impose strict lockdown in capital to try to stop rally against removal of 130m names from electoral roll
Author: Hannah Ellis-Petersen
Headline: Authorities impose strict lockdown in capital to try to stop rally against removal of 130m names from electoral roll
Content: 1:34Police detain anti-government 'Cockroach' party leader amid Delhi protests – videoDelhi‘Cockroach’ leader among thousands detained in Delhi protest crackdownAuthorities impose strict lockdown in capital to try to stop rally against removal of 130m names from electoral rollHannah Ellis-PetersenandAakash Hassanin DelhiSat 10 Oct 2026 07.17 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 01.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIndian authorities have placed Delhi under a severe lockdown and detained tens of thousands of people, including the leader of the youth-led “Cockroach” movement, in an attempt to stop an anti-government protest.Thousands of people from across India were blocked from attending the demonstration, which had been called by the “Cockroach Janata party” (CJP) to protest against an exercise that has stripped 130m names from India’s electoral roll.TheCockroach movement, as well as opposition parties, civil society and student groups, have alleged that the process of “purifying” India’s voter roll was done toentrench the power of Narendra Modi‘s government, and have called for India’s chief election commissioner, Gyanesh Kumar, who oversaw the exercise, to resign.View image in fullscreenPolice detain and carry a protester away in Delhi.Photograph: Manish Swarup/APDelhi police denied permission for the protest to take place in the centre of the capital, and in the days leading up to Saturday, officials began to barricade roads throughoutDelhi. More than 25,000 police and security personnel were deployed across the city, many pulled from other states.Abhijeet Dipke, the founder and leader of the CJP, accused the government of being scared of the young people who were rising up in protest. “The mass crackdown on protesters and the shutdown of Delhi are not signs of strength but of a leader terrified of his own people,” said Dipke.Millions in India stripped of vote before critical state election, as government seeks to ‘purify’ electoral rollRead moreOn Saturday morning, police boarded Dipke’s plane as it landed at Delhi airport and detained him, alongside several other senior figures in the Cockroach movement. In a video recorded just before police detained him, Dipke said: “If you think you can stop us by threatening us with jail, then you have it wrong. Put us in jail if you want … but we will keep fighting to protect the democracy of this country.”View image in fullscreenA protester being detained by security personnel.Photograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersOthers in the CJP movement were detained across India, with arrests and detentions reported to be in the tens of thousands. One of India’s most popular YouTubers, Dhruv Rathee, who has 33m followers and has become a supporter of the CJP, was among those put under house arrest, while Delhi’s former chief minister Arvind Kejriwal was detained at the protest site.Student groups, who have also been calling for Kumar to resign, had described the march as India’s “second freedom struggle”, akin to Gandhi’s fight for independence. As police began mass detentions on Friday night, Neha Bora, a student leader at the forefront of the protests, said: “History is repeating itself. Just like in 1942, the arrest of leaders could not stop the Quit India movement; this movement will also not stop.” By Saturday afternoon, Bora had been detained.Over its 14 years in power, the Modi government has been rigidly intolerant of dissent. However, few protests have prompted such a draconian nationwide crackdown, signalling the government’s concern that this unrest could present a serious political challenge.In major disruption to travel, all trains arriving into Delhi’s two main stations on Saturday were cancelled for 10 hours and almost 50 metro stations were shut. Delhi’s schools and courtrooms were instructed to go online for the day and hotel owners were told to turn away customers.View image in fullscreenSecurity personnel chase a protester.Photograph: Manish Swarup/APTraffic diversions were in place across Delhi and police checkpoints were set up along the main highways from neighbouring states into the capital, with passengers being stopped and interrogated about their final destination. Delhi police told Uber drivers not to drop people near the protest area and said they were “tracking and stopping” bulk orders on food delivery services to Jantar Mantar.In Mumbai, housing societies sent out mass WhatsApp messages, telling parents to “mind your kids” and make sure they didn’t attempt to travel to join the protest.Around Jantar Mantar, which had previously been Delhi’s designated protest site and where the Cockroach supporters had hoped to gather, most of the main thoroughfares were shuttered and barricaded, surrounded by police and paramilitary officers. Riot-control vehicles and trucks fitted with water cannon stood nearby.View image in fullscreenPolie try to stop a detained protester escaping from a bus.Photograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersBuses were used to transport more than 6,000 people who were detained while attempting to reach Jantar Mantar. Paravin Singhal, a 75-year-old lawyer, said he had left home at 5am and shown his court identity card at checkpoints along the way, only to be stopped about 200 metres from Jantar Mantar.Singhal said he had come to stand with young people fighting to save the country from a “lawless regime playing with the constitution”. He accused Modi’s government and the election commission of using the revision of electoral rolls to influence future votes.After voting in elections for 50 years, he said, he had recently been told that his name had been removed from the rolls. “How can this happen to someone who has been voting for 50 years? What is even more disturbing is that the government is taking away our most fundamental right – the right to vote.”Singhal said he would stay put in the hope that more protesters would arrive. “The government is afraid because young people in this country are awake. They know their rights and are fighting for them. That is why the government is behaving like a dictatorship.”View image in fullscreenPolice patrol the streets of Delhi.Photograph: Adnan Abidi/ReutersAmina Minnath, an undergraduate student at Delhi University, had also travelled to the area with friends. They had left before sunrise and navigated the checkpoints. The police barricading of Delhi, she said, had only strengthened her determination to protest.“These restrictions show that the government does not care about people’s rights,” she said. “This will not stop us. We may be detained, but we will come back in greater numbers. This will not end in a single day.”The revision of electoral rolls, in a process known as “special intensive revision (SIR), began last year and attracted criticism from civil society groups and the opposition alliance after it emerged that millions of names were being deleted.The backlash grew when SIR was held in the state of West Bengal and it became clear that Muslims and other minorities, who traditionally do not vote for Modi’s Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata party (BJP), were being disproportionately stripped of their vote.View image in fullscreenA protester is detained.Photograph: Rajat Gupta/EPAYet it didn’t become an issue of national outrage until late last month, when the Indian Express newspaper published an investigation that exposed multiple irregularities in the SIR process, which had been flagged in more than a dozen internal objections but had been unilaterally overruled by Kumar.Opposition parties, the Cockroach movement and student groups began to call for the resignation of Kumar, who was appointed by a committee led by Modi. This week, India’s main opposition Congress party, also tried to reach Jantar Mantar to protest but were blocked by police, and the Congress leader, Rahul Gandhi, was detained twice.This week,the supreme courtordered the Modi government and the election commission to respond to the allegations. A BJP spokesperson said they had “no base, not an iota of evidence” and accused them of being driven by “an irresponsible, anarchist opposition”.Saturday’s protest follows the triumph of the Cockroach movement in July, when it led mass protests that forced the resignation of Modi’s education minister. Since then, India’s youth have proved more willing to criticise the Modi regime and have expressed mounting anger at the obstruction of their freedom to protest.By Saturday evening, young people continued to gather in central Delhi neighbourhoods as the police continued pick up protesters en masse. Many, such as Prakhar Vashishth, who is in his early 20s, remained defiant despite the aggression of Delhi police. He had recently been asked to submit additional documents to establish his eligibility to remain on the electoral rolls.“We are living in extraordinary times, and young people in this country must come out to defend their future,” he said, as he stood near the police barricades around Jantar Mantar.“This government will go to any lengths to stay in power, even changing election rules or removing people it believes will not vote for it. But they cannot keep us away for ever.”Explore more on these topicsDelhiIndiaNarendra ModiSouth and central AsiaProtestActivismCivil liberties - internationalnewsShareReuse this content

title: Skies across the UK illuminated by the northern lights | Northern lights | The Guardian
description: Though mostly visible near the Arctic Circle, the natural phenomenon dazzled sky-gazers as far south Devon, Hampshire and Kent
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Though mostly visible near the Arctic Circle, the natural phenomenon dazzled sky-gazers as far south Devon, Hampshire and Kent
Content: The breath-taking aurora borealis was visible from locations as far south as Sheerness in Kent – pictured here – despite heavy light pollution in the area.Photograph: James Bell/Alamy Live News/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenThe breath-taking aurora borealis was visible from locations as far south as Sheerness in Kent – pictured here – despite heavy light pollution in the area.Photograph: James Bell/Alamy Live News/Alamy Live News.Northern lightsSkies across the UK illuminated by the northern lightsThough mostly visible near the Arctic Circle, the natural phenomenon dazzled sky-gazers as far south Devon, Hampshire and KentNadeem BadshahSat 10 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 18.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe northern lights illuminated the skies across the UK on Friday and Saturday evening.Sky-gazers as far south as Devon, Hampshire and Kent were treated to the dazzling natural phenomenon, also known as the aurora borealis.The Met Office said sightings could continue during clear skies until Tuesday.0:38Spectacular aurora captured from space by Russian cosmonaut – videoSuch occurrences are mostly visible near the Arctic Circle and northern Scotland.The aurora borealis is a natural light display in Earth’s sky, driven by solar activity and geomagnetic storms interacting with the upper atmosphere.Sightings will remain possible until Tuesday across Scotland and similar geomagnetic longitudes during clear skies, the Met Office said.Aurora displays occur when charged particles collide with gases in the Earth’s atmosphere around the magnetic poles. As they collide, light is emitted at various wavelengths, creating colourful displays in the sky.According to the Met Office, the sun emits charged particles known as solar wind, which travel at bout 1m mph.Intense geomagnetic storms could make auroras visible in southern USRead moreThe forecaster said: “When these particles interact with Earth’s magnetic field – especially when the solar wind’s polarity is opposite to Earth’s – they are funnelled toward the magnetic poles.“As these energetic particles collide with gases in the upper atmosphere, they release energy in the form of light. Oxygen produces green and, at higher altitudes, rare red auroras, while nitrogen creates blue and purple hues.”Last year, experts said 2026 will be a peak year for aurora-spotting, as the sun has been in a heightened state of activity as part of its 11-year natural cycle.Explore more on these topicsNorthern lightsThe sunSpacenewsShareReuse this content

title: Man dies after jumping into tiger enclosure at Yorkshire zoo | Zoos | The Guardian
description: Police say man was pronounced dead at the scene after being attacked by tiger
Author: Nadeem Badshah
Headline: Police say man was pronounced dead at the scene after being attacked by tiger
Content: Police at Yorkshire Wildlife Park which has been evacuated and closed after an incident in the tiger enclosure.Photograph: Charley Atkins/SWNSView image in fullscreenPolice at Yorkshire Wildlife Park which has been evacuated and closed after an incident in the tiger enclosure.Photograph: Charley Atkins/SWNSZoosMan dies after jumping into tiger enclosure at Yorkshire zooPolice say man was pronounced dead at the scene after being attacked by tigerNadeem BadshahSat 10 Oct 2026 13.13 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 12.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man has died after being attacked by a tiger after jumping into its enclosure at a zoo inYorkshire, police have said.Emergency services were contacted shortly after 1.30pm on Saturday when the man entered the enclosure at Yorkshire Wildlife Park, nearDoncaster, and was set upon by the tiger.He was pronounced dead at the scene, South Yorkshire police said, adding his family had been informed.Videos circulating online appear to show a man being pawed at and grappled by a tiger in an enclosure.A police spokesperson said the tiger attacked the man and inflicted “serious injury”.“Emergency services attended and sadly, despite the best efforts of medical personnel, the man was pronounced dead at the scene,” they added.“Regarding rumours surrounding the condition of the tiger, the animal was uninjured and remained in the enclosure following the incident and there is no wider risk to the public.”The force urged people not to share “distressing” video footage of the attack, circulating on social media.Yorkshire Wildlife Park said a “serious incident” occurred inside the enclosure.It said in a statement: “Our emergency response procedures were immediately activated, and emergency services are currently attending the scene.“We are working closely with the authorities to ascertain exactly what happened.” It added that the “safety and wellbeing of visitors, staff and animals remain our highest priority”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines UKGet the day’s headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionYorkshire Wildlife Park opened in 2009, with the Land of the Tigers attraction opening in 2011.The attraction is on a purpose-built two-acre reserve for Amur tigers, an endangered subspecies with about 500 left in the wild.Photos of the enclosure on the park’s website shows a high walkway for visitors and fencing above the section where the tigers can roam.A Yorkshire ambulance service spokesperson said it sent a number of resources to the scene including two ambulances, Yorkshire air ambulance and a doctor.Explore more on these title: Camden council was warned about paedophile nursery worker years before arrest | Children | The Guardian
description: Vincent Chan went on to abuse children after being cleared of ‘significant concerns’ following council-overseen inquiry
Author: Sirin Kale
Headline: Vincent Chan went on to abuse children after being cleared of ‘significant concerns’ following council-overseen inquiry
Content: Chan, who was jailed for 18 years in February, was described by prosecutors as a ‘prolific sexual predator’.Photograph: Metropolitan police/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenChan, who was jailed for 18 years in February, was described by prosecutors as a ‘prolific sexual predator’.Photograph: Metropolitan police/AFP/Getty ImagesChildrenCamden council was warned about paedophile nursery worker years before arrestVincent Chan went on to abuse children after being cleared of ‘significant concerns’ following council-overseen inquirySirin KaleSat 10 Oct 2026 11.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA paedophile nursery worker was cleared by an investigation overseen by a local authority three years before he was arrested.In February, Vincent Chanwas jailed after pleading guilty to 56 offences, including assault by penetration on three-year-old girls in his care at a Bright Horizons nursery on Finchley Road in north-west London. After his conviction, prosecutors described him as a “prolific sexual predator”.The Guardian can now reveal that Chan was the subject of an earlier safeguarding investigation, carried out by Bright Horizons, with the oversight of Camden council. It followed what were described as “significant concerns” raised with the nursery in 2021 about Chan’s conduct and behaviour by the parent of a young girl, including concerns about what her daughter was saying to her about Chan.Bright Horizons referred the matter to Camden council, which advised the nursery to investigate. Chan was put on duties that involved no contact with children while the investigation by Bright Horizons took place. After it was completed, Chan was cleared to return to his role caring for young children in the nursery.A year later, in 2022, Chan filmed himself sexually abusing three-year-old girls at the Bright Horizons nursery.Chan was first arrested in June 2024, initially on suspicion of child cruelty, after nursery staff discovered videos Chan had filmed of distressed children in his care.After Chan’s devices were searched by police as part of this investigation, they discovered that he was a prolific sexual offender, with tens of thousands of child abuse images on his computer. He had also committed sexual offences in his previous job as a teaching assistant at St Mary’s Church of England primary school in Dollis Park, northLondon, including upskirting female pupils. In February this year, Chan was sentenced to 18 years in prison.The revelation that Camden council and Bright Horizons were aware of concerns about Chan three years before his arrest, and that there had been an investigation into his behaviour, will raise questions about whether there were earlier opportunities to stop him. It will also raise wider questions about whether existing safeguards for nurseries are adequate.In early 2024, prior to Chan’s arrest, other parents say that they raised concerns with Bright Horizons about Chan’s conduct at work. They say they warned Bright Horizons that their children were telling them that Chan shouted at them, was “angry” and a “bad man”. These parents say these concerns were dismissed. After Chan’s first arrest, the Bright Horizons nursery on Finchley Road closed in June 2025.Nurseries have a responsibility to refer to local authority designated officers (LADOs) when there are concerns that a nursery worker has been accused of harming or posing a risk of harm to children, may be guilty of criminal conduct, or has exhibited behaviour that makes them unsuitable to work with children.Local authorities have the ultimate responsibility for managing allegations raised that relate to adults who work with children.LADOs can recommend that a matter be referred to the police if they believe it meets a criminal threshold. It is understood that the Metropolitan police did not receive a referral in 2021 regarding Chan, and were only notified of the concerns subsequently.After Chan’s sexual offending came to light, Camden council carried out a rapid review of the decision to clear him to return to work after the Bright Horizons investigation. The review concluded in November 2025, and Camden council subsequently commissioned a local child safeguarding practice review, led by an independent reviewer, to examine how Chan was able to abuse children at the Finchley Road nursery, in addition to offences committed in his previous role.The review, which has been pushed back repeatedly, is expected to be published in early 2027 according to Camden council. It is expected to be critical of the safeguarding culture within Bright Horizons. But Camden council has said publicly that it cannot investigate Bright Horizons under health and safety laws because it is conflicted due to its participation in the safeguarding review. Local authorities have the power to prosecute businesses that do not comply with health and safety legislation.In a letter to the parent of a child at the nursery, seen by the Guardian, Camden council said that the purpose of the safeguarding review was “not conducted to hold individuals, organisations, or agencies to account”. The review is not expected to satisfy the parents of Chan’s victims because it is unlikely to apportion blame to executives at Bright Horizons.There has been no explanation of why the review was pushed back from summer 2026, when the independent reviewer was initially expected to submit her report. The council has also rejected a freedom of information request from the Guardian relating to Chan’s employment at the nursery, citing a desire to “manage” the release of information.It is understood that, in addition to the 2021 referral involving Chan, Camden council received other unrelated safeguarding referrals from Bright Horizons between 2017 and 2024, the time Chan worked at the nursery.Get in touchContact our investigations teamThe best public interest journalism relies on first-hand accounts from people in the know. If you have something to share on this subject, you can contact us confidentially using the following methods:Secure Messaging in the Guardian appThe Guardian app has a tool to send tips about stories. Messages are end to end encrypted and concealed within the routine activity that every Guardian mobile app performs. This prevents an observer from knowing that you are communicating with us at all, let alone what is being said.If you don’t already have the Guardian app, download it (iOS/Android) and go to the menu.
