Select ‘Secure Messaging’.EmailIf you don’t need a high level of security or confidentiality you can emailinvestigations.contact@theguardian.com.SecureDropIf you can safely use the tor network without being observed or monitored you can send messages and documents to the Guardian via ourSecureDrop platform.Finally, our guide attheguardian.com/tipslists several ways to contact us securely, and discusses the pros and cons of each.Show moreA spokesperson for Camden council said: “Children deserve the best care in a safe environment and the ongoing independent local child safeguarding review into this case presents a pivotal opportunity to prevent abuse like this from happening again. Our participation in the review is thorough, and we have disclosed all relevant documents and information.“We are ready to receive the review’s recommendations once it is published and take action. We are determined to make a real and tangible impact on safeguarding arrangements for the future.”A spokesperson for Bright Horizons said: “Our thoughts remain with the victims of Chan’s shocking crimes and their families. As the Camden local authority’s child safeguarding practice review is ongoing, we will not be able to comment without the express written authorisation of that committee as we do not wish to prejudice that process. We will respond as soon as we are able, once we have received the committee’s response.”In the UK, theNSPCCoffers support to children on 0800 1111, and adults concerned about a child on 0808 800 5000. The National Association for People Abused in Childhood (Napac) offers support for adult survivors on 0808 801 0331. In the US, call or text theChildhelpabuse hotline on 800-422-4453. In Australia, children, young adults, parents and teachers can contact theKids Helplineon 1800 55 1800; adult survivors can seek help atBlue Knot Foundationon 1300 657 380. Other sources of help can be found atChild Helpline InternationalExplore more on these topicsChildrenEarly years educationCrimeLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: How a South African billionaire is turning a corner of Somerset into ‘one man’s estate’ | The super-rich | The Guardian
description: Koos Bekker’s Newt estate encompasses luxury hotels, pubs and high street business, with local concerns including flooding
Author: Helena Horton
Headline: Koos Bekker’s Newt estate encompasses luxury hotels, pubs and high street business, with local concerns including flooding
Content: The Newt is a beloved destination for celebrities such as Charli XCX and Kate Moss.Photograph: Commission Air/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe Newt is a beloved destination for celebrities such as Charli XCX and Kate Moss.Photograph: Commission Air/AlamyThe super-richHow a South African billionaire is turning a corner of Somerset into ‘one man’s estate’Koos Bekker’s Newt estate  encompasses luxury hotels, pubs and high street business, with local concerns including floodingHelena HortonandMichael GoodierSat 10 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 09.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen South African billionaire Koos Bekker bought an old country estate in a sleepy corner ofSomersetto turn it into a luxury hotel, residents thought it was a sign their area was on the up.Walking through his peaceful manicured gardens, which feature a maze of apple trees twisted into perfect shapes using the espalier method, it’s easy to feel that all is well in this quiet, picturesque pocket ofEngland.But if you venture beyond the orchards and into the local pubs, where the local cider sets tongues wagging, you’ll hear a very different story.Bekker has been embroiled in a row with local people over a number of issues ranging from the vast expansion of his estate, the use of pesticides on it and branding deals – described as “brazen” by one local person – which have seen the local train station named after his hotel, the Newt in Somerset.View image in fullscreenKoos Bekker has been buying thousands of acres around Bruton and Castle Cary.Photograph: Dave Benett/Getty Images for The Newt in Somerset & BurberryThe businessman has a net worth of about £3bn and is the chair of Naspers, one of the world’s biggest technology firms. He has been buying thousands of acres around Bruton and Castle Cary – more than 2,700 acres (1,090 hectares), according to Guardian analysis – through his company Emily Estate (UK) Limited, which trades as the Newt.As well as swathes of the countryside, Bekker has also snapped up high street businesses from a deli to a beauty parlour, as well as pretty former farmhouses and local pubs.map of the area of Somerset with the lands owned by Emily Estate marked according to date of purchase.And it is this expansion of Bekker’s influence beyond the boundaries of the Newt – beloved of celebrities such as Charli xcx and Kate Moss – into the heart of the local Somerset villages where tensions have begun to emerge.Bekker is not the only moneyed arrival in this corner of Somerset. The area boasts famous residents including former chancellor George Osborne, fashion designer Stella McCartney, and broadcaster Mariella Frostrup.The George pub in the centre of Castle Cary currently serves senior citizens a hot dinner for just £12, but local people do not expect these prices will remain now the Newt has bought the inn: a bag of chocolate buttons in its farm shop costs £11.95, while a bottle of “cyder” grown on the estate is £12.50.View image in fullscreenBekker acquired Hadspen House in 2013, along with 16 acres of land, and converted it into the luxury hotel.Photograph: Nick Scott/AlamyBekker bought the 17th-century manor Hadspen House in 2013, along with 16 acres of land, converting it into the luxury hotel. Last year he acquired Yarlington Lodge, a Grade II-listed Georgian house a mile away, and converted it into a 32-guest property with its own pool, tennis court and cinema room.He is hardly a silent investor – the sign for the local train station, Castle Cary, now reads “Castle Cary for the Newt”. By the tracks is the new Creamery cafe, which serves afternoon tea in a vintage Pullman carriage at £45 a head.Hugh Thomas, afood writerfrom Frome, said the renaming of the station seemed “arrogant and brazen”, adding: “The station does feel somewhat colonised by the Newt regardless, which I find an encroaching thing, given it is supposed to be a public service.”View image in fullscreenGardens at the Newt.Photograph: Victor Watts/AlamySome, though, have welcomed the investment, saying it has cheered up a previously unloved train station and the Bekker family were creating jobs as well as bringing new people to the area to eat in the restaurants and drink in the pubs.Visitors to the £800-a-night Newt hotel are invited to enjoy being immersed in the nature of deep Somerset. The hotel recently welcomeda cage of endangered red squirrels. But there, too, lay a problem.The Newt consulted rewilding expert Derek Gow about keeping five red squirrels in a pen. They became extinct in most of England after invasive grey squirrels were introduced from America which carry a virus that causes a disease called squirrelpox, which kills off the reds.Gow said: “The Newt did talk to me about it; we did have one conversation. I said: ‘It is not going to be viable.’ It is performative – [the squirrels] are in the cage to show guests. That’s it. Keeping five squirrels in a cage does nothing for wildlife. If they do release them, they will just get squirrelpox and die.”While the Newt has created spectacular gardens around the hotel, including a historically accurate Roman villa, a “four seasons” garden featuring marble water fountains and a treetop walkway, these are not freely accessible to the public. Only hotel guests and those with an £85 annual pass can enter the grounds.View image in fullscreenThe grounds of the Newt are only accessible to hotel guests and those buying an £85 annual pass.Photograph: OBNW/AlamyPeople living nearby have also been concerned that there has been an increase in flooding since the Newt was built. The hotel has acknowledged this, and has been digging pools to hold any run-off water from the farm and paved areas.Local people have set up a group to coordinate complaints about the issue. Emma Craigie, a writer who lives nearby, said: “I live in a village below the hill the Newt is on. In our immediate locality there were incidents of flooding which seemed clearly exacerbated by their road building and hardcore use.”The worst incident was in May 2023, when rain over the Newt caused flash-flooding down the Pitt and Cam valleys, which the local council described as “beyond levels seen in living memory”. The local authority declared an emergency that evening.Villagers have also set up a petition against the spraying of pesticides on the Newt’s farmland.The model and actor Gabriella Wilde, who also lives locally, said: “I was surprised and a little disappointed to learn that they are using such harmful chemicals in their farming operations. That is certainly not the image they project to their guests and local fans. Is it really necessary, especially given how many local farms are making great strides in moving away from old school harmful practices, and towards more nature friendly farming?”View image in fullscreenThe croquet lawn to the rear of the hotel building.Photograph: Peter Titmuss/AlamyFarmers have been suspicious that new boreholes drilled by the hotel have dried up sections of the River Brue, the stream that Bruton is named after. The cider-maker Oliver Dowding, the nextdoor neighbour of the hotel, has entered negotiations with the Newt via the Environment Agency over his section of the river, which runs through his land. He said, ironically, that the newts which used to live on his land had disappeared.Though the Newt boasts that its food is “locally produced”, its farms do not have organic certification. John Sykes, who lives nearby, pointed to the severely trimmed hedges around the estate as well as the sterile lawns.“Look, there are no berries for the birds here. And what bothers me is the land immediately adjacent to our village used to be an organic farm, now they’ve bought it, and it isn’t any more. They are continuing to buy farmland, and I don’t know when they will stop. I don’t want to live somewhere that’s just one man’s estate,” Sykes said.A spokesperson for the Newt in Somerset said: “Fundamental to our philosophy is a love of gardens, respect for the land and a determination to share that passion with a broad audience. To ensure best practice, we employ experts across our operations, including agronomists, horticulturists, arborists, conservationists, educationalists, beekeepers, nutritionists, livestock and wildlife specialists, alongside our hospitality teams.“We are equally committed to our local community, maintaining close relationships with local organisations and proudly employing more than 650 people, who are either from or live within the local area.”Explore more on these topicsThe super-richHospitality industrySomersetFarmingEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Study explores links between 19th-century Manchester workers and enslaved Africans in Caribbean | Peterloo massacre | The Guardian
description: Global Threads research project reveals how slavery hung ‘like a spectre’ over the Peterloo massacre and other Mancunian struggles for equality
Author: Chris Osuh
Headline: Global Threads research project reveals how slavery hung ‘like a spectre’ over the Peterloo massacre and other Mancunian struggles for equality
Content: The Global Threads project is part of research into the history of the Portico Library.Photograph: Richard Saker/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe Global Threads project is part of research into the history of the Portico Library.Photograph: Richard Saker/The GuardianCotton Capital: ongoing seriesPeterloo massacreStudy explores links between 19th-century Manchester workers and enslaved Africans in CaribbeanGlobal Threads research project reveals how slavery hung ‘like a spectre’ over the Peterloo massacre and other Mancunian struggles for equalityChris OsuhCommunity affairs correspondentSat 10 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 08.03 EDTShareThey were the killings that changed Britain, paving the way for working-class people’s right to vote, as well as leading to the founding of the Manchester Guardian. In thePeterloo massacreof 1819, peaceful protesters were shot and trampled to death by the Manchester and Salford Yeomanry at St Peter’s Field in the city.A study byGlobal Threads, a public history project, has examined how the exploitation of Africans enslaved in the Caribbean was linked with the struggles of cotton workers at Peterloo. Though these workers were divided by thousands of miles and led different lives, they were exploited by the same forces – asRobert Wedderburn, a Black abolitionist in London, said at the time.As well as looking atWedderburn’s story, Global Threads’ research looks at the life of Hugh Hornby Birley, the yeomanry commander who led the fatal charge on the crowd at Peterloo. It found Birley’s family fortune was intimately linked with transatlantic enslavement.View image in fullscreenRobert Wedderburn, a Black abolitionist based in London.Photograph: History and Art Collection/AlamyMeanwhile, the story ofSir George Philips, also examined in the project, reflects the contradictions of 19th-century liberal politics. While Philips helped fund the Manchester Guardian as a liberal reaction to Peterloo, he was personally invested in the exploitation of enslaved Africans in the Caribbean, as owner of theSuccessplantation in Hanover, Jamaica.Birley and Philips weremembers of the Portico Library, Manchester’s historic members’ library. In the 19th century it was a centre of information exchange for Manchester’s business elite, helping ensure their place at the apex of global capitalism. The Global Threads project is part of research into the history of the Portico, which stands a few yards from where the Peterloo massacre took place.Introducing the study, Global Threads said: “Drawing together just three of the thousands of threads connecting Peterloo with Africa and the Americas, we can see how the leaders of each wing of Manchester’s elite – Hugh Hornby Birley and Sir George Philips – owed their positions and power to their family and business activities drawing on colonialism and slavery.“They actively described the system they had created as a transatlantic one. It was not just profit that connected Peterloo … Birley and his reactionary colleagues brought colonial-style coercion more akin to the putting down of uprisings of enslaved people, working people themselves were connected to transatlantic people and places, and slavery hung like a spectre over the Mancunian struggles for justice and equality.”On 16 August 1819, 60,000 people converged in the centre of Manchester to campaign for political representation. Conditions for those workers were better than those endured by the trafficked and enslaved African workers at the other end of the transatlantic commodity boom, who were classed as property. But Britain’s working class were disenfranchised. Only 10% of men in the country could vote, and while landowners were enriched by the tariffs placed on foreign grain by the Corn Laws, workers could barely afford bread.The protest at St Peter’s Field ended in tragedy when the yeomanry – a militia of Tory businessmen – charged the crowd. In the aftermath, the authorities blamed protesters. But Wedderburn, a Jamaican-born Unitarian preacher, was quick to challenge the official narrative.In September 1819, at a meeting at his Soho chapel, he described Peterloo as “an act of murder … committed by the magistrates and yeoman”. In his preaching and writings, Wedderburn had long argued Africans and English labourers were being denied by the same forces.View image in fullscreenThe Peterloo tapestry in Albert Square, Manchester.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThe backstory ofBirleyshows how. Ella Sinclair, writing for Global Threads, found Birley’s family’s business financially benefited from the estate of Daniel Backhouse, an enslaver whofunded and profited from 103 voyages that set out from Liverpool between 1773 and 1807, trafficking more than 27,000 Africans.In the late 18th century, three of those voyages exported people to St Lucia, where Backhouse’s company funded and profited from the Rabot sugar estate. Early 19th-century records reveal that workers there included families trafficked from Guinea and Cape Verde.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |MonthlySign up toCotton CapitalStarting with the Guardian’s own history, Guardian journalists explore the legacies of enslavement and reparative justice around the worldEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter the emancipation of enslaved Africans in the British empire in the 1830s, the Birley family supported the enslaving US confederacy, which was integral to their cotton interests. Birley was closely involved with the development of Manchester institutions, including “the Liverpool and Manchester Railway – designed to more easily transport slave-produced cotton”, Sinclair found.Wedderburn’s family was also embedded in the plantation economy. His uncle, John Wedderburn, owned the Blackheath, Blackness, Bluecastle and Glen Islay plantations in Westmoreland, Jamaica. Workers on those plantations included people trafficked from Old Calabar, in modern-day Nigeria, to Montego Bay in 1773, on a ship carrying textiles woven in Manchester.Robert Wedderburn’s mother was an enslaved woman called Rosanne, while his father was the plantation owner who raped her. Raised in Jamaica by his African grandmother, Talky Amee, Wedderburn served in the Royal Navy and sailed to London, settling in multicultural St Giles and became a leading radical.Global Threads found that the Dreadnought, the ship that trafficked some enslaved workers to Wedderburn plantations, had also trafficked workers to Success, the plantation later owned by Philips.At the time of Peterloo, Wedderburn was in prison, accused of inciting slaves to kill their masters. He believed in armed struggle against enslavement across the Caribbean, and that a revolution had begun at Peterloo.Around the same time as Peterloo, hundreds ofabolitionists who had escaped slaverywere staging raids on plantations in St Catherine, Jamaica. The British governor at the time was, coincidentally, titled the Duke of Manchester.In a paper on Wedderburn, Global Threads historians write: “In the weeks following the [Peterloo] massacre, Wedderburn gave the most clear contemporary articulation of a transatlantic understanding of liberation and justice. He drew direct parallels for his followers … showing that the oligarchy profiting from the labour of working people in Manchester – while denying their rights to representation and improved working and living conditions – were part of the same elite and system that imposed the violence and coercion of slavery upon enslaved Africans.”Explore more on these topicsPeterloo massacreCotton Capital: ongoing seriesManchesterSlaveryColonialismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nine people, including children, dead after mass shooting in Pennsylvania | Pennsylvania | The Guardian
description: Authorities say suspect among dead in house after standoff with police in Erie and there is no ongoing threat
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Authorities say suspect among dead in house after standoff with police in Erie and there is no ongoing threat
Content: Police stand outside the home where nine members of a family were killed in an apparent domestic dispute on 10 October in Erie, Pennsylvania.Photograph: Jeff Swensen/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPolice stand outside the home where nine members of a family were killed in an apparent domestic dispute on 10 October in Erie, Pennsylvania.Photograph: Jeff Swensen/Getty ImagesPennsylvaniaNine people, including children, dead after mass shooting in PennsylvaniaAuthorities say suspect among dead in house after standoff with police in Erie and there is no ongoing threatMarina DunbarandUwa Ede-OsifoSat 10 Oct 2026 19.24 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 11.45 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA man fatally shot eight people, including a pregnant woman and children, at aPennsylvaniaresidence on Friday before killing himself, police say.The victims have not been publicly identified, but seven relatives and a family friend died in the rampage.At a Saturday news conference, Erie’s police chief, Rick Lorah, said it was premature to speculate about the suspected gunman’s motive but noted mental health may have played a role.US man arrested as second suspect in Canada mass school shooting planned with ChatGPTRead morePolice discovered the killings about 5pm Friday when officers were called to a residence following reports of gunfire. Witnesses told authorities that they had seen an attacker with a gun outside the property before making his way inside.Responding officers discovered two women lying dead in the street, both having suffered gunshot wounds. Inside the home, police said they made a devastating discovery, finding six additional victims, including a five-year-old boy and a one-year-old girl, as well as the suspected assailant. Investigators believe the attacker died from a self-inflicted gunshot wound.Video footage showed the women arriving in distress at the residence. They paced outside, pounded on the door and tried to alert neighbors.Authorities believe the suspected shooter came out of the residence, exchanged words with the women and then fired at them.“They knew something was going on at that house. We have to figure out what that is,” Lorah said on Saturday.The suspect had a history with law enforcement, but its nature remains unclear.At the news conference, Erie officials also addressed criticism that they were slow to share details of the shooting with the public.Some of the family members who also lived at the residence had been away, according to Erie’s mayor, Daria Devlin.“We could not allow this to be received on the news, numbers of people, before we had the opportunity to speak with them,” she said.Lorah previously spoke about the scale of the mass shooting, describing the scene as among the most distressing and heartbreaking he had witnessed.“The loss of life is devastating and the circumstances we are working through are deeply disturbing,” Lorah said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHe added: “Our hearts are with the victims, their families and everyone affected by this tragedy. There are no words that can adequately express the magnitude of the loss of life here.”Man with gun kills one Philadelphia police officer and injures anotherRead moreFigures from theGun Violence Archiveindicate that the killings in Erie marked at least the 19th mass murder of the year. Such cases are defined as ones in which four or more victims are murdered.Many of those mass murders have been what are consideredfamily annihilations, in which an attacker kills multiple close family members.The nonpartisan archive alsoindicatedthat the killings in Erie were among more than 500 mass shootings across the US since the beginning of January. Mass shootings are defined as cases in which four or more victims are shot whether fatally or non-fatally.Mass shootings for years have remained a persistent problem in the US, often intensifying public demands for stronger gun control measures at the federal level.Despite those calls, Congress has not enacted such restrictions sought over the years.In the US, you can call or text the988 Suicide & Crisis Lifelineat 988 or chat at988lifeline.org. In the UK and Ireland,Samaritanscan be contacted on freephone 116 123. In Australia, the crisis support serviceLifelineis 13 11 14. Other international helplines can be found atbefrienders.orgExplore more on these topicsPennsylvaniaGun crimeUS crimenewsShareReuse this content

title: Four dead as Isaias weakens to post-tropical cyclone after striking Florida panhandle | Hurricane Isaias | The Guardian
description: Some of deaths came from falling trees as half a million people without power and rain and flooding still a concern
Author: Alba Asenjo Domínguez
Headline: Some of deaths came from falling trees as half a million people without power and rain and flooding still a concern
Content: A home damaged by Hurricane Isaias in Milton, Florida, on 10 October 2026.Photograph: Dan Anderson/EPAView image in fullscreenA home damaged by Hurricane Isaias in Milton, Florida, on 10 October 2026.Photograph: Dan Anderson/EPAHurricane IsaiasFour dead as Isaias weakens to post-tropical cyclone after striking Florida panhandleSome of deaths came from falling trees as half a million people without power and rain and flooding still a concernAlba Asenjo Domínguezand agenciesSat 10 Oct 2026 19.20 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 10.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAt least four people were reported dead on Saturday amidIsaiasafter itmade landfalllate on Friday on Florida’s panhandle as a category 2 hurricane, according to authorities.The storm also took down trees, knocked out electricity for hundreds of thousands and flooded highways – but as Saturday evening approached, the region was reopening.Key things to know about Hurricane Isaias as millions under evacuation ordersRead moreDespite warnings of storm surges ahead of the storm, several major routes along the coast were open by daybreak on Saturday and free of downed trees and power lines typically seen after major hurricanes.Two of the deaths reported during Isaias occurred in Escambia county,Florida, and two others were reported inAlabama, as the storm moved inland, local officials said. Of those deaths, one each occurred in Escambia and Birmingham, Alabama, when trees fell on homes.Another person whose death was linked to Isaias was found in a closed garage with a running generator in Escambia county. Four members of that person’s family have been transported to the hospital with carbon monoxide poisoning, the Escambia sheriff’s office said.“Don’t run any generators inside your home, it can be very, very hazardous,”Floridagovernor Ron DeSantis said in a press conference.View image in fullscreenPeople retrieve belongings from a collapsed boat house in the aftermath of Hurricane Isaias in Destin, Florida, on Saturday.Photograph: Gerald Herbert/APInAlabama, governor Kay Ivey said Isaias – predicted to dissipate on Sunday – “cannot clear fast enough”.Meanwhile, though it had weakened on Saturday to a post-tropical cyclone as it passed through central Alabama, Isaias still posed flooding and tornado threats as it moved inland, forecasters and officials warned.Hurricane-force winds in the Florida panhandle blew the roof off a Pensacola hotel, and the city’s mayor said the airport “took some damage”. The storm flattened a boathouse in Destin and ripped away part of the facade of a high-rise in Panama City Beach.A worker in a condominium parking lot swept piles of the building’s insulation while others put back beach chairs that had been tossed about.View image in fullscreenLee Glessner begins to remove tree limbs from a fallen tree block a road after the landfall of Hurricane Isaias in Milton, Florida, on 10 October.Photograph: Dan Anderson/EPA“Remember, there can still be flooding from rising rivers,” Jared W Perdue, the secretary of Florida’s state transportation department, said at a news conference. “I’m just going to remind all of you – please, if there’s standing water or flowing water on top of a road, please do not drive through it.“It does not have to be that deep, and it can wash away your car, it can wash away a human, it can become very dangerous very quickly.”Nearly 550,000 customers were still without power across Florida, Alabama and Georgia on Saturday afternoon as those in the path of the storm began the cleanup process, according toPowerOutage.us. Though still high, the number of outages was down from more than 900,000 earlier on Saturday.View image in fullscreenDark clouds loom over a historic Catholic church on Friday in Mobile, Alabama.Photograph: Octavio Jones/APStorm surge and tropical storm warnings associated with Isaias by then had been discontinued, the National Hurricane Center (NHC) warned there would still likely be “considerable impacts” associated with Isaias across much of southern Alabama, Florida’s panhandle and south-westernGeorgia.“Flash, urban and river flooding is possible across the region,” the NHC said in a Saturday-morning advisory, adding that there was a considerable potential for flash flooding and landslides across the southern Appalachians. “A risk for tornadoes will persist … through [Saturday] afternoon across parts of the eastern Florida panhandle, Georgia and the Carolinas.”Isaias through Sunday is expected to produce rainfall amounts of 4-8in across southern Alabama, Florida’s panhandle and Big Bend regions, and south-west Georgia. Localized totals up to 15in are possible, particularly within rain bands across the Florida panhandle and Big Bend.View image in fullscreenIn an aerial view, an apartment complex is seen after the roof was blown off when Hurricane Isaias passed through the area on Saturday in Milton, Florida.Photograph: Joe Raedle/Getty ImagesAcross much of the remainder of the south-east US, rainfall amounts of 2-5in are expected, and localized higher amounts up to 10in are possible, especially across the southern Appalachians and coastal Carolinas.The hurricane’s maximum sustained winds were 105mph (169km/h). That was intense enough to sound like “a train whistle”, Tim Mowrytoldthe Associated Press after enduring the storm as his home in Pensacola, Florida.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Around 2-3 times a daySign up toBreaking News USGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHurricane Isaias makes landfall in Florida and hammers Gulf coastRead moreMowry described losing power on Friday afternoon but said could rely on a generator. He said his son tried to drive to his home after his place about 15 minutes away lost power but had to turn around because downed trees and power lines blocked the road.All things considered, Mowry said he was “really fortunate” with respect to how he fared during Isaias.Along Alabama’s Gulf coast, authorities in Mobile reported numerous downed trees and power lines.Maranie Adams, who rode out the storm with her family and their chickens in Gulf Shores, Alabama, said the winds rocked their home, but it was nothing like Hurricane Sally, which left water under their elevated house.“I feel very much more relieved today,” she said.Donald Trump has allowed the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) to provide resources to Georgia to help grapple with the ongoing storm, including possible tornadoes, the agency said on Saturday.Several roads have already been blocked by fallen trees around Atlanta, local outlets have reported.View image in fullscreenPeople line up for gas at one of the few open stations after the landfall of Isaias in Milton, Florida, on Saturday.Photograph: Dan Anderson/EPATrump previously approved emergency declarations for Florida and Alabama ahead of the landfall ofHurricane Isaias.While the stronger El Niño seemed to limit the number of hurricanes in the Atlantic for the year so far, Isaias forming in October with maximum sustained winds of 105mph marked a stark contrast from historical trends.The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) predicted a quiet year in terms of hurricanes at the beginning of a season that officially begins annually on 1 June. Noaa anticipated between three and six hurricanes, well below the average of seven. An August forecast from Noaa cut the expected number to between two and six.Isais is one of the twolatest-forming Atlantic hurricaneson record, tying a record set on 8 October 1905. Otherwise, the second-latest date for the first Atlantic hurricane was 11 September – in 2002 and 2013.None of the eight previous named storms of the 2026 Atlantic season intensified above tropical storm status.The Associated Press contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsHurricane IsaiasFloridaAlabamaGeorgiaHurricanesExtreme weatherUS weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: Hurricane Isaias updates: at least four people dead and hundreds of thousands without power – as it happened | Hurricane Isaias | The Guardian
description: First Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season has now weakened to post-tropical cyclone over central Alabama
Author: Taz Ali
Headline: First Atlantic hurricane of the 2026 season has now weakened to post-tropical cyclone over central Alabama
Content: 14.58 EDTAt least four dead from Hurricane IsaiasUwa Ede-OsifoThe death toll from Isaias is rising.InFlorida, one person was killed after a tree fell on their home, the state’s governor,Ron DeSantis, said at an afternoon news conference on Saturday. Another individual was found dead in their garage with the generator on.InAlabama, two people are dead, according to that state’s governor,Kay Ivey.Earlier reports indicated one casualty due to a downed tree hitting a home, but details around the second death remain unknown.“This storm cannot clear fast enough,” Ivey wrote in a Saturday statement to social media.“It brought heavy winds throughout Alabama, taking down trees, knocking out power and doing some damage. Unfortunately, we have also learned that two Alabamians have lost their lives. I am praying for their loved ones this morning.”ShareUpdated at15.33 EDT

title: Despair after 200-year-old ‘grandmother’ tree toppled for Trump’s border wall: ‘It crushes your heart’  | US immigration | The Guardian
description: Protesters spent months occupying an ancient cottonwood. Then a tense standoff with US border patrol came to a head
Author: Douglas Main
Headline: Protesters spent months occupying an ancient cottonwood. Then a tense standoff with US border patrol came to a head
Content: A drone view shows the mangled remains of the ancient cottonwood tree where activists staged a tree-sit to protest the construction of the US-Mexico border fence, in Lochiel, Arizona.Photograph: Rebecca Noble/ReutersView image in fullscreenA drone view shows the mangled remains of the ancient cottonwood tree where activists staged a tree-sit to protest the construction of the US-Mexico border fence, in Lochiel, Arizona.Photograph: Rebecca Noble/ReutersUS immigrationDespair after 200-year-old ‘grandmother’ tree toppled for Trump’s border wall: ‘It crushes your heart’Protesters spent months occupying an ancient cottonwood. Then a tense standoff with US border patrol came to a headDouglas MainSat 10 Oct 2026 16.57 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 16.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA200-year-old cottonwood tree near theUS-Mexico border, known as the “grandmother”, has been destroyed to make way for the construction ofDonald Trump’s border wall, despite a months-long effort by protesters trying to save it.In late July, land defenders begana tree-sitin the ghost town of Lochiel,Arizona, taking turns occupying a platform high in the tree’s canopy. The group remained there for more than 70 days.Protesters occupy 200-year-old tree at US-Mexico border to stop its destruction: ‘She’s our Statue of Liberty’Read moreThen, on Monday at dawn, more than 80 federal agentsswarmedthe protesters’ camp, which is located on private land, making arrests and preventing people from reaching the cottonwood. Some agents in a steel basket on an extendable crane lift forcibly removed the person in the tree platform, according to videos andphotosshared on social mediaand descriptions of people there at the time. Others were shoved and tackled as they tried to rush toward the tree to prevent its destruction, according to witnesses.Contractors with Fisher Sand & Gravel, a company building this section of wall, then used an excavator topush over the tree, which cracked and crashed to the earth. Land defenders shrieked, cried and yelled at the federal agents.“Seeing that – it crushes your heart,” said Erick Meza, the Sierra Club’s Borderlands coordinator who has been working to save the trees for months, beginning with a series of letters to US Customs and Border Protection (CBP).“That tree brought a lot of people together,” he said. Now, he added, “there’s a community response of outrage. People are pissed off.”The cottonwood’s toppling was filmed by a team fromTurning Point USA, the far-right political group, who appeared to be embedded with border patrol andallowed free access to roamthroughout the closed off public road.View image in fullscreenA tree-sitter on 29 July 2026 in the ancient cottonwood tree at the US-Mexico border in Lochiel, Arizona.Photograph: Rebecca Noble/ReutersOne of the land defenders had scaled another ancient cottonwood tree situated right on the border with Mexico. On Thursday, CBP and Mexican police, who have been present for several days and visibly working with American authorities,removedthe tree-sitter’s platform, food and water supplies, according to Alex Chabbott, a land defender who has been present at the camp on and off for over a month.Late on Friday, the tree-sitter came down on their own volition after not being resupplied for several days.double quotation markWe’re not going anywhere. We are rooted, like the grandmothersKate Scott, a tree-sit leaderThe agents involved include border patrol officers, part of CBP, and a special forces tactical unit calledBortac, whose self-described purpose is to “respond to terrorist threats”.The tree-sit began shortly after contractors knocked over and killed three other ancient cottonwood trees nearby on 27 July.Two 30ft-tall walls are being built throughout this area, known as the San Rafael valley, a remote and once idyllic high elevation prairie where the movie Oklahoma was filmed. The valley, and the Patagonia and Huachuca mountains on either side of it, form one of the most important regional wildlife corridors between the US and Mexico,providingpassagetoanimals includingjaguars, ocelots, bears and even beavers and porcupines in recent years.Already, government contractors have finished 88 miles (140km) of secondary wall, which is a second 30ft fence set at some distance from a primary wall of the same height. Another 444 miles of secondary wall are under construction,according to DHS, much of that in Arizona, using billions of dollars allocated by Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act.View image in fullscreenMembers of the Nogales fire department use a cherrypicker to remove a platform from another tree on the border with Mexico, leaving a protester stranded.Photograph: Rebecca Noble/ReutersProtesters say that construction in the area is progressing rapidly, 24 hours a day. In recent days, Fisher Sand & Gravel has completed the secondary wall, which includes placing 30ft steel panels within a trench filled with rebar and cement, along a part of the private property where the camp is located, including up to the point where the tree stood.These trees, which depend on a regular supply of water underground, are a hallmark of riparian forests, an endangered ecotype throughoutArizonaand the south-west, said Russ McSpadden, an advocate with the Center for Biological Diversity. The ecological importance of these trees is one of the animating factors behind the land defenders.Water usefor wall construction hasdepletedwells throughout the south-west, threatening natural featuressuch as Quitobaquito Springs. CBP does not say how much current construction uses, but in 2008 itestimateda smaller wall nearby could use up to 710,00 gallons per mile for construction; the current project likely uses more, as it is larger.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines USGet the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion‘We are starting a movement’Since Monday, dozens of land defenders have beenarrested, many for entering the road between the private property and the border, which wasordered closedby federal authorities in late September due to wall construction. Protesters have been doingprayersin the road near the tree every morning.Some of those arrested were physically hit and came back with bruises and black eyes, Chabbott claimed.Several more people attemptedto use nonviolent tacticsto halt or delay construction, including one woman wholocked herselfto a cement truck on 7 August, according tovideos sharedon social media.View image in fullscreenProtesters face off with US border patrol as Fisher Sand & Gravel construction crews work on 8 October 2026.Photograph: Rebecca Noble/ReutersThe protester was sprayed in the face with mace and wrestled by several agents, and her limbs forced into painful positions, according to witnesses and social media videos.The truck was later drivenawaywhile the land defender was still attached, and cut from the vehicle later that evening, according to witnesses. She is now in custody, according to what authorities have told the land defenders’ lawyers.double quotation markThat tree brought a lot of people together. People are pissed offErick Meza, Sierra ClubJulia Butterfly Hill,whospent two yearsliving in a redwood in California’s Humboldt county in the late 1990s, said she was horrified to see how roughly border patrol treated this woman on a livestreamed video, she said.This land defender’s courage and commitment to nonviolent resistance in the face of brutality “brought tears to my eyes”, Butterfly Hill said. “She’s a hero of the highest order.”CBP did not respond to a request for comment about this and other clashes, but has previously said that walls in areas like this will help combat unauthorized immigration. The sheriff of Santa Cruz county, David Hathaway, who did not respond to a request for comment for this story, haspreviously saida wall in this area is senseless since this remote valley has no history of significant illegal activity. Fisher Sand & Gravel did not respond to a request for comment.View image in fullscreenA drone view shows the remains of two other ancient cottonwood trees in Lochiel, Arizona, on 27 July.Photograph: Rebecca Noble/ReutersIn a press conference on 8 October, Adelita Grijalva, a congresswoman who represents the area, said she was “heartbroken” about the loss of the “grandmother” trees, and said she plans to try to introduce a bill that will revoke the DHS’s ability to waive any and all laws in building border infrastructure.The tree-sit began shortly after contractorsknocked over and killedtwo other ancient cottonwood trees nearby on 27 July.In felling the tree, the contractors and federal agents “try to break us, but we are not broken”, said Kate Scott, one of the leaders of the tree-sit. “We are starting a movement, and we’re not going anywhere. We are rooted, like the grandmothers.”Explore more on these topicsUS immigrationArizonaUS-Mexico borderTrump administrationDonald TrumpUS politicsTrees and forestsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘People are pissed’: union decries TSA’s removal of chairs for checkpoint staff | US unions | The Guardian
description: Order for workers to remain standing to ‘reinforce professionalism’ draws rebuke amid plunging morale
Author: Michael Sainato
Headline: Order for workers to remain standing to ‘reinforce professionalism’ draws rebuke amid plunging morale
Content: TSA workers at Albany airport in New York.Photograph: Lori Van Buren/Albany Times Union via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTSA workers at Albany airport in New York.Photograph: Lori Van Buren/Albany Times Union via Getty ImagesUS unions‘People are pissed’: union decries TSA’s removal of chairs for checkpoint staffOrder for workers to remain standing to ‘reinforce professionalism’ draws rebuke amid plunging moraleMichael SainatoSat 10 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 07.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUnion officials have launched a campaign to allow airport security staff to sit once more after theTrump administrationunilaterally removed all the chairs for Transportation Security Administration (TSA) staff at checkpoints.“People are pissed,” said Johnny Jones, secretary-treasurer of American Federation of Government Employees (AFGE) TSA council 100 and president of AFGE local 1040, which represents TSA workers in Dallas-Fort Worth.TSA officials ordered that chairs be removed from travel document check stations on September 25, arguing “maintaining a standing posture helps reinforce professionalism, attentiveness and active engagement with passengers” and that the policy change “reinforces both our security posture and our commitment to hospitality”.Jones said his members had been flooded with calls and messages about the agency removing chairs.“People are calling, members are mad, employees are upset because they literally started their day, everything was normal, and by halfway through their shift, they’re (TSA) taking all the chairs out and replacing them with inadequate mats,” said Jones. “The amount of phone calls I received is almost the same as if everybody got fired all at once, almost similar to when we have government shutdowns.”“Our officers screen millions of people a day and they do it right, sitting or standing,” said Hydrick Thomas, president of AFGE TSA council 100, in a statement. “Nobody who works a checkpoint asked for this. Nobody who flies asked for this.”Jones noted the TSA checkpoint podiums are one of two places where TSA officers can rest their legs while screening passengers. Chairs were not removed from x-ray machines because the manufacturersrecommendsitting while operating the machines.Jones cited the union was not informed on the policy change and it was not negotiated, rather unilaterally implemented by the agency, and its unclear where it leaves TSA employees who require light duty accommodations.Following the policy change, TSA workers were alsorequiredto sign a pledge that promises to support “the well-being and morale of our colleagues,” according to the union.“They didn’t notify the union at all, obviously, nor the employees. They decided it would be a great idea to make their employees upset,” said Jones.He said he is unsure what is being done with the chairs in airports around the US.Jones explained the policy worsens the working conditions of TSA officers who no longer have the option of taking time off of their feet, and noted that border patrol officers and customs officers are still using chairs while screening travel documents.US Customs and Border Patrol said it has not adopted this policy.“A lot of people don’t have adequate footwear to need to stand up for that long,” Jones said. “The agency didn’t allow us to bargain any of these changes. They just implemented them. It’s very demoralizing, upsetting that the agency would do this to transportation security officers.”AFGE, the largest union representing federal workers and representing TSA employees,launcheda letter-writing campaign calling on the public to tell TSA to “restore the chairs”.Union leaders criticized the policy change, TSA’s justification for it, and the agency requiring workers sign a morality pledge the same week the policy was unilaterally implemented.“Nobody who works a checkpoint asked for this. Nobody who flies asked for this,” said Thomas in a statement. “If TSA leadership truly believes standing makes people better at their jobs, I look forward to watching every manager in the building prove it for eight hours straight. We will bring the pledge. They can bring their own chair, if they are allowed one.”The policy change is just the latest issue to impact workers at TSA under the Trump administration, who are also currently facingpossible pay freezesandsignificant increasesto their health insurance premium costs.Under the Trump administration, the Department of Homeland Security has attempted twice to cancel the collective bargaining agreement between the agency and TSA unions, with a judgerulingin January to reinstate the contract, ruling the agency’s attempt to cancel it violated a court injunction.TSA workers also continued working during two government shutdowns without pay since Trump began his second presidential term, which included a government shutdown from 1 October to 12 November 2025, followed by a partial government shutdown that impacted TSA workers for 76 days from February to April this year.The Trump administration has also beenexpandingprivatization of work done by TSA workers to private contractors through the TSA Gold+ program; however, following criticism of the plan, Tampa airportabandonedits plan to join the program.TSA did not respond to multiple requests for comment on the policy change and union’s criticisms of the policy and morale pledge. TSA stillrequiresa chair must be available upon request for travelers.“This welcome change reinforces both our security posture and our commitment to hospitality by having these officers on their feet and alert,” a TSA spokesperson said in astatement to ABC Newson the policy change, but did not cite why the agency did not negotiate the change with the union.“All officers must meet fitness for duty requirements to be capable of performing their vital national security function while simultaneously creating a welcoming and professional environment for travelers.”Explore more on these topicsUS unionsTrump administrationUS politicsAir transportnewsShareReuse this content

title: United Auto Workers president Shawn Fain easily wins re-election | US unions | The Guardian
description: Fain was dogged by investigation but still decisively beat challenger Rich Boyer, who received just 13% of vote
Author: Michael Sainato
Headline: Fain was dogged by investigation but still decisively beat challenger Rich Boyer, who received just 13% of vote
Content: Shawn Fein speaks at the the national conference of the UAW’s political arm in Washington DC on 9 February 2026.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersView image in fullscreenShawn Fein speaks at the the national conference of the UAW’s political arm in Washington DC on 9 February 2026.Photograph: Evelyn Hockstein/ReutersUS unionsUnited Auto Workers president Shawn Fain easily wins re-electionFain was dogged by investigation but still decisively beat challenger Rich Boyer, who received just 13% of voteMichael SainatoSat 10 Oct 2026 09.46 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 09.48 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe president of the United Auto Workers, Shawn Fain, haseasily wonhis re-election bid after an campaign period marred by accusations of corruption and election interference.The union’s election of leadership for a four-year termbeganwith mail-in ballots being sent out in late August 2026, with vote tabulating commencing on 6 October.Fain won withover 68%of the vote as of Friday evening, with additional 13 candidates on his slate, United UAW, winning their elections. The closest opponent to Fain, Rich Boyer, received just over 13% of the vote.“The membership has spoken. UAW members are united and want us to keep fighting and building on what we’ve done,” said Shawn Fain in a statement on his re-election win, citing upcoming contract negotiations at John Deere, Volvo and General Dynamics Land Systems in 2027, and the big three automaker contracts expiring on May Day in 2028.“These results are about taking on corporate America and reversing the worst out-of-control wealth inequality in America’s history,” added Fain. “We are fighting for the entire working class, whether that’s at the bargaining table, organizing new members or in the political arena.”In July 2026, the Department of Justiceannouncedit was investigating Fain over allegations he pressured Boyer, another union official, to provide benefits to his fiancee and sister and then retaliated against him when Broyer refused to cooperate. Fain denied the allegations and characterized them as an attempt to interfere in the election.Fain won his firstelectionto serve as the union’s president as a reform candidate in March 2023.He has clashed with the union’s independent monitor, Neil Barofsky,claimingthe monitor was weaponized by his re-election opponent. The monitor was alsoaccusedof pressuring Fain over the UAW’s passing of a resolution calling for a ceasefire in Gaza.Fainledthe union during a roughly six-week strike in September 2023 through October 2023 at the big three automakers, General Motors, Ford and Stellantis, highlighting corporate greed through the strike and citing the companies’ stock buy-backs and record profits.Joe Biden joined the union on the picket line, thefirstsitting president to ever join a strike picket line.Explore more on these topicsUS unionsAutomotive industryUS politicsShareReuse this content

title: USWNT exposed by ruthless Spain as early goals settle heavyweight friendly | USA women's football team | The Guardian
description: The world champions scored twice in the opening 14 minutes before saving a second-half penalty to secure a 2-0 win over Emma Hayes’s side in Washington
Author: Ella Brockway
Headline: The world champions scored twice in the opening 14 minutes before saving a second-half penalty to secure a 2-0 win over Emma Hayes’s side in Washington
Content: USA midfielder Lindsey Heaps challenges Spain’s Eva Navarro for the ball during Saturday’s international friendly at Audi Field in Washington DC.Photograph: Patrick Smith/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenUSA midfielder Lindsey Heaps challenges Spain’s Eva Navarro for the ball during Saturday’s international friendly at Audi Field in Washington DC.Photograph: Patrick Smith/Getty ImagesUSA women's football teamUSWNT exposed by ruthless Spain as early goals settle heavyweight friendlyGuijarro and Navarro score in opening 14 minutesUS midfield and defensive lapses exposed by SpainYohannes misses penalty as US fightback falls shortElla Brockwayat Audi FieldSat 10 Oct 2026 16.53 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 19.59 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn less than a year’s time, the United States and Spain will almost certainly arrive in Brazil as the top two contenders to win the Women’s World Cup. Spain, holders of the top spot in Fifa’s rankings for the past 60 weeks, are the defending champions; the second-ranked US won gold at the 2024 Paris Olympics.This month’s pair of friendlies between the two sides are taking place with caveats. Both sides are missing several of their most important players to injuries. The opening match in Brazil is 258 days away. Spain have booked their place, but the US still have to actuallyqualifyfor the World Cup, through a regional tournament that begins next month.‘A lot of people counted me out’: Ashley Sanchez on goal records, grit and potential USWNT returnRead moreEven without full-strength rosters, a meeting between these two teams is a compelling bill. And in their first of two friendlies, on Saturday in Washington DC, Spain had the upper hand, scoring twice in the first 14 minutes of a 2-0 win.“You can’t afford to go 2-0 down against the best team in the world, especially the way we conceded those goals,” US coachEmma Hayessaid. “That’s the learning.”In just the fifth meeting between the two sides and the first since 11 October 2022 – before Spain broke through to win the 2023 World Cup – the reigning champions took advantage of defensive lapses and the US midfield’s struggles. After trailing by two goals for the first time under Emma Hayes, the Americans played a much-improved second half, but failures to convert chances and a stopped penalty kept them scoreless.In many ways, Saturday’s game and the rematch on Tuesday in Chester, Pennsylvania, are more stress tests than clashes of titans – or causes for alarm bells. Hayes has intentionally crafted this year’s calendar to pit the US against elite competition. The Americans played Japan three times in April, winning twice and losing once, and split a pair of away friendlies against Brazil in June. Saturday was the first time the US ever played the world No 1 in Fifa’s rankings on home soil.“There’s going to be games like that, and I’m happy it’s not the World Cup right now,” forward Trinity Rodman said. “You take what you can from this game and go into the next game.”View image in fullscreenTrinity Rodman controls the ball during the United States’ international friendly against Spain at Audi Field in Washington DC on Saturday.Photograph: Patrick Smith/Getty ImagesA matchup with both sides closer to full strength would have perhaps been more instructive as a preview of a potential World Cup meeting, but such a clash had been ruled out this week. Center-back Naomi Girma and midfielder Sam Coffey, the two players most vital to the US defensive spine, are out with injuries. Spain are missing two-time Ballon d’Or winner Aitana Bonmatí, Vicky Lopez, Mariona Caldentey and Cata Coll with injuries; Clàudia Pina and Mapi León withdrew from camp on Friday.If the lengthy list of absentees affected Spain, it didn’t show. They went ahead in the third minute on a 20-yard screamer by Patri Guijarro. The US struggled to assemble their shape after a turnover and left the Barcelona midfielder with significant space.The second goal came just 11 minutes later, the result of another defensive breakdown. Salma Paralluelo isolated Tierna Davidson on the left side and sent a cross to a wide-open Eva Navarro, who fired it for a one-touch finish on the run. All 11 US players huddled above the box for several minutes after conceding.The US’s connections looked off throughout the first half, from giveaways to overhit clearances. Rose Lavelle attempted to lay off a forward pass with Sophia Wilson and Alyssa Thompson on the break, but both players mistimed their runs and the ball rolled out of bounds to a groan from the Audi Field crowd. Wilson’s best attempts of the half hit the post and rolled wide. The issues in themidfield– for the first 65 minutes, Lavelle, Lily Yohannes and Lindsey Heaps – that predate the Hayes era were evident again.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMoving the GoalpostsNo topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenSpain’s Natalia Ramos reacts during Saturday’s international friendly against the United States at Audi Field.Photograph: Patrick Smith/Getty ImagesThe Americans looked improved and composed in the second half after adjusting their high press. Spain did not produce a shot on target in the second half, and the US outshot them 13-6 on the day. Wilson thought she had scored the US’s first goal in the 53rd minute, but it was waved for offside after video review.The US earned a penalty in the 67th minute after Wilson drew a foul by Natalia Ramos in the box. The taker was Yohannes – a surprise choice, given the 19-year-old has never attempted a penalty in four seasons at Ajax and OL Lyonnes. Wilson, a regular taker for the Portland Thorns, is a perfect 11 for 11 on penalties in the NWSL. (Yohannes told reporters after the game she was second on the US’s list of takers, behind Heaps.) Adriana Nanclares saved Yohannes’s stutter-step attempt and the Americans remained off the board.Forward Mallory Swanson and midfielder Ashley Sanchez were among the second-half substitutes. Swanson, who was out for all of 2025 on maternity leave, made her first game appearance in 710 days. Sanchez was recalled to the national team amida strong NWSL seasonwith the North Carolina Courage and earned her first US minutes since October 2023. She nearly scored off a cross in the 88th minute but slid as her foot connected with the ball.Spain increased the physicality for the final quarter-hour. They committed 12 fouls to the US’s four and went down to 10 players in stoppage time after Athenea del Castillo saw red for a hair pull.The US will have a chance to remedy their finishing issues in Tuesday’s rematch in Pennsylvania. They have not gone consecutive games without scoring since the 2023 World Cup.Explore more on these topicsUSA women's football teamSpain women's football teamUS sportsWomen's footballEmma HayesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Oklahoma stun No 1 Texas as Sandell’s last-second kick seals Red River upset | College football | The Guardian
description: Tate Sandell kicked a 47-yard field goal as time expired to give Oklahoma a stunning 27-24 victory over top-ranked Texas in Dallas
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Tate Sandell kicked a 47-yard field goal as time expired to give Oklahoma a stunning 27-24 victory over top-ranked Texas in Dallas
Content: Texas quarterback Arch Manning looks to pass on the run during the Longhorns’ 27-24 loss to Oklahoma in the Red River rivalry game on Saturday at the Cotton Bowl in Dallas.Photograph: Brian Rothmuller/Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenTexas quarterback Arch Manning looks to pass on the run during the Longhorns’ 27-24 loss to Oklahoma in the Red River rivalry game on Saturday at the Cotton Bowl in Dallas.Photograph: Brian Rothmuller/Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesCollege footballOklahoma stun No 1 Texas as Sandell’s last-second kick seals Red River upsetSandell’s 47-yard kick seals 27-24 upset in DallasSooners overcome offensive struggles to stun TexasManning throws three TDs but two costly picksAgenciesSat 10 Oct 2026 19.52 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 20.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTate Sandell kicked a 47-yard field goal on the final play and Oklahoma overcame their continued offensive ineptness with touchdowns on special teams and defense in a 27-24 win over No 1 Texas in the Red River rivalry game on Saturday.The Sooners (3-2, 1-1 Southeastern Conference) beat a No 1 team for the first time since a 38-17 win over Missouri in 2007. They had been 0-4-1 when facing a top-ranked Texas team.Arch Manning threw three touchdowns for the Longhorns (4-1, 1-1), but both of his interceptions were costly.Texas had two late chances, but Gianni Spetic was wide right on a 53-yard field-goal attempt with 1:55 left. After the Sooners went three-and-out for the seventh time in the game, Manning’s last pass was intercepted by Courtland Guillory with 19 seconds left.That set up the Sooners at their 39, and John Mateer completed passes of 13 and 20 yards to Isaiah Sategna on opposite sides of the field, both upheld on replay review.Oklahoma then ran a play to set up the kick by Sandell, who earlier had made a 53-yarder and missed another from the same distance.Dakoda Fields recovered a blocked punt in the end zone and Peyton Bowen returned an interception 42 yards for a touchdown for the Sooners, who in their previous game two weeks earlier lost 41-13 at No 2 Georgia.The pick-six by Bowen came after Manning was scrambling away from pressure and throwing to Cam Coleman, who had an earlier touchdown. But the ball instead went to the Oklahoma safety, whose return with 10:07 left put the Sooners up 24-17.Texas responded with a tying 75-yard drive and Manning’s third TD pass, a 15-yarder to Jermaine Bishop Jr with 6:32 left.Manning finished 19 of 31 passing for 260 yards.Mateer completed 18 of 26 passes for 155 yards. The Sooners had only 238 total yards, well below their average of 321 coming into the game that was last in the SEC.Explore more on these topicsCollege footballCollege sportsUS sportsShareReuse this content

title: LeBron James is everything Philadelphia wants. And everything it can’t stand | LeBron James | The Guardian
description: The city has embraced its new superstar with open arms, even as he choppers in from Manhattan and makes no secret of the fact that Philadelphia was never his first choice
Author: Bryan Armen Graham
Headline: The city has embraced its new superstar with open arms, even as he choppers in from Manhattan and makes no secret of the fact that Philadelphia was never his first choice
Content: LeBron James made his pre-season debut with the 76ers on Thursday.Photograph: Ishika Samant/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLeBron James made his pre-season debut with the 76ers on Thursday.Photograph: Ishika Samant/Getty ImagesLeBron JamesLeBron James is everything Philadelphia wants. And everything it can’t standBryan Armen GrahamThe sports-mad city has embraced its new superstar, even as he choppers in from Manhattan and makes no secret of the fact that Philly was never his first choiceSat 10 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 09.24 EDTSharePhiladelphia has always had an instinctive affinity with athletes who embrace the grind over the glamour. In a place where sports mean a littletoomuch, commitment has traditionally counted for more than celebrity. What it demands above all, sometimes unreasonably, is the sense that they have bought in, that the city and its fortunes matter to them as much as they do to the people who devote their lives to backing its teams.Few embodied that ethic more completely than Lane Johnson, the Eagles’ revered right tackle and best player for more than a decade,who abruptly announced his retirementTuesday after 14 seasons, two Super Bowl titles and acareer spent neutralizingsome of the most freakish physical specimens to walk the earth. Johnson’s quotidian greatness on the offensive line was almost perversely workmanlike. According to Pro Football Focus, he allowed just 10 sacks across close to 7,000 pass-blocking snaps in the last 13 years, goingentire seasonswithout letting his man bring down the quarterback. The Eagles won nearly two-thirds of their games when he played and lost nearly two-thirds when he didn’t.LeBron James once raged against the machine. Increasingly, he helps prop it upRead moreSurely a first-ballot Hall of Famer when he’s eligible in 2031, he earned a place in the first rank of Philadelphia sporting legends alongside Mike Schmidt, Julius Erving and Bobby Clarke, despite playing a position where success is largely measured by how little anyone notices you. But perhaps the most revealing thing Johnson did was decide when to stop. At 36, he walked away from millions in future earnings to prioritize his mental wellbeing and focus on his parents’ health. For a man who made his living holding the line, there was something fitting about knowing when to let go.Johnson’s departure comes at a particularly anxious moment on the local sports scene. The ageing Phillies’desultory wildcard exit against the Atlanta Braveslast week marked a fifth consecutive playoff appearance with diminishing returns. The Flyers have opened their season with five straight losses, splashing cold water on themounting optimismthat had surrounded them. The Union have US soccer’s most exciting prospect ingenerational talent Cavan Sullivan, but they remain a decidedly niche concern in a town dominated by its four traditional major-league teams. And the Eagles, almost comicallybeset by injuryand suddenly without one of their franchise cornerstones as they travel to London this week, appear consigned to a rebuild. Across the city, the sensation is less of a championship window closing than of several slamming shut at once.All of which has left the new-look 76ers, whodebuted their tricked-out starting fiveon Thursday night in Brooklyn, carrying an almost inordinate share of the city’s sporting hopes. The timing makes for an uncomfortable juxtaposition. Philadelphia is losing an athlete who spent 14 years making the city his own, just as it welcomesthe greatest basketball player to ever live, who has given precious little indication that he intends to do the same.View image in fullscreenLeBron James poses with a new-look Philadelphia 76ers team alongside Jaylen Brown, Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and VJ Edgecombe (from left) during the team’s media day in Camden, New Jersey, on 28 September 2026.Photograph: Chris Szagola/APThe Philly sporting identity has always been shaped by its uneasy relationship with New York, the northern neighbor that eclipsed it as America’s commercial and cultural capital a long time ago and has spent the intervening centuries reminding it of that fact. That history has bred a peculiar combination of civic pride and insecurity, a conviction that Philadelphia is entitled to better and a gnawing suspicion that deep down it doesn’t even deserve it. The 76ers, third on the NBA’s all-time wins list, haven’t won a championship since 1983, spending more than four decades watching Boston and Los Angeles pile up the sport’s prizes. The city’s athletes are expected to understand that burden, or at least pretend to share it.James admitted at last month’s media day that Philadelphia had not been his preferred landing spot in free agency. The 41-year-old had dreamed of finishing his career at Madison Square Garden, only to abandon the idea after the Knicks ended their 53-year title drought in June, wary of being perceived as a ring-chaser. For a city that has spent generations bristling at New York’s perceived superiority, the confession carried a particular sting. Nearly a century after WC Fields quipped that he would rather see Paris before he died but Philadelphia would do, the NBA’s most famous star appeared to have reached the same conclusion. Even now, James seems reluctant to commit to the place geographically. Asked where he would live, he answered: “Both. Multiple residences.” That apparently means commuting from New York in a Fanatics-branded helicopter that gets roughly 1.6 miles to the gallon.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueThe Leonardo AW139, suppliedthrough his sponsorship arrangementwith Michael Rubin’s sports merchandising empire, has become James’s preferred mode of transport between the two cities. Publicly availableflight-tracking datashowed 18 trips between Manhattan and Northeast Philadelphia Airport in the first days of October alone. Never mind that Amtrak’s Acela service connects the cities in about 90 minutes, with comfortable seats, wifi and enough legroom even for a 6ft 9in basketball player.The environmental optics have raised eyebrows. The AW139, accordingto a Defector report, is unusually emissions-intensive, even by the standards of private helicopters. But in Philadelphia, the symbolism is as offensive as the carbon footprint. It’s hard to imagine a more exquisitely calibrated insult to the city’s sporting psyche. Philly fans have never cared much where their sporting heroes come from. What matters is whether, somewhere along the way, they come to regard the city as their own. Johnson gave the city 14 years of his body, his loyalty and his labor. James appears determined to give it his working hours.Which is fine. James isn’t the first gun-for-hire to find himself in an arranged marriage in the winter of his career. Yet the helicopter is merely the latest indignity in James’s increasinglydepressing transformationfrom athlete-activist into walking corporate billboard. Not so long ago, James was helping lead More Than a Vote, the organization he co-founded in 2020 to combat voter suppression, register voters and mobilize Black communities. He leveraged his extraordinary celebrity to encourage civic participation and tell people that their voices mattered. It was a meaningful demonstration of what an athlete with virtually unlimited cultural influence could accomplish. Six years later, he’s hawkingonline gamblingandbrown liquor.View image in fullscreenThe abrupt retirement of Lane Johnson (above) has added to a growing sense of uncertainty around Philadelphia’s sporting fortunes.Photograph: Michael Owens/Getty ImagesHis reported $15m-a-year partnership with Polymarket, a prediction-market platform encouraging ordinary marksto wager on everythingfrom basketball to elections to war, is all the more dispiriting. The mainstreaming of prediction markets, and the relentless creep of gambling into news, politics and virtually every corner of society, are one of the bleaker developments in American public life. The same cultural capital that once encouraged people to participate in democracy is now being deployed to encourage them to speculate on it with their disposable income, all so a handful of techno-fascist investors can become obscenely rich. His involvement with Fanatics, with its ever-expanding connections to the gambling industry, makes the whole spectacle even harder to reconcile with his cultivated image as a socially conscious athlete. It’s the kind of corporate exploitation couched in cultural legitimization and the aesthetics of cool thatfeels ripe for a Spike Lee satire… were the Bamboozled director notappearing in glossy Polymarket adshimself.Nobody begrudges James the fortune his extraordinary talent and longevity has earned him. Nor should anyone expect professional athletes in his echelon to move like ascetics. His philanthropic work, most notably the I Promise School in Akron, remains meaningful regardless of whatand whohe chooses to align himself with. But there’s something grotesque aboutthe NBA’s first active billionairecollecting millions more to promote an industry fueling an emerging public-health crisis, while burning extraordinary quantities of fuel to avoid the mild inconvenience of the train.Johnson spent 14 years protecting Philadelphia’s quarterbacks before deciding there were things more important than football and money. James has accumulated enough wealth to say no to almost anything, yet he keeps finding reasons to say yes. Perhaps that’s the most lamentable part of the spectacle: a man who once seemed determined to change the world now seems more concerned with what it will pay him to fly over it.Explore more on these topicsLeBron JamesPhiladelphiaPhiladelphia 76ersPhiladelphia EaglesUS sportsNBABasketballcommentShareReuse this content

title: Bruno Guimarães completes Arsenal comeback to end Leeds’ unbeaten run | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Second-half goals from Riccardo Calafiori and substitute Bruno Guimarães earn Arsenal a win over Leeds after the visitors took a shock first-half lead.
Author: Paul MacInnes
Headline: Second-half goals from Riccardo Calafiori and substitute Bruno Guimarães earn Arsenal a win over Leeds after the visitors took a shock first-half lead.
Content: Bruno Guimarães shows his delight after scoring Arsenal’s winner against Leeds.Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenBruno Guimarães shows his delight after scoring Arsenal’s winner against Leeds.Photograph: Julian Finney/Getty ImagesPremier LeagueBruno Guimarães completes Arsenal comeback to end Leeds’ unbeaten runPaul MacInnesat the Emirates StadiumSat 10 Oct 2026 09.41 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 16.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleArsenal built the foundations of their new success on a desire for competition, an appetite for battle. But what happens when that spirit is insufficient, when your opponents play just as hard as you do? Well, then you bring on Bruno Guimarães and you play even harder.Arsenal had just snatched an equaliser against a dominant Leeds side when Mikel Artetaintroduced his key summer signing. The former Newcastle captain has been having to bide his time but when he entered the field just after the hour, he turned the game on its head.Arsenal 2-1 Leeds: Premier League – liveRead moreArsenal had been ponderous until this point, even uncertain at times. The passing had been intricate, not incisive, and echoes of familiar weaknesses had put the crowd on edge. Guimarães put paid to all that. Not only snapping into tackles, not only moving the ball at pace, he was desperate for everything to go faster, more aggressively, with sharper intention. Nine minutes after coming on, he scored the winner.It was a goal that deserved to decide the contest and reflected the best of what the home side had been trying to achieve. Play developed down the left where Noni Madueke had shone, but here it was Bukayo Saka playing a one-two with Martin Ødegaard. The captain then poked a short pass to Declan Rice who – with Guimarães now covering him – had burst into the opposition area. Rice back-heeled the ball to the edge of the area and there was the Brazilian waiting, poised, to steer the ball unerringly into the corner of James Trafford’s goal.In the time between Leeds’ opener and the winner, Arsenal had five efforts on goal, the same as in the preceding 55 minutes. Once the lead was established, they should have had at least two more goals, with Ødegaard somehow missing from two yards out and Trafford denying Saka in a one-on-one in the final move of the match. Leeds did not feature as an attacking threat in the final half hour, so decisive was the switch in momentum.View image in fullscreenRiccardo Calafiori equalises for Arsenal against Leeds.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersArteta said his team had to “pinch our desire to win” to overcome a visiting side who appear no longer to be punching above their weight, but rather have moved up a class.“We had to face the challenge because [Leeds] are a team that hadn’t lost in thePremier League,” he said. “They’re in a great position because they fully deserve it. They are incredibly dangerous and we got into a situation, [a goal down] after that defeat against Brighton, 12:30 kick-off.“It is a bad mixture and we got out of it through … pinching our desire to win, by showing the personality and courage that we have in this team.”Arteta will be able to take satisfaction from the way his team managed the result, the effectiveness of his substitutes and other smaller details such as the continuing creative contributions of Rice – now with three assists to his name – and a second goal for Riccardo Calafiori, whose buccaneering inside runs have been a feature of the season.On the other hand, his midfield was outmuscled and outplayed in the first hour, with the opening 10 minutes of the second half a period of dominance for the visitors that deservedly delivered a goal when James Justin finished Gabriel Gudmundsson’s cross after the Swede had run off the back of Ben White.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenJames Justin (centre) fires Leeds ahead.Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Action Images/ReutersArsenal’s centre-halves, are looking like less of the sum of their parts, with Ezri Konsa and Gabriel uncertain when faced with the accuracy and variation of Leeds’ deliveries.“It’s a credit to the mentality that Mikel Arteta has created, that even on a tough day they found a way to win”, said Daniel Farke.
