The German bemoaned the Arsenal equaliser, bundled home by Calafiori after White had knocked down a Madueke cross, believing that if Trafford had got a hand to it, “we would have gone on to take three points.”With the proviso that there can be no back-slapping in defeat, however, Farke said the match showed his team’s improvement since returning to the Premier League. “We have developed in all aspects,” he said. “You can speak about game management, you can speak about pressing, about compactness against the ball, or quality in possession, or in counterattacks. We were able to compete much better with set pieces.“Today we came very close to winning an away game against one of the best sides in the world and we played exactly on their level, more or less.”Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueArsenalLeeds Unitedmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m supposed to be here’: Angel Reese’s road from ridicule to the WNBA finals | Angel Reese | The Guardian
description: After years of mockery and doubts about her game, Reese has helped carry Atlanta to the WNBA’s biggest stage. Her critics might want to start forming an apology queue
Author: Bryan Armen Graham
Headline: After years of mockery and doubts about her game, Reese has helped carry Atlanta to the WNBA’s biggest stage. Her critics might want to start forming an apology queue
Content: Angel Reese (center) celebrates with her Atlanta Dream teammates after completing a three-game sweep of New York to reach the WNBA finals.Photograph: Ishika Samant/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAngel Reese (center) celebrates with her Atlanta Dream teammates after completing a three-game sweep of New York to reach the WNBA finals.Photograph: Ishika Samant/Getty ImagesAngel Reese‘I’m supposed to be here’: Angel Reese’s road from ridicule to the WNBA finalsAfter years of mockery and doubts about her game, Reese has helped carry Atlanta to the WNBA’s biggest stage. Her critics might want to start forming an apology queueBryan Armen Grahamat Barclays CenterSat 10 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 13.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA lot of folks oweAngel Reesean apology after Friday night. They should probably form an orderly queue.Not that the bad-faith take merchants who have spent three years gleefully circulating her missed layups, likening her occasionally awkward footwork to “Bambi on ice” and marveling atthe supposed comic genius of “mebounds”are likely to join it. Theright-wing culture warriorswho turned one of the WNBA’s most naturally gifted rebounders into a joke were never particularly interested in an honest assessment of her basketball abilities. But after Friday the punchline has never worn thinner.Angel Reese powers Atlanta past New York into first WNBA finals since 2013Read moreReese’s careerhas been measured against Caitlin Clark’salmost from the moment the two became household names, their rivalry inflatedinto a culture-war proxy battlethat neither player could fully control. Now Reese has reached the WNBA finals before her more celebrated contemporary, a delicious reversal for those who have spent three seasons insisting she didn’t belong in the same conversation.On Friday in Brooklyn, Reese poured in a team-high 22 points with nine rebounds and two blocked shots as the Atlanta Dreamcompleted a three-game sweepof the New York Liberty with an 85-83 victory, reaching the WNBA finals for the first time since 2013. The 24-year-old scored 18 points before half-time, including a pair of three-pointers, and helped eliminate the2024 championson their home floor.As it happens, Reese had been expecting this moment.“I manifested this when I came to Atlanta. I knew what I was getting. The finals. The finals,” she said afterward. “This team has poured so much into me. We poured so much into each other.”Exactly 364 days earlier, while watching last season’s championship series from the couch, Reese hadposted a predictionon social media: “Manifesting the finals.”“I was watching the finals from home for the last two years and kept saying, just give me one playoff game,” she said. “I manifest a lot of things and think it’s important to speak positively into your life and your team, but this is all God. I’m thankful and blessed to be here and won’t take it for granted.”View image in fullscreenAngel Reese celebrates during Atlanta’s Game 3 victory over New York on Friday night, which sent the Dream into the WNBA finals.Photograph: Mike Lawrence/NBAE/Getty ImagesThe former Chicago Sky forward, who arrived in Atlantain an offseason trade, has found more than a new basketball home.“We have a praying group; eight of our 12 players go to chapel, and we take that seriously,” she said. “It’s a blessing to be around the girls in that locker room.”Reese’s offensive limitations were always real enough. Her finishing around the basket could be erratic, her shooting needed work and her impatience sometimes got the better of her. But there was an enormous difference between acknowledging those weaknesses and insisting they rendered her accomplishments fraudulent.Friday’s post-game news conference in the bowels of Brooklyn’s Barclays Center offered a revealing glimpse of the work she has put into addressing them.Clay Travis: inside the Maga permadad’s world of sports bros, trans panic and mortgagesRead more“For me, it’s really hard for me to not wan to rush success,” Reese admitted.She recalled a particularly demanding shooting drill under Dream coach Karl Smesko, who stopped the exercise until Reese made the required shot. Her teammates were left waiting, and her frustration mounted.“I was upset with him that day, for sure,” she said. “Because I didn’t want to let the team down.”Smesko remembered the episode, explaining that Atlanta had undertaken substantial changes to Reese’s offensive game. He warned her that the adjustments would not feel natural immediately, but that the work would begin to pay off as the season progressed.For much of her first two professions seasons, Reese seemed destined to become a Dennis Rodman for the modern WNBA: a generational rebounder, an indefatigable competitor and the sort of complementary piece whose singular gifts could turn a good team into a great one. That was hardly a modest projection. Rodman was a Hall of Famer and one of basketball’s most influential role players.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBut in her third year, Reese is making even that comparison look increasingly restrictive. She’s becoming the sort of player a championship contender can build around.Her reflections on Friday extended beyond basketball. Reese spoke movingly about her mother, Angel Webb Reese, who raised her and her brother with help from their grandparents and remains her most dependable source of support.“She’s really proud because she knows the dark moments that I’ve been through,” Reese said. “I can pick up the phone at three in the morning, call her crying, and she’s just been there for me.”View image in fullscreenAtlanta’s Rhyne Howard separates teammate Angel Reese and New York’s Sabrina Ionescu during a heated exchange in Friday’s WNBA semi-final Game 3 in Brooklyn.Photograph: Ishika Samant/Getty ImagesHer mother, she explained, asks for little beyond the opportunity to be present.“Support me, show up, and love me, and I’ll give you the world,” Reese said. “She’s not very hard on me, but she’s very loving, and she’s very caring.”It was a reminder of the human being behind the online caricature, and of the private difficulties that cannot be captured in a compilation of missed shots.Friday’s victory came without injured second-leading scorer Allisha Gray, whose absence placed additional demands on Reese and Atlanta’s already depleted rotation. Reese said she had promised Gray that she would help finish the job.“This is what you brought me here for. I got your back. You got my back,” she recalled telling her. “And I’m glad to have her back for the finals.”Atlantawill face the Golden State Valkyriesin the best-of-seven championship series beginning on 17 October. For Reese, who spent her first two seasons hoping for even a single playoff appearance, the prospect of playing for a WNBA title remains almost surreal.“I knew I belonged here and wanted to help this team do whatever it took – not just get out of the first round or semi-finals, but make the finals and win a championship,” she said.“The job isn’t done. We’re happy, but not satisfied.”Explore more on these topicsAngel ReeseAtlanta DreamNew York LibertyGolden State ValkyriesWNBAUS sportsBasketballShareReuse this content

title: Max Verstappen takes F1 Singapore GP pole from Leclerc after sprint win | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: Max Verstappen’s good weekend in Singapore continued on a day when George Russell crashed out of the sprint from the lead
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: Max Verstappen’s good weekend in Singapore continued on a day when George Russell crashed out of the sprint from the lead
Content: Max Verstappen enjoys his pole, flanked by second-placed Charles Leclerc (right) and Lewis Hamilton.Photograph: Mark Thompson/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenMax Verstappen enjoys his pole, flanked by second-placed Charles Leclerc (right) and Lewis Hamilton.Photograph: Mark Thompson/Getty ImagesFormula One 2026Max Verstappen takes F1 Singapore GP pole from Leclerc after sprint winHamilton qualifies third with Antonelli fourthRussell crashed out of sprint when leading on lap oneGiles RichardsSat 10 Oct 2026 11.17 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 14.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile Red Bull andMax Verstappenwere very much on a roll at the Singapore Grand Prix with victory in the sprint and then pole position, Britain’s George Russell was left having to roll with the punches. His vanishingly slight title hopes took another blow after he crashed out of the sprint race on the streets of the Marina Bay circuit.Verstappen’s pole was a mighty lap to beat the Ferrari of Charles Leclerc into second by five-hundredths of a second as the Dutchman enjoys his best form of the season. A 50th pole, his first in Singapore coming on theback of a pole and win at the last round in Malaysiaand pole and victory in the sprint at Marina Bay.Singapore Formula One Grand Prix – updates as Verstappen adds pole to sprint victoryRead moreBehind him, the title is edging close to being decided. The championship leader, Kimi Antonelli, was fourth in qualifying for Mercedes, a decent return after he has struggled with the car over the weekend and of greater import given Russell, his teammate and title rival, will start from the back of the grid on Sunday.Russell qualified in sixth – in the process saving soft tyres for use on Sunday – but will be opening at the back of the field because of the penalties applied for taking a new engine this weekend. He had no control over the reliability issues that saw his engine fail at the last round in Malaysia but his weekend in Singapore was compromised on Saturday after he made an error in the sprint and crashed out from the lead of the race.He had taken the lead, passing Verstappen into the first corner but put his wheels on to the white lines at the final corner at the end of the opening lap. In the wet conditions, he lost the rear, spun and went into the barriers, out of the race and the team had to work fast just to repair the car before qualifying. Russell held his hands up for the mistake and it once more played into Antonelli’s hands.“Miscalculation,” Russell said. “Came through the corner had more battery deployment than I thought, pushed me a little bit wider than I hoped and went onto the white line. Silly mistake. Big consequences.”View image in fullscreenGeorge Russell crashes out of the sprint race in Singapore.Photograph: Mark Sutton/Formula 1/Getty ImagesBig consequences indeed. Antonelli’s advantage over his teammate is now 89 points. If he leaves Singapore with a lead of 101 points, he can seal his first championship at the next round in Austin.Verstappen was all but flawless in Singapore. Having thrown himself into the lap on the absolute edge, he found the limit with precision, his time of 1min 31.373sec on his first run in Q3 could not be matched. Lewis Hamilton chased him hard and then Leclerc edged into second place, but no one could better Verstappen’s effort. Hamilton finished third for Ferrari, with Lando Norris in fifth for McLaren.It was another demonstration of how the recent upgrades have improved the Red Bull and how much more comfortable Verstappen was with the car in Singapore. It is a track where he has yet to win a GP and one of two, along with the Madring, on the current calendar where he has yet to take victory.Verstappen won the sprint, which had been delayed because of heavy rain, with complete control from the front once he had inherited the lead after Russell’s crash. He had enough pace to comfortably see off Hamilton in second, who had made a superb start to move from sixth to third off the line. It was very much a processional affair, with overtaking all but impossible as drivers managed their tyres to the flag.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe short-form dash was enlivened by late drama when Norris made a move on his teammate, Oscar Piastri, on the final lap, the pair clashed, taking the Australian out and dropping Norris to eighth, to the consternation of his McLaren team.“Seeing two McLarens making contact like that is simply not acceptable,” said the team principal, Andrea Stella. “Something we will discuss with out drivers, we will iterate that the team interest is far bigger than any of us.”That moved Antonelli up from sixth to fourth place, another indication that simply everything seems to be going the Italian’s way, even when he is just keeping his head down and grinding out a result.The track was holding a sprint for the first time as F1 looks to enliven some of the more processional circuits, including having Monaco host a sprint next season. However, it was not welcomed with any enthusiasm by the drivers. “If it was dry that would probably have been the most boring race to have watched,” said Hamilton. An opinion echoed by his teammate Leclerc, who was third in the race.“I don’t think it makes sense to have any sprint races on city tracks in general,” he said. “Here or Monaco, I don’t think it adds anything to the weekend.”Explore more on these topicsFormula One 2026Formula OneMotor sportMax VerstappennewsShareReuse this content

title: Seixas makes Giro di Lombardia history after riders stage safety protest | Cycling | The Guardian
description: The 20-year-old French prodigy Paul Seixas ended his breakout season as a history-making youngest Monument winner with a stunning victory at the Giro di Lombardia
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The 20-year-old French prodigy Paul Seixas ended his breakout season as a history-making youngest Monument winner with a stunning victory at the Giro di Lombardia
Content: Paul Seixas celebrates at the finish line ending an incredible season as a Monument winner.Photograph: Dario Belingheri/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPaul Seixas celebrates at the finish line ending an incredible season as a Monument winner.Photograph: Dario Belingheri/Getty ImagesCyclingSeixas makes Giro di Lombardia history after riders stage safety protestFrench prodigy is youngest winner of the ClassicEvenepoel highlights death of Finlay TarlingAgenciesSat 10 Oct 2026 11.33 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 07.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePaul Seixas ended his breakout season as a history-making Monument winner with a stunning victory at the Giro di Lombardia. The 20-year-old French prodigy became the youngest winner of the Classic of the Falling Leaves and the fourth-youngest winner of a Monument.The Vuelta champion Enric Mas took second place, 48 seconds back, with Giulio Ciccone rounding out the podium just over a minute behind the winner.Earlier, riders staged a brief protest, delaying the start of the race by five minutes to draw attention to safety concernsafter a series of incidentsinvolving non-race vehicles.Once organisers completed the countdown for the start, the peloton remained stationary, creating a moment of confusion before Remco Evenepoel addressed the crowd. “There’s too many incidents happening with vehicles in the race,” he said.“Unfortunately we lost the life of a brother and of a colleague of us, so we want to make this statement to show to the world we cannot keep accepting the fact that guys are getting injured or dying in what we like the most to do.”Evenepoel was referring tothe death of Finlay Tarling, the younger brother of Netcompany Ineos rider Josh Tarling. Finlay died after a collision with a vehicle during the Tour of Portugal on 14 August. On Wednesday, Thomas Gloag and Marcel Camprubi werestruck by a police motorcycle travelling in the opposite directionduring the Tre Valli Varesine.Seixas launched a devastating attack on the Civiglio climb with around 19km of the 239km one-day classic remaining, and within a kilometre, he had dropped all of his remaining challengers.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe RecapThe best of our sports journalism from the past seven days and a heads-up on the weekend’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPidcock ‘mad’ after two teammates collide with police motorcyclist in ItalyRead moreEvenepoel was the first to flounder, followed shortly by pre-race favourite Isaac del Toro and then world champion Brandon McNulty. Evenepoel and McNulty eventually came home in fourth and fifth.With Tadej Pogacar, the winner of the last five editions of Lombardia, missing due to injury, Seixas took his chance to end an incredible season as a Monument winner. It was only his third Monument – the five most prestigious one-day classics on the calendar – having finished seventh at Lombardia last year and second at Liège-Bastogne-Liege in April. Pogacar had won both of those.This success completes a remarkable first full season in the professional ranks for Seixas. He was fourth at the Tour de France – his debut Grand Tour – in July, having won the Tour of the Basque Country and La Flèche Wallonne earlier in the year. He had also impressed in second-placed finishes at Strade Bianche, Liège and the Montreal GP.But he endured a disappointing world championships last month, cramping up in the final stages and finishing 15th, although a week earlier he had won the time-trial bronze medal behind specialists Evenepoel and Filippo Ganna.Explore more on these topicsCyclingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Portugal suspend Cristiano Ronaldo after walking out on national team  | Cristiano Ronaldo | The Guardian
description: Cristiano Ronaldo has been provisionally suspended by the Portuguese football federation following his decision to walk out on the national team
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Cristiano Ronaldo has been provisionally suspended by the Portuguese football federation following his decision to walk out on the national team
Content: Cristiano Ronaldo walked out on the Portugal squad during the international window.Photograph: NTB/ReutersView image in fullscreenCristiano Ronaldo walked out on the Portugal squad during the international window.Photograph: NTB/ReutersCristiano RonaldoPortugal suspend Cristiano Ronaldo after walking out on national teamFederation opens disciplinary proceedingsVeteran has been critical of coach Jorge JesusAgence France-Presse and ReutersSat 10 Oct 2026 16.48 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 09.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleCristiano Ronaldo has been provisionally suspended as the Portuguese football federation (FPF) opened disciplinary proceedings against the 41-year-old after hisdecision to walk out on the national team.Ronaldo apologised to supporters on Tuesdaywhile criticising the Portugal coach, Jorge Jesus, and said he would serve any “suspension that is imposed” on him.“Disciplinary ​proceedings have been initiated against Cristiano ‌Ronaldo dos Santos Aveiro, following ‌a decision by the non-professional section on 9 October 2026,” the FPF said in ‌a statement released on Saturday.Ronaldo gave his ⁠account of the dispute ⁠that promptedhis ​departure from Copenhagenbefore Portugal’s Nations League match against Denmark last week.Ronaldo said Jesushad agreed a planunder which the forward would ⁠miss the Norway and Denmark matches to manage his fitness. However, on the day of the Norway game, the coach told him he would play for 30 ⁠minutes.“Everyone knows the rest. I warmed up from half-time onwards, watched the minutes tick by and wasn’t called ​on,” Ronaldo said. “The manager had broken his ‌word to me.”In the games where Ronaldo was either an unused substitute or absent,Portugalwon all three and his replacement, Gonçalo Ramos, seized his chance by scoring three times. Portugal’s next Nations League games will come against Denmark and Wales in November.Ronaldo ended the international break with a long post to his 679 million followers on Instagram, where he asked Jesus to acknowledge a mistake in asking him to warm up on the sidelines and then not send him on the field against Norway. The Portugal coach did not acknowledge any mistake.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRonaldo wrote that he expected a suspension under federation rules but promised his fans “we will have one or more farewell matches.” He has already returned to his club team, Al Nassr in Saudi Arabia, and scored in a 3-0 victory over Diriyah on Friday.Explore more on these topicsCristiano RonaldoPortugalnewsShareReuse this content

title: Carrick ‘massively disappointed’ after United drop points against 10-man Spurs | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: After a 1-1 draw that left Roberto De Zerbi praising 10-man Spurs’ character, his Manchester United counterpart reflected on the club’s worst start since 1986
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: After a 1-1 draw that left Roberto De Zerbi praising 10-man Spurs’ character, his Manchester United counterpart reflected on the club’s worst start since 1986
Content: Michael Carrick had a lot to reflect on after Manchester United conceded a late equaliser to a team with 10 men.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersView image in fullscreenMichael Carrick had a lot to reflect on after Manchester United conceded a late equaliser to a team with 10 men.Photograph: Phil Noble/ReutersManchester UnitedCarrick ‘massively disappointed’ after United drop points against 10-man SpursSix points from six games is worst start since 1986De Zerbi praises Spurs’ character after late equaliserJamie Jacksonat Old TraffordSat 10 Oct 2026 16.19 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 16.25 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMichael Carrick was left “massively disappointed” by Manchester United’s 1-1 draw with Tottenham at Old Trafford and admitted they need more points after managing six from their opening six league games.This is United’s poorest start to the season since 1986, Saturday’s draw coming when concedingDominic Solanke’s added-time equaliserfor 10-man Spurs, following Rodrigo Bentancur’s 78th-minute red card. The midfielder was sent off five minutes after Bryan Mbeumo’s opener had left United heading for only a second league victory.Solanke strikes late as 10-man Spurs salvage point at Manchester UnitedRead moreCarrick said: “I am massively disappointed with the result, for sure. A mixed performance. I’m not happy with the amount of points that we’ve had so far. There’s no hiding from that. I think it could have been different for a couple of little things here or there, but the reality is the reality, we’ve got to accept it, you know. We need to put things in a direction, in a positive direction quite quickly, that’s pretty plain.”United were disjointed throughout. The manager was asked if he felt let down by the players. “I don’t feel let down, because you can make mistakes. You can make mistakes, things go against you,” said Carrick. “I’ve made mistakes in games, and it’s not so much letting everyone down. We’ve all got standards, we’ve all got levels, the players have got levels and standards, and they hold their hands up at times when something goes against them.”United’s fans jeered at times during the game. “When things aren’t quite going to plan, I understand the reaction at times,” said the manager. “Obviously, it hurts a lot. It’s not nice to go through, but sometimes you have to go through it, that’s how it is.“I care as much as anybody about this place, so sometimes you could say too much because then it overspills. But it’s coming from a good place, really, and so I understand it.”View image in fullscreenLuke Shaw (right) clashes with Rodrigo Bentancur (centre) and other Tottenham players.Photograph: Ash Donelon/Manchester United/Getty ImagesBentancur might have caused a serious injury had a scissors-challenge on Shaw connected.Roberto De Zerbibacked his midfielder, who was sent off for a head-butt in the resulting melee.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“I kiss Rodrigo and say thanks,” said the Spurs manager. “It is clear it is a mistake from Rodrigo, it is not the right reaction in football but in that moment maybe with 10 players we played with more courage, more energy and for a long time Tottenham played without this blood this character. I am the coach and I want to see this character every game.”While Spurs have only three points and remain winless, they are now off the bottom though remain in the relegation zone. “Today has been the game where for the first time this season we showed we are a team, we played for the teammates, we played together,” said De Zerbi.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedMichael CarrickTottenham HotspurRoberto De ZerbinewsShareReuse this content

title: Why we’re stuck with a Premier League in the clutches of the global mega-rich  | Premier League | The Guardian
description: There’s little prospect of a troubled model changing in a country that welcomes wealthy international owners with open arms
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: There’s little prospect of a troubled model changing in a country that welcomes wealthy international owners with open arms
Content: The Etihad Stadium at sunset. Manchester City’s Gulf-based owners are a world away from the local businessmen who once coveted English clubs.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe Etihad Stadium at sunset. Manchester City’s Gulf-based owners are a world away from the local businessmen who once coveted English clubs.Photograph: Ed Sykes/Action Images/ReutersInside footballPremier LeagueWhy we’re stuck with a Premier League in the clutches of the global mega-richJonathan WilsonThere’s little prospect of the model changing in a country that welcomes wealthy international owners with open armsSat 10 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTShareFootball, the world’s most popular sport, played by laws drawn up in London in 1863. ThePremier Leagueis the UK’s greatest soft power export. Premier League clubs are owned by a deputy prime minister of Abu Dhabi, the public investment fund of Saudi Arabia, a billionaire based in Monaco for tax reasons and a disappointing assortment of investors and private equity funds. And what, really, could be more British than that? Football truly is the national game.Whatthe Manchester City casehas exposed is just how difficult it is to regulate some of the richest and most powerful bodies in the world. While the wait for the verdict was frustrating, it’s perhaps unavoidable given the possibility of legal objection at every turn when a leaked email from City’s in-house lawyer during Uefa’s action against the club had threatened to “spend 30 million on the 50 best lawyersin the world to sue them for the next 10 years”. You didn’t get that with Albert Alexander Sr or Peter Swales.Everton owner The Friedkin Group exploring sale of club after two yearsRead moreFootball clubs in England and Wales still represent their communities, a relationship that may be strained in certain cases by the pressures of a globalised entertainment economy, but remains broadly true. Arsenal can feel like the club of choice for the nouveau fan from across the world, butthe scenes of celebrationwhen they ended their 22-year wait for the league title last season were an undeniable expression of local pride.The idea that there was ever an idyll when clubs were run by benevolent potentates for the good of those communities is romantic nonsense. But just because there was no golden age is not to say that the situation has always been as bleak as this.How did we get into a situation in which clubs are flotsam on the swirling currents of geopolitics and the world economy? Chelsea alone in the past four years have had aRussian oligarch forced to sell the clubafter falling under UK government sanctions, while a subsequent American co-owner has been forced to sell his minority stake after his insurance business came under federal investigation in the US. It’s a curious world in which the professional gamblers feel like a welcome breath of fresh air.View image in fullscreenChelsea fans hold banner during a peaceful, fan-led protest calling for accountability and structural change at Chelsea Football Club in January. Fans criticised the club’s ownership model, recruitment strategy, and overall leadership since the takeover, urging an end to micromanagement and a return to long-term ambition at the top level of English and European football.Photograph: Martin Pope/Getty ImagesThe days of the local businessmen, the owners of mines, shipyards and factories, the hauliers and scrap-metal dealers, are gone. Some invested because they genuinely wanted to give back to their communities or liked the sport. Others did so because it was easier to fund a local football club than to improve working conditions or pay a proper wage. And some did so because, wrongly in most cases, they thought there may be money to be made.But nobody should think those were days of purity. The decrepitude of English stadiums in the 1980s should caution anybody who thinks football was uncomplicatedly better then.The contradiction has always lain at the heart of English football. Clubs represent their communities and for fans support becomes an aspect of identity, a link to family and place and past, a role that has only become more significant as the influence of traditional institutions – the church, the workplace, the social club – has faded. Yet fans in England have almost never owned their club, which in part underlies the present crisis.That is not to say fan ownership is a panacea. There is much to be admired about the German 50+1 model which, to oversimplify, ensures outside investors can never own a majority of the club. But it has not prevented Bayern Munich from winning 13 of the past 14 Bundesliga titles. Some sort of recognition that a club is not just a business, that it has a community function might, though, have prevented the free-for-all that has led to this mess.At least when most owners were local, there was some understanding of what the club meant to its area, and a recognition that exploitation or neglect could have direct consequences. No owner wanted demonstrations at the directors’ entrance, or to be jeered as he drove the streets in his Rolls-Royce, or to have his car showroom boycotted because he put up ticket prices then sold a popular centre-forward at a knockdown price. The distant majority shareholder in his boardroom in Los Angeles, his penthouse in Monte Carlo or his luxury villa on the Gulf feels the sting less keenly.Richard Scudamore, the former chief executive of the Premier League, who did more to shape the modern competition, for good and for ill, than any other individual always spoke of being “neutral about ownership models”. Essentially that meant taking the money without worrying too much about where it came from. The current Premier League is the consequence: a gleaming, world-leading edifice, but built on what?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPerhaps it’s not fair to be too harsh on the Premier League. This is not just modern football; it is modern Britain. As Miguel Delaney and Jack Pitt-Brookeargued on the Libero podcast this week, the Premier League is a direct outcome of Blairite economic policy, a point made clear inOliver Bullough’s Butler to the WorldIn the book he described the classic New Labour approach as “allowing something, making money from it and attempting to solve the problems it causes after they’ve occurred”.Premier League: 10 things to look out for this weekendRead moreBut how do you solve those problems in football? How can football extricate itself from the clutches of the mega-rich? Regulation, up to a point, helps – and there may at least now be a sense that there can be enforcement. Whatever the flaws of theprofitability and sustainability rules, or thesquad cost ratiothat has replaced them, it may be useful if football could accept the basic premise that the game shouldn’t just be about how rich your owner happens to be. But that can only go so far; a door open to the world has admitted a world of problems.Short of some sort of financial crash in football, the sort of apocalyptic event that would make the sport unappealing to big finance and require the game to be built anew, with a fresh spirit that might recategorise football clubs as community assets rather than simple businesses, we’re probably stuck with it.How, after all, could football ever escape the society that produced it?Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueInside footballBusinessManchester CityChelseacommentShareReuse this content

title: Henderson and João Pedro lead Chelsea charge against Bournemouth | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Jordan Henderson scored his first two goals for Chelsea in a 5-1 thrashing of Bournemouth at Stamford Bridge
Author: Jacob Steinberg
Headline: Jordan Henderson scored his first two goals for Chelsea in a 5-1 thrashing of Bournemouth at Stamford Bridge
Content: Jordan Henderson celebrates with Cole Palmer (right) after scoring his second goal, and Chelsea’s fifth, against Bournemouth.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenJordan Henderson celebrates with Cole Palmer (right) after scoring his second goal, and Chelsea’s fifth, against Bournemouth.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersPremier LeagueHenderson and João Pedro lead Chelsea charge against BournemouthJacob Steinbergat Stamford BridgeSat 10 Oct 2026 12.18 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 16.28 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWatch and learn, kids. The day began with one for the youth audience, Cole Palmer appearing on a live stream to explain the thinking behind his latest contract extension. It finished with the oldest player to joinChelseaduring the BlueCo era stealing the show with an all-action midfield display.Even Palmer was happy to step aside as Jordan Henderson used his right foot to curl home a free-kick that drew comparisons with one of David Beckham’s specials. It was Henderson’s second spectacular strike – he marked his home debut by opening the scoring with a bending effort from 20 yards and also laid on an assist for Morgan Rogers to make it 2-0 – although it is fair to assume that Xabi Alonso did not bring the veteran to Stamford Bridge for his goalscoring prowess.The idea was more to lift standards in the dressing room. Chelsea needed experience and are surely better off now a 36-year-old starting for them in midfield is no longer a laughable notion.Aston Villa’s wait for home win goes on after Ajer hits back for BrentfordRead more“We signed him for everything,” Alonso said of Henderson. “If he’s able to score two beauties as today, we are more than happy for him. But apart from the goals he’s done many good things. He’s always involved in the action, always giving solutions to teammates.”Henderson set the tone for Chelsea, driving into tackles and raising the tempo with the urgency of his passing. He joined from Brentford in the summer and is keen to do more than make up the numbers. Chelsea, up to fifth after their first win in four league games, were more stable with Henderson alongside Moisés Caicedo, who lasted 72 minutes on his long-awaited return from a calf injury.View image in fullscreenMoisés Caicedo (left) returned to the Chelsea team after a spell on the sidelines due to injury.Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesAlonso, who was without Reece James after the captain picked up a knee injury in training on Friday, was still disappointed his side have now gone 22 league games without a clean sheet. They were 3-0 up when Evanilson pulled a goal back forBournemouth, who are finding the transition from Andoni Iraola to Marco Rose trickier than anticipated and must manage games better.Even so, Alonso was pleased with Chelsea’s level. They have scored in the first 10 minutes in five of their six league games this season and are a match for anyone when the front three of Palmer, Rogers and João Pedro take full flight.Palmer had a point to prove after having his desire to play for England questioned by Thomas Tuchel last month. His impact was immediate, although it owed much to Bournemouth’s naivety. The visitors lined up in a flat 4-4-2 formation and gave Palmer far too much space when he sauntered down the right in the first minute.It was encouraging to see Palmer moving freely, especially after Alonso’s admission that the playmaker’s decision to sit out the international break was related to last season’s groin pain, but Bournemouth were a soft touch. There was no challenge on the 24-year-old, who has displayed his commitment to Chelsea by signing on until 2034.Palmer floated into the area, turned and rolled the ball to Henderson, who hit it first time with the inside of his right foot and saw his bending effort go in off the inside of the right post.View image in fullscreenJordan Henderson (centre) give Chelsea an early lead with a fine finish.Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/ReutersThere were 68 seconds on the clock when Henderson became Chelsea’s oldest scorer in thePremier Leaguesince John Terry in May 2017. “We knew Chelsea are a team that starts well,” Rose said. “It was our responsibility that we didn’t react the right way with this information.”Bournemouth were overwhelmed. Chelsea pushed again in the third minute, Palmer’s flick freeing Pedro Neto to test Djordje Petrovic. The ball broke loose and Henderson swept a pass to Rogers, who cut in from the left and his shot flew in via a deflection off Antonio Silva.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIpswich’s O’Shea and Ouattara stun Fulham with last-gasp comeback winRead moreThe focus switched to Bournemouth’s long list of absentees. Justin Kluivert and Eli Junior Kroupi are big losses in attack. Alex Scott, the subject of multiple bids from Chelsea in the summer,exacerbated a thigh problemduringa scintillating displayforEngland against Croatia last Saturday.These are worrying times for Bournemouth, who are winless after six league games. Goal difference is keeping them out of the bottom three and they struggled without Scott’s energy and quality in midfield. Ryan Christie and Tyler Adams were overrun and Silva had a nightmare at the back, his error at the start of the second half allowing Neto to nip in and set up João Pedro to make it 3-0 with an emphatic shot.Bournemouth had chances during the first half, Christie, Rayan and Silva drawing saves from Emiliano Martínez, but it suited Chelsea for a basketball game to develop.View image in fullscreenA tidy finish from close range gave João Pedro a second goal of the game and Chelsea a fourth.Photograph: Darren Walsh/Chelsea FC/Getty ImagesThere were echoes of past battles between Alonso and Rose in the Bundesliga. Rose, who ended Alonso’s 35-game unbeaten run with Bayer Leverkusen when he was RB Leipzig’s manager, was a distinct second-best this time. Evanilson bundled in from a corner, but Chelsea were rampant.The fourth goal arrived when Rogers found the overlapping Pep Chavarria, whose low cross was gobbled up by João Pedro. Alonso, who had become increasingly frantic on the touchline, relaxed. He was a great midfielder in his day and will have appreciated the technique when Henderson’s free-kick flew beyond the reach of Petrovic.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueChelseaBournemouthmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Real Madrid’s Vinícius Júnior sent off for hair-pulling in victory over Villarreal | La Liga | The Guardian
description: Vinícius Júnior’s goal was disallowed and the substitute was dismissed after a VAR review showed he had pulled Nathan Saliba’s hair
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Vinícius Júnior’s goal was disallowed and the substitute was dismissed after a VAR review showed he had pulled Nathan Saliba’s hair
Content: Real Madrid’s Vinícius Júnior is held back by Antonio Rüdiger after being sent off.Photograph: Ángel Martínez/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenReal Madrid’s Vinícius Júnior is held back by Antonio Rüdiger after being sent off.Photograph: Ángel Martínez/Getty ImagesLa LigaReal Madrid’s Vinícius Júnior sent off for hair-pulling in victory over VillarrealAFPSat 10 Oct 2026 17.38 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 18.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYan Diomandé earned Real Madrid a tight 1-0 victory over Villarreal to keep them six points behind La Liga leaders Barcelona, even though wingerVinícius Júniorwas sent off for hair pulling.Vinícius, on as a substitute, scored but his goal was disallowed and then he was dismissed after a VAR review showed he had pulled the hair of Villarreal’s Nathan Saliba.European football: Gordon boosts Barcelona and Bayern battle backRead moreJosé Mourinho’s side battled through the final stages with 10 men, holding on to win and provisionally going third. But the red card left a bitter taste for Real, with Vinícius running the risk of a potential ban which could keep him out of El Clásico on 25 October.“I don’t know what’s going on with the referees, with this red card, I don’t understand,” said the Madrid midfielder Aurélien Tchouaméni. “But the most important thing is the victory.”Kylian Mbappé was fit to start the match for Madrid after suffering a knee problem playing for France during the international break. There were a smattering of whistles for the superstar forward, with some fans believing he has been unprofessional in recent weeks, but also applause from others.Mbappé, acandidate for the Ballon d’Ortrophy later this month, was Madrid’s most threatening player in the first half, although he had little competition.View image in fullscreenPlayers react as the referee, Isidro Díaz de Mera Escuderos, sends off Vinícius Júnior.Photograph: Denis Doyle/Getty ImagesMourinho started with out-of-form Vinícius on the bench, following his trips to Australia and India with Brazil during the international break.Madrid improved defensively, giving Villarreal few chances of note, but struggled to build much in attack themselves in a drab opening half.Mbappé struck the post from Álvaro Carreras’s lay-off as Madrid pushed Villarreal back early on. Villarreal soon gained a foothold and restricted Madrid’s opportunities, until Mbappé forced a good save from Peter Gulacsi.There was some more mild whistling for Madrid’s display from their fans at half-time, but soon they were able tocelebrate summer arrival Diomandé’s first goal for the club. The Ivorian winger, Madrid’s record signing, produced a sharp low finish into the far corner after good work from Federico Valverde to play him in.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenYan Diomandé scores the only goal of the game at the Bernabéu.Photograph: Óscar del Pozo/AFP/Getty ImagesVinícius thought he had doubled Madrid’s lead after Jude Bellingham charged in down the left and cut the ball back for him. However the winger’s joy turned to anger after the referee, Isidro Díaz de Mera Escuderos, was called to watch Vinícius’s hair pull on Saliba in the buildup by VAR and sent off the Brazilian, disallowing his goal.Madrid’s Belgian goalkeeper Thibaut Courtois, who had made a couple of smart saves earlier in the half, then produced an acrobatic stop to thwart Carlos Romero.Mbappé was denied again by the Hungarian goalkeeper Gulasci as the forward left the Bernabéu frustrated in his hunt for goals, although his team were able to clinch three important points to stay on Barcelona’s trail.Explore more on these topicsLa LigaReal MadridVinícius JúniorVillarrealmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Ten-man Brighton continue fine form with battling win at Sunderland  | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Two second-half goals secured Brighton’s third consecutive win in the Premier League, despite Pascal Struijk’s red card at Sunderland
Author: Louise Taylor
Headline: Two second-half goals secured Brighton’s third consecutive win in the Premier League, despite Pascal Struijk’s red card at Sunderland
Content: Maxim De Cuyper (left) scored Brighton’s first goal in their win at Sunderland.Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/ReutersView image in fullscreenMaxim De Cuyper (left) scored Brighton’s first goal in their win at Sunderland.Photograph: Lee Smith/Action Images/ReutersPremier LeagueTen-man Brighton continue fine form with battling win at SunderlandLouise Taylorat the Stadium of LightSat 10 Oct 2026 12.20 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 16.32 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Jaouen Hadjam lashed Brighton’s second goal low beyond Robin Roefs, it sparked a mass exodus. With a smattering of boos, the Stadium of Light emptied at a speed of knots and frown lines creased the forehead of Sunderland’s manager, Régis Le Bris.Undaunted by Pascal Struijk’s second-half red card, Brighton had not merely cemented their hold on third place but boosted an already healthy points tally to 13.Henderson and João Pedro lead Chelsea charge against BournemouthRead moreThis was not quite as fluent asBrighton’s 3-0 deconstruction of Arsenalbefore the international break, but no one can possibly underestimate their supreme defensive organisation now.“It wasn’t easy but we always had this belief we could get something here,” said the Brighton manager, Fabian Hürzeler. “We keep clean sheets and we always have chances to score. We’ve always played good football, but I don’t want us just to be known as a nice team anymore.”Sunderland are stuck on four points with a solitaryPremier Leaguevictory to their name this season. They head to central Portugal for Thursday’s Europa League meeting with Torreense in introspective mode.View image in fullscreenJaouen Hadjam sealed the win for Brighton at the Stadium of Light.Photograph: Allstar Picture Library Ltd/Ed Sykes/Allstar Picture Library Ltd/SportsphotoAs a cagey first half unfolded, Kyril Louis-Dreyfus looked on anxiously from the directors’ box. Sunderland’s owner and chair has added the title chief executive to his club portfolio after Tom Burwell’s abrupt departure just five months into the role of interim CEO.Among the 29-year-old’s more pressing tasks in this hands-on role is to secure a front-of-shirt sponsor after the collapse of a deal with Visit Ghana.At the interval, Louis-Dreyfus was probably relieved the scoreboard read 0-0. Deep in stoppage time at the end of the first period, Struijk had headed against an upright with Roefs beaten.View image in fullscreenEnzo Le Fee shows his disappointment after Sunderland’s defeat to Brighton.Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty ImagesIt was the best chance of a half low on clearcut chances and only really enlivened by some beautiful calibrated deliveries from Enzo Le Fée. Sunderland’s attacking playmaker created decent early openings for Wilson Isidor – deputising for the hamstrung Brian Brobbey – and Thomas Meunier. Significantly, though, Le Fée faded badly in the second half.In the 53rd minute, a home defence missing the hamstrung Dan Ballard paid the price for a failure to clear a long throw when Pascal Gross’ clever through ball cued up Maxim De Cuyper to slide the crispest of low first-time shots between Roefs and a post. It was the 35-year-old Gross’s seventh direct goal involvement in a Brighton goal in his last six Premier League appearances, but his team were soon reduced to 10 men.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWhen a poorly positioned Struijk felled Isidor as he accelerated towards the area the £20m summer signing from Leeds denied a clear goalcoring opportunity, but initially the referee, Tom Bramall, did not see it that way. The video assistant referee urged Bramall to visit the pitchside monitor, which prompted a change of heart and a red card for Struijk.View image in fullscreenBrighton defender Pascal Struijk was shown a red card after a VAR review for this challenge on  Sunderland's Wilson Isidor.Photograph: Oli Scarff/AFP/Getty ImagesDespite their numerical disadvantage, Brighton continued to look comfortable. It did not help Sunderland’s cause that, unusually, Granit Xhaka proved untypically slapdash in possession.Perhaps the strain of admitting to obtaining a fake Covid vaccination certificateduring the pandemic – the authorities in Lucerne issued Switzerland’s captain with a suspended £136,000 fine last week – took its toll.Recent social media footage shows Xhaka demonstrating commendable restraint in the face of jibes from Newcastle fans while out shopping with his wife near their home in Gosforth, but he could have perhaps done with a little more trademark aggression here. In its absence, the visiting substitutes Georginio Rutter and Hadjam combined for the Algeria left-back to strip the shine expertly from Sunderland’s Portuguese trip.“It was a tight, intense game,” said Le Bris. “But we weren’t at our best. It’s a question of composure. We have to change the momentum.”Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueSunderlandBrighton & Hove Albionmatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Ipswich stun Fulham with last-gasp comeback to increase heat on Arbeloa | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Ryan Sessegnon’s a 55th-minute goal put Fulham on the verge of a first victory but Abdoul Ouattara and Dara O’Shea gave Ipswich a dramatic 2-1 win
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Ryan Sessegnon’s a 55th-minute goal put Fulham on the verge of a first victory but Abdoul Ouattara and Dara O’Shea gave Ipswich a dramatic 2-1 win
Content: Dara O'Shea celebrates scoring Ipswich’s winner in added time, after Abdoul Ouattara equalised against Fulham in the 89th minute.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAView image in fullscreenDara O'Shea celebrates scoring Ipswich’s winner in added time, after Abdoul Ouattara equalised against Fulham in the 89th minute.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PAPremier LeagueIpswich stun Fulham with last-gasp comeback to increase heat on ArbeloaPress AssociationSat 10 Oct 2026 14.29 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 12.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleÁlvaro Arbeloa bristled at suggestions he cannot handle the pressure after Fulham’s at Ipswich extended their winless start in thePremier Leagueto six matches. The former Real Madrid manager was minutes away from a first managerial victory in the competition after Ryan Sessegnon’s brilliant 55th-minute strike, but the visitors collapsed late on in abject fashion.Abdoul Ouattara produced a thunderbolt from 30 yards to level for Ipswich after 88 minutes and Dara O’Shea headed home Jack Clarke’s free-kick in the second minute of stoppage time to consign the visitors to a painful loss. Tottenham securing a point at Manchester United pushedFulhamto the bottom of the table.Ten-man Brighton continue fine form with battling win at SunderlandRead moreWith his side facing another week in the relegation zone, Arbeloa pushed back at suggestions he is feeling the scrutiny, saying: “I never worry about my position.“I don’t feel fear. You cannot be a coach if you feel it. You have to work, take the decision and you need to show confidence to your players. I am so happy with many things they are doing. I know it is not easy for them.“It’s not about my position, it is about Fulham’s position. That is the most important thing. It is just six games, but it is true we need points.”View image in fullscreenÁlvaro Arbeloa reacts during Fulham’s defeat at Ipswich.Photograph: MB Media/Getty ImagesArbeloa walked straight down the tunnel at full-time after shaking hands with his opposite number, Gary O’Neil. Fulham are seven points behind promoted Ipswich as they switch focus to Saturday’s visit of Hull.Asked how he would block out the noise, Arbeloa said: “Maybe you don’t know me, but I played for the best team in world. I have coached the best team in the world. Maybe you don’t know, but just to let you know, that pressure is part of my life since I was a kid.View image in fullscreenDara O’Shea (centre) scores Ipswich’s dramatic late winner at Portman Road.Photograph: Ben Whitley/PA“It is normal in football. It is normal for players, it is normal for coaches and everybody that is around a team. Pressure is something that is important for me and I like it.”This defeat made it four league losses this season for Fulham and they have conceded after 75 minutes in matches with Sunderland, Crystal Palace, Manchester United and now Ipswich.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionO’Neil struck a different tone after he celebrated a third victory of the campaign with substitutes Chuba Akpom and Clarke able to make telling contributions during a dramatic finale.“On the result, I’m proud of the players and proud of the way we finished the game,” O’Neil said. “They showed exactly what they are – together, hard-working, have quality, never going to stop.“Looked fitter than the opposition, I thought. The last 20 minutes, it looked like they were starting to tire and we were able to keep pushing. The subs helped with that.“That Fulham side have been in the Premier League for a while now and for us to be able to compete with them the way we did was impressive.”Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueIpswich TownFulhammatch reportsShareReuse this content

title: Aston Villa’s wait for home win goes on after Ajer hits back for Brentford | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Kristoffer Ajer’s second-half equaliser earned Brentford a 2-2 draw to leave Aston Villa winless at home in the Premier League this season
Author: Ben Fisher
Headline: Kristoffer Ajer’s second-half equaliser earned Brentford a 2-2 draw to leave Aston Villa winless at home in the Premier League this season
Content: Kristoffer Ajer leaves Aston Villa trailing in his wake to equalise in the second half.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAView image in fullscreenKristoffer Ajer leaves Aston Villa trailing in his wake to equalise in the second half.Photograph: Nick Potts/PAPremier LeagueAston Villa’s wait for home win goes on after Ajer hits back for BrentfordBen Fisherat Villa ParkSat 10 Oct 2026 12.09 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 14.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKristoffer Ajer spent a chunk of the extended international window fielding questions about the state of mind of his Norway teammate Erling Haaland and perhaps in recent weeks he also picked up some finishing tips. Two minutes after John McGinn’s shot cannoned in via Ajer’s calf, the centre-back strode into the Villa box and kept three defenders at arm’s length before equalising, his side-foot shot also catching a nick off a defender, on this occasion Victor Lindelöf.For the second time in the game, one team cancelled out the other within two minutes; just 88 seconds separated Yehor Yarmolyuk’s opener, born from Jaidon Anthony pressing Tyrone Mings, from Nicolas Jackson’s simple equaliser. It was a strange, seesawing and tempestuous game and a busy one for Ajer, who was also booked late on for questioning a decision by Craig Pawson, who managed the impressive feat of drawing ire from both sets of supporters.Chelsea 5-1 Bournemouth, Sunderland 0-2 Brighton, and more: football – liveRead moreUnai Emery had dipped into expletive to make it clear he was not enamoured of Villa’s previous home performance, describing their displayin defeat by Nottingham Forestas “very shit”, and his side’s failure to hold on to the lead against Brentford extended their winless record since the Villa Park revamp left the ground with just three stands in play.“We are not happy, we are sad, but I am optimistic because we improved things we needed after the match against Nottingham,” said Emery, conceding his team are struggling to control games in the manner they have so often across his near four-year tenure. “To draw at home is not a good result.”This feisty draw also maintained Keith Andrews’s fine, unbeaten record against Emery across four meetings, though the visitors also had chances to snatch victory with the left-back El Hadji Malick Diouf’s delivery into the box keeping Villa’s defenders on their toes and the Brazil striker Igor Thiago a constant threat.Ajer’s equaliser – his first goal in club football for two and a half years – served as confirmation that Villa had threats coming at them from all angles. “When he goes on one of those mazy runs, I encourage him to stay involved in the attack,” Andrews said. “It can be quite off-putting for the opposition defence when they see someone of his size and technical ability around the 18-yard box.”Brentford, who remain one of four unbeaten sides in the league this season, seized the lead when Anthony forced Mings into a loose pass and Kevin Schade located Thiago, whose cross was cleared by Lindelöf to the edge of the box. Yarmolyuk hammered the ball in but Villa quickly replied. Emi Buendía’s shot deflected off Jannik Schuster and Jackson nipped around the back of Ajer to finish unmarked from the six-yard box.View image in fullscreenJohn McGinn pulls his shorts up in response to chants from the Brentford fans about his weight.Photograph: Tony O Brien/ReutersBuendía missed a chance to gain the lead in the first half, crashing to his knees theatrically, just after Michael Kayode, fresh from scoring on his Italy debut during the break, had superbly blocked Johan Manzambi’s low strike.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCaoimhín Kelleher made a brilliant, instinctive double save on the verge of half-time to deny Jackson and then McGinn. After the interval his opposite number was called into a fine save, Zion Suzuki pushing wide a Schade volley. Emery clenched both fists and momentarily basked in the joy of Villa taking the lead on 77 minutes. Manzambi had the coolness of mind to locate McGinn, who celebrated by dragging his shorts high above his waist in a retort to the chants about his weight. But a roaming, towering Ajer had the final say at the end.“I sensed Villa were starting to click before the international break, embedding new and talented players and trusted lieutenants that Unai has had for numerous years,” Andrews said. “We could’ve won it, could’ve lost it and I’m a tad disappointed that we couldn’t take advantage of situations in the last 10-15 minutes where I felt we were coming on strong and had the opportunity to win the game.“But to come away [disappointed] at a club that is playing in the Champions League, won the Europa League, with a manager who has just been nominated for the Ballon d’Or [coach of the year], it probably says where we’re at the moment.”Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueAston VillaBrentfordmatch reportsShareReuse this content
