title: European football: Gordon boosts Barcelona, Neuer errors cost Bayern in draw | European club football | The Guardian
description: Anthony Gordon’s first Barcelona goal sparked a 3-0 win over Getafe, while Bayern Munich drew 2-2 after conceding the fastest Bundesliga goal
Author: Guardian sport
Headline: Anthony Gordon’s first Barcelona goal sparked a 3-0 win over Getafe, while Bayern Munich drew 2-2 after conceding the fastest Bundesliga goal
Content: Anthony Gordon celebrates scoring Barcelona’s opener against Getafe, his first goal for the club.Photograph: David Ramos/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAnthony Gordon celebrates scoring Barcelona’s opener against Getafe, his first goal for the club.Photograph: David Ramos/Getty ImagesEuropean club footballEuropean football: Gordon boosts Barcelona, Neuer errors cost Bayern in drawBarcelona 3-0 Getafe, Inter 3-0 Parma, PSG 3-1 Le MansBayern concede fastest Bundesliga goal in Augsburg drawGuardian sportand agenciesSat 10 Oct 2026 15.05 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 12.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthony Gordon scored his first goal forBarcelonaas they extended their perfect start in La Liga with a 3-0 home win overGetafe. The England international opened the scoring in the second minute and Gabriel Jesus added another after half an hour for the league leaders, who have won every match they have played this season.Gordon, who has impressed since joining from Newcastle this summer, grabbed his first Barça goal with a low deflected effort after bundling his way past three players.Getafedefender Zaid Romero gave the ball away in his own box for Barça’s second, passing it straight to Jesus who stroked into the bottom corner.Real Madrid’s Vinícius Júnior sent off for hair pulling in victory over VillarrealRead moreJules Koundé tucked home the third from Lamine Yamal’s cross to cap a solid win at Camp Nou. Barcelona are five points clear of second-placed Atlético Madrid, who won 2-1 at Alavés earlier. Real Madrid are a further point back in third, afterthey edged past Villarreal 1-0despite Vinícius Júnior’s red card for hair-pulling.Rayo Vallecano’s match againstAthleticClubwas abandoned because of home fans at Vallecas stadium throwing objects on to the pitch in a protest against the club president, Raúl Martin Presa.In the 13th minute, Rayo fans threw paper planes, rubber balls and other objects, leading the referee to pause the game and send the players off the pitch. After the teams came back out to resume play, the fans continued to throw objects and the match was abandoned with the score goalless.View image in fullscreenJosé María Sánchez looks at rubbish thrown on to the field by Rayo Vallecano fans shortly before the referee called off the game.Photograph: Mariscal/EPAIn Germany,Augsburg’s Robin Fellhauer scored after eight ⁠seconds againstBayern Munichon Saturday to record the fastest ⁠goal in Bundesliga ⁠history, ​but the visitors twice came from a goal down to snatch a 2-2 ⁠draw.Fellhauer benefited from a blunder by Bayern’s Manuel Neuer to ​beat the record, held ‌jointly by Kevin ‌Volland and Karim Bellarabi, by one second. Bayern, whose only league defeat in their past 48 matches was by their Bavarian rivalsAugsburgin January, upped their game after the break, and Ismael Saibari scored the equaliser.Another Neuer error put Augsburg ahead again in the 64th ​minute, the 40-year-old punching Calvin Brackelmann’s shot into the path of Rodrigo Ribeiro, who only had to push the ball over the line. Bayern earned a draw ⁠when Harry Kane, who hit the woodwork in ​the first ​half, cut the ball ​back for Nathaniel Brown to tap in 10 ‌minutes from ​time.View image in fullscreenManuel Neuer reacts to conceding a goal after eight seconds at Augsburg.Photograph: Matthias Schräder/APThere was also drama elsewhere, asBayer Leverkusengrabbed a rollercoaster 4-3 win inMainzwhileHamburgsnatched a late 3-2 win atHoffenheim.Robert Andrich gave Leverkusen the lead with a superb volley after just five minutes, before Patrik Schick doubled the lead four minutes later. Anthony Caci dragged Mainz back into the game, scoring twice to make it level before half-time. Second-half goals from Jarell Quansah and Moussa Diaby put Leverkusen back in control, before Benedict Hollerbach grabbed a late third for Mainz.Yussuf Poulsen bundled in an early opener forHamburg, before Fisnik Asllani jabbed home an equaliser for Hoffenheim. Bambasé Conté put Hoffenheim in front with a brilliant long-range finish, but a red card for his teammate Bernardo swung the game back in Hamburg’s favour. Terem Moffi equalised with an 83rd-minute header and Miro Muheim grabbed a stoppage-time winner.In the late game,RBLeipzigrampaged to a 6-0 win overEintracht Frankfurtthanks to a Christopher Nkunku hat-trick. Goals from Ezechiel Banzuzi and Nkunku put Leipzig 2-0 up within five minutes, and the former Chelsea forward added two more quickfire goals on the stroke of half-time. Antonio Nusa swept in a fifth after the break and Tidiam Gomis ran through the Frankfurt defence to add a sixth late in the game.In Saturday’s other games, goals from Jeff Chabot and Chris Führich sealed a comfortable 2-0 win forStuttgartatPaderborn, while Livan Burcu struck late to handUnion Berlina nervy 1-0 win at home toElversberg.In Ligue 1,Paris Saint-Germaineased to a 3-1 home victory over⁠Le Mans, played out in a tense atmosphere amid student protests ​across France. Scuffles broke out as police tried to remove a ⁠banner and eventually an entire stand was temporarily emptied of spectators.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenLucas Beraldo (left) celebrates with Ferran Torres after scoring PSG’s opener.Photograph: Sarah Meyssonnier/ReutersPSG took the lead with a penalty converted by Lucas Beraldo, butLe Manslevelled in the second half ⁠through Louis Mafouta, who blasted home for his fourth goal this season. Substitute Khvicha Kvaratskhelia fired PSG ahead two minutes after coming on as he reacted quickest to a ‌rebound.MaghnesAkliouche then wrapped up victory with the third, his first goal since switching from Monaco at the start of the season. PSG were awarded a penalty in added time but Désiré Doué’s effort was saved by Nicolas Kocik. The defending champions move up to fifth, three points behind leadersMonaco, who were held 2-2 at home byToulouse.Edan Diop scored Monaco’s opener and then turned provider for Matthis Abline to net his first goal since a move from Nantes, but the hosts could not hold on to their half-time lead. Casper Tengstedt pulled ​one back for the visitors with a penalty just after the break, before teenager Sion Oppong netted his first Toulouse goal to earn the visitors a point.Lillesit in second place after beating bottom clubLe Havre,Dilane Bakwa scoring the only goal in the fifth minute. The winless visitors lost Ayumu Seko to a red card for ​a professional foul just past the ​hour mark.LorientendedParis FC’s unbeaten start with a 1-0 win, whileBrestscored four first-half goals in a 5-1 rout ofAngers.In Italy,Intersurged to the top ofSerie Athanks to three goals in the first half-hour to defeat an outclassedParma3-0 at San Siro. Petar Sucic opened the scoring in the 13th minute, before Hakan Calhanoglu doubled the lead from the penalty spot. Marcus Thuram then made it 3-0 after 31 minutes with his third goal of the campaign.View image in fullscreenScott McTominay returned for Napoli as they eased to a 3-0 home win over Frosinone.Photograph: Ciro Fusco/EPANapolicruised to a 3-0 victory at home toFrosinonewith Scott McTominay making his comeback after heart surgery. Scotland midfielder McTominay came on in the second half, a welcome return for the player who has been his team’s powerhouse for the last two seasons.The opener came when Rasmus Højlund was fouled as he surged towards goal and Kevin De Bruyne converted the penalty. Dutch forward Noa Lang slotted in the second on 29 minutes after Højlund’s effort was saved, and De Bruyne added his second to complete the job in second-half stoppage time.Elsewhere,Genoaclimbed out of the relegation zone with a 2-1 home win overFiorentina, who replace them in the bottom three. Milutin Osmajic and Junior Messias put the hosts 2-0 up inside 15 minutes before a Johan Vásquez own goal in the second half.Explore more on these topicsEuropean club footballBundesligaAugsburgBayern MunichRayo VallecanoAthletic BilbaoLa LiganewsShareReuse this content

title: Scottish Premiership: Naderi puts Rangers top and Hearts rout St Mirren | Scottish Premiership | The Guardian
description: Ryan Naderi scored twice as Rangers moved top of the Premiership overnight with a 3-1 win over Kilmarnock, while Hearts beat St Mirren 5-0
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Ryan Naderi scored twice as Rangers moved top of the Premiership overnight with a 3-1 win over Kilmarnock, while Hearts beat St Mirren 5-0
Content: Ryan Naderi heads home Rangers’ opener against Kilmarnock.Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRyan Naderi heads home Rangers’ opener against Kilmarnock.Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty ImagesScottish PremiershipScottish Premiership: Naderi puts Rangers top and Hearts rout St MirrenGers beat Kilmarnock 3-1 to go ahead of Celtic overnightCalvin Miller scores two penalties in Hearts 5-0 St MirrenPress AssociationSat 10 Oct 2026 14.17 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 12.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDerek McInnes praised hisRangersplayers as they moved to the top of the league and blamed the extended international break for some disjointed play in a 3-1 win overKilmarnock.Rangers went into the break three up at Ibrox after Ryan Naderi twice headed home either side of a Kevin Kelsy strike. But Killie had chances throughout, especially after the interval, before finally getting their reward when substitute Nicky Clescenco struck on a last-minute counterattack. The visitors ended the game with six efforts on target to Rangers’ four, but the home goalkeeper, Ivor Pandur, was seriously troubled once before being beaten.Rangers moved a point ahead of Celtic, who face Motherwell on Sunday, thanks to a sixth consecutive league win.McInnes, who started with eight of the 13 players who had been away on international duty, said: “The fact we went top of the league, we shouldn’t lose sight of that. There’s a lot of positives, but the performance was disjointed at times.“I was really pleased with how clinical we were in the first half. We put the ball in the box, we scored goals. We just didn’t do it enough for whatever reason. But we have to be honest, for long spells we looked like a team that hadn’t been together for the last three weeks.“There’s a bit of understanding for me where the players have been. Whoever came up with this idea, it’s such a long time for your players to be away. We pay their wages, we look after our players and for them to be away for nearly three weeks is too long. But we’ve got the job done and credit the players for digging deep and getting three points.”Heartseased to their biggest home win in the league for three-and-a-half years as they dismantledSt Mirren5-0 to remain on the coattails of Rangers and Celtic.View image in fullscreenHearts’ Calvin Miller scores his side’s second from the spot against St Mirren.Photograph: Zak Mauger/Getty ImagesThe third-placed Jambos dominated from the start and Laurent Mendy fired them ahead in the 20th minute. Calvin Miller scored two penalties, either side of half-time, before goals from Cláudio Braga and Josh McPake ensured a smooth afternoon for Hearts before their Conference League opener at home to Nordsjaelland on Thursday.It was Hearts’ biggest league win at Tynecastle since they defeated Ross County 6-1 under Steven Naismith in April 2023 and they are now comfortably the top scorers in the league.Their manager, Wouter Vrancken, said: “We try to play a kind of football that is positive and constructive and proactive, and not a reaction. I think people come to the stadium to see nice football, to see goals from your side.“Also for the players, we try to play a style of football that, when you were a little boy, when you started playing on the street, you played to score goals, not to stay in front of your goal and prevent the goals.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“You want to score goals because this is the nicest feeling you have in football. Some days it will work better than other days, but it’s nice to see that it worked well today.”Ashley Hay scrambled in a stoppage-time winner to secureDundeea 2-1 victory atFalkirk. The striker, out since early August with a ligament sprain, converted from close range after latching on to Ethan Hamilton’s free-kick in the first minute of added time.His goal completed the turnaround after Owen Bevan’s second goal for the Dark Blues had cancelled out Jacob Murrell’s first-half penalty at Falkirk Stadium.Marink Reedijk endured a disappointing first game asHibernian’s manager as his side suffered a 1-0 defeat againstDundee Unitedat Tannadice. The hosts scored in the first half through winger Daniel Bennie, on loan from QPR, and the visitors finished the game with 10 men after Jacob Devaney was sent off.This story will be updatedExplore more on these topicsScottish PremiershipRangersKilmarnocknewsShareReuse this content

title: Championship roundup: Swansea fight back to beat Norwich; Middlesbrough go second | Championship | The Guardian
description: Adam Idah’s goal puts Swansea top of the Championship, while Middlesbrough are up to second after a 1-0 home victory over Wolves
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Adam Idah’s goal puts Swansea top of the Championship, while Middlesbrough are up to second after a 1-0 home victory over Wolves
Content: Swansea's Adam Idah (left) heads home the winner against Norwich.Photograph: Steven Paston/PAView image in fullscreenSwansea's Adam Idah (left) heads home the winner against Norwich.Photograph: Steven Paston/PAChampionshipChampionship roundup: Swansea fight back to beat Norwich; Middlesbrough go secondLeaders earn 2-1 home win, Boro beat Wolves 1-0Burnley rout Watford; Birmingham edge West BromPress AssociationSat 10 Oct 2026 12.32 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 10.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVítor Matos praised hisSwanseaside for overcoming a lack of training as they strengthened their position at the top of theChampionshipwith a 2-1 comeback win overNorwich. Second-half goals from Moussa Yeo and the Republic of Ireland striker Adam Idah wiped out Jacob Wright’s strike just before the half-hour mark.West Ham’s penalty pain costs them top spot in Championship after QPR drawRead moreIt was the third time Swansea had come from behind this season to win, and, afterWest Ham’s draw the previous night, it gave them top spot in the table. Idah, though, limped out of the action and could be a doubt for Tuesday’s visit to Millwall.“I’m really happy with the boys,” said Matos. “Players had been flying around because of the international break, joining on the last days of training as well before the game. It’s not the easiest way to prepare. It’s all about trying to reconnect everyone.”It was a fourth defeat in a row in all competitions for Norwich, who have now conceded 19 goals in nine league matches.Middlesbroughcelebrated their 150th anniversary game in style as Will Lankshear’s second-half header secured a 1-0 victory overWolvesat the Riverside Stadium. A sold-out crowd helped mark the occasion, and Lankshear’s header from Tommy Conway’s cross ensured the home fans went home happy. The win enabledMiddlesbroughto climb above West Ham into second spot. Wolves were second best as they suffered a second league defeat since their relegation last season.View image in fullscreenA tifo marks Middlesbrough’s 150th anniversary before their win over Wolves at the Riverside.Photograph: Richard Sellers/PAWest Brom’shead coach, James Morrison, defended Nat Phillips as a “strong character” after a second successive derby mistake led to the only goal in a 1-0 defeat toBirminghamat The Hawthorns. Phillips gave away the 41st-minute penalty when he fouled August Priske, who slotted home from the spot. The former Liverpool defender’s back pass let in Fer López to win the Black Country derby for Wolves last time out, but Morrison said: “I understand he’s made two errors but it was just a misjudgement.”Quick GuideLeague One: Plymouth on top; dream start for SavageShowPlymouthcame from behind to beatWimbledon2-1 with a stoppage-time goal from substitute Xavier Amaechi which put them clear at the top of  League One. Jayden Stockley had put the Dons ahead in the 16th minute, with Caleb Watts equalising ahead of the break. It looked like the points would be shared before Amaechi swept the ball home in the fifth minute of added time.NewPeterboroughmanager Robbie Savage had a dream start with a 3-1 win atLeicester, to pile more pressure on Foxes’ manager Russell Martin. Posh took an early lead through Owura Edwards and Harry Leonard before an own goal from Warren O’Hora made it 3-0 just before the break. Emil Riis scored a second-half consolation for the hosts.Mark Harris and Cameron Brannagan scored as high-flyingOxfordsecured a 2-1 win overNottsCountyat Meadow Lane.Bradfordwere held to a goalless draw byLeyton Orientat Valley Parade, slipping two points behind Plymouth.Huddersfieldmissed the chance to go second afterSheffield Wednesdayfought back with two late goals to snatch a 2-2 draw at the Accu Stadium after Jamal Lowe scored a penalty deep into stoppage-time. Kyle Wootton scored twice asStockportcame from behind to beatBarnsley3-1 at Edgeley Park to sit third.Gassan Ahadme’s late goal gave fifth-placedCambridgea 1-0 win over 10-manBlackpoolat the Abbey Stadium, where there had been a 15 minute delay to kick-off because of issues affecting supporters entering the ground.Readingare sixth after a 5-1 away win at strugglersMK DonswhileLutonwere comprehensive victors atWycombewith a dominant 4-1 display to spoil a day of celebration for Tom Hounsell. Efforts from Kasey Palmer, Nahki Wells, Jamie Donley and Devante Cole were more than enough against a home side who announced Hounsell as permanent head coach before the game.Leon Ayinde’s first EFL goal was enough to moveDoncasterout of the bottom four with a 1-0 home win overBurton.Mansfieldedged home 2-1 in their first ever game againstBromleyto halt a run of four games without a victory.Wiganremain adrift at the bottom of the table after a 1-0 defeat atStevenage.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Burnley’sfirst win of the season, and their first away from home since February, sentWatfordfans into open revolt as the Clarets cruised home 4-0 at Vicarage Road. While Alessio Dionisi’s fifth defeat in six games increased the pressure on the Hornets head coach, counterpart Nicky Hayen’s first victory liftedBurnleyoff the bottom.Three goals in the space of 12 first-half minutes put the visitors out of sight and extended the Hornets’ wretched defensive record to 29 weeks without a clean sheet. When Stoke won 2-1 at Vicarage Road last month, it ended 251 days without a win on the road for the Potters. Here,Watfordextended more charity to the Clarets, who ended 241 days without an away win comfortably.Asked about the furious reaction of fans, and the rising tide of opinion on social media that his job was at risk, Dionisi said: “In football it’s normal. It’s probably better to say only one thing – I’m sorry for this match. I’m very angry because after 30 minutes the match was finished, it was impossible to come back. But I believe in my team and I believe in my job. I’m here and we work every to improve: now it is important to work well, to work better.”Dionisi’s decision to take off popular Spaniard Iker Bravo after just 35 minutes was roundly booed, and he admitted: “Iker is a good player and, for me, he must play every match, but I had to change something and it was impossible to change everyone.”View image in fullscreenWatford fans leave early as their side crumbles at home to Burnley.Photograph: Peter Tarry/PABristol City’smanager, Michael Skubala, feltCharltongoalkeeper Arthur Okonkwo should have been sent off in the 1-1 draw at The Valley. Referee Tom Reeves did not give a foul after the Wrexham loanee raced out of his box to halt Japanese winger Yu Hirakawa in the 15th minute. By that stage the Addicks already had a lead through Karlan Grant’s smart finish but Scott Twine’s penalty in the 27th minute put City back on level terms after Conor Coventry brought down Dom Ballard.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPatrick Bamford scored twice to helpSheffield Unitedto a comfortable 3-0 victory overLincoln. The result, with Tahith Chong also on the scoresheet, ended a three-match losing run for Chris Wilder’s men in all competitions against a side which had won three of their previous four away matches.Quick GuideLeague Two: Grant strikes twice to keep Salford topShowJorge Grant’s late double sealed a 2-0 win forSalfordat 10-manCheltenhamto keep them top of the table. The result extends the Ammies’ winning run in League Two to four and it was also their first victory at Cheltenham.Kabongo Tshimanga’s stoppage-time strike sealed an impressive 3-1 come-from-behind victory forBarnetatBristolRovers. Rovers’ record home winning streak came to an end after a two-on-one counter-attack resulted in Tshimanga tucking home under Brad Young to seal all three points.Crewekept up the pace with a 1-0 away win overSwindon, who suffered a fourth defeat in five league games.Gillinghammoved into fourth spot after a 4-1 win atRotherhamandPort Valeclimbed out of the bottom two after a 1-0 win overGrimsby.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Lamine Cissé and Ben Wilmot were on target as 10-manStokeextended their unbeaten league run to six games with a 2-1 win overBolton. Mark Robins’ in-form side played for 70 minutes without Maksym Talovierov after the defender’s dismissal for bringing down Kyliane Dong. However, the Potters shrugged off the disadvantage to gain a first win in Bolton since October 1990. Their fifth win in six games lifted them up to fourth while Bolton dropped to 17th.Blackburnmade it back-to-back home wins with a battling 2-1 victory overCardiff. Andri Gudjohnsen gave Rovers the lead with a composed finish just before the half hour and Todd Cantwell doubled the advantage 10 minutes later with a shot that Bluebirds goalkeeper Nathan Trott will be disappointed not to have saved. The visitors struck just after the break through Callum Robinson’s first of the campaign.View image in fullscreenTodd Cantwell watches his effort cross the line, putting Blackburn two up against Cardiff.Photograph: Dave Howarth/CameraSport/Getty ImagesDerbyare still without a home win after Ollie Rathbone scored late on to earnWrexhama 1-1 draw at Pride Park. The Rams were on course for victory through Sam Szmodics’ superb early strike only for the Welsh side to rescue a point two minutes from the end.Camiel Neghli ensured it was a baptism of fire for the newPrestonmanager, Graham Alexander, as his late strike sealed a 1-0 win forMillwallat Deepdale. It was coolness personified from the Dutch-born Algerian, who slotted Luke Cundle’s cut-back into the far corner for what turned out to be a 79th-minute winner.PosTeamPGDPts1Swansea98202Middlesbrough95183West Ham911164Stoke92165Wolverhampton84146QPR93147Birmingham92148Millwall91149West Brom911410Bristol City9-11411Charlton9-31312Blackburn911213Sheff Utd911214Wrexham9-31115Lincoln City9-41116Southampton891017Bolton9-51018Norwich9-2919Portsmouth7-1820Watford9-7821Cardiff9-3722Burnley9-4723Derby9-7624Preston North End9-84Explore more on these topicsChampionshipSwansea CityNorwich CityMiddlesbroughWolverhampton WanderersWest Bromwich AlbionBirmingham CitynewsShareReuse this content

title: Matt Renshaw’s epic 190 helps Australia turn tables on South Africa in Durban | Australia cricket team | The Guardian
description: Matt Renshaw scored his first century in Tests for nine years and 280 days as Australia notched 390 with a second highest ninth wicket partnership of 134
Author: Geoff Lemon
Headline: Matt Renshaw scored his first century in Tests for nine years and 280 days as Australia notched 390 with a second highest ninth wicket partnership of 134
Content: Australia's Matt Renshaw acknowledges the crowd after his dismissal having scored 190 runs.Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAustralia's Matt Renshaw acknowledges the crowd after his dismissal having scored 190 runs.Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty ImagesAustralia cricket teamMatt Renshaw’s epic 190 helps Australia turn tables on South Africa in DurbanRenshaw’s century was his first in Tests for nine yearsLyon helps build second-highest ninth-wicket partnershipGeoff LemonSat 10 Oct 2026 11.51 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 20.19 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf the choice to ask Nic Maddinson to open in Durban was a bust, the upside for Australia was that it pushed Matthew Renshaw down to number five. From there, the Queenslander returned from 10 years on the periphery to the centre of the spotlight in the first Test against South Africa, with an innings of 190 that saved Australia from peril, settled them into stability, then lifted them to dominance.Staunch support from the lower order was the other part of the equation, as Renshaw batted through two extended sessions until he was last man out, just after tea, with Australia’s 390 followed by South Africa’s 27 for one before stumps.South Africa v Australia: first men’s cricket Test, day two – liveRead moreImagine the likelihood, with the score at 124 for six on the first day, that Renshaw might go on, not just to score his second Test century, but to exceed that career high of 184? His secret was that there was no secret, just the most common formula known to the game: patience, concentration and pacing. Continuing in the style of his unbeaten 46 from day one, Renshaw defended calmly, kept the score moving with singles and picked off the odd poor ball.He was aided by an often passive approach to fielding, despite some tough spells of bowling from Marco Jansen and Anrich Nortje. Resuming after 65 overs, they had a morning burst with the old ball, then a short rest before the new one, often dropping short and hitting gloves or body. But it was the more modest velocity and bounce of Wiaan Mulder in between times that reaped rewards.Pat Cummins carried on the previous day’s partnership to 86, but lost concentration eight overs into the morning to poke the old ball to slip for 43. With the slightest bit of inswing from the new ball, Mulder bowled Mitchell Starc an unplayable that pitched on leg stump before seaming away to take middle and off.At 230 for eight, South Africa would have imagined a quick finish, but Temba Bavuma let things drift by spreading the field for Renshaw. Against players with the right temperament, this tactic often backfires, and so it was here. Renshaw happily defended or added a few runs early in each over, turned over strike from the fourth or fifth ball, and watched Nathan Lyon defend what was left.Lyon did not score for 16 overs either side of lunch, facing 24 balls. When Renshaw for once failed to farm the strike, Nortje immediately came back on to target Lyon, Australia’s spinner flicked him for four.By the second session the pitch had gone to sleep and with it went the South African bowling. Even with two specialist spinners in the side, part-timer Aiden Markram was called upon. Lyon had never been part of a century stand, but up that landmark came: no cricketer has played more Tests than his 144 before achieving that feat.When Jansen finally ended his team’s pain by dishing some out, smashing Lyon in the foot with a fierce yorker from around the wicket, the partnership was 134, Australia’s second-highest for the ninth wicket.View image in fullscreenSouth Africa’s Marco Jansen (centre) celebrates the wicket of Australia’s Nathan Lyon (right) who helped notch up the second highest ninth wicket partnership of 134 runs.Photograph: Marco Longari/AFP/Getty ImagesLyon made 27 from 92 balls and Renshaw was up to 169. He went up a gear, uppercutting Nortje for six and nailing a pull for four. Josh Hazlewood was able to help him bat through a monster session, ending up at two hours and 45 minutes after one extension to make up lost overs and a second one for being nine wickets down.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to our cricket newsletter for our writers' thoughts on the biggest stories and a review of the week’s actionEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRenshaw fell two balls after the resumption, driving the off-spinner Simon Harmer to slip, but it had been a flawless innings otherwise. It set records for Durban: the highest score by an Australian, past the Phil Hughes 160 that is part of folklore; and the highest score by any batter at five or below, past the 2019 Kusal Perera epic that was Ben Stokes at Headingley before Ben Stokes went to Headingley.Australia bowled fewer than nine overs in the last session before bad light once again stopped play, although that was enough time for Hazlewood to have Ryan Rickelton edge a drive to slip from a ball that was not full enough. South Africa will start the third day 363 runs behind.For Renshaw, though, the day was eventful enough. Treated as a prodigy at 20 years old, then discarded summarily by 21, he has loitered on the sidelines with occasional nibbles at a Test return. Now he will get a proper second chance.His century celebration was chiefly a smile of vast relief. At nine years and 280 days, the only Australians to have waited longer between hundreds are monochrome memories, Bob Simpson and Warren Bardsley.Where Renshaw bats next may still be an open question, as the shuttle continues between number five and opening. Usman Khawaja went from five to the top, then Travis Head did the same to replace him. Renshaw was just shunted from opening to five, but may soon have to go back to accommodate Cam Green, who was the most convincing batter in Australia’s previous series but is injured. That will be next week’s problem. Renshaw is this week’s solution.Explore more on these topicsAustralia cricket teamSouth Africa cricket teamCricketAustralia sportnewsShareReuse this content

title: Future Champions Festival: Darkness Falls sparks Triple Crown dreams with Dewhurst win – as it happened | Horse racing tips | The Guardian
description: Darkness Falls could become the first Triple Crown winner since Nijinsky in 1970 after a narrow win in the Dewhurst Stakes
Author: Greg Wood
Headline: Darkness Falls could become the first Triple Crown winner since Nijinsky in 1970 after a narrow win in the Dewhurst Stakes
Content: 11h ago11.34 EDTDARKNESS FALLS SPARKS TRIPLE CROWN DREAMSDarkness Fallswill be given every chance to go one better than his sire,Camelot, and become the firstTriple Crownwinner since Nijinsky in 1970 after a narrow defeat of Desert Castle, the odds-on favourite, in the Group One Dewhurst Stakes here on Saturday.Camelot went down to a narrow and slightly unfortunate defeat to Encke in the 2012St Legerafter registering wins in the first two legs of the Triple Crown: the2,000 Guineasin May and theDerbyat Epsom a month later. There was then a further twist to the disappointment a few months later, when Mahmood al Zarooni, Encke’s trainer, was found to have been systematically doping horses at his Newmarket yard with steroids.Modern breeding favours speed over stamina and the field for the 2,000 Guineas, the opening leg of the Triple Crown, tends to be dominated by specialist milers.Darkness Falls,though, proved on Saturday that he has both speed and stamina, as he dropped back to seven furlongs for hisDewhurstwin following a Group One success over nine furlongs at Leopardstown last month.“It was a big call to come here and it’s incredible to bring a horse back from nine furlongs to win a Dewhurst,”Aidan O’Brien,Darkess Falls’s trainer, said.“You saw what he did over nine furlongs and I don’t think he’ll have any problem going further either, he has a lot of quality.“When they have as much class as he has, they can do anything, and the Triple Crown is the dream. His dad was an incredible horse who went very close. This lad is very like him, but quicker.”Darkness Falls is quoted at odds of between 12-1 and 25-1 to complete the Triple Crown.Darkness Falls completed a double for his trainer afterDrumbeat’svictory in theZetland Stakesearlier on the card, and gave O’Brien a major boost in his bid to beatAndrew Baldingto the trainers’ championship.The reigning champion picked up nearly £400k in prize money from his two wins and is now neck-and-neck with Balding ahead of the Champions Day card at Ascot next week, with more than £4m on offer in prize money.Share

title: Post-its, homework breaks and karaoke: inside the Women’s Pro Baseball League’s debut season | Baseball | The Guardian
description: The first league of its kind in 70 years brought players from all around the world to Illinois for eight weeks, writing a new chapter in the history of women’s sports
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The first league of its kind in 70 years brought players from all around the world to Illinois for eight weeks, writing a new chapter in the history of women’s sports
Content: New York Heights players surround Keira Izumi after a home run during a WPBL game against the LA Queens.Photograph: Jaclyn LichtView image in fullscreenNew York Heights players surround Keira Izumi after a home run during a WPBL game against the LA Queens.Photograph: Jaclyn LichtBaseballPost-its, homework breaks and karaoke: inside the Women’s Pro Baseball League’s debut seasonThe first league of its kind in 70 years brought players from all around the world to Illinois for eight weeks, writing a new chapter in the history of women’s sportsPhotographs and text by Jaclyn LichtSat 10 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTShareOn the morning of 14 September, Rocky Henley sat at her rental home’s dining room table amid scattered rulebooks, colorful markers and graph paper. The New York Heights manager drew a chart on a large poster – her method of sketching plays for the evening’s playoff game. Her assistant manager, Jackson, trudged in from the kitchen in flannel pajama pants and a Heights hoodie and watched her work. He also happens to be her son.View image in fullscreenRocky Henley draws out gameplans at her dining room table on the morning of the Heights’ WPBL playoff game.Photograph: Jaclyn LichtView image in fullscreenHenley’s son, Jackson, assists her in gameplanning.Photograph: Jaclyn LichtView image in fullscreenHenley prepares a list of messages to leave on the lockers of her players before a game.Photograph: Jaclyn LichtView image in fullscreenHenley and her coaches gather during a game.Photograph: Jaclyn LichtTheWomen’s Pro Baseball League(WPBL) is the first league of its kind in 70 years. Players hailed from across the US and 11 different countries to play for four teams: the Heights, Boston Hunters, San Francisco Firebells and Los Angeles Queens. While each team’s namesake city was selected for their market value and reputations for sports fandom, the eight-week inaugural season was played in entirety in Springfield, Illinois.View image in fullscreenFrom left to right: Gabrielle Haas, Maïka Dumais and Hyeonah Kim of the Boston Hunters wait in the dugout before their first WPBL game.Photograph: Jaclyn LichtView image in fullscreenAlyssa Zettlemoyer of the New York Heights celebrates as she steals second base during a WPBL game against the Boston Hunters.Photograph: Jaclyn LichtView image in fullscreenAddisyn Baird of the LA Queens dances in the dugout.Photograph: Jaclyn LichtView image in fullscreenFirebells players greet Alexia Jorge at the plate after a home run.The inaugural season of the WPBL marked a pivotal moment in the women’s sports history books. The players, coaches and crew fashioned the paper, the pen and the ink to write this new chapter.The broadcast producer consulted on merchandise stock. Catchers doubled as assistant coaches. The league doctors taught and studied at the local university.View image in fullscreenBroadcasters call a game in the booth at Robin Roberts Stadium.View image in fullscreenFans buy merchandise during the WPBL’s first playoff game.Photograph: Jaclyn LichtBefore her players arrived for games at Robin Roberts Stadium, Rocky Henley would consult a list of adjectives scribbled on a piece of notepad paper, crossing out repetitions and racking her brain for synonyms. Each Heights player received two Post-it notes on their locker: a green Post-it with a mantra they needed to keep in mind during the game – “stamina,” “determination” and “spirit”, to name a few examples – and a pink one to highlight an adjective reflective of their general personalities – such as “comical”, “ridiculous” or “fun!”View image in fullscreenBefore each game, Rocky Henley wrote out Post-it notes with inspirational messages for her players.View image in fullscreenOne message read “fortitude”.Most of the players balanced the WPBL season with schoolwork or second jobs. Days outside of games consisted largely of practice – often at the local YMCA, where many of the players bought memberships for the summer.Addisyn Baird, the youngest player in the league, is long accustomed to multitasking. Baird, 18, was called up to play with the LA Queens in late August, just weeks before she was set to start her senior fall semester of high school at the Hill School in Pennsylvania. She juggled Queens games with AP Psych assignments, hockey practice, babysitting and being scouted for colleges. She has spent years navigating the typically male-dominated world of baseball; her father Travis was once removed as head coach of the local youth team for allowing his daughter to play alongside the boys.“I was kind of used to being the only girl,” she says. “But I mean, you get used to the stares, you get used to the eyes on you. At that point, it’s just all the time.”View image in fullscreenAddisyn Baird, the only high schooler in the WPBL, works on a school assignment in a hotel room.Photograph: Jaclyn LichtView image in fullscreenBaird sits in the stands to watch a playoff game between the Hunters and the Firebells.Photograph: Jaclyn LichtView image in fullscreenBaird, 18, holds her niece, Preston, on the field after a game.Photograph: Jaclyn LichtView image in fullscreenFrom left: Ayuri Shimano, Baird and Mayao Hirano, Japanese interpreter for the WPBL, gather for an LA Queens cookout.Photograph: Jaclyn LichtWhile young players like Baird were accustomed to game-time pressure and their roles as pioneers of women in sports, adjusting to life alongside dozens of other fellow athletes in a small city was its own unique journey. Many tried to absorb Illinois culture as much as possible. The Hunters’ Ticara Geldenhuis, who normally lives full-time near Sydney, Australia, enjoyed swimming at the local lake, playing with teammates at the local golf course or day tripping to Chicago. On game nights, whether win or lose, players often frequented the bars in town afterward to play pool or sing karaoke.View image in fullscreenFirebells players hold balls in the dugout.Photograph: Jaclyn LichtView image in fullscreenLexi Hastings and Ticara Geldenhuis of the Boston Hunters take a selfie at Clique, a local bar in Springfield.Photograph: Jaclyn LichtView image in fullscreenLondon Studer of the New York Heights sings karaoke at Clique as a groundskeeper looks on.Photograph: Jaclyn LichtView image in fullscreenRobin Roberts Stadium during Game 2 of the WPBL Championship Series on 17 September.Photograph: Jaclyn LichtThe Post-It notes and gameplans Henley spent that morning preparing did not deliver a win that night. The LA Queens defeated the Heights 15-11, eliminating New York from the playoffs.Two days later, the Queens would beat the Fireballs in Game 1 of the WPBL Championship Series, en route to becoming the league’s inaugural champions. Rocky and Jackson were there in the bleachers watching with their players, inspecting every play with sharp attention and already taking notes for next season.

title: UK must not be beholden to foreign AI, says head of Alan Turing Institute | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: George Williamson says ‘national resilience’ is key focus of ATI amid US and China’s runaway leadership in field
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: George Williamson says ‘national resilience’ is key focus of ATI amid US and China’s runaway leadership in field
Content: George Williamson: ‘As AI becomes more embedded in domains like defence, national security, critical infrastructure and healthcare we shouldn’t depend solely on systems we can’t inspect or control.’Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGeorge Williamson: ‘As AI becomes more embedded in domains like defence, national security, critical infrastructure and healthcare we shouldn’t depend solely on systems we can’t inspect or control.’Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianAI (artificial intelligence)UK must not be beholden to foreign AI, says head of Alan Turing InstituteGeorge Williamson says ‘national resilience’ is key focus of ATI amid US and China’s runaway leadership in fieldDan MilmoGlobal technology editorSat 10 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK must not become dependent on foreign AI systems that can be switched off at short notice and must develop its own versions of the technology, according to the head of the Alan Turing Institute.The country needs a stronger domestic position in AI in response to the US and China’s runaway leadership in the field, with “national resilience” a key focus for ATI said George Williamson.The institute is the UK’s leading AI research body and isunder new leadershipafter the government, its main source of funding, demanded a strategic shift.Palantir’s Tom Watson says ‘mob rule’ must not dictate awarding of government contractsRead more“As AI becomes more embedded in critical services, in domains like defence, national security, critical infrastructure and healthcare we shouldn’t depend solely on systems we can’t inspect or control, or that could be restricted or even switched off,” said Williamson.In June Washington temporarily blocked the release outside the US of Anthropic’s latest models, and has reportedly asked leading AI labs to withhold their models from being tested by the UK’s AI Security Institute until they have been examined by AISI’s US counterpart.“We’ve seen now that both political and commercial pressures mean we may not have access [to AI] in all the circumstances when we want it. That is not a place where a nation wants to be,” he said.Williamson added: “There’s a set of circumstances where it would be a good idea for us to have something that we don’t have to ask other people’s permission to use.”He said national resilience would be a focus of ATI’s work amid concern about the geopolitical situation and the risk posed by increasingly powerful AI systems.Those concerns were highlighted last month by the UK prime minister, Andy Burnham, announcing a new national centre to tacklestate-backed disinformation, and Anthropic predicting the technology had agreater than 10% chance of wiping out humanity by 2030.“It’s a moment when national resilience is definitely what the country needs and it’s definitely a thing I think the Turing institute can help with,” he said.“We are facing a more adversarial world, more frequent shocks to our critical infrastructure and now powerful AI amplifying these threats. To strengthen national resilience, the Turing will focus on securing critical systems against disruption, countering threats from AI itself and helping to shape the right strategic AI capability for the UK.”Williamson said the institute could assist in building such resilience by helping produce uses for AI “for the public good”, working on areas from weather forecasting to farming, as well as helping spot disinformation. Referring to state-led disinformation campaigns, he said: “It’s very dangerous for the state of democracy and it’s an area that we can monitor.”Williamson is the former head of His Majesty’s Government Communications Centre, a secretive government body that makes gadgets for UK spy agencies and counts Alan Turing – the second world war codebreaker and AI pioneer after which ATI is named – among its former staff.Williamson said it had become clear in recent months that the UK needed “more agency on access to technology” and a stronger sovereign position in AI. “It feels pretty uncomfortable if you don’t have some control or ability to use technologies when you want them, and also harder to imagine how you build an economy on the top of stuff that can disappear,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn recent weeks Christine Lagarde, the president of the European Central Bank, and Ursula von der Leyen, the president of the European Commission, have urged Europe to be more self-sufficient in AI, withLagarde speaking about the threat of being “cut off”from US and Chinese technology.Williamson cited China as another reason for boosting domestic AI, amid concerns that Chinese-made systems might not “coincide with our values”. He said: “Try asking some of these models about some events in the recent past in China and you’re not going to get an answer that’s particularly helpful if you’re doing GCSE history.”“This is the defining technology of our time. We want to be able to shape that technology … in a way that accords with who we are and our values,” he said, adding that while ATI and the UK probably could not match the financial resources of major AI labs, they could still produce “nationally owned IP” or smaller models that could be made available to startups.“We can be ambitious here without trying to copy what frontier labs are doing,” he said.Williamson said ATI, a registered charity, could be an “objective and helpful” arbiter of concerns about AI, including existential threat. “A national institute should be an active partner to government and the public more generally in helping to navigate some of this stuff.”He said there was a “a lot of stuff being tossed around” on the existential threat risk that “is not always well grounded in science”. Referring to the penchant among some in the sector for expressing the risk of AI-triggered extinction in percentage terms, he said: “I’m not sure it’s helpful trying to assign particular percentages to it because I have not seen anyone show me a convincing evidence of how they’ve arrived at the number they then start throwing around.”Williamson indicated that the focus on national resilience would enable ATI to keep doing work on the environment that Keir Starmer’s government had wanted to sideline. In 2025 the then technology secretary, Peter Kyle, wrote to ATI’s chair demanding the institute switch its main focus to defence and security. Williamson’s predecessor Jean Innesresigned soon afterwards.“For me climate is as much a national security issue as defence. For me, it [national resilience] is a frame that enables us to cover the range of threats and opportunities to the UK,” he said.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)Defence policyUK security and counter-terrorismComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: Nuclear war and malicious use of AI threaten end of humanity by 2100, says Lancet assessment | Global health | The Guardian
description: Newly established commission identifies 17 catastrophic threats to human health but says ‘realistic route to act’ on each exists
Author: Kat Lay
Headline: Newly established commission identifies 17 catastrophic threats to human health but says ‘realistic route to act’ on each exists
Content: An environmental protest at Cop28, the UN climate summit in Dubai, 2023.Photograph: Karim Sahib/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAn environmental protest at Cop28, the UN climate summit in Dubai, 2023.Photograph: Karim Sahib/AFP/Getty ImagesGlobal healthNuclear war and malicious use of AI threaten end of humanity by 2100, says Lancet assessmentNewly established commission identifies 17 catastrophic threats to human health but says ‘realistic route to act’ on each existsSupported byAbout this contentKat LaySat 10 Oct 2026 19.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHumans could become extinct by the year 2100 due to malicious use of AI or nuclear conflict, according to a new global risk assessment.They top a list of 17 major threats to human health over the next 75 years, which also includes cuts to aid spending by wealthy countries, the climate crisis and childhood malnutrition.The experts behindThe Lancet Commission on 21st Century Global Threats to Healthsaid all the threats interact, meaning they must be addressed together – but stressed that there was “a realistic route to act” on each.“Decisions made by leaders today will shape the health and wellbeing of the next generation,” said Prof Christopher Murray, commission co-chair and the director of the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation, University of Washington.To create its list, the commission modelled how many years in good health might be lost due to sickness, disability or early deaths due to each threat, based on current trajectories – a measure known as disability-adjusted life years (Dalys).“Malicious use of AI, including bioweapons, and nuclear conflict with nuclear famine carry risks of extinction in the next 75 years,” the report said, adding that while their likelihood remained low, they had the potential to end humanity in the case of nuclear conflict by injecting enough particles into the upper atmosphere to block sunlight and cause famine, or via AI-created biological weapons. An accompanying Lancet editorial, published alongside the report, warned: “The scale of harm, should they be realised, would inflict an apocalypse on humanity.”Other risks that could cause more than 1bn cumulative Dalys, and therefore deemed “major catastrophic threats”, includedair pollution,antimicrobial resistance,childhood malnutritionand climate breakdown, as well as conventional conflict,declining overseas aid,high alcohol use, high blood pressure, income inequality, low educational attainment,naturally occurring pandemics,obesity, poormental health,smokingand unhealthyageing.To be included on the list, threats not only had to potentially cause a high number of lost healthy years, but also to have potential solutions.Ibrahim Abubakar, commission member and professor of infectious disease epidemiology at UCL, said: “We are not starting from a point of view of ‘oh look, we want to scare you – we’ve got X many threats facing humanity’. We’re starting from the premise that if you are a policymaker today, whether at the global multilateral level or at the national level, these are the potential threats that you could face, and this is the magnitude by which, if you act, you can actually make a difference.”Action to limitglobal heating to about 1.8C (3.2F)rather than letting it reach 4.4C could prevent 1.89bn years of healthy life being lost, according to the report, which modelled best and worst case scenarios for each threat.In higher income regions, non-communicable diseases such as obesity and poor mental health were the dominant threats, while in lower income regions health loss was driven by issues such as low educational attainment.Many major donor nations, including the US and UK, have announcedlarge cuts to aid spendingover the past year. The potential collapse of, or steep reduction in, international health aid could cause up to 1.5bn Dalys before 2100, the commission found, nearly 70% of which would be in sub-Saharan Africa. The region also bears the brunt of child malnutrition.The commission was made up of 35 experts, and its findings will be shared on Sunday at the World Health Summit in Berlin, Germany. Their assessment will be updated annually to re-evaluate the 17 threats identified, incorporating new data and any emerging hazards.The authors urged leaders to address the risks before they escalated into crises, including via investment in technological innovations and by strengthening health systems.“We started this process three years ago, thinking that there were three big threats: conflict, climate, and pandemics,” said Murray. “There’s a much larger number of threats that we need to worry about, and governments really need to dedicate some money and staff to the task of anticipation, prevention and preparation for this more diverse set of threats.”Explore more on these topicsGlobal healthAI (artificial intelligence)Nuclear weaponsClimate crisisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Recruitment boss accused of being behind ‘doxxing’ campaign against RNLI and anti-racism activists | RNLI | The Guardian
description: Tom Watson, of Worcester, alleged to be behind Big Time Charlie X account that created so-called Traitorbase
Author: Ben Quinn
Headline: Tom Watson, of Worcester, alleged to be behind Big Time Charlie X account that created so-called Traitorbase
Content: Tom Watson is accused of being behind the X account Big Time Charlie.Photograph: FacebookView image in fullscreenTom Watson is accused of being behind the X account Big Time Charlie.Photograph: FacebookRNLIRecruitment boss accused of being behind ‘doxxing’ campaign against RNLI and anti-racism activistsTom Watson, of Worcester, alleged to be behind Big Time Charlie X account that created so-called TraitorbaseBen QuinnPolitical correspondentSat 10 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 03.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe owner of a recruitment firm has been accused of being at the centre of a so-called “doxxing” campaign against the Royal National Lifeboat Institution (RNLI), anti-racism activists and business executives who recruit black, Asian and minority ethnic workers.Tom Watson, from Worcester, is alleged to be behind anXaccount calling itself “Big Time Charlie”, which was deactivated shortly after he was named by the campaign group Hope Not Hate.The account had almost 50,000 followers and had become increasingly prominent in recent weeks as RNLI staff found themselves being harassed and attacked online as far-right activists targeted them over their involvement in rescuing people trying to cross the Channel in small boats.The account, which has a history of racist comments, appears to have been using AI to scrape data from LinkedIn and other sites to build a so-called Traitorbase. The Big Time Charlie account was removed almost immediately after Hope Not Hate alleged that Watson was behind it, and after the Guardian approached him for comment.Like the posts on Watson’s LinkedIn account, the X account has frequently praised the hard-right MP Rupert Lowe. It also claimed to have donated £2,500 to Lowe’sRestore Britainparty and joined its “Cromwell Club” for those activists who pay a certain level of donation.Targets of doxxing by the Big Time Charlie account told the Guardian of the impact.They included Chantelle Lunt, a Green party councillor in Merseyside who has already been targeted by the far right, and who made a report to the police after details about her were published online by the account.She said: “Someone told me that I had been doxxed and when I went to look I saw that details about me appeared to be on a spreadsheet which included reference to other people who were involved in Stand Up to Racism.“The climate at the moment is horrendous and I’m no stranger to people targeting me and my family, but there’s a big concern when this information is actively put out there. You can see people engaging with it and actively encouraging each other.”A spokesperson for a charity that was targeted told the Guardian: “This is another example of a cynical attempt to spread misinformation that has unfortunately gone unchecked on social media platforms.“This is an attempt to sow discord and division among communities and prevent organisations trying to help the most vulnerable communities in this country from operating at their full potential.“Time spent combating misinformation and bigotry is a distraction from these organisations’ programme work here at home, which actually makes a difference in the ordinary lives of people in the UK.Social mediacompanies, the media and politicians have a responsibility to clamp down on misinformation and the division it causes.”RNLI warns supporters their personal information may have been hackedRead moreA number of businesses, big and small, were also doxxed on the account, which posted the photographs and names of executives who were said to have been involved in hiring minority ethnic staff.A businessperson who was also targeted described their doxxing by the account as “bizarre”.“Thankfully it doesn’t seem to have led to any problems, but it’s not something that you expect to have to contend with. It’s a pretty unpleasant thing to do, especially if it’s someone who is involved in their own business,” they added.Watson divides his time between the UK and US and founded the recruitment firm Futura Energy Group, which describes itself as “a specialist recruitment and build-with talent partner for companies operating across AI”.Archived online records show that the Big Time Charlie account originally bore the name Tom Watson, while a range of other evidence links him to it.That included regular references by the account to being in Puerto Rico, where Futura is based according to its LinkedIn account, and references to working in recruitment for technical roles.The Big Time Charlie account posted on 20 July that they were in Zurich and shared a photo taken in the grounds of the Vitznauerhof hotel. Two days later, Watson posted on his LinkedIn profile that he was in Switzerland and shared another image taken from the Vitznauerhof hotel.Watson was approached for comment.Explore more on these topicsRNLIRupert LoweRestore BritainAI (artificial intelligence)XSocial medianewsShareReuse this content

title: The Jane Doe in the Cornell seven case is getting threats | Arwa Mahdawi | The Guardian
description: Every time a story about a woman being raped becomes headline news, the same pattern repeats without fail
Author: Arwa Mahdawi
Headline: Every time a story about a woman being raped becomes headline news, the same pattern repeats without fail
Content: A Stop Sexual Violence protest in the wake of the Cornell University rape allegations, in Seattle, Washington, on Thursday.Photograph: David Ryder/ReutersView image in fullscreenA Stop Sexual Violence protest in the wake of the Cornell University rape allegations, in Seattle, Washington, on Thursday.Photograph: David Ryder/ReutersThe Week in PatriarchyRape and sexual assaultThe Jane Doe in the Cornell seven case is getting threatsArwa MahdawiEvery time a story about a woman being raped becomes headline news, the same pattern repeats without failSat 10 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 09.03 EDTShareIf she really was raped, why didn’t she speak up earlier? Why did she get drunk? Why was she wearing such a short skirt? Why did she walk home by herself?God, it’s exhausting, isn’t it? Every time a story about a woman being raped becomes headline news, the same pattern repeats without fail. People accuse the woman of asking for it. They question her motives; they scrutinize her looks; they attack her character. And without fail, she is punished for speaking up.It happened to Christine Blasey Ford when she accused Brett Kavanaugh, then a supreme court nominee, of assaulting her when they were both teenagers in the 1980s. Ford and her familyreportedlyhad to flee their home because of threats and harassment.According to her lawyers, her email was hacked and she was impersonated online. Her entire life was turned upside down. Meanwhile, Kavanaugh waspraisedby Donald Trump and now has a lifetime appointment on the supreme court.It happened with E Jean Carroll, who accused Trump of sexually assaulting her back in 1996. Trump said Carroll was not his “type” and “totally lying”. His lawyer asked Carroll why shedidn’t screamduring the alleged attack and why she didn’t go to the police at the time. Carroll’s life was upended and the Trump administration opened a criminal investigationinto her.Now we’re seeing the cycle repeat with the woman known as Jane Doe in theCornell gang-rape case. According to her attorney, Thomas Giuffra, Doe is receiving threats from people who have discovered her identity and is terrified for her safety. Doe was even the victim of aswattingepisode this week, a form of harassment where someone places a false call to emergency services with the goal of sending armed officers to the victim’s location. Giuffratold CNNthat officers pointed weapons at Doe’s family after a fake tip about someone “killing people in the house” on Tuesday evening. “If you had a trigger-happy cop, or somebody had done the wrong thing, somebody could have ended up dead,” Giuffra said.Nobody ended up dead on that particular occasion, but Doe’s character is systematically being assassinated. “What attracts women to those parties – late at night, like Jane Doe – to walk alone to a fraternity house and take her chances?” Caitlin Flanagantut-tutted in the Free Press. “What she’s really looking for is a man. And she has no idea how to find a good one.” The underlying message here? She should have known better than to go to a frat party. Silly little girl: she was asking for it.Rightwing commentator Megyn Kelly, who has been vocal about her experience ofsexual harassmentat Fox News and should really know better, went even further and attacked Doe’s looks. “No one will even consider the possibility that this woman made a decision to get it on with four men total, not seven, and enjoyed it because, I’m just going to be honest, she’s not the most attractive gal,” Kelly said on arecent episode of her podcast. “She’s extremely beefy in like her arms and her legs. She has a whole video online talking about her cankles. And she possibly enjoyed being admired. This is how women make these mistakes.”It should go without saying that being raped is not a “mistake”. It should go without saying that a woman should be able to go to a party and have a drink and walk home at night and wear whatever she likes without it being an invitation for men to rape her. And yet it seems that women have to keep saying all this over and over again.Arizona congressional candidate says she was raped while repairing campaign signBernadette Greene Placentia told thePhoenix New Timesthat she was attacked in August while walking across a parking lot in the middle of the night to fix a damaged campaign sign.“Speaking publicly about what happened has been incredibly difficult for Bernadette,” a campaign spokespersonsaid. “She chose to share her story because she knows many survivors struggle in silence, and she hopes that by speaking about her experience, others will know they are not alone.”A Pentagon influencer said liberal women will ‘end Western civilization’“The Pentagon has secretly installed several conservative military veterans with large online followings in government roles … [to] amplify Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth’s viewpoints,” the Washington Postreportedin August. One of these influencers is a retired army colonel called Kurt Schlichter who is, surprise, surprise, a raging misogynist.This week, Wired highlighted a number of Schlichter’s disturbing writings, including an article for Townhall in which he argues “liberal women” could end western civilization. “These self-righteous crones are a pestilence, a plague upon Western society … whose antics, if unchecked, will inevitably lead to the fall of civilization,”he wrote.Child killed in Gaza every 71 minutes for the past three yearsNearly 22,000 Palestinian children have been killed in Israeli attacks on Gaza over three years, with more than 71,000 orphaned, according to a report by Gaza’s health ministrysummarized by Drop Site news. That number includes 5,444 children under five and 1,125 infants under one year old.Israeli politician says Israel should have left Gaza ‘empty’The Zehut party chair, Moshe Feiglin, who is running in the October elections with the finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, toldthe Jerusalem Postthat the whole of Gaza should have been emptied of Palestinians and annexed by Israel. Inanother interviewon i24News’s Israel Out Loud, Feiglin said everyone in Gaza should leave, “down to babies born prematurely”.JD Vance does not seem to know what ‘socialism’ meansWhen asked to define the term during a Thursday press conference,he said: “Classically, you would think socialism is about prioritizing workers … [But now] what it actually means in the American context is, that you want to replace American workers with foreign workers, and you want boys to play in girls’ sports.”Kimberly Guilfoyle allegedly asked Trump donor to pay $100,000 credit card billGuilfoyle is the US ambassador to Greece and the former fiancee of Donald Trump Jr. She is also a former prosecuting attorney, Fox News host, and first lady of San Francisco during her ex-husband Gavin Newsom’s tenure as mayor of the city. All of which to say: the woman should be more than capable of paying her own credit card bills. But, as we know, Maga types don’t like paying foranything themselves. According to the Wall Street Journal, days before her confirmation hearing last year, Guilfoyle asked a Trump donor to payher $100,000 American Express billin exchange for access to the administration. (Guilfoyle’s attorney has disputed the authenticity of text messages cited in reporting.)Margaret Hamilton, the woman whose work allowed men to walk on the moon, dies aged 90The pioneering computer scientist helped launch software engineering as an industry and was hired as the first programmer for theApollo project at MIT. In that role, she led a team of software engineers who poweredthe first moon landing.Flag football is all the rage among US teen girls“According to data from the National Federation of State High School Associations, more than 100,000 American high school girlsplayed flag footballat school during the 2025-26 academic year, which constitutes a 48% jump from the previous year and an increase of more than 550% from just five years ago,”Bloomberg reports. This is largely because the NFL has poured $192m into the sport, which is safer and simpler than traditional US football. The idea is that participation as a kid will translate into fandom (and profits for the NFL) as an adult.A naked Trump statue has been unveiled inside the European parliamentIt’s called the Orange Plague and shows an unrobed and gold Trump sitting on the shoulders of another man while wielding a large golf club. It was only on display for a day at the parliament’s Winston Churchill building in France, but the sculptorhas saidhe was “astonished” that the exhibition took place at all.The week in pawtriarchyAs if the Orange Plague in the US and the “possible” plague in Siberia weren’t enough to worry about, Los Angeles county recently documented its firstrabid raccoonin more than 50 years. Somehow this feels paw-tentous.Explore more on these topicsRape and sexual assaultThe Week in PatriarchyUS universitiesWomencommentShareReuse this content

title: LeBron James is everything Philadelphia wants. And everything it can’t stand | LeBron James | The Guardian
description: The city has embraced its new superstar with open arms, even as he choppers in from Manhattan and makes no secret of the fact that Philadelphia was never his first choice
Author: Bryan Armen Graham
Headline: The city has embraced its new superstar with open arms, even as he choppers in from Manhattan and makes no secret of the fact that Philadelphia was never his first choice
Content: LeBron James made his pre-season debut with the 76ers on Thursday.Photograph: Ishika Samant/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenLeBron James made his pre-season debut with the 76ers on Thursday.Photograph: Ishika Samant/Getty ImagesLeBron JamesLeBron James is everything Philadelphia wants. And everything it can’t standBryan Armen GrahamThe sports-mad city has embraced its new superstar, even as he choppers in from Manhattan and makes no secret of the fact that Philly was never his first choiceSat 10 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 09.24 EDTSharePhiladelphia has always had an instinctive affinity with athletes who embrace the grind over the glamour. In a place where sports mean a littletoomuch, commitment has traditionally counted for more than celebrity. What it demands above all, sometimes unreasonably, is the sense that they have bought in, that the city and its fortunes matter to them as much as they do to the people who devote their lives to backing its teams.Few embodied that ethic more completely than Lane Johnson, the Eagles’ revered right tackle and best player for more than a decade,who abruptly announced his retirementTuesday after 14 seasons, two Super Bowl titles and acareer spent neutralizingsome of the most freakish physical specimens to walk the earth. Johnson’s quotidian greatness on the offensive line was almost perversely workmanlike. According to Pro Football Focus, he allowed just 10 sacks across close to 7,000 pass-blocking snaps in the last 13 years, goingentire seasonswithout letting his man bring down the quarterback. The Eagles won nearly two-thirds of their games when he played and lost nearly two-thirds when he didn’t.LeBron James once raged against the machine. Increasingly, he helps prop it upRead moreSurely a first-ballot Hall of Famer when he’s eligible in 2031, he earned a place in the first rank of Philadelphia sporting legends alongside Mike Schmidt, Julius Erving and Bobby Clarke, despite playing a position where success is largely measured by how little anyone notices you. But perhaps the most revealing thing Johnson did was decide when to stop. At 36, he walked away from millions in future earnings to prioritize his mental wellbeing and focus on his parents’ health. For a man who made his living holding the line, there was something fitting about knowing when to let go.Johnson’s departure comes at a particularly anxious moment on the local sports scene. The ageing Phillies’desultory wildcard exit against the Atlanta Braveslast week marked a fifth consecutive playoff appearance with diminishing returns. The Flyers have opened their season with five straight losses, splashing cold water on themounting optimismthat had surrounded them. The Union have US soccer’s most exciting prospect ingenerational talent Cavan Sullivan, but they remain a decidedly niche concern in a town dominated by its four traditional major-league teams. And the Eagles, almost comicallybeset by injuryand suddenly without one of their franchise cornerstones as they travel to London this week, appear consigned to a rebuild. Across the city, the sensation is less of a championship window closing than of several slamming shut at once.All of which has left the new-look 76ers, whodebuted their tricked-out starting fiveon Thursday night in Brooklyn, carrying an almost inordinate share of the city’s sporting hopes. The timing makes for an uncomfortable juxtaposition. Philadelphia is losing an athlete who spent 14 years making the city his own, just as it welcomesthe greatest basketball player to ever live, who has given precious little indication that he intends to do the same.View image in fullscreenLeBron James poses with a new-look Philadelphia 76ers team alongside Jaylen Brown, Joel Embiid, Tyrese Maxey and VJ Edgecombe (from left) during the team’s media day in Camden, New Jersey, on 28 September 2026.Photograph: Chris Szagola/APThe Philly sporting identity has always been shaped by its uneasy relationship with New York, the northern neighbor that eclipsed it as America’s commercial and cultural capital a long time ago and has spent the intervening centuries reminding it of that fact. That history has bred a peculiar combination of civic pride and insecurity, a conviction that Philadelphia is entitled to better and a gnawing suspicion that deep down it doesn’t even deserve it. The 76ers, third on the NBA’s all-time wins list, haven’t won a championship since 1983, spending more than four decades watching Boston and Los Angeles pile up the sport’s prizes. The city’s athletes are expected to understand that burden, or at least pretend to share it.James admitted at last month’s media day that Philadelphia had not been his preferred landing spot in free agency. The 41-year-old had dreamed of finishing his career at Madison Square Garden, only to abandon the idea after the Knicks ended their 53-year title drought in June, wary of being perceived as a ring-chaser. For a city that has spent generations bristling at New York’s perceived superiority, the confession carried a particular sting. Nearly a century after WC Fields quipped that he would rather see Paris before he died but Philadelphia would do, the NBA’s most famous star appeared to have reached the same conclusion. Even now, James seems reluctant to commit to the place geographically. Asked where he would live, he answered: “Both. Multiple residences.” That apparently means commuting from New York in a Fanatics-branded helicopter that gets roughly 1.6 miles to the gallon.Allow Instagram content?This article includes content provided byInstagram. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as they may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueThe Leonardo AW139, suppliedthrough his sponsorship arrangementwith Michael Rubin’s sports merchandising empire, has become James’s preferred mode of transport between the two cities. Publicly availableflight-tracking datashowed 18 trips between Manhattan and Northeast Philadelphia Airport in the first days of October alone. Never mind that Amtrak’s Acela service connects the cities in about 90 minutes, with comfortable seats, wifi and enough legroom even for a 6ft 9in basketball player.The environmental optics have raised eyebrows. The AW139, accordingto a Defector report, is unusually emissions-intensive, even by the standards of private helicopters. But in Philadelphia, the symbolism is as offensive as the carbon footprint. It’s hard to imagine a more exquisitely calibrated insult to the city’s sporting psyche. Philly fans have never cared much where their sporting heroes come from. What matters is whether, somewhere along the way, they come to regard the city as their own. Johnson gave the city 14 years of his body, his loyalty and his labor. James appears determined to give it his working hours.Which is fine. James isn’t the first gun-for-hire to find himself in an arranged marriage in the winter of his career. Yet the helicopter is merely the latest indignity in James’s increasinglydepressing transformationfrom athlete-activist into walking corporate billboard. Not so long ago, James was helping lead More Than a Vote, the organization he co-founded in 2020 to combat voter suppression, register voters and mobilize Black communities. He leveraged his extraordinary celebrity to encourage civic participation and tell people that their voices mattered. It was a meaningful demonstration of what an athlete with virtually unlimited cultural influence could accomplish. Six years later, he’s hawkingonline gamblingandbrown liquor.View image in fullscreenThe abrupt retirement of Lane Johnson (above) has added to a growing sense of uncertainty around Philadelphia’s sporting fortunes.Photograph: Michael Owens/Getty ImagesHis reported $15m-a-year partnership with Polymarket, a prediction-market platform encouraging ordinary marksto wager on everythingfrom basketball to elections to war, is all the more dispiriting. The mainstreaming of prediction markets, and the relentless creep of gambling into news, politics and virtually every corner of society, are one of the bleaker developments in American public life. The same cultural capital that once encouraged people to participate in democracy is now being deployed to encourage them to speculate on it with their disposable income, all so a handful of techno-fascist investors can become obscenely rich. His involvement with Fanatics, with its ever-expanding connections to the gambling industry, makes the whole spectacle even harder to reconcile with his cultivated image as a socially conscious athlete. It’s the kind of corporate exploitation couched in cultural legitimization and the aesthetics of cool thatfeels ripe for a Spike Lee satire… were the Bamboozled director notappearing in glossy Polymarket adshimself.Nobody begrudges James the fortune his extraordinary talent and longevity has earned him. Nor should anyone expect professional athletes in his echelon to move like ascetics. His philanthropic work, most notably the I Promise School in Akron, remains meaningful regardless of whatand whohe chooses to align himself with. But there’s something grotesque aboutthe NBA’s first active billionairecollecting millions more to promote an industry fueling an emerging public-health crisis, while burning extraordinary quantities of fuel to avoid the mild inconvenience of the train.Johnson spent 14 years protecting Philadelphia’s quarterbacks before deciding there were things more important than football and money. James has accumulated enough wealth to say no to almost anything, yet he keeps finding reasons to say yes. Perhaps that’s the most lamentable part of the spectacle: a man who once seemed determined to change the world now seems more concerned with what it will pay him to fly over it.Explore more on these topicsLeBron JamesPhiladelphiaPhiladelphia 76ersPhiladelphia EaglesUS sportsNBABasketballcommentShareReuse this content

title: A banner along the Pacific Highway speaks volumes about why some communities are turning to One Nation | Julianne Schultz | The Guardian
description: ‘Centrelink is evil’ isn’t a call to slash welfare payments – it’s a sign people are frustrated about the ability to access government support
Author: Julianne Schultz
Headline: ‘Centrelink is evil’ isn’t a call to slash welfare payments – it’s a sign people are frustrated about the ability to access government support
