Content: ‘The drive north from Sydney along the Pacific Highway is lined with towns that are potentially prey for One Nation,’ Julianne Schultz writes.Photograph: Ellen Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘The drive north from Sydney along the Pacific Highway is lined with towns that are potentially prey for One Nation,’ Julianne Schultz writes.Photograph: Ellen Smith/The GuardianOpinionOne NationA banner along the Pacific Highway speaks volumes about why some communities are turning to One NationJulianne Schultz‘Centrelink is evil’ isn’t a call to slash welfare payments – it’s a sign people are frustrated about the ability to access government supportSat 10 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 18.29 EDTShareThe drive north from Sydney along the Pacific Highway is lined with towns that are potentially prey forOne Nation.For years, handmade roadside signs disputed climate change and objected to the voice to parliament referendum.Now they stridently support the angry party of despair.One Nation celebrated stunning success in Queensland in 1998 – then it all fell apart. What happened?Read moreThe signs have given way near Port Macquarie to what can best be described as a homemade installation. It is a tribute to Ben Roberts-Smith, One Nation and a foundation that declares Fire the Liars. A plinth is topped by the Australian flag –“Great Britain by night”as Jerry Seinfeld once described it.A banner strung between trees hints at one of the grievances fuelling disappointment and anger in these communities. It says: CENTRELINK IS EVIL.The electorate of Cowper, bookended by Port Macquarie and Coffs Harbour, is one of the“least resilient”communities in Australia, according to a Redbridge survey. If you didn’t know this, you may think the banner was a protest against social security payments. After all, theOne Nation promise to slash government spendingwould not, if realised, leave welfare payments untouched.Instead, the banner speaks to the frustration of people in an area with above average unemployment, more poverty, lower education, experience when trying to secure the benefits they are due.Even the local National party MP has argued thatthe Centrelink payment for jobseekers is not enoughand needs to be increased so fewer people are forced to live by their wits and in poverty.View image in fullscreenThe banner beside the Pacific Highway.Photograph: Julianne SchultzCalling Centrelink evil speaks to the exasperation of completing endless, complicated forms, the hours spent on the phone to call centres and the fear that, as withrobodebtand theautomated aged careanddisability assessment tools, the computer may just say no.On an international scale, Australia is better than most nations in providing some income support to some of those who need it – the swift delivery of jobkeeper during the pandemic to most, if not all, who needed it, was exemplary. Insome US statesthe pandemic was over before cheques arrived.But it is far from perfect. Nearly 4 million Australians including 757,000 childrenlive in poverty, with insecure food and housing and manifestly inadequate public support.Those at the pointy end of disadvantage are likely to have fewer physical and emotional resources at hand, and many are worn down by the experience of applying for government support.The frustration they feel is acute and personal. Security guards stand to attention at Services Australia offices – they may be necessary but do not make anyone feel welcome. Even resilient people are often reduced to tears as they attempt to navigate a system that seems to imply they are cheats.The US journalist Annie Lowrey documents in her book,The Time Tax, how the frustration with an overly bureaucratic system targets the most needy and eroded trust in government, and helped create the conditions that led to theelection of Donald Trump. Despite promises to improve their lives, he has failed to deliver.The US system with its more than 10,000 jurisdictions, countless support programs and endless complicated forms makes the Australian model look effective and responsive. But that is not how it feels to many of those who depend on it.In both nations, politicians spend too much time talking about how much they are distributing, and not enough time explaining how to receive it.The bamboozlingly big numbers used in political debate don’t always translate into actual dollars in the bank accounts of the neediest.Cutting government spendingwon’t make things better.The polling group Redbridge’s survey on the resilience of Australian electorates assessed resilience not just in terms of incomes but their access to health services and the strength of community networks.It paints a chilling picture of inequality – with the most resilient communities in the inner suburbs of the major cities where people have the money they need in an emergency, access to quality health resources, and strong social networks. In the outer suburbs, financial security shrinks and community networks are also weaker.View image in fullscreenAnother Pacific Highway sign.Photograph: Julianne SchultzCowper, where theCentrelinkbanner flies, is Australia’s sixth least resilient electorate in terms of health, followed by the nearby electorates of Paterson and Hunter. Paterson, two hours’ south, is the 10th least resilient electorate – in terms of health, finance and social relations.One Nation to establish headquarters in multimillion-dollar Brisbane office bought by Gina RinehartRead moreThe tendency to dismiss One Nation as racist and inept,which it no doubt is, misses the point. People who feel left behind will inevitably lash out. Theubiquity of online propagandafeeds this and leads to some wacky conclusions.One example, the Lowy Institute’s long-running survey ofAustralian attitudes to international leaderssuggests that most Australians give the prime minister a net positive score, are sceptical but still positive about Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, but deeply distrustful of Vladimir Putin and Kim Jong-un.One Nation voters, by contrast, put the prime minister between Putin and Kim, with anet negative score of 82.Whatever Anthony Albanese’s shortcomings, to suggest that he is on par with these men is delusional.At thelaunch of George Megalogenis’s bookThree Shocks last month, Albanese disputed the suggestion that Labor was vulnerable to One Nation. He argued that there was always a rightwing rump in Australia.Tactically that may be true but real people are hurting and being egged on by dishonourable agents who sense their pain but have no capacity to address it.Addressing inequity is the job of a progressive government, not treating the suffering like political playdough.Julianne Schultz is the author of The Idea of AustraliaExplore more on these topicsOne NationOpinionAustralian politicsCentrelinkRural and regional AustraliaInequalityWelfarePovertycommentShareReuse this content

title: The more Putin escalates his attacks on Europe, the more Europe should support Ukraine | Timothy Garton Ash | The Guardian
description: Moscow’s imperialist strongman believes decadent European democracies can be cowed. Our job is to prove him wrong, says Guardian columnist Timothy Garton Ash
Author: Timothy Garton Ash
Headline: Moscow’s imperialist strongman believes decadent European democracies can be cowed. Our job is to prove him wrong, says Guardian columnist Timothy Garton Ash
Content: A mural depicting Vladimir Putin at a polling station in Donetsk, in Russian-controlled Ukraine, during Russia’s parliamentary elections, 20 September 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA mural depicting Vladimir Putin at a polling station in Donetsk, in Russian-controlled Ukraine, during Russia’s parliamentary elections, 20 September 2026.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionVladimir PutinThe more Putin escalates his attacks on Europe, the more Europe should support UkraineTimothy Garton AshMoscow’s imperialist strongman believes decadent European democracies can be cowed. Our job is to prove him wrongSat 10 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 12.35 EDTShareVladimir Putin is escalating both his full-scale war against Ukraine and hisshadow war against the rest of Europe. His main purpose in the shadow one is to break European support for Ukraine so he can subjugate that country, something he regards as existential for Russia’s future and his own. While we in the rest of Europe must prepare as best we can to defend ourselves against every kind of hybrid attack, the central thrust of our response should be to redouble our support for Ukraine. Ukraine is his main target. It’s there, and only there, not in a contest of a thousand hybrid pinpricks, that Putin’s Russia can in a meaningful sense be defeated and deterred.In a powerful new book, Warum Russland nicht aufhören wird (Why Russia Won’t Stop), the German historian Martin Schulze Wessel shows how Putin’s policy fits into a much older Russian tradition of territorial expansionism and striving for hegemony, combined with a religiously infused imperial ideology. Hereminds usthat in 2016 Putin said “Russia’s frontier ends nowhere” and in 2025, “wherever the boot of a Russian soldier steps, that is ours”. West Europeans, fondly imagining that we have consigned such brute territorial imperialism to the dustbin of history, tend to think there must be some other explanation (eg something we did “wrong”, like the eastward expansion of Nato). Finns, Estonians and Poles know better. Despite Russia’s weaknesses, the author concludes, it is “the most dangerous country in the world”. Some in Asia might question that large claim, but certainly Russia is the most dangerous countryfor Europe.Schulze Wessel makes another simple but very pertinent point: Russia’s expansion was always facilitated by cooperation with other great powers and arrested when it faced equal and opposing powers. Since Donald Trump’s return to the White House last year, the United States has ceased to be the latter and has at times looked like the former. So now it’s Europe that is shouldering the burden of being the equal and opposing power. Europe (including the UK)has now given more aid to Ukrainethan the US. Its combined economies are 10 times larger than Russia’s; Germany’s economy alone is twice the size.And it’s Germany that’s now central to this European effort. Cumulatively, since the beginning of the full-scale war in 2022, Germany has been the biggest individual country donor apart from the US. According to theKiel Institute’s Ukraine support tracker, it has given twice as much as Britain or France. As people in Kyiv and Odesa are daily pounded by Putin’s ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones, it’s worth looking at the Kiel tracker’s figures for air defence systems. Germany has so far donated 19 of them, including five of the vital US-built Patriot air defence batteries – two more than the US itself has given.In the first year of this war,I arguedthat Germany “has a unique historical responsibility to help defend a free and sovereign Ukraine”. At that time, I felt strongly that Germany was not yet doing what it should. Now, in the fifth year of a conflict that has already lasted longer than the first world war and shows no sign of ending, I can say without hesitation that it is. This is not just a matter of the numerical scale of its support for Ukraine and its own increased defence spending, which, on thelatest projectionsfrom the German finance ministry, will reach €154bn (£130bn) in 2028 (Roughly the same asRussia’s total estimated military expenditurefor this year).It’s also a matter of political will. Chancellor Friedrich Merz has shown that will, and courage, by taking thetrain from Germany to Ukraineon the evening of 3 October, the 36th anniversary of German unification, with a strong delegation including defence industry leaders. The Russian bombardment of civilian targets in central Kyiv, including Ukraine’s National Academy of Sciences and bridges across the Dnipro River, did not stop even though – or perhaps exactly because – Moscow knew the German leader would be there.0:49Russian drone hits key bridge in Kyiv on German chancellor’s visit – videoFor a historian, there’s something very familiar here. Oh no, it’sGermanyand Russia again! Yet each time is different. Historically, Germany is one of the powers that has done most to facilitate Russian expansion (just think of the 1939 Hitler-Stalin pact) but also most to threaten it. In the first world war, and even at the margins in the second, some Ukrainian nationalists saw in a conflict between Germany and Russia a chance for their independence. Instead, they got imperial Germany’s colonialism (and then German defeat) in the first case and Hitler’s genocidal fascism (and then German defeat) in the second.Now, at last, Germany is genuinely engaged, at some cost and risk to itself, for the sovereignty ofUkraine. To anyone who knows this tangled history, there is something not just redemptive, but frankly inspiring in this sight: a democratic Germany playing a leading role in supporting an independent Ukraine’s bid to assume its proper place in a wider European community of free countries.But for how long? And with how much support elsewhere in Europe? Precisely because Putin sees Germany’s centrality, it’s one of the main targets of his hybrid war, fromexplosive-laden dronesat Leipzig airport that the German government has firmly attributed to Russia andassassination threatsagainst defence industry bosses, all the way to covert political interference and disinformation. While Ukraine faces its most difficult winter yet, three closely connected things will be put to the test: Germany’s will to stay committed on the right side of history; the capacity of democracies to sustain the fight against a dictatorship (a perennial concern); and Europe’s ability to remain united in this cause.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionPutin’s escalating bombing campaign won’t break Ukrainians’ resolve. History shows that it’s doomed to fail | Rajan MenonRead moreA sceptic can point to many grounds for pessimism. Merz is unpopular at home. Alternative für Deutschland (AfD), the party currently making the running in German politics, would abandon Ukraine to Russia. In France, the National Rally’s presidential candidate, Marine Le Pen, says her country can’t afford to go on giving so much to Ukraine. Solidarity with Ukraine is also crumbling on the right in Poland, with two smaller parties sounding frankly anti-Ukrainian. In one Italianopinion polllast month, more than half those asked were opposed to continued weapons deliveries to Kyiv.In Brussels recently, I found alarge audience seemingly stalwartin support of Ukraine – until, right at the end, our discussion turned to the issue of using the Russian frozen assets held in Belgium. Ah now, that’s a different matter … Yet with the terrible damage being inflicted on the Ukrainian economy, including its grain exports via the Black Sea, experts estimate that as much as €100bn of additional support for Kyiv may be needed in 2027 alone – and hard-pressed European taxpayers are in no mood to cough that up.Putin believes decadent European democracies will crumble before the iron determination of an imperialist strongman. Our job is to prove him wrong.Timothy Garton Ash is a historian, political writer and Guardian columnist. His new book,Europe in 7½ Chapters, is published next weekExplore more on these topicsVladimir PutinOpinionUkraineRussiaGermanyFriedrich MerzEuropecommentShareReuse this content

title: Angry French students take to the streets. British students don’t – and I think I know why | Kitty Sayers | The Guardian
description: I grew up in France, where all children are taught about the revolutionary roots of their nation and the responsibility of the state towards its citizens, says Kitty Sayers, a master’s student in journalism
Author: Kitty Sayers
Headline: I grew up in France, where all children are taught about the revolutionary roots of their nation and the responsibility of the state towards its citizens, says Kitty Sayers, a master’s student in journalism
Content: Student protesters in the Place de la Bastille in Paris, 8 October 2026Photograph: Orin Louis/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenStudent protesters in the Place de la Bastille in Paris, 8 October 2026Photograph: Orin Louis/ZUMA Press Wire/ShutterstockOpinionFranceAngry French students take to the streets. British students don’t – and I think I know whyKitty SayersI grew up in France, where all children are taught about the revolutionary roots of their nation and what the state owes its citizens. The lessons leave their markSat 10 Oct 2026 05.45 EDTFirst published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTShareYoung British people have plenty to be angry about. Crushing student debt, private-school privilege, a housing market they can’t enter. Yet unlike their French counterparts, they have little tradition of turning that frustration into collective action. I grew up inFranceas a Briton, and for years I have watched my French friends do something my British ones never seem to: take to the streets.“To arms, citizens! Form your battalions! Let’s march, let’s march!” It shouldn’t be too surprising, given the rousing lyrics of La Marseillaise, that France’s revolutionary spirit is not a relic of the past.Thelycéeprotests in the past week have displayed the organisation and bravery of the French students. In Lens, a 15-year-oldlost his handto a police grenade during a blockade. More than6,000 people have been arrested, many of them under 18. Hundreds of schools across France are either blockaded or closed. These teenagers know the risks and commit to turning up anyway, day after day. I can’t imagine that happening in Britain, so what makes the French so different?First, there’s the history. France’s republic was born of insurrection and has never forgotten it. French pupils learn that protest, uprising and rioting are the origin story of their freedoms, so these methods are championed in promoting change. We grew up in school with the idea that if you don’t like something, you have the power to change it. The language of rights, citizenship and collective power is woven into French education. The French Revolution appears in the curriculum twice, for pupils aged 12 and then again at 16; the student protests of 1968 are taught at age 14 and again at 17. Debating is encouraged in schools from as early ascollège, or at about 11 years old.Young peopleare expected to have an opinion and not be afraid to defend it.Even I, at 11, started to feel patriotic during our moral and civic education classes, despite not having a French passport. Protesting is taught as a legally framed fundamental right and a civic responsibility. Of course, withlycéensnot yet being old enough to vote, protest is the next best thing.In the final year oflycée, pupils study Rousseau’sDu Contrat Social(The Social Contract), which argues that citizens should only surrender their unrestricted natural liberty in exchange for civil and moral freedoms. You give up your individual interests for thevolonté générale(general will) – put simply, you pay heavy taxes and in return you expect the country to work. That bargain is how the French understand their relationship with the state. When the government raises the retirement age, lets electricity bills soar or cuts school budgets, that is seen as a breach of the social contract. Protest is the automatic response.Britons, on the other hand, are subjects of the UK and are characterised more by an American-style individualism and a desire to live and let live. There is less collective spirit.Britain has an extraordinary history of protest, spanning Peterloo, the Chartists, the suffragettes and the poll tax riots, but there is arguably a different cultural relationship to these events. They can be remembered as stand-alone episodes and interruptions to the national story rather than as the story itself. The Thatcher era also did permanent damage to unions, contributing to the British public being a grumbling but compliant one, lacking in organising power.I see what’s happening here in Paris: reasonable student demands met with awful violence | Helen Massy-BeresfordRead moreBecause these values are ingrained across French society, and in every generation,the student protestersare emboldened by the firefighters, nurses, lawyers and teachers who have joined them in solidarity. Across social media, you can see these moments of support and unity. Aviral videoof the mayor of Saint-Denis,Bally Bagayoko, protecting students from the police is a striking example of this. It’s difficult to imagine British teenagers taking to the streets, because they would be alone.Parents have joined their children in protesting, and have called on other parents to do the same for the planned general strike on 17 October. (This is also a response to the police brutalitywitnessedin the past week.) Many parents were themselveslycéestudents and marched against education reforms and cuts. The anti-Macroniste parents (of whom there are many) don’t treat their children as delinquents, but as citizens exercising their rights.That does not mean every French parent supports every protest, or that French society is wholly united behind its students. While the French state technically encourages protest through the curriculum, the force and violence with which it has met its students says otherwise. And there is resentment of the protests among some students, particularly those who come from conservative households and believe that the blockades are a leftwing plot.Students in France are not necessarily more political than their British counterparts – young British people are active, but tend to take part in established and larger movements such as Extinction Rebellion or the Gaza protests rather than initiate protests themselves. The biggest difference lies in the French willingness to take to the streets, suddenly and en-masse. Unlike in the UK, the state is something the French are taught to engage with as citizens, and to challenge when necessary. If anything, thelycéensare just being good students.Kitty Sayers is a master’s student in journalismExplore more on these topicsFranceOpinionProtestYoung peopleEuropeStudentscommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘Jelliness is my life motto’: jackpot theatre prize winner Jaha Koo on kimchi, K-pop and his robotic eel | Stage | The Guardian
description: Feted for cooking up shows that can be mouthwatering as well as thought-provoking, the artist discusses his fusion of South Korean and European culture
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: Feted for cooking up shows that can be mouthwatering as well as thought-provoking, the artist discusses his fusion of South Korean and European culture
Content: ‘Did you have a good meal?’ … Jaha Koo.Photograph: Bea BorgersView image in fullscreen‘Did you have a good meal?’ … Jaha Koo.Photograph: Bea BorgersStageInterview‘Jelliness is my life motto’: jackpot theatre prize winner Jaha Koo on kimchi, K-pop and his robotic eelChris WiegandFeted for cooking up shows that can be mouthwatering as well as thought-provoking, the artist discusses his fusion of South Korean and European cultureSat 10 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 08.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I meet Jaha Koo in Oslo, where he has just been honoured with the prestigious International Ibsen award, I hand him a congratulatory packet of Haribo. The alternative would be a jar of kimchi but one of the many things you learn from Koo’s captivating theatre shows is that air travel and fermented vegetables can be a disastrous combo. When he moved to Berlin fromSouth Koreawith 10kg of his grandma’s finest kimchi, it became “bloated like a dead whale” and exploded on his balcony. His new neighbours were unimpressed.In Koo’s current touring production,Haribo Kimchi, he examines how this unlikely fusion of two foods represents his cultural identity. He does so while preparing an onstage banquet for two lucky audience members. Despite spending many years in Europe, where Haribo gummies originated around a century ago, Koo still finds himself considered foremost as Korean by Europeans. But when he returns to his original homeland he is not always seen as Korean either.We meet the day after the ceremony for the Ibsen award, founded by the Norwegian government and rewarding the winner with a huge 2.5m kroner (£200,000). Its past recipients include Lola Arias, Taylor Mac and Forced Entertainment. Koo cheerfully packs away my sweets for the next day’s flight to Belgium, where he is now based, and outlines his life motto of “jelliness”. It was only when he arrived in Europe that he started to eat gummy bears. “When you push jelly, it can shrink and change form but after a few seconds, it recovers its shape,” he says. “That is the same resilience I need to improve when I live outside Korea.” In the show, he explains how the bears’ smiley faces cheer him up when he’s feeling down.View image in fullscreenA kimchi diaspora … Jaha Koo cooks for theatregoers while he performs at the Edinburgh international festival 2026.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianIf Haribo was a new discovery, kimchi “was there before I was born and it was waiting for me”. As a Korean, he says, it is impossible to think about food without this quintessential side dish and he is part of “a kimchi diaspora”. The exact ingredients may differ around the world, depending on what’s available, but that doesn’t make any recipe inauthentic, he says: “Kimchi can be very diverse.” When he prepares the dish in Belgium, it sums up how he is true to his roots yet adapting to a new environment – “a kind of cultural assimilation”.Koo is an artist adept at setting out his stall – literally so in the case of Haribo Kimchi, where the set is a Korean snack cart called apojangmacha.It’s a movable feast, typically frequented by hungry customers of all backgrounds and generations – “kind of like a soul place,” he says. “They want to find comfort, eat quite humble food.” The roof of Koo’s bar has a Haribo-red glow that is translucent – a signifier, he suggests, of in-between states, much as thepojangmachassuggest lives in transit. “They are movable. There is no address. They appear in the evening and then disappear.” He draws a parallel with the country’s pop-up shop culture, which can transform a street over night, and Korea’s rapid pace of change which, viewed from Europe, makes him feel far behind as well as far away.A simple kimchi pancake is on the menu for Haribo Kimchi, its aroma filling the room in a show where Koo’s narrative is often sensory – such as the persimmon fruit trees he remembers from his youth. The theatregoers who take a seat at his bar are first given asomaek, a cocktail made with soju and beer, then several dishes including cold seaweed soup. As you’d expect from the theatrical cookery genre, which has included productions as different asTravis Alabanza’s BurgerzandHannah Khalil’s My English Persian Kitchen, each item on the menu has a different emotional resonance – Koo likens it to a score of carefully chosen compositions. Seaweed, for example, has links with birthday traditions in Korea and with ocean myths.View image in fullscreenA movable feast … the set for Haribo Kimchi with projected scenes from South Korea.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianThat brings us to Koo’s unusual co-star: a robotic eel who slithers around the stage and even delivers a ballad. (A giant gummy bear and a snail break out in song too.) It’s not as random as it sounds – Koo says he was drawn to the way eels leave their birth home, journey afar, but “then go back to their home before they die”.Haribo Kimchi, designed by Eunkyung Jeong (who is married to Koo) and with dramaturgy by their regular collaborator Dries Douibi, had its UK premiere at this summer’s Edinburgh international festival, where the audience invaded the stage for his end-of-show buffet. It’s not the first time Koo has found that mealtimes can make perfect metaphors for a show. In Korea, he says, “When we say hello, we always ask: ‘Did you have a good meal?’ Korean people call familysikku,which means ‘people who eat together’.” His earlier productionCuckoo, which he revived in Oslo, uses rice cookers as a symbol of both “economic imperialism and the pressure upon society”.Cuckoo delves into the longterm impact of Korea’s late 90s financial crisis and its neoliberal shift after the International Monetary Fund intervened with a $58bn rescue package. The part played by US treasury secretary Robert Rubin in what Koo calls “economic imperialism” is given a catchy electro-pop tune to rivalBo Burnham’s Jeff Bezostakedown. Koo describes, in a show as angry and raw as Haribo Kimchi is gentle and warm, a severe spike in unemployment, inequality and isolation – “a generation without a future”, including an account of his close friend’s suicide.View image in fullscreenAngry and raw … Jaha Koo’s Cuckoo, 2019.Photograph: Eunkyung JEONGCuckoo is the name of Korea’s brand of ubiquitous talking rice cookers – Koo appears on stage with three of them which have been hacked so that they gripe at each other and even sing. Listening to an answerphone message from his father, Koo cradles one cooker as if it’s his own child. The show also has much of the poppy melancholy of Haribo Kimchi and blurs with performance art: in the climax, he tips a mound of rice from the cooker, steam rises, and he feverishly prepares it in portions – an act of control and division as much as cheffing.His other shows take in linguistic colonisation: Lolling and Rolling is about the tongue surgery some South Koreans pursue in order to pronounce the English “R”. The History of Korean WesternTheatreexamines what you could call theatrical imperialism. “I studied at university in Korea and it was quite a conservative environment in terms of what theatre can be,” he says. In this classical western definition of drama, there was no room for a robotic eel or a chatty rice cooker and Koo is intent on putting tech on stage. “When we think about our contemporary world, it’s impossible to think and understand only with a human perspective. If we want to understand our time, then we have to think about different perspectives – nature, animals – and also technology like robotics.”In his Oslo ceremony speech, Koo duly reflected on the irony of receiving an award named after a canonical figure such as Ibsen: “But he was also an artist who questioned the theatre and society of his own time.” His next project will grapple with another artform that has become “a force for change”:K-pop, whose fans have wielded the genre’s bangers and glow sticks as a form of political protest, notably against former President Yoon’s martial law attempt in 2024. It will be the first of Koo’s shows where he will not perform; the cast will comprise singers. “I want to examine our global society through the lens of K-pop,” he says. “It has strong power as a new form of pop culture … On the other hand, the industry has a really dark side.”Theatre, for Koo, is an arena for us “to think together” he says. “This kind of solidarity is very important,” he adds. It’s drama as an act of breaking bread with the audience – or slurping cold seaweed soup.Haribo Kimchiis touring Europe until 21 November. Chris Wiegand’s trip to Oslo was provided by the International Ibsen award.Explore more on these topicsStageTheatreSouth KoreaAwards and prizesK-popFoodEdinburgh festival 2026interviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘People forgot I existed’: Audrey Niffenegger on taking 14 years to write a sequel to The Time Traveler’s Wife | Audrey Niffenegger | The Guardian
description: Her debut made her a global star. Now she has finally written a follow-up – and this time, it’s political. She talks about impostor syndrome, screen adaptations and becoming radicalised
Author: Sophie McBain
Headline: Her debut made her a global star. Now she has finally written a follow-up – and this time, it’s political. She talks about impostor syndrome, screen adaptations and becoming radicalised
Content: Audrey Neffenegger at her home in Chicago.Photograph: Lucy Hewett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAudrey Neffenegger at her home in Chicago.Photograph: Lucy Hewett/The GuardianAudrey NiffeneggerInterview‘People forgot I existed’: Audrey Niffenegger on taking 14 years to write a sequel to The Time Traveler’s WifeSophie McBainHer debut made her a global star. Now she has finally written a follow-up – and this time, it’s political. She talks about impostor syndrome, screen adaptations and becoming radicalisedSat 10 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 10.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe artist and novelistAudrey Niffeneggerbegan writing the long-awaited sequel to her bestselling debut, The Time Traveler’s Wife, in 2012, just after Obama’s re-election. It was a “rosy” time in American politics, “as good as it gets over here”, she says now, but her new novel required her to imagine what the world might look like in 20, 40, 60 years’ time. In the 14 years she spent exploring various dystopian futures, American politics moved on. And her imaginings began to look worryingly realistic.An early scene in the new book involves a group of neo-Nazis at a house party. When she was writing it, few people believed the US would witness a resurgence of neo-nazism. It’s not like she is “psychic or anything”, she tells me, the clues were all there. “The first thing I remember reading in the news was Watergate, and so I’ve grown up with Reagan, and the Republicans coming on stronger and stronger, so that every Republican president we get is more of a disaster. And I thought the logical progression of that would be fascism,” she says.Listen to an extract from the audiobook of Audrey Niffenegger’s Life Out of OrderSorry your browser does not support audio - but you can download here and listen $https://uploads.guim.co.uk/2026/10/09/Life_Out_Of_Order_Chapter_1_Audio_Clip.mp300:00:0000:05:24The Time Traveler’s Wife – the 2003 novel so popular it became a cultural phenomenon – is about an artist named Clare who falls in love with Henry, a man who is forever disappearing on her because he has a rare genetic condition that causes him to lurch involuntarily forwards and backwards in time. Henry is condemned to keep revisiting the most painful chapters of his life, and knows – but cannot change – hardships that will happen in their shared future. Niffenegger’s sequel, Life Out of Order, tells the story of their daughter, Alba, who was born with the same condition, but has a little more control over her time travel, and a greater willingness to try to harness her special abilities to serve her personal and political ends.double quotation markYes, The Time Traveler’s Wife is romantic, but it’s also heavy. Things don’t all work outNiffenegger always saw The Time Traveler’s Wife as a much “darker book” than many of her readers. People would tell her the story was “so romantic” – “and I’m like yes, it’s so romantic. It’s also kind of heavy,” she says. “Because there’s a lot of inevitability, and they’re choosing to be happy in the moment, knowing that things are not going to work out so well.” With this new novel, there’s no missing the darkness.We meet in the book-filled Chicago home that she shares with the Scottish artist Eddie Campbell, her husband of just over a decade. The walls are hung with Niffenegger’s bold, dreamlike paintings, and she has an impressive taxidermy collection: a rhea in the front room, two doves in a bell jar, a pangolin on the coffee table (bought long ago, as an antique). She used to have much more taxidermy on display, but her three cats are “barbarians” and as kittens they started “interacting with it in weird ways”. She worried one would skewer itself on the huge porcupine that used to reside on the kitchen sideboard, which she has since sequestered upstairs.At 63, Niffenegger exudes a bookish bohemianism, with her cat-eye glasses, dangly earrings and cropped silver hair. She is softly spoken, but when she talks about politics, where the conversation keeps veering, she resorts to scathing sarcasm. She is currently recovering from a long and serious illness, something she doesn’t want to talk about, because she does not want it to detract from her work. People are always obsessed with how an artist’s life influences their work, she observes, and they forget how much art can change the person who made it. Every book she has written has transformed her life. The Time Traveler’s Wife opened up the world to her.When she started writing it, Niffenegger was working as an artist and a professor at the Columbia College Chicago’s Centre for Book and Paper Arts. She made her own hand-bound, hand-printed books, sumptuously illustrated gothic fairytales that she produced in editions of 10. She was sketching one day when the phrase “The Time Traveler’s Wife” popped into her head. “It’s a good title, because it gives you two people, their relationship with each other, and their situation,” she says. She imagined the novel, which was published in 2003 by MacAdam/Cage, a small independent press, might sell a few thousand copies. In fact it sold more than9m globally.She had a few lucky breaks, Niffenegger explains. At the time she didn’t know many other writers, but she gave the book to a fellow Chicago-based artist, Annette Turow, who liked it and passed it on to her husband, the novelist Scott Turow, who then recommended it during an interview with the US Today show. In the UK, the novel was picked for Richard and Judy’s Book Club. Quickly, it became apparent that the romance and tragedy of time travel struck a chord. She began receiving emails, often from people struggling in long-distance relationships. “A lot of the resonance comes from people having that absence in their lives. So, you know, my husband is in the military, my friend is in prison, my wife is in school far away … we’re both reading it together and talking about it over the phone,” she says. She received notes from young people who were sharing the novel with their boyfriends or girlfriends and knows of a “surprising number” of children who were subsequently named Henry or Clare.Becoming a sudden commercial success was “very odd”, she recalls: “all the running around and doing interviews and having people dig really deep into the novel and have very intricate questions was extraordinary”. The scrutiny didn’t trouble her too much – it reminded her of being critiqued at art school – but she struggled with “impostor syndrome”.For most of her life so far, Niffenegger had few opportunities to travel. She’d never been west of the Mississippi and, if she had a chance to leave Chicago, she tended to either go to New York or Europe. Suddenly, she went everywhere. Once, she visited a different American city every day for two weeks, which she found too much. At a literary festival in Australia, she knew almost no one – as was often the case back then – but the writer Neil Gaiman, who was interviewing her on stage, introduced her to a young journalist named Hayley Campbell. Hayley would eventually introduce her to her father, Eddie, and for many years the couple somehow made a long-distance relationship between Brisbane and Chicago work, meeting for dates all over the world.View image in fullscreenRose Leslie and Theo James in a scene from the HBO series of The Time Traveler’s Wife (2022).Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyMeanwhile, the ordinary Chicago restaurants she mentioned in The Time Traveler’s Wife got a lot of attention “which I’m sure confused them”. The city’s Newberry Library, where Henry works, had so many visitors that they had to print a Time Traveler’s Wife FAQ sheet for the front desk and an unremarkable stairwell, featured in the story, became a destination in itself. In 2009, The Time Traveler’s Wife was made into a Hollywood film, starring Rachel McAdams. The adaptation was panned by the critics. Niffenegger has never watched it. “I mean you can let people do their own thing, and not have anything to say about their thing, that’s OK,” she says. In 2022, it was also made into a series by HBO.Thanks to her runaway success, Niffenegger received a $5m advance for her second book,Her Fearful Symmetry(2009), a ghost story set in London. For her research, she moved to the city and became a tour guide in Highgate Cemetery. “I didn’t expect people to know about it,” she says when I ask her about the advance, her manner polite, her meaning very clear. “I didn’t understand that it was going to be news and that people would know about it and ask me about it. It was like ‘That’s just my finances. Why would anybody care what’s going on with my bank account?’.” And then she answers her own question: “People are kind of fascinated because it’s weird that I would make money – ever.”Her paintings were never very “fashionable”, she says, and in the art world she is relatively unknown. “Something where you kind of need a long explanation from the artist seems to be very in,” she observes, while her work has always been narrative and figurative. She paints self-portraits with butterflies, monkeys and birds, and skeletons are a recurring motif, a skeleton wearing a party hat, curled around a cat, skeletons intertwined with people, a child skeleton holding up his mother’s face like a giant inflatable balloon.The great advantage of earning money is that it buys you time to do creative work, she says: “Like if you own your day, that’s great.” Over the years she has cut back on teaching so that she can focus on her writing and art, and run a small nonprofit arts school, Artists Book House, which she founded in 2019. While she has been doing all this, in the many years since Her Fearful Symmetrywas published, something nice happened. “People just forgot I existed,” she says, which seems to suit her just fine.Niffenegger was raised in Evanston, a city north of Chicago and a short drive from where she lives now. “I think people imagine I had some baroque childhood. I actually just had a very American middle-class, suburban childhood,” she says. Her father was a civil engineer working for the department store chain JC Penney and her mother was a quiltmaker. Niffenegger studied at the School of Art Institute in Chicago, took a few years out to teach and work, mostly as a picture framer, and then did her MFA at Northwestern University. One of her graduate projects, the illustrated novel Three Incestuous Sisters, is currently being adapted as a silent film with a very illustrious cast: the novelist Ottessa Moshfegh worked on it alongside the director Alice Rohrwacher, and Dakota Johnson, Saoirse Ronan and Jessie Buckley will star as the sisters, whose suffocatingly close bond is ripped apart over their love for the lighthouse keeper’s son. Niffenegger has read the screenplay, and this time she plans to “watch the hell out of” the film. “It’s going to be wild,” she says approvingly. “It was just so over the top, I mean it’s far weirder than the book, and I can appreciate that.”double quotation markWhatever you can be doing, now’s the time. If all you can do is vote, then voteOver the decades, her artistic interests have not wavered: “Love and loss, death, rock and roll, sex and romance, to me those are the biggest issues,” she says. Except now, because she has been writing about the future, she’s been thinking much more about politics. Both Alba and Henry find it easier to move backward than forward in time, because the future is harder to imagine, but the more they do so, the more concrete the future becomes. Niffenegger realised this is true more generally. We find it hard to respond to the threat posed by, say, the climate crisis, because we find climate meltdown hard to visualise. In her book, she describes scenes in which whole cities are underwater, utilities no longer work, food is in short supply, and the weather is apocalyptically weird in an attempt to make extreme global warming feel less abstract. And she found the more time she spent trying to imagine 2040, the more jarring the disconnect with the US’s political discourse. “I’m just like OK, sure, build a bunker for yourself,” she says of Trump, oozing contempt. “Like OK, billionaires, go to Mars, that’s OK.”The current administration has radicalised her, she says. “Until the recent Trump debacle I was not a person who used to go to demonstrations. I was political in some ways, but I was not somebody who would drop everything and, you know, hit the street yelling. Now I am,” she says. She feels a sense of urgency. “I feel like whatever you can be doing, now’s the time. If what you can do is vote, vote. If that’s all you can do, cool. If you can give money to a cause, yay. If you can, go to a demonstration. Excellent. People should be paying attention and acting accordingly.”She says one advantage of being a slow writer is that she is able to respond to current events. It would have been strange, she realises now, if she’d published the book before the pandemic and the coronavirus lockdowns had not been mentioned at all. Part of the reason the writing took so long, she says, is that she was “waiting to find out the resolution to certain real world events”. Some outcomes felt predictable, others not at all. While imagining civil unrest in a fictitious future, she watched the protests over the police killing of George Floyd rock the US and felt sure something would finally change, “But no, it just seems to have been like a rock falling into a pond,” she says, sounding despondent.Niffenegger will leave on her book tour soon, though it will be a small one. There is art to make and new writing projects to get stuck into. She’s thinking of expanding her graphic novel, The Night Bookmobile, into a series of interlinked short stories. She’s also thinking about not doing too much at all. “After spending 14 years on one thing, I’m happy to have a little rest,” she says.Life Out of Order by Audrey Niffenegger is published by Jonathan Cape (£22). To support the Guardian order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Hear Audrey in conversation with Steven Moffat at Conway Hall London on 28 Oct.
