title: Time: David Tennant and Siobhan Finneran are stellar in this horrifying and exceptional TV drama | Television | The Guardian
description: Jimmy McGovern’s grab-you-by-the-throat prison show is back and it could hardly be more urgent, prescient or excellent. Brace yourself though … Bake Off it is not
Author: Frances Ryan
Headline: Jimmy McGovern’s grab-you-by-the-throat prison show is back and it could hardly be more urgent, prescient or excellent. Brace yourself though … Bake Off it is not
Content: Behind bars … Siobhan Finneran, Chukwubuikem Molokwu and David Tennant star in Time.Photograph: BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyView image in fullscreenBehind bars … Siobhan Finneran, Chukwubuikem Molokwu and David Tennant star in Time.Photograph: BBC/BBC Studios/Peter MarleyThe watcherTelevisionTime: David Tennant and Siobhan Finneran are stellar in this horrifying and exceptional TV dramaJimmy McGovern’s grab-you-by-the-throat prison show is back and it could hardly be more urgent, prescient or excellent. Brace yourself though … Bake Off it is notFrances RyanSat 10 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt takes a lot to drag me away from comfort TV in the autumn. Blame the shrinking hours of light or the apocalyptic news cycle but the closest thing I like to get to televisual trauma in October is watching comedians get into their own graves in The Celebrity Traitors. I doubt I’m alone. I don’t want to psychoanalyse the British public but I’d take a punt that collectively we are just about capable right now of looking at Josh Widdicombe trying to find a purpose next to Emma Willis on the Strictly dancefloor (andreportedly, even that’s a struggle).Enter legendary Jimmy McGovern with a new series of the Bafta-winning prison drama Time (Sunday, 9pm, BBC One) to drag the nation out of its Bake Off-related coma. Having already covered the devastation of men’s and women’s prisons in the first two series, the good news is that McGovern and co-writer Samuel Bailey’s trilogy surely can’t get any more distressing. The new episodes will be set in*checks notes* a youth offending institution for boys. OK great. It’s about children in prison. Thank you, Jimmy! I hope you’re happy! No one else is going to be.Of course, McGovern – long known for tackling social realism and institutional injustice in iconic shows such as Cracker, The Lakes and Hillsborough – is not going to put the viewer through the wringer without proper reason. Asprison overcrowdingdominates the headlines, alongside themultifaceted crisisamongyoung men, Time series three is so urgent and prescient that you wonder if the BBC were tempted to change the title to Time(ly).Still, best brace yourself before going in. Within 90 seconds, a teenage boy is being dragged horizontally by five adult guards to his cell; a hand half-covering his jaw as he screams obscenities. That hand belongs toDavid Tennant, playing veteran prison officer Bobby Bailey. Tennant is an impressively blank slate as Bailey: a figure who is almost always on screen but has such sparse dialogue and emotion that at times he is – in classic McGovern fashion – defined by his ordinariness and hard to box as “goody” or “baddy.”He’s joined by Happy Valley’s Siobhan Finneran who returns as prison chaplain Marie-Louise – the only common thread through all three series and a rare merciful sign of, dare I say it, hope.Tennant and Finneran both give stellar performances but it’s the three young actors playing new offenders who will surely be stars of the future. There’s Peter (Ollie McNulty), caught between the death of an innocent man and loyalty to his community, and James (Louis McCartney), struggling to face his broken parents after a life-changing act of violence. Then there’s Christopher (a heartbreaking Chukwubuikem Molokwu) battling a stammer and reconnecting with his birth mother.‘Me and the lads would not survive a day in here’: inside TV’s utterly stunning, Bafta-winning prison dramaRead moreOne of Time’s strengths is its exceptional writing, but it is not afraid to say plenty without a word. The white vans that transport the boys to jail with tiny square black windows for pockets of light. The gates in D-wing that are rarely opened and keep its violent not-yet-men apart (“Gates are dangerous,” Tennant tells Finneran ominously). Cells named “Room 29”, as if the boys are on a hostel break for the week – an illusion that’s only broken when you realise there’s not a scene that takes place in the wing that’s not accompanied by the sound of screaming.The whole thing is a lesson in tension, each minute in the prison dragging the viewer further into the claustrophobia of dread and despair.I won’t give any spoilers but I will say you will be thinking about a moment in the first episode for days. This is not easy viewing but nor should it be. McGovern is not delivering content that plays in the background while you’re scrolling Instagram. It grabs you by the throat, asking you to question whether it’s possible to change or if the horrors of the human-made system dooms certain people – certain children – before they ever really get a chance. All of us should watch it, not least politicians across the political spectrum. Just maybe stick Bake Off on afterwards to decompress.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionThe watcherDavid TennantfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Edge Control: the art exhibition using hidden camera images to explore race and beauty | Art | The Guardian
description: Artist Deana Lawson uses beauty supply store surveillance images to analyze power and personhood in her exhibition at the Gagosian in New York City
Author: Morgan Jerkins
Headline: Artist Deana Lawson uses beauty supply store surveillance images to analyze power and personhood in her exhibition at the Gagosian in New York City
Content: Edge Control – Deana LawsonPhotograph: Deana Lawson/Courtesy GagosianView image in fullscreenEdge Control – Deana LawsonPhotograph: Deana Lawson/Courtesy GagosianArtEdge Control: the art exhibition using hidden camera images to explore race and beautyArtist Deana Lawson uses beauty supply store surveillance images to analyze power and personhood in her exhibition at the Gagosian in New York CityMorgan JerkinsSat 10 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 08.03 EDTShareIn her essay The Oppositional Gaze: Black Female Spectators, writer and philosopher bell hooks explains that the relationship between Black people and the act of “looking” has been traumatic since slavery. Black people, many of whom are still subject to the constant surveillance that originated during enslavement, have historically been punished with severe consequences, such as lynching, for looking back at those who subjugate them. Despite these risks, hooks writes, they rebelled by secretly looking at white people, as well as their surroundings, rejecting the white gaze as the singular framework of reality. We can, as bell hooks writes, “interrogate the gaze of the Other but also look back, and at one another, naming what we see”.I thought of this analysis when I visited Edge Control, artist Deana Lawson’s latest photography exhibition at the Gagosian gallery inNew YorkCity. Edge control refers to the gels and pomades that slick the hairs along the edges of a Black woman’s hairline, but in Lawson’s exhibit, the phrase takes on an additional meaning. It’s at once a styling product for Black haircare devotees as well as a tool to examine the beauty industry, consumerism and how surveillance and race intersect.To explore these intersections, Lawson uses photos of alleged beauty supply store shoplifters, presented in large scale and outside their original contexts. As a warning to customers, many beauty supply stores post surveillance photos of alleged shoplifters caught in the act of stealing products. The stores, which almost exclusively sell Black haircare products within Black neighborhoods, are rarely owned by Black people. The small, indistinct images tend to fade in the background amid the various colors of shampoo bottles and hair accessories.View image in fullscreenDeana LawsonPhotograph: Courtesy the artist and GagosianLawson’s images, however, are large portraits framed by mirrors, forcing the onlooker to simultaneously see themselves looking at these shoplifters. The viewer is small and narrow while the shoplifters are life-size, and what was once quiet, passive spectatorship immediately becomes active participation. This evolution is further emphasized once a viewer moves to the middle of the gallery room where two holograms stand, revealing Black women’s bodies that shift depending on the viewer’s angle. These pieces demonstrate how Lawson manipulates perception: these alleged shoplifters are not frozen in time, they are in motion, just as the viewers are.The notion of wrongdoing is questionable as the exhibition becomes a house of mirrors exploring who is and is not being watched. Lawson accomplishes exactly what bell hooks wrote about – the rebellious gaze – by looking at her subjects, challenging viewers to evaluate them, and therefore exploring how perception functions within a space full of unequal power relations.The exhibit’s official description proclaims that Lawson does not intend to cast moral judgment over these images, but rather “foregrounds the implications of agency and transformative potential of beauty products within our late capitalist society”. Lawson is not trying to villainize or glorify these shoplifters, but she does protect them. The shoplifter photos are evasive – the original images are low resolution, some of the shoplifters are masked and a few of the photos are so blurry that the viewer is unable to make out the subject’s face. Lawson’s deliberate refusal to clarify these images causes the viewer to contemplate what or who they are looking at. Who is the regular customer and who is the criminal?She aims for neutrality in the depiction of her subjects by making the artistic decision to show them in stark contrast to other Black people whose images were not gathered from surveillance cameras. On the right wall opposite Lawson’s shoplifter images, the photographer’s signature style portraits hang: lush images of Black men and women in very private settings.In all these artworks, the subjects’ gaze always meets the viewers’, reinforcing their humanity and leveling the playing field. In fact, due to their size, the subjects seem to be looking down at you. In the early 20th century,Black photographers would immortalize their Black subjectsin suits, nuns’ habits or graduate gowns to usher in a new form of race pride – and respectability – into the mainstream. Lawson’s subjects are casually dressed – if at all. She’s not interested in a dignified kind of Blackness, but rather the beauty of Blackness within the mundane. By placing all of these images together within the same space, Lawson forces the viewers to view Blackness through a continuum of life in all of its contradictions, rather than a flat binary of good and bad behavior.The relationship between the Black subjects on both sides of the room is contingent upon the viewer’s own judgment. How different is the Black female shoplifter near the braid extensions aisle from the naked Black woman squatting with her knees apart? How different is the Black male shoplifter from the Black man with a busted eye posing with others in a living room? However the viewer judges these subjects reveals their own biases. But in this exhibition, one’s biases are not private, inconsequential flaws. They’re ideological constraints that must be confronted.Edge Control succeeds at capturing the extreme vulnerability of people who are being surveilled without their knowledge in active pursuit of beauty. At the same time, Lawson narrows the gap between spectator and participant as the viewer is confronted with multiple gazes–including their own–so that no one person is valued differently than the other. With power being briefly reassembled, parity is achieved.Edge Control is on view at the Gagosian in New York City until 24 October

title: ‘I just wasn’t going to give up’: the fight to free the longest-serving political prisoner in the US | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: Leonard Peltier was imprisoned for 49 years before his sentence was commuted. A new Netflix documentary exposes the ‘corrupt’ system that allowed it to happen
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: Leonard Peltier was imprisoned for 49 years before his sentence was commuted. A new Netflix documentary exposes the ‘corrupt’ system that allowed it to happen
Content: Leonard Peltier in Coleman, Florida, on 18 February 2025 after his release from prison.Photograph: Angel White Eyes/NDN Collective/ReutersView image in fullscreenLeonard Peltier in Coleman, Florida, on 18 February 2025 after his release from prison.Photograph: Angel White Eyes/NDN Collective/ReutersDocumentary films‘I just wasn’t going to give up’: the fight to free the longest-serving political prisoner in the USLeonard Peltier was imprisoned for 49 years before his sentence was commuted. A new Netflix documentary exposes the ‘corrupt’ system that allowed it to happenAdrian HortonSat 10 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOn 20 January 2025, with 14 minutes remaining in his term as president, Joe Bidencommutedthe life sentence ofLeonard Peltier, after years of pressure to release a figure seen by many as the longest-serving political prisoner in the US. The Indigenous activist, a leader within the American Indian Movement (Aim) and an icon of Native American resistance, served nearly 50 years in prison for allegedly killing two FBI agents during a shootout on the Pine Ridge reservation in South Dakota, in 1975 – killings he has always denied, prosecuted in a railroaded trial widely seen as corrupt.‘He’s going home’: new film documents the fight to free Leonard PeltierRead moreOutside the Florida prison where Peltier was being held that morning were several of the many activists and lawyers who fought for his release, as well as film-makers David France and Jesse Short Bull. The two directors’ long-gestating documentary on Peltier’s fight for justice was set topremierejust a week later at the Sundance film festival with a very different ending, the octogenarian still awaiting a chance to return home to the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa reservation in North Dakota. That morning, there was “a sinking feeling that it wasn’t going to happen”, France said.When it did, while the cameras rolled, the line of supporters erupted in joy for a commutation that allowed Peltier to serve the rest of his consecutive life sentences on house arrest, though it did not pardon him – not quite justice, but a victory so uncertain and so hard-fought, over more than half a lifetime, that I have cried every time I’ve rewatched it.Free Leonard Peltier, out on Netflix for Indigenous Peoples’ Day in the US, makes clear why, as Peltier put it to me over Zoom from his new home, “I just wasn’t going to give up.” Over 110 minutes, Short Bull and France retrace not only what happened that day at Pine Ridge, but the long arc of Indigenous activism in the US, from Peltier’s childhood resistingNative boarding schools, the government-run institutions used to forcibly separate Native families and force assimilation, to Aim’s occupation of the Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) in 1972 and the many decades of work to free Peltier. For years, as more evidence of railroaded justice emerged, Peltier’s name became synonymous with Indigenous resistance, another abuse in a long chain of abuses by the US federal government. “His name was definitely said on the daily,” Short Bull, who is Oglala Lakota, told me. “It was just like, the sky is blue.” Still, “it wasn’t until I started gaining access to the history where I started to understand that this was a bad deal.”‘We’re not going to go away’: the mom fighting for social media reform after her son’s suicideRead moreMuch of the first half of the film relies on archival material and interviews with the now-elderly former members of Aim, introducing a new audience to the movement’s origins, in response to the crisis of boarding schools, forced evictions and the steady encroachment on tribal territory. Peltier joined the movement in the 1960s, after experiencing anti-Native police brutality while working at a power plant on the Navajo Nation, and participated on Aim’s “trail of broken treaties” caravan to Washington. He served as a security guard when Aim members occupied the BIA building, where things devolved after the discovery of paperwork confirming future plans to use tribal lands for mining.Such tribal lands included Pine Ridge, which held some of the richest uranium deposits in the United States. Peltier arrived on the reservation during a tense and dangerous time, as a corrupt tribal government, led by Dick Wilson and enforced by his BIA-backed private “goons” (Guardians of the Oglala Nation), clashed with tribal members and Aim, sent to help defend residents from routine violence; one former resident recalls in the film that there were 68 murders in Pine Ridge during that time, and no arrests. The day of the shootout, in which a militarized FBI – archival footage shows dozens of tanks and military-style assault weapons – traded fire with a handful of Aim security members, Wilson unilaterally ceded one-eighth of the reservation to the federal government.View image in fullscreenLeonard Peltier and Holly Cook Macarro in Free Leonard Peltier.Photograph: Courtesy of Netflix“We took this on as historians, really,” said France. “Our job wasn’t to do a whodunnit. We weren’t going to try to solve the case. It wasn’t our job to figure out who pulled the trigger – we know it wasn’t Leonard.” What became clear through extensive archival research was that “people knewthenthat this was all about land. And none of that had been brought out before in the telling of Leonard’s story or the telling of the American Indian Movement. It’s all about the land.”Almost every film participant, as well as France, Short Bull and Peltier himself, assert that given the land deal, the FBI at minimum escalated the violence that day, which killed agents Jack Coler and Ronald Williams, as well as Aim member Joe Stuntz, if not outright staged it. (No arrest was ever made in Stuntz’s death.)The ICE documentary as chilling as a horror movie: ‘We’re trying to put the audience in a position of terror’Read moreThe film’s second half details the numerous miscarriages of justice after Peltier, who escaped that day and hid out for a time in an RV loaned by Marlon Brando, was arrested in Canada. The litany of dubious maneuvers used to incarcerate Peltier plays like a who’s-who of prosecutorial misconduct on every level: Peltier’s extradition was secured via fabricated testimony from a “girlfriend” he had never met, and who later recanted, citing coercion; he was tried separately from his co-defendants Dino Butler and Bob Robideau, who were allowed to argue self-defense and acquitted, in a court presided over by a known racist judge in North Dakota; the FBI’s limited evidence, claiming with certainty that Peltier shot the two agents at point-blank range, was later revealed to be unreliable. “They had no evidence to even indict us,” Peltier told me. “That was not a trial.” Nevertheless, Peltier was sentenced to life in prison in 1977.In 1984, at a hearing prompted by international activism toward Peltier’s release, the defense presented a firing pin test conducted by the FBI demonstrating that Peltier’s AR-15 was not used to shoot the agents that day. Still, the case was not overturned. By the mid-1990s, Peltier was running out of options for a verdict reversal. At times, he was presented the option to plead guilty or admit wrongdoing for clemency, but refused. “I said, ‘they’ve been saying for 46 years I’ve been found guilty beyond a reasonable doubt, beyond a shadow of a doubt, that there’s overwhelming proof against me, and now they want me to plead guilty? No, that’s not going to happen,’” he recalled.View image in fullscreenLeonard Peltier while imprisoned in 1999.Photograph: Joe Ledford/Associated Press“We’re not the guilty party here,” he added. “We weren’t killing them. We weren’t trying to exterminate them.” During his half-century of prison, Peltier remained acutely engaged with politics – “he’s the Nelson Mandela of the movement,” said France. “He spent his time in prison still organizing” – so he speaks with conviction: “We’re still in danger right now.” Just this summer, the Trump administrationwent aheadwith its court-contested plan to build 62 miles of its border wall through Tohono O’odham Nation without the tribe’s consent. “There’s the same type of president in there, the fascists who are talking about doing away with our treaties,” he said. “If we do away with our treaties, that means the end of us as a race of people.“And people will say, ‘Why are people doing that?’ Well, as long as we’re alive, as long as we’re still living as a race of people, they could never legitimately claim to be the only and true Americans.”The film ends on an upbeat note – Peltier, at long last, at home, surrounded by friends and family, though he is quick to note that house arrest is not freedom. “I’m still battling for total freedom,” he said, including the ability to travel and meet many of his supporters. “I would like to have my total freedom before I pass, or at least what freedom I could have in America.”But Free Leonard Peltier argues that his legacy is not forgotten. “I’m a beneficiary of the sacrifice that that generation made,” Short Bull said. “Leonard reminds me of so many people here on the Pine Ridge reservation. Even today, young people that are willing to make the sacrifice … hopefully history doesn’t have to ever repeat itself ever again.”Free Leonard Peltier is released onNetflixon 12 OctoberExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsUS justice systemSouth DakotaJoe BidenIndigenous peoplesNative AmericansNetflixdocumentariesShareReuse this content

title: Remember Me review – narrow view of two photographic centuries is like a history of food in three ham sarnies | Photography | The Guardian
description: There are 700 works from François Pinault’s collection on display – more than half of them by Irving Penn – but it’s a blinkered selection and annoyingly didactic
Author: Charlotte Jansen
Headline: There are 700 works from François Pinault’s collection on display – more than half of them by Irving Penn – but it’s a blinkered selection and annoyingly didactic
Content: Extractive images … Irving Penn’s Cuzco Children, 1948.Photograph: © Irving Penn, Condé Nast Pinault CollectionView image in fullscreenExtractive images … Irving Penn’s Cuzco Children, 1948.Photograph: © Irving Penn, Condé Nast Pinault CollectionPhotographyReviewRemember Me review – narrow view of two photographic centuries is like a history of food in three ham sarniesBourse de Commerce, ParisThere are 700 works from François Pinault’s collection on display – more than half of them by Irving Penn – but it’s a blinkered selection and annoyingly didacticCharlotte JansenSat 10 Oct 2026 00.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 00.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Beware … of assuming the sterile attitude of the spectator, for life is not a spectacle” scream the words of Aimé Césaire – writ large and bold by Barbara Kruger, in a giant installation, The History of Tears, that fills Bourse de Commerce’s spectacular Rotunda. Kruger’s angry, menacing, viscerally charged work – words as images, and large-scale video clips of people seething with self-hate – is a thrilling setup for Remember Me, an exhibition that promises a take on 200 years of photography through 700 works by more than 70 artists drawn from the collection of the French billionaire François Pinault. That excitement quickly dissipates as the exhibition moves on.This is the biggest photography show ever held at the Bourse de Commerce. Remember Me has two main problems: first, it tries to say too much with too few artists. For a start, nearly 450 of the 700 or so works are byIrving Penn. It leans heavily on classical, conventional approaches, styles and familiar names, and that creates a very obvious skew in the perception of what photography is, does, and how it is presented.View image in fullscreenLike waves … Remember MeThe organisation makes no real sense. There are two main spaces, in addition to Kruger’s installation, dedicated exclusively to one artist. Penn is one of them. The installation looks undeniably beautiful: following the curving Ando architecture, the works have been hung like waves, expanding in undulating lines across the walls, without chronology or theme, flowing freely into the space. However, when you look closely at the works themselves, this configuration becomes very problematic. There are a large number of colonial-style portraits taken in a temporary tent studio by Penn when he travelled in Cameroon and Benin. Many of the pictures depict men and women in traditional tribal dress, and were taken as a commission for Vogue. These nations were actively negotiating independence from France at that time. When you compare them with portraits byMalick SidibéorSeydou Keïtaof the same time, they look even more like anthropological, ethnographic, extractive images by a westerner who couldn’t even communicate with his subjects.“Primitive subjects respond more to tone than to obscure words,” Penn stated of how he directed the people who appear in these photographs. To me, that says everything about his perspective on African bodies and culture. Then you notice the rest of it: the glamorous white women who appear as pristine models of passive beauty, while all the men are mediocre-looking and wear suits. Still lifes are woven through – presumably to undo the idea of hierarchy between subjects. So, a man who looks at a vase or a plate of fruit the same way he looks at people. The camera has been instrumental in colonialism, and in cultural extraction and appropriation – including in the fashion industry, of which Penn was part. But there’s no attempt to tackle that here, to counter these visions with other perspectives.View image in fullscreenMan Ray’s Noire et Blanche, 1926.Photograph: © Man Ray Trust / Adagp, Paris 2018It’s not the last you’ll see of Penn, unfortunately – his works keep popping up through the upper floor, where various major names reappear in different sections that each try to heavy-handedly explain and demystify, in an annoyingly didactic way, what photography is and how it’s made. We jump between sections on composition, abstraction, portrait and seriality, to nudes – where the women have gorgeous bums and breasts turned alluringly to the camera, and the men are small and, so we’re told to think, weak and vulnerable, with very large penises. My biggest issue here was why the sumptuous, elegant nude portrait of Zanele Muholi (by the artist themself, but not technically a self-portrait) needed a lengthy wall text, justifying the work via the western painting tradition – where none of the nudes of white women seemed to warrant one. Yet a quirky series of small 1933 nude shots by Man Ray – an erotic performance featuring the younger artist Méret Oppenheim, unclothed, and Man Ray in a suit and bowler hat – are left with no explanation about the power dynamics of the camera and male surrealism’s issues with women.This is a show that’s too afraid to let people think for themselves. We’re told Richard Avedon’s trio of 1963 portraits of William Casby, a former enslaved person who was 106 when Avedon photographed him, elevate his subject, giving him back his dignity. They’re glaringly close and unflattering photographs that resemble mug shots. Compare them with Avedon’s smaller, slightly blurred, portrait of Malcolm X. Decide for yourself what Avedon felt, whose image is claimed and whose is handed to them.View image in fullscreenPerfect vision of a seascape … Gustave Le Gray’s Effet de soleil dans les nuages – Océan, 1856.Photograph: Pinault CollectionOnce the exhibition lets go of the binaries, the anxiety to overexplain, or to adhere to the techniques of photography, when it allows active participation or just to be with the work, it gets better. The looser, thematic unions between images are intelligible and interesting, such as sections on “hands” and a glorious room exploring photographs of the sea. These rooms make you feel something, and reflect photographic resonances through history in a more meaningful way. By the Sea, for example, moves seamlessly from the 19th century in Gustave Le Gray’s painterly wet collodion prints, where he spliced two negatives together, one for the sea and one for the sky, to create his perfect vision of a seascape, to Hiroshi Sugimoto and Wolfgang Tillmans’ elegiac and laconic black and white ruminations. I think about why artists keep returning to look at the sea, looking for the infinite, for continuity, for obliteration and enormity. This room captures the feeling of gazing out at the sea, the ocean’s soothing violence and impervious calm.Photography is an inherently accessible medium, and they take it seriously in France. This show feels fumbling, and an unnecessary dumbing-down. Trying to bend two centuries of one of the most prolific mediums around these particular artists is like trying to tell the history of food through three ham sandwiches. There are more than 8,000 photographs in the wider collection: perhaps it’s more varied in perspective than appears in this show – but as it is, it shirks the responsibility of retelling photography’s history with nuance and multiplicity. Remember Me forgets Kruger’s invocation at the start.Remember Meis at Bourse de Commerce, Paris, until 18 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsPhotographyArtExhibitionsParisFranceIrving PennreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Guide #264: Why is Hollywood obsessed with the tech-bro baddie? | Culture | The Guardian
description: In this week’s newsletter: Dead-eyed, detached billionaires can’t hold a candle to the maniacal cinematic villains of old – it’s time Hollywood rewrote its source code
Author: Gwilym Mumford
Headline: In this week’s newsletter: Dead-eyed, detached billionaires can’t hold a candle to the maniacal cinematic villains of old – it’s time Hollywood rewrote its source code
Content: With great power comes no responsibility … clockwise from top left: The Altruists, The Audacity, Artificial and The Social Reckoning.Composite: VariousView image in fullscreenWith great power comes no responsibility … clockwise from top left: The Altruists, The Audacity, Artificial and The Social Reckoning.Composite: VariousThe Guide newsletterCultureThe Guide #264: Why is Hollywood obsessed with the tech-bro baddie?In this week’s newsletter: Dead-eyed billionaires can’t hold a candle to the maniacal cinematic villains of old – it’s time Hollywood rewrote its source codeDon’t get The Guide delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereGwilym MumfordSat 10 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSixteen years ago The Social Network was released and the first stirrings of a new cinema archetype were seen: the tech-bro villain. Perhaps that’s too damning a description for the Mark Zuckerberg portrayed by Jesse Eisenberg in David Fincher’s 21st-century classic about the dawn of Facebook; he’s certainly not a villain in the mwah-ha-ha, moustache-twirling sense. But he is, at the very least, on the wrong side of antiheroic: brilliant, brittle, status-craving, cruel and in charge of a social network with an exploding user base. Back then of course, the ramifications of this combination of troubling personality traits and transformative technology hadn’t quite dawned on us all: to many, social media sites still seemed a societal net positive. But the character was chilling enough to give even the most Pollyanna of tech evangelists a moment of pause.Fast forward to 2026, when faith in social media – and technology more broadly – is at Mariana Trench lows, and a sequel to Fincher’s drama has arrived in cinemas, this time both written and directed by the first film’s writer, Aaron Sorkin. The Social Reckoning whizzes the action forward to the tail end of the 2010s, by which time Facebook has grown into a near-trillion-dollar monolith. It follows real-life data engineer Frances Haugen (played by Mikey Madison), whose concerns over the radicalising qualities of Facebook’s algorithm prompt her to leak confidential files to investigative journalist Jeff Horwitz (Jeremy Allen White), resulting in the release of theWall Street Journal’s Facebook Files. Right around the same time as this damaging publication, and also depicted in the film, is the small matter of a riot-slash-insurrection at the Capitol, egged on by the outgoing US president on, among other places, Facebook, prompting his belated ban from the platform by Zuckerberg.The stakes for The Social Reckoning then are immeasurably higher than those of its predecessor, which ultimately concerned corporate manoeuvres at a swiftly growing but still small-potatoes company; not nothing, but definitely not overthrowing-the-government levels of drama. Zuckerberg has transformed too. Played in the sequel by Jeremy Strong, he does now resemble a full-on tech-bro baddie: remote, uncaring, monomaniacal and willing to blow a hole in the social fabric if it means his company can grow ever bigger. So why then does he feel less threatening than Eisenberg’s Zuckerberg?Partly it comes down to the performance. As sensational as Strong can be, his Zuckerberg feels strangely undercooked, the robotic mannerisms on point, but the matter of the character badly lacking. At times he seems to revert to Kendall Roy (his character inSuccession) at his most dead-eyed, rather than conjuring something new. It probably doesn’t help that Sorkin’s script shifts Zuckerberg to the side for much of proceedings – an absent, ambiguously defined monster to be slayed by the film’s heroes. But there’s a larger problem too, I think, and it’s one that’s hardly unique to The Social Reckoning: in 2026, tech bros don’t make for terribly great baddies.Lord knows they should, given the disruptive, damaging role these seemingly unaccountable figures play in our lives. And it’s not like Hollywood hasn’t tried to make the archetype stick. There have been attempts across horror (Channing Tatum’s creepy mogul inBlink Twice), superhero movies (a Bluetooth headset-wearing Lex Luthor in 2025’s Superman), whodunnits (the billionaire disruptor at the centre of Knives Out sequelGlass Onion), dark comedies (Don’t Look Up), and plenty of other genres aside. And don’t forget the numerous dark depictions of real-life figures like Zuckerberg: Theranos fraudster Elizabeth Holmes (portrayed by Amanda Seyfried in Hulu’s The Dropout) or WeWork founders Adam and Rebekah Neumann (Jared Leto and Anne Hathaway in Apple TV’s WeCrashed).View image in fullscreenTech baddie … Amanda Seyfried as Elizabeth Holmes in The Dropout.Photograph: Beth Dubber/APThere were enough of them last year, in everything from Jesse Armstrong’s Succession follow-up Mountainhead, to The Naked Gun remake, for the Guardian to declare the tech bro“Hollywood’s go-to baddie of 2025”, though Vulture reckoned that“every movie villain was (still) a tech bro”as far back as 2022. And the coming months promise an absolute deluge of them: alongside The Social Reckoning, there’s Artificial, Luca Guadagnino’s film about OpenAI and its CEO Sam Altman (played by Andrew Garfield); The Altruists, a Netflix series about the fall of cryptocurrency billionaire Sam Bankman-Fried; and The Audacity, a HBO comedy on an unhinged and scandal-ridden tech CEO. Plus two very high-profile documentaries in the form of Alex Gibney’s Musk and Nathan Fielder’s hotly anticipated Holmes film You Can See Everything (pictured above).Some of those films and series are likely to be great (Artificial has received positive reviews out of the New York film festival), as some have been before. But it’s hard not to feel a little fatigued by the trend at this stage. There are only so many slick but socially awkward, jargon-spouting masters and mistresses of the universe you can witness before the whole trope becomes dull and unilluminating. Tech CEOs aren’t often visually interesting either, with their muted-coloured quiet-luxury dress sense. And there’s a familiar endpoint to them too: imprisonment, scandal or, most likely, the software they have foisted on everyone spiralling out of their control. Inevitably the tech becomes as much a villain as its maker.But that’s arguably even less interesting – as the spate ofevil AI moviesin recent times has shown. Anyone who watchedMission: Impossible – The Final Reckoningwould surely agree that the all-conquering, nuke-deploying bot that serves as antagonist for much of the film was sorely lacking when compared to former flesh-and-blood villains like Henry Cavill’s moustachioed malcontent in Fallout or Philip Seymour Hoffman’s brilliant baddie in M:I3 – men animated by violence and spite as much as world domination. Give us them over the robots – or the robotic tech CEO – any day.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTo read the complete version of this newsletterplease subscribeto receive The Guide in your inbox every FridayExplore more on these topicsCultureThe Guide newsletternewslettersShareReuse this content

title: Amélie allowed me to embrace my neurodivergence | Amelie | The Guardian
description: Watching a DVD of the French film alone in my room, I saw for the first time a character who moved through the world like I do
Author: Lillian Crawford
Headline: Watching a DVD of the French film alone in my room, I saw for the first time a character who moved through the world like I do
Content: ‘As my understanding of myself has evolved over the years, so has my understanding of Amélie.’Illustration: Martin O’Neill/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘As my understanding of myself has evolved over the years, so has my understanding of Amélie.’Illustration: Martin O’Neill/The GuardianMy cultural awakeningAmelieAmélie allowed me to embrace my neurodivergenceWatching a DVD of the French film alone in my room, I saw for the first time a character who moved through the world like I doLillian Crawford; as told toOlivia LadanyiSat 10 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAmélie likes the sound of cracking creme brulee with a teaspoon, plunging her hand into a sack of grain, and turning around in the cinema to watch people’s faces in the dark. I like the smell of books and I love cinema, but I hate the sound of people eating popcorn.Amélie was not the first neurodivergent-coded woman I’d seen depicted in film. There had been Margot Tenenbaum in The Royal Tenenbaums and Suzy Bishop in Moonrise Kingdom – two Wes Anderson characters in whom I’d recognised myself. But Amélie was the first who was at the centre of the story; she’s the titular character and we see things through her eyes. It was the first time I’d seen a woman on screen move through the world as I did: overstimulated, a bit lonely and afraid of the unknown, comfortable in her own company, with firm likes and dislikes and a powerful sense of social justice.My parents suspected I was autistic as a child: I didn’t have any friends, preferring my own company or that of my parents, and I couldn’t understand why other children behaved the way they did. They thought I was odd. I had hyperfixations and obsessive special interests. Doctors were trained to look out for the stereotypical signs of autism in boys, and autism can show up differently in girls, who tend to mask (assimilate the behaviours of neurotypical people) a lot more. My sense of humour, empathy and interest in history and culture rather than maths or science meant I wasn’t formally diagnosed until my early 20s. But a diagnosis has never felt important to me. That’s what I love about Amélie: she’s never labelled as autistic in the film, yet it was clear to me, as a neurodivergent person, that she was, too.In the opening credits, young Amélie flaps her hands over her ears, spins a coin and runs a finger round the rim of a glass – behaviours I now recognise as “stimming” (repetitive movements, sounds or words that help process sensory input or manage emotions). Adult Amélie’s overwhelm is communicated not only through Audrey Tautou’s performance, but through the cinematography. When she takes the Paris Métro, the wide lens and intensified sound evoke the experience of sensory overload. When Amélie is happy, everything glows. When she is sad, she literally becomes a puddle on the floor.double quotation markI have the urge to help Amélie, as if by helping her I would also be helping the younger version of myselfTen years ago, I was in my second year at the University of Cambridge when I first watched Amélie, on a DVD player alone in my room. I fell in love with it. After watching it twice that night, I became scared to return to it in case I didn’t connect with it in the same way. But in the past year, I’ve watched Amélie five times in an effort to make up for lost time, and on every watch I see something different.As my understanding of myself has evolved over the years, so has my understanding of Amélie. Now I have the urge to help her, as if by helping her I would also be helping the younger version of myself. To have a conversation with her and say: don’t be so afraid of things that feel alien and new.I had a book launch in August and it made my parents emotional how many people were there from different parts of my life. They never thought having friendships like I do would be possible for me. I wish I could tell my 14-year-old self, locked away in a library, or the 19-year-old who watched Amélie on repeat alone in her room, that she had all of this ahead of her. That she would programme and organise neurodivergent film screenings and have a community of autistic people around her. That her bones aren’t made of glass, and she can take life’s knocks, as the Glass Man tells Amélie in the film. That she would overcome her fears and learn to take up space in her own life, as Amélie had shown her was possible all those years ago.The Mind of the Doctor by Lillian Crawford is published by Darton, Longman & Todd (£14.99). title: TV tonight: Richard Ayoade and Hannah Waddingham’s cartoon comedy | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Rick and Morty fans will love ancient Greece animation Krapopolis. Plus, Danny Dyer takes the SNL UK hosting reins. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Rick and Morty fans will love ancient Greece animation Krapopolis. Plus, Danny Dyer takes the SNL UK hosting reins. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Not your typical ruler … Krapopolis on BBC Three.Photograph: BBC/Fox MediaView image in fullscreenNot your typical ruler … Krapopolis on BBC Three.Photograph: BBC/Fox MediaTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: Richard Ayoade and Hannah Waddingham’s cartoon comedyRick and Morty fans will love ancient Greece animation Krapopolis. Plus, Danny Dyer takes the SNL UK hosting reins. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Ali Catterall,Jack Seale,Hannah J DaviesandSimon WardellSat 10 Oct 2026 01.15 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 01.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleKrapopolis11.40pm, BBC ThreeThis starry-voiced adult cartoon by Rick and Morty creator Dan Harmon quietly dropped on iPlayer last month. Set in ancient Greece, it follows benevolent Tyrannis (Richard Ayoade) – the mortal son of vain goddess Deliria (Hannah Waddingham) and husband Shlub (Matt Berry) – who uses modern ideas as he rules Krapopolis. Served up in fun 20-minute bites, this six-episode bill will race by.Hollie RichardsonStrictly Come Dancing6.15pm, BBC OneChris and Amy were the first couple to cha cha their way from the dancefloor (in their Baywatch gear, no less), which means 14 pairs are left in week three of the competition. Lacey and Vito confirmed one dance at the end of last week’s show: they’ll be getting lively with a samba to Bamboléo by the Gipsy Kings.HR40 Hits of 1976 at the BBC8.40pm, BBC TwoOdd year, 1976. Perhaps the record-breaking heat boiled record buyers’ brains. How else to explain the UK’s best-selling single and Eurovision winner, Save Your Kisses for Me? Or the Wurzels ploughing Combine Harvester to No 1? Thankfully, punk was also battering down the door – along with Abba and Dolly.Ali CatterallMarble Hall Murders9.20pm, BBC OneA classy cast and the lure of gossip among pampered literati are keeping Anthony Horowitz’s convoluted mystery drama going. Book editor Susan (Lesley Manville), working on a roman à clef set in Crete in 1955, now meets the family of the author, who alleges one of them murdered his grandmother. Everyone is wonderfully barbed.Jack SealeSaturday Night Live UK10pm, Sky OneOh, this is going to be a good one: while his daughter hotfoots it on Strictly, actor/geezer/emerging national treasure Danny Dyer is the host of this edition of the show, which is back after a week off. Music comes from south London singer-songwriter Sasha Keable.HRThree Women1.30am, Channel 4If 1.30am is a little late, this candid drama based on Lisa Taddeo’s nonfiction hit about sex and desire is also streamable. In an episode that’s all the more resonant given grim events at Cornell, Lina (Betty Gilpin) tells Gia (Shailene Woodley) about a disturbing event from her student past.Hannah J DaviesFilm choiceMatchbox the Movie, out now, Apple TVView image in fullscreen‘Amiable muscleman’ … Matchbox the Movie on Apple TV.Photograph: Jasin BolandIn the wake of the pink powerhouse that was Barbie, toy giant Mattel is going all-in on adaptations. Before we get the pleasure of Polly Pocket on screen, the line of tiny toy vehicles is given some dramatic spit and polish in Sam Hargrave’s breezy caper. Amiable muscleman Jon Cena plays CIA covert agent Sean, who returns to his home town for a funeral and reconnects with four childhood friends known as the Matchbox Gang, including Jessica Biel’s paramedic – and youthful crush – Aimee. Unfortunately, Sean is the fall guy after a nuclear warhead vanishes, so his mates are thrown into his globe-trotting world of spies, close-quarter violence and, naturally, shiny fast cars.Simon WardellAnimals, out now, NetflixBen Affleck’s knotty kidnap thriller was put on hold in 2024 after it clashed with Spike Lee’s similarly themed Highest 2 Lowest, itself a remake of a Kurosawa classic. It’s finally here, with Affleck casting himself (original pick Matt Damon was stuck on an island in the Med) as an attorney standing for LA mayor and Kerry Washington as his wife. The plot revolves round their son being taken for ransom, as moral and political calculations seriously muddy the waters. Gillian Anderson walks off with her scenes as a cool, collected English fixer called upon to help.SWPoor Things,10pm, Channel 4View image in fullscreenDeeply weird yarn … Poor Things on Channel 4.Photograph: TCD/Prod.DB/AlamyA risk-taking performance from Emma Stone is at the heart of this deeply weird yarn from Yorgos Lanthimos. She plays Bella, a young woman who died but was revived with the brain of her unborn baby by the Frankenstein-esque Godwin (Willem Dafoe). As she learns to walk and talk, she yearns to discover more about life. Lothario Duncan Wedderburn (a hilariously louche Mark Ruffalo) has designs on being her svengali – but Bella has a mind of her own. A delightful, disconcerting comedy adapted from Alasdair Gray’s novel, set in a stunning, not-quite-realistic Victorian era. SWRed Rooms, 11.20pm, Film4In Montreal, Canada, a man goes on trial for the murder of three teenage girls, the torture and killing of whom he had filmed for paying customers on the dark web. Pascal Plante’s increasingly disturbing psychological drama follows the proceedings – and the media frenzy surrounding it – through the eyes of model Kelly-Anne (Juliette Gariépy), who is a regular attendee at court. But why is she there? Is she a groupie of the (clearly guilty) accused? A true-crime obsessive? Or something darker? Gariépy’s enigmatic performance keeps us guessing almost to the end.SWLive sportPremier League Football: Arsenal v Leeds, 11am, TNT Sports 1Man Utd v Tottenham is at 5pm on Sky Sports Main Event.Prem Rugby Union: Northampton v Bath, 3pm, TNT Sports 1Saracens v Bristol follows at 5.15pm.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Spa bliss in the Alps: hot springs and hiking in the shadow of Mont Blanc | Spa breaks | The Guardian
description: An autumn break in the French mountain town of Saint-Gervais-Les-Bains offers thermal treatments and glorious walking trails before the winter ski crowds descend
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: An autumn break in the French mountain town of Saint-Gervais-Les-Bains offers thermal treatments and glorious walking trails before the winter ski crowds descend
Content: Les Thermes de Saint Gervais, which first opened its doors in 1806.Photograph: Saint-Gervais Mont Blanc tourist boardView image in fullscreenLes Thermes de Saint Gervais, which first opened its doors in 1806.Photograph: Saint-Gervais Mont Blanc tourist boardSpa breaksSpa bliss in the Alps: hot springs and hiking in the shadow of Mont BlancAn autumn break in the French mountain town of Saint-Gervais-Les-Bains offers thermal treatments and glorious walking trails before the winter ski crowds descendJane KnightSat 10 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sat 10 Oct 2026 11.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMont Blanc is hiding behind the clouds, but the Aiguille du Midi spears the sky above a mountainside ablaze with russet, gold and tawny tones. The maples flare red; rowan trees are dusted with crimson berries.Our little group has trundled up to Mont Lachat station (altitude: 2,115 metres) on the Tramway du Mont Blanc, the century-old cog railway that climbs improbably steep slopes from the French alpine town of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains. Operational since 1909, the railway was once intended to reach the 4,809-metre summit of Mont Blanc, but war, glacial terrain and waning funds put an end to that ambition. But even from Mont Lachat, the view is a showstopper. On one side, the Bionnassay Glacier slips scenically down the slope, a buzzard soaring over the milky-green glacial lake at its base, while on the other the Chamonix valley basks in soft autumnal sunshine.View image in fullscreenAutumn is golden season in the Alps, when you can find quieter hiking trails, lower prices and air crisp enough to stir the senses without nipping your fingers. Once focused purely on winter sports, the region’s resorts have spent years building up their summer credentials to offer hiking and biking through flower-strewn meadows. Now they’re marketing their shoulder season, too, to meet a growing demand for off-peak escapes.The little spa town of Saint-Gervais-les-Bains, 50 minutes from Geneva and sandwiched between its glitzier neighbours Chamonix and Megève, is perfectly placed to take advantage of this trend. Unlike many resorts, the town of 5,800 doesn’t fall silent once the snow (or summer crowds) melts away, in large part thanks to its thermal waters, which were discovered at the beginning of the 19th century.double quotation markThe secret is that instead of thinking about tourists, you think about the people who live here. Then the tourists will be happy tooA year-round gondola called Le Valléen now links the train station in the village of Le Fayet, farther down the slope where the thermal spa is located, to Saint-Gervais proper. Opened in late 2024, it means you can arrive by rail from London via Paris and reach the heart of the resort without needing a car. “If you go to Megève in the shoulder season there’s no one there,” says long-serving mayor Jean-Marc Peillex. “That’s not the case here. The secret is that instead of thinking about tourists, you think about the people who live here. Then the tourists will be happy too.”View image in fullscreenA gondola heads up Aiguille du Midi.Photograph: KI Photography/AlamySaint-Gervais (850 metres) may lack Megève’s polish but it has its own quiet charm: a medieval fortified house, a 17th-century church with geometric stained glass windows, elegant belle époque buildings near the spa and a thriving market every Thursday. Several excellent restaurants stay open year round, and our hotel, the chocolate-box Coeur des Neiges, offers rooms at less than half the summer or winter rate, making it an ideal base for autumnal exploring.From here we take the Mont Blanc tramway one stop to Motivon, at 1,400 metres, then hike for an hour without seeing another soul; the only sound is the gentle clanging of cowbells. Our destination is the Distillerie Saint-Gervais Mont Blanc, one of Europe’s highest microdistilleries at 1,365m. It’s actually set in a converted donkey shed with windows framing pine forests and plunging valleys, shelves fashioned from old skis and two gleaming copper distillation stills.This is where Scotsman James Abbott, kilt and all, produces some 450 bottles a year of single malt whisky (in a Speyside style), along with vodka, the traditional herbal liqueurgénépiand a superb mountain gin infused with ingredients such as blueberries and wild herbs from the nearby slopes.View image in fullscreenThe Tramway du Mont Blanc, the century-old cog railway that climbs ‘improbably steep slopes’.Photograph: Hemis/Alamy“The locals noticed that when I went to parties, I took whisky, not wine,” James laughs. “They said: ‘Why don’t you make your own – you drink enough of it.’” It turns out he does it rather well: the whisky sells for €95, the gin for €50, and both go down beautifully after a day in the mountain air before we hop back on the tramway.Although the tramway stops running from the end of September, there’s no shortage of scenic hiking trails fanning straight out from town which are accessible later in the year, plus a free, year-round bus service linking the villages that make up the commune of St-Gervais. We’re due to take it the next morning for a walk from Saint-Nicolas-de-Véroce, whose baroque church is resplendent with blue-and-gold interiors and frescoed ceilings, but a heavy rainstorm postpones our plans.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markWe drift between pools of different temperatures, while the gondola glides silently overheadThat’s not a problem when just down the road (or a free cog lift ride down the mountainside) are Les Thermes de Saint-Gervais, which have been soothing weary bodies since 1806, when notary Joseph-Marie Gontard discovered the springs. The mineral-rich waters, packed with sulphur, magnesium, calcium and zinc, bubble up from underground at 39C, feeding a three‑hour wellness circuit.We drift between pools of different temperatures, move lazily from sauna to steam room, enjoy the rainforest spa and wallow outdoors as jets of water pummel our backs while the gondola glides silently overhead. Who cares about the rain?View image in fullscreenLes Thermes de Saint-Gervais.Photograph: Leblanc Catherine/AlamyBy the time we emerge, the storm has cleared, so we continue to Saint-Nicolas. From here, a steep two‑hour trail winds up to theRefuge du Mont-Joly, a century-old wooden inn that smells of woodsmoke and melting cheese. Normally there are sweeping views of Mont Blanc from the terrace, but today the peaks are shrouded in cloud.We might not be able to see the mountains but we can taste their produce, notably in the enormous portion of blueberry tart that follows a tartiflette big enough to satisfy a sumo wrestler. As I tuck in, snow begins to fall. By morning it will be gone, melted by the late-summer sun. But now it lies thick and soft outside, turning the world white, as if the Ice Queen from Narnia might step through the door at any moment. That’s autumn in the Alps for you.The trip was provided by theSaint-Gervais Mont Blanctourist board.Doubles at theCoeur des Neigesfrom €108 room-only, or from€76 room-only atPlan Bat Le Fayet. The Refuge du Mont-Joly is closed from the end of March to late May, and from November to mid-December.The Tramway du Mont Blanc now stops at theNid d’Aigle lookout (2,380 metres), after the line was extended in JulyExplore more on these topicsSpa breaksAlps holidaysRest and relaxationChamonix holidaysFrance holidaysEurope holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Henry Harris’ recipe for tarte Vaudoise à la creme | Dessert | The Guardian
description: This Swiss cream tart is a minor miracle but only needs a few ingredients
Author: Henry Harris
Headline: This Swiss cream tart is a minor miracle but only needs a few ingredients
Content: Henry Harris’ tarte Vaudoise à la crème.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.View image in fullscreenHenry Harris’ tarte Vaudoise à la crème.Photograph: Louise Hagger/The Guardian. Food styling: Emily Kydd. Prop styling: Jennifer Kay. Food styling assistant: Eden Owen-Jones.DessertHenry Harris’ recipe for tarte Vaudoise à la cremeThis fantastic tart is a minor miracle invented by a legendary chef, yet it has very few ingredients and an intriguing technique for baking itHenry HarrisSat 10 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOften, the greatest dishes are made from very few ingredients and with pretty standard techniques, and this tart is one of them. It’s based on an oldFrédy Girardetrecipe that, despite his reputation as one of the all-time greats, calls only for a simple application of process to deliver a knockout result (which is one reason I put it in my latest book). A pastry case is spread with sugar and cream, then dotted with butter and sprinkled with cinnamon. The pastry is not blind baked, but filled and baked in a very hot oven. That sounds wrong, but it is not: a fierce heat is needed to bake the pastry under its filling and to meld the cream, sugar and butter. A pinch of flour is mixed with the sugar and, as it all boils up, that smidgen of flour holds everything together as it bubbles and reduces until it takes on the appearance of condensed milk while the pastry cooks and toasts at the edges. I still use Girardet’s quantities because, unsurprisingly, they work perfectly.Merci, chef.Tarte Vaudoise a la cremePrep10 minCook1 hr + coolingServes4-6For the pastry140g plain flour, plus extra for dusting5gbaking powder1 pinch salt1 generous pinchcaster sugar60g unsalted butter, at room temperature and cut into small pieces50ml cold whole milkFor the filling100g caster sugar1 generous pinchplain flour250mldouble cream50g cold unsalted butter, dicedA little ground cinnamon(freshly ground is worth the faff)Heat the oven to 220C (200C fan)/425F/gas 7. To make the pastry, sift the flour into a large bowl, then mix in the baking powder, salt and sugar. Add the butter, then work it in with your fingertips until the mix resembles coarse breadcrumbs.Pour in the milk and mix with as light a hand as possible to bring the dough into a ball. Don’t rest the pastry, because that will activate the baking powder too soon and the pastry will puff up through the filling while it cooks. Roll out the pastry on a lightly floured surface into a circle big enough to line a 25cm tart tin, then lay it in the tin and prick the pastry all over with a fork.For the filling, mix the sugar and flour, then spread it in an even layer over the base of the pastry case. Pour in the cream, then scatter over the diced butter and a light sprinkling of ground cinnamon. Bake for about 25 minutes, until the edges of the pastry are a good biscuit colour and the cream has bubbled up and looks thick and almost about to split.Remove from the oven and transfer the tin to a rack to cool completely. To serve, carefully remove the tart from its tin and cut into slices.Henry Harris is chef/co-owner ofBouchon Racine, London EC1. His book, The Racine Effect, is published by Quadrille at £40.
